WilderThings — Survival Guide Collection

Comprehensive, field-tested survival knowledge — offline-ready, mobile-first, and built for when it matters most.

How to Use This Guide

This is a Progressive Web App (PWA). Once loaded, all content is cached for offline access — no signal required.

Install on your phone:

  1. Open this site in your mobile browser.
  2. Tap "Add to Home Screen" (iOS Safari: share icon → Add to Home Screen; Android Chrome: menu → Install app).
  3. The app works offline from your home screen like a native app.

Search everything: Use the search bar at the top. It works offline and searches all guide content.

Principles

Every guide in this collection follows these rules:

  • Accuracy over volume. No fabricated advice. Sourced from military field manuals, medical references, and established survival literature.
  • Actionable under stress. Short sentences. Numbered steps. Critical info first. Written for someone who is panicking, injured, or exhausted.
  • Offline-first. Works without internet. Designed for the field, not the couch.
  • No filler. Every sentence earns its place.

First Aid Basics: Wound Care, Burns, and Bleeding Control

Stop bleeding, prevent infection, and manage burns using field-expedient first aid when professional help is unavailable.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Control life-threatening bleeding first — everything else is secondary.
  • Clean all wounds thoroughly to prevent infection, which kills more people in survival situations than the initial injury.
  • Never remove an embedded object from a wound; stabilize it in place.
  • Cool burns immediately with clean, cool water for at least 10 minutes.
  • Reassess every wound at least twice daily for signs of infection.

Wound Classification

Cuts and Lacerations

A cut is a clean, sharp-edged wound. A laceration is a jagged, torn wound with irregular edges. Lacerations carry a higher infection risk due to tissue damage.

Assess every wound for:

  • Depth — can you see fat, muscle, tendon, or bone?
  • Length — wounds longer than 1 inch (2.5 cm) often need closure.
  • Location — face, hands, joints, and genitals require special attention.
  • Contamination — dirt, debris, rust, animal matter.

Puncture Wounds

Puncture wounds appear small on the surface but can be deep. They carry the highest infection risk because debris gets driven deep and the wound seals over, creating an anaerobic environment ideal for tetanus and other infections.

WARNING Puncture wounds to the chest, abdomen, neck, or head are medical emergencies. Do not probe them. Stabilize and evacuate immediately.

Abrasions

Abrasions (scrapes, road rash) remove the outer skin layers. They are painful, prone to contamination, and heal slowly without proper care.

Bleeding Control

Address bleeding in this order — move to the next step only if the current one fails.

Step 1: Direct Pressure

  1. Apply firm, direct pressure using the cleanest material available.
  2. Use your palm over a folded cloth or gauze pad.
  3. Press hard — effective pressure causes discomfort to the patient.
  4. Maintain pressure continuously for at least 10 minutes. Do not lift to check.
  5. If blood soaks through, add more material on top. Do not remove the original dressing.

Step 2: Elevation

Raise the injured limb above the level of the heart while maintaining direct pressure. Gravity reduces arterial pressure at the wound site.

Step 3: Pressure Points

If direct pressure and elevation fail, compress the artery upstream of the wound against underlying bone.

Body Region Pressure Point Location
Arm Brachial artery Inner upper arm, between bicep and tricep
Leg Femoral artery Groin crease, midpoint between hip bone and pubic bone
Scalp/Temple Temporal artery Just in front of the ear
Neck Carotid artery Side of neck — compress ONE side only, never both

Step 4: Wound Packing

For deep wounds that direct pressure cannot control:

  1. Open the wound with gloved fingers to visualize the bleeding source.
  2. Pack gauze tightly into the wound, starting at the deepest point.
  3. Fill the entire wound cavity. Use hemostatic gauze (QuikClot, Celox) if available.
  4. Apply direct pressure on top for a minimum of 3 minutes (5 minutes for hemostatic agents).

Step 5: Tourniquet

Apply a tourniquet when:

  • Direct pressure fails on an extremity wound.
  • A limb is partially or fully amputated.
  • Multiple casualties require you to move on to the next patient.
  • You cannot reach the wound (e.g., trapped limb).

Application procedure:

  1. Place the tourniquet 2-3 inches (5-7.5 cm) above the wound. Never place directly on a joint.
  2. Route the strap through the buckle and pull tight.
  3. Turn the windlass until bleeding stops.
  4. Lock the windlass in place.
  5. Mark the time of application on the tourniquet, the patient's forehead, or tape — write "TQ" and the time.
  6. Do not loosen or remove the tourniquet once applied unless directed by a medical professional.
  7. A properly applied tourniquet causes significant pain. This is expected.
WARNING A tourniquet that is too loose increases bleeding by occluding venous return without stopping arterial flow. Tighten until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent.

Improvised tourniquet: Use a strip of material at least 1.5 inches (4 cm) wide. Never use wire, paracord, or narrow material — these cause tissue necrosis without effectively stopping blood flow. A triangular bandage folded into a cravat with a stick windlass is the most effective improvised option.

Wound Cleaning

When to Clean

Clean every wound that is not actively hemorrhaging. Delay cleaning of life-threatening bleeds until hemorrhage is controlled.

Irrigation Procedure

  1. Use the cleanest water available. Potable drinking water is acceptable. Sterile saline (0.9%) is ideal.
  2. Fill a clean container or zip-lock bag. Puncture a small hole in the bag or use a syringe.
  3. Irrigate under pressure — 8 psi is the target. A 20 mL syringe with an 18-gauge needle produces this pressure. Squeezing a bag with a pinhole approximates it.
  4. Use at least 500 mL (about 1 pint) per inch of wound length.
  5. Direct the stream into the wound from multiple angles.
  6. Remove all visible debris with clean tweezers.

Debridement

Remove dead, contaminated, or devitalized tissue (gray, black, or non-bleeding tissue) using a clean blade or scissors. Healthy tissue bleeds when cut and appears pink or red.

WARNING Do not irrigate puncture wounds aggressively — you risk pushing debris deeper. Soak puncture wounds in clean warm water with mild soap or diluted antiseptic instead.

Antiseptics

Solution Dilution Use
Povidone-iodine (Betadine) 1% solution (dilute 10% stock 1:10) Wound irrigation after initial water flush
Chlorhexidine 0.05% aqueous Wound irrigation — do not use near ears or eyes
Dilute bleach 0.5 teaspoon per 1 quart (1 liter) Last resort wound irrigation
Hydrogen peroxide Do not use Damages healthy tissue, delays healing

Wound Closure

When to Close

Close a wound only if all of the following are true:

  • The wound is less than 6 hours old (12 hours for face wounds).
  • It is thoroughly cleaned and free of debris.
  • The edges can be approximated without tension.
  • There is no sign of infection.
  • It is not a bite wound (human or animal).

Closure Methods

Adhesive strips (Steri-Strips, butterfly bandages):

  1. Dry the skin on both sides of the wound.
  2. Apply tincture of benzoin to the skin (not the wound) to improve adhesion.
  3. Place strips perpendicular to the wound, 1/8 inch (3 mm) apart.
  4. Alternate sides — do not pull both edges from one side.
  5. Leave small gaps between strips for drainage.

Tissue adhesive (skin glue):

  1. Hold wound edges together.
  2. Apply a thin layer across the closed wound surface.
  3. Hold for 60 seconds.
  4. Do not use inside the wound or on wet surfaces.

Suturing (field expedient):

Use only if trained. Improper suturing traps infection and worsens outcomes. If you must suture, use simple interrupted stitches spaced 1/4 inch (6 mm) apart, entering and exiting 1/8 inch (3 mm) from wound edges.

Bandaging Techniques

Basic Principles

  • Cover the wound completely.
  • Secure the dressing without restricting circulation.
  • Check distal circulation (pulse, sensation, color, warmth) after applying any bandage.
  • Change dressings at least once daily, or whenever wet, soiled, or loosened.

Pressure Dressing

  1. Place an absorbent pad directly over the wound.
  2. Wrap an elastic bandage (ACE wrap, Israeli bandage) firmly over the pad.
  3. Each wrap should overlap the previous by one-half.
  4. Secure the end with clips, tape, or by tucking.

Figure-Eight Bandage (Joints)

  1. Anchor the bandage below the joint.
  2. Wrap diagonally across the joint.
  3. Circle above the joint.
  4. Wrap diagonally back across the joint.
  5. Repeat, creating an X pattern over the joint.

Spiral Bandage (Limbs)

  1. Anchor at the narrowest point (distal end).
  2. Wrap upward, overlapping each turn by one-half to two-thirds.
  3. Secure at the widest point.

Improvised Dressings

  • Clean cloth, t-shirt material, or bandana as a dressing.
  • Duct tape as adhesive.
  • Plastic wrap (cling film) as a moisture barrier over burns.
  • Maxi pads or diapers as absorbent wound pads.
  • Sphagnum moss (dried, clean) as an antiseptic wound packing — used historically, but carries contamination risk.

Burn Treatment

Classification

Degree Depth Appearance Sensation Healing
1st (Superficial) Epidermis only Red, dry, no blisters Painful 3-5 days
2nd (Partial thickness) Epidermis + dermis Red, wet, blisters Very painful 2-4 weeks
3rd (Full thickness) Through dermis White, brown, or charred; dry, leathery Painless (nerves destroyed) Requires grafting

Estimating Burn Area

Use the Rule of Nines for adults:

  • Head and neck: 9%
  • Each arm: 9%
  • Chest (front): 18%
  • Back: 18%
  • Each leg: 18%
  • Groin: 1%

For small or irregular burns, the patient's palm (including fingers) equals approximately 1% of total body surface area (TBSA).

WARNING Burns greater than 20% TBSA in adults (10% in children or elderly) are life-threatening emergencies requiring IV fluid resuscitation and evacuation.

First-Degree Burn Treatment

  1. Cool with clean, cool (not cold) running water for at least 10 minutes.
  2. Apply aloe vera or a bland moisturizer.
  3. Take ibuprofen (400-800 mg) or acetaminophen (500-1000 mg) for pain.
  4. Protect from sun exposure during healing.

Second-Degree Burn Treatment

  1. Cool with clean, cool running water for 10-20 minutes.
  2. Do not pop blisters — they are a natural sterile dressing.
  3. If a blister breaks, clean gently and apply antibiotic ointment.
  4. Cover with a non-adherent dressing (Telfa, plastic wrap, or a clean, smooth cloth).
  5. Change dressings daily. Watch for infection.
  6. Elevate burned extremities to reduce swelling.

Third-Degree Burn Treatment

  1. Do not cool with water — hypothermia is a greater immediate risk.
  2. Cover with a clean, dry, non-adherent dressing.
  3. Treat for shock: lay flat, elevate legs 6-12 inches (15-30 cm), keep warm.
  4. Monitor airway — inhalation burns cause progressive airway swelling.
  5. Evacuate immediately.

Burns: Do Not

  • Apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or egg whites.
  • Use cotton balls or fluffy material directly on burns (fibers embed in tissue).
  • Remove clothing that is stuck to a burn — cut around it.
  • Wrap circumferential burns tightly — swelling needs room to expand.

Infection Recognition

Check every wound for these signs at least twice daily:

  • Redness spreading beyond the wound edges (mark the edge with a pen and monitor expansion).
  • Warmth around the wound compared to surrounding tissue.
  • Swelling that increases rather than decreases after 48 hours.
  • Purulent drainage (thick, yellow, green, or foul-smelling discharge).
  • Red streaks extending from the wound toward the heart (lymphangitis) — this is a medical emergency.
  • Fever above 100.4 degF (38 degC).
  • Increased pain after an initial improvement period.

Field Infection Management

  1. Reopen and re-irrigate the wound.
  2. Apply topical antibiotic ointment (bacitracin, mupirocin, or triple antibiotic).
  3. If oral antibiotics are available: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily, or cephalexin 500 mg four times daily.
  4. Change dressings three times daily with re-irrigation.
  5. Elevate the affected area.
  6. Evacuate if infection worsens or red streaking develops.

Common Mistakes

  • Removing a tourniquet too early because the patient complains of pain.
  • Using hydrogen peroxide or full-strength Betadine on open wounds — both damage healthy tissue.
  • Packing a wound loosely — ineffective packing fails to tamponade bleeding.
  • Closing contaminated or bite wounds — this seals in bacteria and creates abscesses.
  • Changing dressings too frequently on healing wounds, disrupting new tissue formation.
  • Failing to check distal circulation after applying bandages or splints.
  • Ignoring puncture wounds because they "look small."
  • Cooling large burns with cold water, causing hypothermia.

Quick Reference

Problem Immediate Action Time-Critical?
Arterial bleed (spurting, bright red) Direct pressure, pack, tourniquet Yes — minutes
Venous bleed (steady, dark red) Direct pressure, elevation Yes — minutes to hours
Deep laceration Clean, close if appropriate, dress Moderate — close within 6 hours
Puncture wound Soak, do not probe, monitor for infection Moderate — watch 48+ hours
1st-degree burn Cool water 10 min, moisturize No
2nd-degree burn Cool water 10-20 min, non-adherent dressing Moderate — infection risk
3rd-degree burn Dry sterile dressing, treat shock, evacuate Yes — life-threatening
Infection (red streaks) Reopen wound, irrigate, antibiotics, evacuate Yes — hours

  • CPR and Choking — airway management and resuscitation.
  • Fractures and Splints — immobilization of injured limbs.
  • Hypothermia and Heatstroke — temperature-related complications of trauma.
  • Trauma and Triage — systematic patient assessment and mass casualty response.

CPR and Choking Response

Restore circulation and clear airway obstructions using standardized resuscitation protocols when professional help is delayed or unavailable.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace hands-on CPR certification from the American Heart Association, Red Cross, or equivalent authority. Practice on manikins before you need these skills for real.

At a Glance

  • Push hard, push fast — compress the chest at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep at 100-120 compressions per minute for adults.
  • Hands-only CPR (compressions without breaths) is effective and recommended for untrained bystanders.
  • Begin CPR immediately if someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally — every minute without CPR reduces survival by 7-10%.
  • Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) clear most choking obstructions in conscious adults and children.
  • Infant choking protocol uses back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

When to Start CPR

Start CPR when a person meets all of the following criteria:

  1. Unresponsive — does not react to shouting or a firm tap on the shoulders.
  2. Not breathing normally — no chest rise, only gasping (agonal respirations), or no breath sounds.
  3. No definite pulse within 10 seconds (check the carotid artery in the neck for adults/children, the brachial artery in the upper arm for infants).
WARNING Agonal breathing (irregular gasps, gurgling, or snoring sounds) is NOT normal breathing. It occurs in up to 40% of cardiac arrest victims. Begin CPR immediately if you see agonal breathing.

If you are unsure whether there is a pulse, start CPR. Performing CPR on someone with a pulse is far less harmful than withholding CPR from someone without one.

Adult CPR (Age 12+)

Preparation

  1. Confirm the scene is safe.
  2. Check responsiveness — shout "Are you okay?" and tap both shoulders firmly.
  3. Call for help. Activate emergency medical services. Send someone for an AED if available.
  4. Place the patient face-up on a firm, flat surface.

Compressions

  1. Kneel beside the patient's chest.
  2. Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum (breastbone).
  3. Place your other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
  4. Position your shoulders directly above your hands. Lock your elbows.
  5. Compress straight down at least 2 inches (5 cm) but no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm).
  6. Allow full chest recoil between compressions — do not lean on the chest.
  7. Compress at a rate of 100-120 per minute (the tempo of "Stayin' Alive" by the Bee Gees).
  8. Minimize interruptions. Pauses in compressions should not exceed 10 seconds.

Rescue Breaths (if trained)

  1. After 30 compressions, open the airway using the head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver.
  2. Place one hand on the forehead and tilt the head back.
  3. Place two fingers under the bony part of the chin and lift upward.
  4. Pinch the nose shut.
  5. Create a complete seal over the patient's mouth with yours.
  6. Deliver 2 breaths, each lasting about 1 second.
  7. Watch for visible chest rise. If the chest does not rise, reposition the head and try again.
  8. Resume compressions immediately after the second breath.

Compression-to-breath ratio: 30:2 (30 compressions, 2 breaths, repeat).

Hands-Only CPR

If you are untrained, unwilling to give breaths, or unable to create a seal:

  1. Perform continuous chest compressions at 100-120 per minute.
  2. Do not stop to give breaths.
  3. Continue until help arrives, an AED is available, or the patient shows signs of life.

Hands-only CPR is nearly as effective as conventional CPR for the first several minutes of adult cardiac arrest.

AED Use

  1. Turn on the AED and follow voice prompts.
  2. Expose the chest. Remove clothing, wipe dry if wet, shave excessive hair if pads do not adhere.
  3. Apply pads: one on the upper right chest (below the collarbone), one on the lower left side (below the armpit).
  4. Ensure no one is touching the patient during analysis and shock delivery.
  5. If the AED advises a shock, confirm everyone is clear and press the shock button.
  6. Resume CPR immediately after the shock — start with compressions.
  7. The AED will re-analyze every 2 minutes.
WARNING Do not use an AED in standing water. Move the patient to a dry surface first. Moisture on the chest between the pads can cause arcing — dry the chest thoroughly before applying pads.

Child CPR (Age 1-12)

The protocol is similar to adult CPR with these modifications:

Compressions

  1. Use one or two hands (depending on the child's size) on the lower half of the sternum.
  2. Compress to a depth of about 2 inches (5 cm), or one-third the depth of the chest.
  3. Rate: 100-120 per minute.
  4. Allow full chest recoil.

Rescue Breaths

  1. Open the airway with head-tilt/chin-lift. Use a neutral (sniffing) position — do not over-extend the neck.
  2. Deliver smaller breaths than for an adult — just enough to see the chest rise.
  3. Ratio: 30:2 for a single rescuer, 15:2 for two rescuers.

Key Difference

For children, respiratory failure is the most common cause of cardiac arrest (unlike adults, where it is typically cardiac). Rescue breaths are more important in pediatric CPR. Give 2 initial rescue breaths before starting compressions if the arrest is witnessed to be respiratory in origin.

Infant CPR (Under Age 1)

Compressions

  1. Place the infant on a firm, flat surface.
  2. Two-finger technique (single rescuer): Place two fingers on the sternum, just below the nipple line.
  3. Two-thumb technique (two rescuers): Encircle the chest with both hands, thumbs side by side on the sternum just below the nipple line. This is the preferred method when two rescuers are available.
  4. Compress to a depth of about 1.5 inches (4 cm), or one-third the depth of the chest.
  5. Rate: 100-120 per minute.
  6. Allow full chest recoil.

Rescue Breaths

  1. Place the infant's head in a neutral position (do not tilt back).
  2. Cover the infant's mouth AND nose with your mouth.
  3. Deliver tiny puffs of air — just enough to see the chest rise. Over-inflation causes gastric distension and vomiting.
  4. Ratio: 30:2 for a single rescuer, 15:2 for two rescuers.
WARNING Do not shake an infant to check responsiveness. Flick the sole of the foot or tap the shoulder gently. Shaking can cause brain injury.

CPR Duration and Stopping

Continue CPR until:

  • Emergency medical services take over.
  • An AED becomes available and delivers analysis/shock.
  • The patient shows definite signs of life (purposeful movement, normal breathing).
  • You are too physically exhausted to continue (switch rescuers every 2 minutes if possible).
  • A qualified medical professional pronounces death.
  • The scene becomes unsafe.

Rescuer Fatigue

Effective compressions degrade after approximately 2 minutes, even when the rescuer does not feel tired. Rotate compressors every 2 minutes. Switch in less than 10 seconds.

Recovery Position

Place an unconscious, breathing patient in the recovery position to maintain an open airway and allow fluids to drain.

  1. Kneel beside the patient.
  2. Place the arm nearest to you at a right angle to the body, palm up.
  3. Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of their hand against the near cheek.
  4. Grasp the far knee and pull it up so the foot is flat on the ground.
  5. Pull the far knee toward you, rolling the patient onto their side.
  6. Adjust the top leg so the hip and knee are at right angles.
  7. Tilt the head back slightly to keep the airway open.
  8. Monitor breathing continuously.
WARNING Do not place a patient in the recovery position if you suspect a spinal injury. Use the jaw-thrust maneuver to open the airway and maintain spinal alignment. See [Fractures and Splints](#fractures-and-splints) for spinal precautions.

Choking: Conscious Adult and Child (Over Age 1)

Recognizing Choking

  • Universal choking sign: hands clutching the throat.
  • Inability to speak, cough, or breathe.
  • High-pitched sounds or wheezing when trying to inhale.
  • Skin turning blue (cyanosis), especially lips and fingertips.
  • If the patient can cough forcefully or speak, encourage continued coughing. Do not intervene physically — a strong cough generates more airway pressure than any maneuver you can perform.

Heimlich Maneuver (Abdominal Thrusts)

  1. Stand behind the patient.
  2. Make a fist with one hand. Place the thumb side against the abdomen, above the navel and below the sternum (xiphoid process).
  3. Grasp the fist with your other hand.
  4. Deliver quick, sharp, inward-and-upward thrusts.
  5. Each thrust should be a distinct, forceful movement — not a squeeze.
  6. Continue until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unconscious.

Chest Thrusts (Alternative)

Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts for:

  • Pregnant patients (late pregnancy).

  • Obese patients whose abdomen you cannot encircle.

  • Stand behind the patient.

  • Place your fist on the center of the sternum (breastbone), between the nipples.
  • Grasp with the other hand.
  • Deliver sharp, backward thrusts.

Self-Administered Heimlich

If you are alone and choking:

  1. Make a fist and place it above your navel.
  2. Grasp with the other hand and thrust inward and upward.
  3. Alternatively, lean your upper abdomen over the back of a chair, countertop edge, or railing and thrust your body weight forward and downward.
  4. Repeat forcefully until the obstruction clears.

Choking: Conscious Infant (Under Age 1)

WARNING Never perform abdominal thrusts on an infant. The liver is proportionally large and unprotected — abdominal thrusts can cause fatal internal injury.

Back Blows and Chest Thrusts

  1. Hold the infant face-down along your forearm, supporting the head and jaw with your hand. Rest your forearm on your thigh for stability. Keep the infant's head lower than the chest.
  2. Deliver 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your free hand.
  3. Turn the infant face-up on your other forearm, keeping the head lower than the chest.
  4. Deliver 5 chest thrusts using two fingers on the sternum, just below the nipple line. Use the same landmark and depth as infant CPR compressions.
  5. Repeat the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until:
  6. The object is expelled.
  7. The infant begins to cry or breathe.
  8. The infant becomes unconscious (switch to CPR — see below).

Choking: Unconscious Victim (Any Age)

If a choking victim becomes unconscious:

  1. Lower the patient to the ground carefully on their back.
  2. Begin CPR immediately, starting with compressions.
  3. Before each set of rescue breaths, open the mouth and look for a visible foreign object.
  4. If you see an object, sweep it out with a finger. Use a hooked finger motion along the inside of the cheek.
  5. Do not perform blind finger sweeps — you risk pushing the object deeper.
  6. Attempt rescue breaths. If the chest does not rise, reposition the head and try again.
  7. If breaths still do not go in, continue compressions. The compressions themselves may dislodge the object.
  8. Continue this cycle until the obstruction clears or help arrives.

Special Situations

Drowning

  1. Remove the patient from the water safely — do not become a victim.
  2. Begin rescue breaths first: deliver 5 initial breaths before starting compressions.
  3. Follow standard CPR protocol (30:2).
  4. Do not attempt to drain water from the lungs — the Heimlich maneuver is not indicated for drowning unless a foreign body is suspected.
  5. Vomiting is common during drowning resuscitation. Turn the head to the side, clear the airway, and continue.

Opioid Overdose

  1. Suspected opioid overdose signs: pinpoint pupils, slow or absent breathing, unresponsiveness.
  2. Administer naloxone (Narcan) if available: 4 mg intranasal spray in one nostril, or 0.4 mg intramuscular injection.
  3. Begin CPR if the patient is not breathing and has no pulse.
  4. If the patient resumes breathing but remains unconscious, place in the recovery position.
  5. Naloxone wears off in 30-90 minutes. The patient may stop breathing again. Monitor continuously.

Hypothermic Cardiac Arrest

  1. Check for a pulse for 60 seconds (not the standard 10) — the heart rate may be extremely slow.
  2. If no pulse is detected, begin CPR.
  3. Rewarm the patient — see Hypothermia and Heatstroke.
  4. Do not pronounce a hypothermic patient dead in the field. The principle: "They're not dead until they're warm and dead."

Common Mistakes

  • Compressing too shallow — this is the most common CPR error. Push hard enough to compress the chest at least 2 inches (5 cm) in adults.
  • Compressing too fast — exceeding 120/min reduces refill time and decreases cardiac output.
  • Leaning on the chest between compressions — this prevents full recoil and reduces blood flow by up to 25%.
  • Interrupting compressions too long for breaths or pulse checks — keep pauses under 10 seconds.
  • Hyperventilating the patient — excessive breaths increase intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous return. One breath per second, visible chest rise only.
  • Performing abdominal thrusts on infants — use back blows and chest thrusts only.
  • Performing blind finger sweeps on choking victims — visualize the object before sweeping.
  • Stopping CPR when agonal breathing occurs — agonal breaths do not indicate recovery.
  • Failing to tilt the head back sufficiently when delivering rescue breaths (the most common cause of failed ventilation).

Quick Reference

CPR at a Glance

Parameter Adult (12+) Child (1-12) Infant (Under 1)
Compression depth 2-2.4 in (5-6 cm) ~2 in (5 cm) ~1.5 in (4 cm)
Compression rate 100-120/min 100-120/min 100-120/min
Hand position 2 hands, center of chest 1-2 hands, center of chest 2 fingers or 2 thumbs, just below nipple line
Ratio (1 rescuer) 30:2 30:2 30:2
Ratio (2 rescuers) 30:2 15:2 15:2
Breath volume Normal breath Small breath Tiny puff

Choking at a Glance

Patient Conscious Unconscious
Adult Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) CPR with airway checks
Child Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) CPR with airway checks
Infant 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts CPR with airway checks
Pregnant/Obese Chest thrusts CPR with airway checks
Self Abdominal thrusts or lean over chair N/A

Medical

Fractures and Splints

Identify fractures, immobilize injuries using improvised and commercial splints, and recognize spinal injuries requiring extreme caution.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. Improper splinting or moving a patient with a spinal injury can cause permanent paralysis or death. This guide does not replace professional medical training. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Splint injuries in the position found — do not attempt to straighten or realign deformed limbs unless circulation is compromised.
  • Always immobilize the joint above and the joint below the fracture site.
  • Check circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) distal to the injury before and after splinting.
  • Suspect spinal injury in any patient with a mechanism of injury involving significant force — falls greater than standing height, vehicle accidents, diving injuries, or direct blows to the head or spine.
  • An open fracture (bone piercing skin) is a surgical emergency. Cover the wound, splint, and evacuate.

Fracture Types

Closed Fracture

The bone is broken but the skin is intact. Signs include:

  • Deformity — angulation, shortening, or rotation compared to the uninjured side.
  • Swelling and bruising at the injury site.
  • Point tenderness — pain localized to a specific spot when pressed.
  • Crepitus — a grinding sensation or sound when the fracture site moves (do not intentionally test for this).
  • Loss of function — inability or unwillingness to use the limb.
  • Guarding — the patient instinctively protects the area.

Open (Compound) Fracture

The bone has broken through the skin or the skin has been lacerated by the force that caused the fracture. This creates a direct path for infection to reach the bone (osteomyelitis).

WARNING Never push a protruding bone back into the wound. Cover the exposed bone with a moist, sterile dressing, splint around it, and evacuate immediately.

Open fracture management:

  1. Control bleeding with direct pressure around (not on) the protruding bone.
  2. Irrigate the wound with at least 1 liter of clean water.
  3. Cover with a sterile, moist dressing — saline-soaked gauze is ideal.
  4. Splint the limb in the position found, building up padding around the protrusion.
  5. Administer antibiotics if available: cephalexin 500 mg four times daily, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily. Begin within 3 hours of injury.
  6. Evacuate. Open fractures require surgical debridement.

Greenstick Fracture

Common in children. The bone bends and partially breaks, like a green twig. The limb may appear bent but not fully deformed. Splint as you would a closed fracture.

Stress Fracture

A hairline crack from repetitive overuse. Presents as localized pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. No deformity. Diagnose by point tenderness over the bone. Treatment: rest and offload the affected bone.

Fracture Assessment

Systematic Examination

  1. Look — compare both sides. Note swelling, bruising, deformity, wounds, skin color distal to the injury.
  2. Feel — palpate along the bone gently. Identify the point of maximum tenderness. Check for crepitus (but do not intentionally manipulate).
  3. Move — ask the patient to actively move the extremity. Do not force passive motion through a suspected fracture. Note range-of-motion limitations and pain.

CSM Check (Circulation, Sensation, Movement)

Perform this check before and after every splinting procedure, and recheck every 15-30 minutes.

Check How Normal Finding
Circulation Press a fingernail or toenail until it blanches white, then release. Check pulse distal to the injury. Color returns in less than 2 seconds (capillary refill). Pulse present.
Sensation Touch the skin distal to the injury. Ask "Can you feel this?" Patient reports normal feeling. No numbness or tingling.
Movement Ask the patient to wiggle fingers or toes. Active movement without excessive pain.
WARNING If CSM is absent — no pulse, no sensation, no movement — the limb is in jeopardy. Gently realign the limb toward its anatomical position using steady traction until circulation returns, then splint in that position. This is the one situation where you move a deformed fracture.

Splinting Principles

General Rules

  1. Splint in position found unless CSM is compromised.
  2. Immobilize one joint above and one joint below the fracture.
  3. Pad all bony prominences — ankles, knees, elbows, wrists. Pressure sores develop rapidly under splints.
  4. Secure the splint firmly but not tightly. You should be able to slide one finger under the wrapping.
  5. Elevate the splinted limb when possible to reduce swelling.
  6. Apply cold — ice or cold water in a bag, wrapped in cloth, 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off. Never apply ice directly to skin.
  7. Recheck CSM after application. If CSM worsens, loosen or reposition the splint immediately.
  8. Document the time of splinting and CSM findings.

Padding

Adequate padding prevents:

  • Pressure sores over bony prominences.
  • Nerve compression causing numbness.
  • Circulation impairment from rigid materials pressing into tissue.

Use any soft material: clothing, towels, moss, dried grass, foam, bubble wrap, socks.

Splinting by Body Region

Forearm and Wrist

  1. Place padding in the palm — a rolled sock or bandage. This maintains the hand in the "position of function" (as if holding a can).
  2. Place a rigid splint along the palmar side of the forearm, extending from the fingertips to past the elbow.
  3. Place a second splint on the dorsal (back) side if available.
  4. Secure with wraps at the hand, mid-forearm, and above the elbow. Avoid wrapping directly over the fracture site.
  5. Support with a sling and swathe.

Upper Arm (Humerus)

  1. Place a padded rigid splint along the outer side of the arm.
  2. Wrap to secure, leaving the elbow at approximately 90 degrees.
  3. Apply a sling to support the forearm.
  4. Apply a swathe (wrap around the torso) to prevent the arm from swinging.

Shoulder and Collarbone (Clavicle)

  1. Place the arm in a sling with the elbow at 90 degrees.
  2. Apply a swathe to bind the arm against the torso.
  3. Place padding (rolled towel) in the armpit.
  4. Do not attempt to reduce a shoulder dislocation without training — you risk damaging the axillary nerve and blood vessels.

Finger

  1. Buddy-tape the injured finger to an adjacent uninjured finger.
  2. Place padding between the fingers to prevent skin maceration.
  3. For severely angulated finger fractures, splint in a slightly flexed position using a tongue depressor, popsicle stick, or small twig, padded and taped.

Femur (Thighbone)

Femur fractures are serious injuries. The thigh can hold 1-2 liters of internal blood loss.

Improvised traction splint procedure:

  1. Cut or find two sturdy poles — one extending from the armpit to 12 inches (30 cm) past the foot, one from the groin to 12 inches (30 cm) past the foot.
  2. Pad the groin and armpit thoroughly.
  3. Secure the poles to the body at the chest, hip, and above and below the knee. Do not wrap directly over the fracture.
  4. Attach an ankle hitch: wrap padding around the ankle, then tie a loop that can be connected to the foot end of the outer pole.
  5. Apply traction by pulling the foot-end of the loop until the injured leg is the same length as the uninjured leg. The patient should report decreased pain when traction is correct.
  6. Secure the traction in place.
WARNING Do not apply a traction splint if the fracture is near the knee, the pelvis is fractured, or the lower leg is also fractured. In these cases, immobilize the entire leg using padded board splints on both sides, from armpit to foot.

Lower Leg (Tibia/Fibula)

  1. Place padded splints on both sides of the leg, extending from above the knee to past the foot.
  2. Alternatively, place one splint along the back of the leg from the buttock to past the foot.
  3. Wrap at the thigh, above and below the knee, mid-calf, and the ankle/foot.
  4. Immobilize the foot at 90 degrees to the leg if possible.

Ankle and Foot

  1. Apply a pillow splint: wrap a pillow or folded blanket around the ankle and foot.
  2. Secure with tape or wraps.
  3. Alternatively, build an L-shaped splint from rigid material, padded, along the back of the calf and under the foot.
  4. Do not remove the boot or shoe if swelling is already present — the boot acts as a compression dressing.

Pelvis

Pelvic fractures are life-threatening. The pelvis can hold 3+ liters of internal blood loss.

  1. Wrap a sheet, belt, jacket, or commercial pelvic binder tightly around the hips at the level of the greater trochanters (the bony bumps on the outer hips).
  2. Tie or clip the binder snugly — it should compress the pelvis to reduce the fracture space and control bleeding.
  3. Do not log-roll or repeatedly move the patient. Every movement can disrupt clots.
  4. Treat for shock — see Trauma and Triage.

Slings and Swathes

Triangular Bandage Sling

  1. Place one point of the triangle at the elbow of the injured arm.
  2. Bring the upper end over the shoulder on the uninjured side.
  3. Bring the lower end up and over the shoulder on the injured side.
  4. Tie the ends behind the neck with a square knot. Pad the knot.
  5. Fold and pin or tie the material at the elbow to secure.
  6. The hand should be slightly higher than the elbow (about 4 inches / 10 cm above elbow level).

Improvised Sling

  • Pin the sleeve of a buttoned shirt to the chest of the shirt.
  • Tuck the hand inside a buttoned jacket between buttons.
  • Use a belt, scarf, rope, or strip of fabric looped around the neck and under the forearm.

Swathe

Wrap a broad band of material around the torso and over the splinted/slung arm to prevent movement. The swathe prevents the arm from swinging away from the body.

Spinal Injury Precautions

Suspect Spinal Injury When

  • The mechanism of injury involves significant force to the head, neck, or back:
  • Falls greater than standing height (approximately 5 feet / 1.5 meters).
  • Motor vehicle, bicycle, or horseback accidents.
  • Diving into shallow water.
  • Direct blows or penetrating injuries to the spine.
  • Lightning strikes.
  • The patient complains of neck or back pain.
  • The patient has numbness, tingling, or weakness in the extremities.
  • The patient is unconscious with an unknown mechanism of injury.

When NOT to Move Someone

Do not move a patient if you suspect spinal injury unless:

  • The scene is immediately dangerous (fire, flood, structural collapse, active threat).
  • You cannot access the airway to manage a life-threatening obstruction or perform CPR.
  • You need to roll the patient to control life-threatening hemorrhage on the posterior body.

In all other cases, stabilize the spine in place and wait for evacuation resources.

Manual Spinal Stabilization

  1. Kneel above the patient's head.
  2. Place your hands on both sides of the head, covering the ears.
  3. Hold the head in a neutral position aligned with the spine. Do not pull traction.
  4. Maintain this hold continuously until the patient is fully immobilized on a backboard or until professional rescuers take over.
  5. If you must release, build improvised padding (rolled towels, clothing, sandbags) on both sides of the head and tape across the forehead and chin.

Log Roll

When you must turn a spinal injury patient (to assess the back, place on a backboard, or manage vomiting):

  1. One person maintains inline head stabilization.
  2. Two or more people position themselves along the patient's body.
  3. On command from the person at the head, roll the patient as a single unit, keeping the spine aligned.
  4. The head, shoulders, hips, and legs must all move together simultaneously.
  5. Assess or intervene, then roll back.

Improvised Spinal Immobilization

  • Use a door, tabletop, wide plank, or ironing board as a backboard.
  • Pad the natural curves of the spine (behind the neck and lower back).
  • Secure the patient to the board at the forehead, chest, hips, and legs.
  • Immobilize the head last — secure the torso first to prevent the head from moving relative to the body.
  • Tape or tie across the forehead (not the neck) with padding on both sides.

Splinting Materials from Nature

Natural Material Best Used For Preparation
Straight hardwood sticks Arm and leg splints Select straight pieces, pad with cloth, moss, or grass
Bark slabs (thick bark from fir, cottonwood, or birch) Curved splints for forearms and lower legs Peel a slab large enough to wrap around the limb
Cattail leaves (bundled) Padding under rigid splints Bundle thick layers; surprisingly rigid when compressed
Bamboo (split) Rigid splints for any limb Split lengthwise, smooth sharp edges, pad generously
Rolled newspaper or magazines Rigid forearm or lower-leg splints Roll tightly and tape; surprisingly strong
Sam Splint equivalent Shape a thin, green branch into a curve Bend a pliable branch into a U or T shape
Mud or clay (dried) Emergency cast for forearm Apply wet, mold into shape, allow to dry. Fragile — temporary only

Constructing a Natural Splint

  1. Select two pieces of rigid material longer than the injured segment (extend beyond the joints above and below).
  2. Pad all surfaces that will contact skin — use clothing, moss, dried grass, or bark strips.
  3. Place splints on opposite sides of the limb.
  4. Secure using strips of cloth, vines, cordage, boot laces, or belts at four or more points.
  5. Do not tie directly over the fracture site.
  6. Check CSM immediately and every 15 minutes after.

Dislocations

Recognition

  • Joint appears deformed — compare to the other side.
  • The limb is locked in an abnormal position.
  • Patient cannot move the joint through normal range of motion.
  • Swelling and severe pain at the joint.

Field Reduction (Wilderness/Austere Setting Only)

Attempt field reduction only when evacuation is delayed more than several hours and when CSM distal to the dislocation is compromised. Attempted reduction can worsen the injury if performed incorrectly.

Shoulder (anterior dislocation — most common):

  1. Lay the patient face down on a raised surface (table, rock ledge) with the affected arm hanging straight down.
  2. Attach 10-15 pounds (4.5-7 kg) of weight to the wrist (a bag of water or rocks).
  3. Allow gravity and the weight to pull the arm downward for 20-30 minutes. Muscle spasm often releases, and the joint relocates with a palpable "clunk."
  4. Alternatively, have the patient lie on their back. Slowly abduct the arm to 90 degrees, then externally rotate (turn the forearm outward) slowly. Stop if pain increases sharply.
  5. After reduction, immobilize with a sling and swathe.
  6. Recheck CSM.

Finger dislocation:

  1. Grasp the finger beyond the dislocated joint.
  2. Apply steady traction (pull) along the axis of the finger.
  3. Gently guide the joint back into alignment.
  4. Buddy-tape to the adjacent finger and splint.
WARNING Never attempt field reduction of hip, knee, elbow, or spinal dislocations without advanced training. Incorrect technique can sever blood vessels or permanently damage nerves.

Common Mistakes

  • Splinting too tightly — restricting circulation causes more damage than the fracture itself. Check CSM every 15 minutes.
  • Failing to immobilize the joints above and below the fracture — the splint is ineffective if the fracture can still move.
  • Attempting to straighten a deformed limb when circulation is intact — splint in position found.
  • Removing footwear from an ankle injury after swelling has begun — the shoe provides compression.
  • Applying ice directly to skin — wrap ice in cloth. Frostbite atop a fracture is a preventable disaster.
  • Moving a suspected spinal injury patient without a compelling reason (immediate danger to life).
  • Using narrow cordage (paracord, wire) to secure splints — this creates pressure points that impair circulation.
  • Forgetting to pad bony prominences under the splint — pressure sores develop within hours.
  • Neglecting to check and document CSM before and after splinting.

Quick Reference

Injury Immobilize Key Concern Evacuate?
Finger fracture Buddy tape + small splint Loss of fine motor function When possible
Forearm fracture Elbow to fingertips, sling Compartment syndrome (swelling in tight spaces) Yes
Humerus fracture Shoulder to elbow, sling + swathe Radial nerve damage (wrist drop) Yes
Clavicle fracture Sling + swathe Usually heals without surgery When possible
Femur fracture Traction splint or full-leg immobilization 1-2 L internal blood loss, shock Urgent
Tibia/fibula fracture Knee to foot Compartment syndrome Yes
Pelvis fracture Pelvic binder, do not move 3+ L blood loss, life-threatening Emergency
Spinal injury Full spinal immobilization Paralysis risk Emergency — do not move
Open fracture (any) Splint around wound, moist dressing Infection, surgical emergency Emergency

  • CPR and Choking — recovery position and spinal considerations.

Medical

Hypothermia and Heatstroke

Recognize, prevent, and treat cold and heat injuries in the field using protocols adapted from wilderness medicine and military standards.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. Temperature emergencies can be fatal. This guide does not replace professional medical training or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Hypothermia begins at a core temperature below 95 degF (35 degC) and can kill at temperatures well above freezing, especially when wet and windy.
  • Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency defined by core temperature above 104 degF (40 degC) with altered mental status — cool aggressively and immediately.
  • Afterdrop — a continued decline in core temperature after rewarming begins — can trigger cardiac arrest in moderate-to-severe hypothermia patients.
  • Frostbite should not be thawed in the field if there is any chance of refreezing — refreezing causes far more tissue destruction than remaining frozen.
  • Prevention is vastly more effective than treatment for all temperature-related injuries.

Hypothermia

How Heat Is Lost

Understand these mechanisms to prevent and treat hypothermia:

Mechanism Description Example Mitigation
Radiation Body emits infrared heat to cooler surroundings Standing in cold air Insulate, cover head and neck
Conduction Direct contact with cold surfaces Sitting on cold ground, wet clothing Insulate from ground, remove wet layers
Convection Moving air or water strips heat Wind, swimming Windproof outer layer, shelter
Evaporation Water changing to vapor absorbs heat Sweating, wet clothing Stay dry, manage exertion
Respiration Inhaling cold air, exhaling warm moist air Breathing in subzero conditions Cover mouth with scarf or balaclava

Stages of Hypothermia

Mild Hypothermia: 95-90 degF (35-32 degC)

Recognition:

  • Shivering — vigorous, uncontrollable. This is the body's primary heat-generation mechanism.
  • Impaired fine motor coordination — difficulty with zippers, buttons, knots.
  • Pale, cold skin. Goosebumps.
  • Increased heart rate and respiratory rate.
  • Mild confusion, poor judgment, apathy ("I'm fine, leave me alone").
  • Increased urination (cold diuresis).

Treatment:

  1. Remove from the cold environment. Get into shelter, out of wind and precipitation.
  2. Remove all wet clothing. Replace with dry layers.
  3. Insulate from the ground — use a sleeping pad, branches, dry leaves, or any barrier.
  4. Add insulation — sleeping bag, blankets, extra clothing. Cover the head, neck, and torso.
  5. Provide warm, sweet drinks if the patient is alert and can swallow. No alcohol or caffeine.
  6. Provide high-calorie food — sugar, chocolate, energy bars. Shivering burns 400+ calories per hour.
  7. Apply external heat sources: chemical heat packs, warm water bottles, or warmed rocks wrapped in cloth. Place against the neck, armpits, and groin (areas where major blood vessels are near the skin surface).
  8. Encourage gentle movement — mild exercise generates heat. Do not allow exhaustive activity.

Mild hypothermia responds well to field rewarming. Most patients recover fully.

Moderate Hypothermia: 90-82 degF (32-28 degC)

Recognition:

  • Shivering slows and eventually stops — this is an ominous sign, not improvement.
  • Severe mental impairment — confusion, slurred speech, irrational behavior.
  • Loss of fine and gross motor coordination — stumbling, inability to walk.
  • Paradoxical undressing — the patient removes clothing due to a false sensation of warmth.
  • Muscle rigidity.
  • Drowsiness, difficult to rouse.
  • Heart rate slows. Breathing becomes shallow.

Treatment:

  1. Handle the patient gently. Rough movement can trigger cardiac arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation) in moderate-to-severe hypothermia.
  2. Place the patient in a horizontal position. Do not allow them to sit up or stand.
  3. Remove wet clothing — cut it off rather than having the patient move.
  4. Insulate aggressively: place the patient in a hypothermia wrap.

Hypothermia Wrap (Burrito Wrap):

  1. Lay a ground insulation layer (sleeping pad, branches).
  2. Lay a vapor barrier (tarp, plastic sheet, emergency blanket reflective side in).
  3. Lay insulation (sleeping bag, blankets).
  4. Place the patient on top.
  5. Place heat sources at the neck, armpits, and groin.
  6. Wrap the insulation around the patient.
  7. Wrap the vapor barrier over everything — the goal is to trap heat and block wind and moisture.

  8. Cover the head, leaving the face exposed for airway monitoring.

  9. Do not give food or drink to a patient with altered mental status — aspiration risk.

  10. Monitor breathing and pulse continuously.
  11. Evacuate. Moderate hypothermia requires professional medical care.
WARNING Afterdrop — when rewarming begins, cold blood from the extremities returns to the core, causing core temperature to drop further. This can trigger cardiac arrest. Rewarm the core (torso, neck, head) first. Do not rub or warm the extremities actively in moderate-to-severe cases.

Severe Hypothermia: Below 82 degF (28 degC)

Recognition:

  • No shivering.
  • Unconscious or semi-conscious.
  • Rigid muscles.
  • Very slow or undetectable pulse (check for 60 seconds).
  • Very slow or absent respirations.
  • Dilated pupils (this alone does not indicate death).
  • Skin may appear gray or blue.
  • May appear dead.

Treatment:

  1. Handle with extreme care — the heart is extremely irritable and prone to fibrillation from any jarring.
  2. Check pulse and breathing for a full 60 seconds before initiating CPR.
  3. If no pulse or breathing is detected, begin CPR. See CPR and Choking for hypothermic arrest protocol.
  4. Apply a hypothermia wrap as described above.
  5. If rescue breathing is needed, warm and humidify the breaths if possible (breathe through a warm cloth).
  6. Do not attempt active external rewarming of extremities.
  7. Evacuate immediately. Severe hypothermia patients need core rewarming (warm IV fluids, warm lavage) available only in a hospital setting.
WARNING Do not pronounce a hypothermic patient dead in the field. The cold protects the brain and organs. Cases of full recovery after prolonged cardiac arrest in severe hypothermia are documented. Continue CPR and rewarming. "They are not dead until they are warm and dead."

Frostbite

Classification

Degree Depth Appearance Sensation Prognosis
Frostnip Surface skin only Red, then white or gray Painful, tingling Full recovery
1st degree Epidermis White/yellowish plaque, surrounding redness Numbness, then burning on rewarming Full recovery
2nd degree Full skin Clear or milky blisters, redness Numbness, then severe pain on rewarming Usually recovers
3rd degree Skin and subcutaneous tissue Blood-filled blisters, blue-gray skin Numbness, loss of sensation Tissue loss likely
4th degree Through muscle and bone Mottled, deep red to black, firm No sensation Amputation likely

Field Treatment

  1. Do not thaw frostbitten tissue if there is any possibility of refreezing. Thaw-refreeze cycles cause far worse damage. A patient can walk on a frozen foot with minimal additional damage, but not on a thawed one.
  2. Protect the frozen area from further injury. Do not rub, massage, or apply snow.
  3. Remove wet clothing and constrictive jewelry (rings, watches) before swelling occurs.
  4. Insulate the affected area. Place dry padding between frostbitten fingers or toes.
  5. Do not break blisters.
  6. Do not apply direct heat (fire, heater, hot water bottle) — frozen tissue burns easily because the patient cannot feel temperature.

Controlled Rewarming (Only When Refreezing Can Be Prevented)

  1. Prepare water at 98.6-102 degF (37-39 degC). Test with an uninjured hand — it should feel warm but comfortable, not hot.
  2. Immerse the frostbitten area completely.
  3. Maintain the water temperature by adding warm water as it cools. Do not let it exceed 102 degF (39 degC).
  4. Rewarming takes 20-40 minutes. The process is complete when the tissue is soft, pliable, and red or purple.
  5. Rewarming is extremely painful. Administer the strongest available pain medication before beginning — ibuprofen 800 mg plus acetaminophen 1000 mg at minimum. Opioids are appropriate if available.
  6. After thawing, loosely wrap with dry, sterile dressings. Place padding between digits.
  7. Elevate the affected extremity.
  8. Give ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours — it has specific anti-prostaglandin effects that reduce frostbite tissue loss.
  9. Do not allow weight-bearing on thawed feet.
WARNING Frostbitten tissue looks worse before it looks better. Final determination of tissue viability takes weeks. Do not amputate or debride frostbitten tissue in the field.

Heat Illness

Contributing Factors

  • High ambient temperature and humidity.
  • Direct sun exposure.
  • Heavy physical exertion.
  • Dehydration.
  • Restrictive clothing or heavy gear.
  • Medications: antihistamines, beta-blockers, diuretics, stimulants, antidepressants.
  • Alcohol consumption.
  • Obesity, poor physical conditioning.
  • History of prior heat illness.
  • Age extremes (children and elderly are more vulnerable).

Heat Cramps

Recognition: Painful muscle spasms, usually in the calves, thighs, or abdomen, during or after heavy exertion in heat.

Treatment:

  1. Rest in a cool, shaded area.
  2. Drink an electrolyte solution: 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon of salt per 1 quart (1 liter) of water. Commercial sports drinks are adequate.
  3. Gently stretch and massage the affected muscle.
  4. Do not resume activity until cramps have fully resolved and adequate hydration is restored.

Heat Exhaustion

Recognition:

  • Core temperature elevated but below 104 degF (40 degC).
  • Heavy sweating — skin is cool and clammy.
  • Weakness, fatigue, dizziness.
  • Headache, nausea, vomiting.
  • Rapid, weak pulse.
  • Pale or flushed skin.
  • Mild confusion but oriented — the patient knows who they are, where they are, and what happened.
  • Muscle cramps.
  • Dark, concentrated urine.

Treatment:

  1. Move to shade or the coolest available environment.
  2. Remove excess clothing and gear.
  3. Lay the patient down, elevate the legs 6-12 inches (15-30 cm).
  4. Cool actively:
  5. Apply cool, wet cloths to the neck, armpits, and groin.
  6. Fan the patient to promote evaporative cooling.
  7. Spray or sponge the skin with water and fan.
  8. Rehydrate orally: small, frequent sips of cool electrolyte solution. Target 1-2 liters (1-2 quarts) over the first hour.
  9. Monitor for progression to heatstroke — check mental status every 5 minutes.
  10. Rest for the remainder of the day. Resume activity gradually over 24-48 hours.

Heatstroke

WARNING Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency. Without aggressive cooling, mortality exceeds 50%. Every minute of delay in cooling increases organ damage and death risk.

Recognition — Heat Exhaustion vs. Heatstroke:

Feature Heat Exhaustion Heatstroke
Core temperature Below 104 degF (40 degC) Above 104 degF (40 degC)
Mental status Alert, mildly confused Altered — confusion, combativeness, seizures, unconsciousness
Sweating Heavy May be present (exertional) or absent (classic)
Skin Cool, clammy Hot, may be dry or wet
Severity Moderate — treat and monitor Critical — cool immediately or patient dies

The defining distinction is altered mental status. If the patient is confused, combative, delirious, having seizures, or unconscious and the core temperature is elevated, treat as heatstroke.

Heatstroke Treatment:

  1. Cool first, transport second. Do not delay cooling to evacuate. Begin cooling immediately.
  2. Move to shade.
  3. Remove all clothing.
  4. Best method — cold water immersion: Submerge the patient in cold water (any natural water source — creek, pond, lake) up to the neck. This is the gold standard and cools fastest. If a tub or container is available, fill it.
  5. Alternative methods (use the most aggressive available):
  6. Pour cold water continuously over the entire body while fanning aggressively.
  7. Apply ice packs or cold packs to the neck, armpits, groin, palms, and soles of the feet.
  8. Wrap in a wet sheet and fan.
  9. Evaporative cooling: mist skin with water and maximize airflow.
  10. Target a core temperature of 101 degF (38.3 degC). If you do not have a thermometer, cool for at least 15-20 minutes or until the patient's mental status noticeably improves.
  11. Monitor the airway. Heatstroke patients may seize or vomit.
  12. Place in the recovery position if unconscious. See CPR and Choking.
  13. If the patient can drink, provide cool fluids slowly.
  14. Do not give aspirin or acetaminophen — they are ineffective against heatstroke and may worsen organ damage.
  15. Evacuate to definitive medical care after initial cooling. Heatstroke patients need monitoring for rhabdomyolysis, kidney failure, and coagulopathy.

Exertional vs. Classic Heatstroke

  • Exertional heatstroke — occurs in healthy, active individuals during intense physical activity. Often still sweating. Common in military, athletes, laborers.
  • Classic heatstroke — occurs in elderly, chronically ill, or medicated individuals during heat waves. Often NOT sweating (hot, dry skin). Develops over days.

Both are treated identically: aggressive, immediate cooling.

Hydration Guidelines

Prevention of Heat Illness

  • Pre-hydrate: drink 500 mL (about 1 pint) of water 2 hours before exertion in heat.
  • During activity: drink 250 mL (about 1 cup) every 15-20 minutes.
  • Do not exceed 1.5 liters (1.5 quarts) per hour — overhydration causes hyponatremia (low blood sodium), which can be fatal.
  • Add electrolytes for activity lasting longer than 1 hour or in heavy sweating: 1/4 teaspoon salt per liter of water, or use commercial electrolyte tablets.
  • Monitor urine color — target pale yellow. Dark urine indicates dehydration. Clear urine with frequent urination may indicate overhydration.

Oral Rehydration Solution (Field-Expedient)

  • 1 quart (1 liter) clean water
  • 6 teaspoons sugar
  • 1/2 teaspoon salt

Dissolve completely. Sip frequently. This formula approximates the World Health Organization oral rehydration solution.

Cold Weather Prevention

The COLD Acronym

  • Clean — keep clothing clean for maximum insulation.
  • Overlayer — dress in layers (base layer wicks moisture, insulation layer traps air, outer layer blocks wind and water).
  • Loose — wear clothing loose to allow air circulation and avoid constricting blood flow.
  • Dry — stay dry. Change out of wet clothing immediately. Moisture increases heat loss by 25x.

Additional Prevention

  • Eat high-calorie food frequently — your body needs fuel to generate heat. Consume 4,000-6,000 calories daily in cold environments.
  • Stay hydrated — dehydration impairs circulation and heat distribution.
  • Cover the head, neck, and hands — these areas have high surface-area-to-mass ratios and lose heat rapidly.
  • Keep moving — but do not overexert and sweat.
  • Use the buddy system — check each other for signs of hypothermia and frostbite regularly. Individuals often do not recognize their own symptoms.
  • Insulate from the ground. Conductive heat loss to cold ground is rapid.

Common Mistakes

  • Giving alcohol to a hypothermia patient — alcohol dilates blood vessels, accelerating heat loss.
  • Placing a moderate-to-severe hypothermia patient in a warm shower or bath — rapid external rewarming of extremities drives cold blood to the core and can cause fatal afterdrop and arrhythmia.
  • Rubbing frostbitten skin with snow or hands — this causes further mechanical tissue damage.
  • Thawing frostbite in the field when refreezing is possible — thaw-refreeze cycles destroy tissue that would otherwise survive.
  • Confusing heat exhaustion with heatstroke — the critical difference is altered mental status. If in doubt, treat as heatstroke.
  • Giving aspirin or acetaminophen for heatstroke — these drugs do not lower core temperature in heatstroke and may increase liver or kidney damage.
  • Stopping cooling efforts too early — cool until core temperature reaches 101 degF (38.3 degC) or mental status clearly improves.
  • Overhydrating — hyponatremia is as dangerous as dehydration. Do not exceed 1.5 L/hour.
  • Ignoring early mild symptoms — both hypothermia and heat illness are progressive. Early intervention prevents emergencies.
  • Allowing a hypothermia patient to walk or stand — exertion and upright posture circulate cold blood to the core and can trigger cardiac arrest.

Quick Reference

Hypothermia Stages

Stage Temp Range Key Signs Shivering? Field Treatable?
Mild 95-90 degF (35-32 degC) Shivering, confusion, clumsiness Yes, vigorous Yes
Moderate 90-82 degF (32-28 degC) Shivering stops, severe confusion, paradoxical undressing Slowing/stopped Partially — evacuate
Severe Below 82 degF (28 degC) Unconscious, rigid, appears dead No No — evacuate immediately

Heat Illness Progression

Stage Core Temp Mental Status Skin Action
Heat cramps Normal-slight elevation Normal Sweating Rest, electrolytes, stretch
Heat exhaustion Below 104 degF (40 degC) Alert, mild confusion Cool, clammy, sweating Cool, hydrate, rest
Heatstroke Above 104 degF (40 degC) Altered — confused, combative, seizing, unconscious Hot, may be dry or wet Cool aggressively NOW, evacuate

Frostbite Decision Matrix

Question Answer Action
Can refreezing be prevented? No Keep frozen, protect, evacuate
Can refreezing be prevented? Yes Rewarm in 98.6-102 degF (37-39 degC) water for 20-40 min
Blisters present? Clear fluid Do not break, protect
Blisters present? Blood-filled Do not break, protect — deep injury
Can patient walk on affected feet? Feet are frozen Yes, if necessary for evacuation
Can patient walk on affected feet? Feet are thawed No — carry or sled the patient

  • CPR and Choking — hypothermic cardiac arrest protocol, recovery position.
  • Fractures and Splints — immobilized patients are at high risk for hypothermia.
