Medical

Trauma Assessment and Field Triage

Systematically assess trauma patients, prioritize casualties in mass-casualty situations, and manage life-threatening injuries using TCCC and wilderness medicine protocols.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. Trauma management requires hands-on training and practice. This guide does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Stop massive hemorrhage first — it kills faster than airway or breathing problems in trauma.
  • Use the MARCH mnemonic for tactical trauma: Massive hemorrhage, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia/Head injury.
  • The primary survey (ABCDE) takes 60-90 seconds and identifies all immediately life-threatening conditions.
  • START triage categorizes casualties by survivability in under 30 seconds per patient.
  • Treat shock aggressively — lay flat, control bleeding, keep warm, and evacuate.

Scene Safety and Approach

Before touching any patient:

  1. Assess the scene for hazards — fire, unstable structures, downed power lines, traffic, active threats, chemical exposure, hostile actors.
  2. Determine the mechanism of injury — this tells you what injuries to suspect before you examine the patient.
  3. Count the patients — if multiple casualties exist, shift to triage mode immediately.
  4. Use personal protective equipment — gloves at minimum. Eye protection if blood exposure is likely.
  5. Establish a plan — decide who does what before rushing in. Disorganized responders become additional casualties.

Mechanism of Injury Clues

Mechanism Suspect
Fall > standing height Spinal injury, pelvis fracture, bilateral calcaneus (heel) fractures, wrist fractures
Vehicle accident (unrestrained) Cervical spine, aortic tear, liver/spleen laceration, femur fracture
Blast Primary: lung blast injury, TBI; Secondary: penetrating fragments; Tertiary: blunt trauma from being thrown
Penetrating (knife, bullet) Organ damage along the wound track, vascular injury
Crush injury (prolonged entrapment) Crush syndrome — hyperkalemia upon release, kidney failure

MARCH Protocol (Tactical Trauma)

The MARCH mnemonic reorders traditional ABCDE to prioritize the leading cause of preventable death in trauma: hemorrhage.

M — Massive Hemorrhage

  1. Identify and control all life-threatening external bleeding immediately.
  2. Apply direct pressure to compressible hemorrhage.
  3. Pack deep wounds with hemostatic gauze (QuikClot Combat Gauze, Celox). Pack tightly from the deepest point outward. Hold pressure for 3-5 minutes.
  4. Apply a tourniquet to any extremity hemorrhage that direct pressure cannot control. Place it 2-3 inches (5-7.5 cm) above the wound. See First Aid Basics for full tourniquet protocol.
  5. For junctional hemorrhage (groin, axilla, neck) where a tourniquet cannot be placed, use wound packing with direct pressure. Commercial junctional tourniquets (SAM JT, CRoC) are ideal if available.
  6. Note the time of tourniquet application.
WARNING Do not delay hemorrhage control to assess the airway. A patient can bleed to death from a femoral artery wound in 3-5 minutes. Hemorrhage kills faster than any airway problem in trauma.

A — Airway

  1. Open the airway. Use a jaw-thrust maneuver if spinal injury is suspected; head-tilt/chin-lift if not.
  2. Clear visible obstructions — blood, vomit, teeth, debris. Use a finger sweep only if the object is visible.
  3. Place an unconscious patient with an intact airway in the recovery position (if spinal injury is not suspected).
  4. Insert a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) if available — lubricate and insert into one nostril with the bevel toward the septum. Size: measure from the nostril to the earlobe.
  5. Insert an oropharyngeal airway (OPA) if the patient has no gag reflex. Size: measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe.
WARNING Do not insert an NPA if there is suspected mid-face or basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle's sign behind the ear, CSF leaking from the nose or ears). Use an OPA instead.

R — Respiration

Expose the chest and assess breathing:

  1. Look — chest rise symmetry, open wounds, flail segments (paradoxical movement).
  2. Listen — breath sounds bilaterally, equal or unequal.
  3. Feel — chest wall stability, subcutaneous emphysema (crackling sensation under the skin indicating air leak).

Manage immediately:

  • Open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound): An open wound in the chest wall that allows air into the pleural space.
  • Apply a chest seal (vented if available) — commercial chest seals (HyFin, SAM) are ideal.
  • Improvised seal: petroleum gauze, plastic wrap, or any airtight material taped on three sides (creating a flutter valve) or on all four sides if using a vented seal.

  • If a fully sealed dressing is used and the patient worsens (increasing difficulty breathing, dropping oxygen), suspect tension pneumothorax and burp the seal — lift one corner to release trapped air, then reseal.

  • Tension pneumothorax: Air enters the pleural space with each breath but cannot escape, progressively compressing the lung and shifting the heart.

Field signs: - Severe, worsening respiratory distress. - Absent breath sounds on the affected side. - Tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side (late sign — do not wait for this). - Jugular vein distention (JVD) — engorged neck veins (may be absent if also hypotensive from blood loss). - Hypotension, tachycardia, cyanosis. - Hyperresonance (hollow, drum-like sound) when tapping the affected side. - Subcutaneous emphysema spreading from the chest.

Field treatment — needle decompression: 1. Locate the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line (two finger-widths below the collarbone, at the midpoint of the collarbone) on the affected side. Alternative: 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line (nipple level, at the front of the armpit). 2. Insert a 14-gauge needle (at least 3.25 inches / 8 cm long for adults) perpendicular to the chest wall, just above the top of the 3rd rib (to avoid the neurovascular bundle that runs beneath each rib). 3. A rush of air confirms the diagnosis. 4. Leave the catheter in place. Secure with tape. 5. Reassess breathing. The patient should improve rapidly. 6. This is a temporizing measure — definitive treatment requires a chest tube.

WARNING Needle decompression is a life-saving but invasive procedure. Perform it only when you are confident in the diagnosis and the patient is deteriorating. An incorrect diagnosis results in an iatrogenic pneumothorax.
  • Flail chest: Three or more adjacent ribs broken in two or more places, creating a free-floating segment that moves paradoxically (inward during inhalation).
  • Position the patient with the injured side down (if no spinal injury suspected) to splint the flail segment against the ground.
  • Alternatively, apply a bulky dressing and tape firmly over the flail segment.
  • The real danger is the underlying pulmonary contusion. Monitor for worsening respiratory distress.

C — Circulation (Shock)

Assess and treat circulatory shock. See the Shock section below for details.

H — Hypothermia / Head Injury

  1. Prevent hypothermia in every trauma patient. Trauma patients lose thermoregulatory ability. The "lethal triad" of trauma death is hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy. See Hypothermia and Heatstroke.
  2. Manage head injuries — see the Head Injury section below.

Primary Survey (ABCDE)

The civilian primary survey uses the ABCDE framework. Complete it in 60-90 seconds.

A — Airway (with cervical spine protection)

  • Is the patient talking? If yes, the airway is open.
  • If not talking, open and assess as described in the MARCH section.
  • Maintain cervical spine immobilization if mechanism suggests spinal injury.

B — Breathing

  • Respiratory rate: count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
  • Normal adult: 12-20 breaths/min.
  • Tachypnea (>20): pain, anxiety, chest injury, shock, metabolic acidosis.
  • Bradypnea (<12): head injury, drug effect, fatigue, impending respiratory failure.
  • Assess for the three immediately treatable chest injuries: open pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, flail chest.

C — Circulation

  • Check pulse: rate, rhythm, strength.
  • Radial pulse present: systolic blood pressure is at least 80 mmHg.
  • Femoral pulse present: systolic BP is at least 70 mmHg.
  • Carotid pulse only: systolic BP is at least 60 mmHg.
  • Assess skin: color, temperature, moisture. Cool, pale, clammy skin indicates shock.
  • Capillary refill: press a fingernail and release. Normal refill is under 2 seconds.
  • Control any remaining hemorrhage not addressed in the M step.

D — Disability (Neurological Status)

Use AVPU for rapid assessment:

Level Response
Alert Eyes open spontaneously, oriented, follows commands
Verbal Responds to voice (eyes open, withdraws, moans)
Pain Responds only to painful stimulus (sternal rub, nail bed pressure)
Unresponsive No response to any stimulus

Check pupils: size, equality, reactivity to light. Unequal pupils after head trauma suggest herniation — this is a neurosurgical emergency.

E — Exposure / Environment

  1. Expose the patient completely — cut away clothing to find hidden injuries. Check the back by log-rolling.
  2. Immediately cover and insulate after examination to prevent hypothermia.
  3. Look for injuries you might have missed: posterior bleeding, impaled objects, deformities, bruising patterns.

Secondary Survey

Perform the secondary survey only after all life-threatening conditions identified in the primary survey have been addressed. This is a head-to-toe systematic examination.

SAMPLE History

Gather this information from the patient or bystanders:

  • Signs and symptoms — what happened, what hurts?
  • Allergies — medications, foods, environmental.
  • Medications — current prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, supplements.
  • Past medical history — chronic conditions, surgeries, hospitalizations.
  • Last oral intake — when did they last eat or drink?
  • Events leading to the injury — what happened before, during, and after?

Head-to-Toe Examination

Examine systematically. Use "look, feel, listen" at each body region:

  1. Head and face — palpate the skull for depressions, lacerations, swelling. Check the ears for blood or clear fluid (CSF). Check the eyes for pupil size, equality, and tracking. Check the nose for deformity and drainage. Check the mouth for loose teeth, lacerations, airway obstructions.
  2. Neck — palpate the cervical spine for tenderness, step-offs, or deformity. Check for JVD, tracheal position, subcutaneous emphysema. Do not remove a cervical collar if one is in place.
  3. Chest — palpate each rib, the sternum, and clavicles. Listen for breath sounds in four quadrants (if a stethoscope is available). Check for paradoxical motion, crepitus.
  4. Abdomen — palpate all four quadrants gently. Note rigidity, guarding, distension, or tenderness. A rigid, board-like abdomen indicates peritonitis.
  5. Pelvis — apply gentle inward and downward pressure once. If unstable or painful, stop immediately and apply a pelvic binder. Do not rock the pelvis back and forth. See Fractures and Splints.
  6. Extremities — check all four limbs for deformity, swelling, lacerations, pulse, sensation, movement. Compare sides.
  7. Back — log-roll (with spinal precautions if indicated) and inspect the entire posterior surface. Run a gloved hand along the spine from the base of the skull to the tailbone, feeling for deformity or tenderness.

Vital Signs

Take and record baseline vital signs. Reassess every 5-15 minutes depending on patient stability.

Vital Sign Normal Adult Range Concerning Values
Heart rate 60-100 bpm >100 (tachycardia in trauma = shock until proven otherwise)
Respiratory rate 12-20 breaths/min <10 or >30
Blood pressure (systolic) 100-140 mmHg <90 (hypotension — late sign of shock)
Temperature 97.8-99.1 degF (36.5-37.3 degC) <95 degF (35 degC) hypothermia
Pulse oximetry (if available) 95-100% <90%

Shock Recognition and Treatment

Types of Shock in Trauma

Type Cause Key Signs
Hypovolemic Blood loss (most common in trauma) Tachycardia, cool/pale/clammy skin, weak pulse, altered mental status
Obstructive Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade JVD, muffled heart sounds (tamponade), absent breath sounds (tension)
Neurogenic Spinal cord injury Bradycardia (slow heart rate) with hypotension, warm/dry skin below injury level
Septic Infection (delayed presentation) Fever, warm/flushed skin initially, progresses to cool/clammy

Estimated Blood Loss by Class

Class Blood Loss Heart Rate Blood Pressure Mental Status Skin
I <750 mL (<15%) Normal Normal Normal Normal
II 750-1500 mL (15-30%) 100-120 Normal (narrowed pulse pressure) Anxious Pale, cool
III 1500-2000 mL (30-40%) 120-140 Decreased Confused Cold, clammy, pale
IV >2000 mL (>40%) >140 or absent Severely decreased Lethargic/unconscious Cold, mottled, gray

Shock Treatment (Field)

  1. Control the bleeding source. Shock treatment is futile if hemorrhage continues.
  2. Lay the patient flat. Elevate the legs 6-12 inches (15-30 cm) if no spinal injury, pelvic fracture, or head injury is suspected.
  3. Keep the patient warm — insulate from the ground and cover with blankets. Prevent hypothermia aggressively.
  4. Do not give oral fluids to a patient with altered mental status, abdominal trauma, or who may need surgery.
  5. If the patient is alert with no abdominal injury, small sips of water are acceptable.
  6. If IV access and fluids are available, administer a 500 mL bolus of normal saline or lactated Ringer's. Reassess after each bolus. Target a systolic BP of 80-90 mmHg in hemorrhagic shock (permissive hypotension) — aggressive fluid administration dilutes clotting factors and can worsen bleeding.
  7. Reassess vital signs every 5 minutes.
  8. Evacuate. Definitive shock treatment requires surgery and blood products.
WARNING Do not elevate the legs of a patient with a suspected head injury — this increases intracranial pressure. Keep the head of the bed elevated 30 degrees for isolated head injuries.

Head Injury Management

Classification

  • Mild (concussion): GCS 13-15, brief or no loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, confusion.
  • Moderate: GCS 9-12, prolonged confusion, repeated vomiting, worsening headache.
  • Severe: GCS 3-8, prolonged unconsciousness, focal neurological deficits, seizures.

Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

Response Score
Eye Opening
Spontaneous 4
To voice 3
To pain 2
None 1
Verbal
Oriented 5
Confused 4
Inappropriate words 3
Incomprehensible sounds 2
None 1
Motor
Obeys commands 6
Localizes pain 5
Withdraws from pain 4
Abnormal flexion (decorticate) 3
Extension (decerebrate) 2
None 1

Total: 3-15. Document and track over time. A declining GCS is more significant than a single reading.

Field Management of Head Injury

  1. Maintain the airway — vomiting and loss of consciousness are common. Suction or position to drain.
  2. Control scalp bleeding — scalp wounds bleed profusely. Use direct pressure. Avoid clamping without visualization.
  3. Elevate the head 30 degrees (unless spinal injury is suspected with an unstable mechanism).
  4. Do not pack the ears or nose if clear fluid (CSF) is draining — this indicates a basilar skull fracture. Allow drainage and cover loosely.
  5. Monitor neurological status using GCS and pupil checks every 15 minutes.
  6. Note and document any seizure activity — duration, type, and body parts involved.
  7. Do not give aspirin or ibuprofen (increase bleeding). Acetaminophen is acceptable for headache.
  8. Keep the patient calm and minimize stimulation.

Signs of Deterioration (Herniation)

These indicate rising intracranial pressure and impending brain herniation — a fatal progression without surgical intervention:

  • Decreasing level of consciousness (declining GCS).
  • Unilateral pupil dilation (blown pupil) — the pupil on the side of the lesion dilates and stops reacting to light.
  • Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations — a late, pre-terminal sign.
  • Posturing: decorticate (arms flexed, legs extended) or decerebrate (all extremities extended) — indicates severe brain injury.
WARNING A single dilated, non-reactive pupil after head trauma is a neurosurgical emergency. Hyperventilate the patient briefly (20 breaths/min in an adult) as a temporizing measure to reduce intracranial pressure. This buys minutes, not hours. Evacuate immediately.

START Triage (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment)

Use START triage when casualties exceed available resources. Assess each patient in under 30 seconds.

Triage Categories

Category Color Priority Criteria
Immediate RED 1st Life-threatening but salvageable with immediate intervention
Delayed YELLOW 2nd Serious but can tolerate a delay of hours without dying
Minor GREEN 3rd (Walking wounded) Ambulatory, minor injuries
Expectant/Dead BLACK Last Dead or injuries incompatible with survival given available resources

START Triage Algorithm

Step 1: Can the patient walk? - Yes → tag GREEN (Minor). Direct them to a collection point. Move to the next patient. - No → proceed to Step 2.

Step 2: Is the patient breathing? - No → open the airway (head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw thrust). - Starts breathing → tag RED (Immediate). - Does not start breathing → tag BLACK (Expectant/Dead). Move to the next patient. - Yes → proceed to Step 3.

Step 3: What is the respiratory rate? - Greater than 30 breaths/minute → tag RED (Immediate). Move to the next patient. - Less than 30 → proceed to Step 4.

Step 4: What is the capillary refill? - Greater than 2 seconds (or radial pulse absent) → control any major bleeding, tag RED (Immediate). Move to the next patient. - 2 seconds or less (or radial pulse present) → proceed to Step 5.

Step 5: Can the patient follow simple commands? ("Squeeze my fingers," "What is your name?") - No → tag RED (Immediate). - Yes → tag YELLOW (Delayed).

Triage Principles

  • Do the greatest good for the greatest number. This means not spending all resources on one unsalvageable patient while others die of treatable injuries.
  • Triage is dynamic. Reassess patients as resources become available or as conditions change.
  • Triage decisions are among the hardest in medicine. Accept that imperfect decisions made quickly save more lives than perfect decisions made slowly.
  • Tag patients clearly — use commercial triage tags, colored tape, or write directly on the patient's forehead.

Field Decision-Making

Evacuation Priorities

Evacuate these patients first:

  1. Uncontrolled hemorrhage despite tourniquet and packing.
  2. Tension pneumothorax after needle decompression (needs chest tube).
  3. Declining neurological status (head injury with herniation signs).
  4. Open fractures.
  5. Abdominal trauma with signs of peritonitis (rigid abdomen).
  6. Pelvic fracture with shock.
  7. Burns greater than 20% TBSA.
  8. Crush injury patients before release from entrapment (if possible — crush syndrome can cause cardiac arrest upon release).

When to Stay vs. When to Go

Factor Stay and Treat Go (Evacuate)
Bleeding Controlled with pressure/tourniquet Uncontrolled, worsening
Airway Patent, maintainable Threatened, burns to face/neck
Breathing Adequate after intervention Deteriorating despite intervention
Neuro status Stable or improving Declining
Environment Safe, shelter available Hostile, exposed
Resources Adequate for current needs Exhausted or insufficient
Distance to help Very far, transport dangerous Feasible and transport available

Documentation in the Field

Write directly on the patient with a marker if no forms are available:

  • Time of initial assessment.
  • Injuries found.
  • Treatments given (especially tourniquet time, medications, doses).
  • Vital signs.
  • Allergies.
  • Triage category.

Use the patient's forehead, chest, or a piece of tape. Information that travels with the patient saves lives at the next level of care.

Common Mistakes

  • Tunnel vision on one dramatic injury while missing a second life-threatening problem — always complete the full primary survey.
  • Focusing on the airway before controlling massive hemorrhage — in trauma, hemorrhage kills faster.
  • Moving a patient with a suspected spinal injury before immobilization.
  • Not rechecking tourniquet effectiveness — a tourniquet that has loosened during transport is worse than no tourniquet.
  • Failing to check the back — log-roll every trauma patient. Posterior wounds are missed constantly.
  • Over-resuscitating with IV fluids — aggressive fluid boluses dilute clotting factors and raise blood pressure, which dislodges clots and restarts hemorrhage. Target 80-90 mmHg systolic (permissive hypotension).
  • Pronouncing a hypothermic patient dead in the field.
  • Spending excessive time on one patient during mass casualty events — triage demands 30 seconds per patient, not 30 minutes.
  • Not documenting tourniquet time — without this, downstream providers cannot make informed decisions about limb salvage.
  • Elevating the legs of a patient with a head injury — this worsens intracranial pressure.
  • Removing impaled objects — stabilize them in place. Removal can cause uncontrolled hemorrhage. The only exception is objects in the cheek obstructing the airway.

Quick Reference

MARCH Mnemonic

Letter Focus Key Interventions
M Massive hemorrhage Tourniquet, wound packing, direct pressure
A Airway Jaw thrust, NPA/OPA, recovery position
R Respiration Chest seal, needle decompression, flail management
C Circulation Shock treatment, IV fluids if available, leg elevation
H Hypothermia / Head injury Insulate, hypothermia wrap; elevate head, monitor GCS

ABCDE Primary Survey

Letter Assessment Time
A Airway + C-spine 10 sec
B Breathing 15 sec
C Circulation 15 sec
D Disability (neuro) 10 sec
E Exposure/Environment 20 sec

    │

    │                              │

Medical

Bites and Stings: Identification and Field Treatment

Recognize, treat, and triage venomous and non-venomous bites and stings when professional medical care is unavailable.

DISCLAIMER: This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Envenomation can be fatal. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Most bites and stings are not life-threatening — anaphylaxis and envenomation are the two emergencies that kill.
  • Never cut, suck, or tourniquet a bite wound. Immobilize the limb, keep it at or below heart level, and evacuate.
  • Recognize anaphylaxis early: hives, throat swelling, wheezing, dropping blood pressure. Administer epinephrine immediately.
  • Remove stingers and ticks promptly — delay worsens envenomation and disease transmission.
  • Photograph or clearly note the animal's appearance if safe to do so. Identification guides treatment.

Anaphylaxis

WARNING Anaphylaxis can kill within minutes. Treat it before addressing the bite or sting itself.

Recognition

Anaphylaxis typically develops within 5-30 minutes of exposure. Watch for:

  • Skin: Widespread hives, flushing, itching, swelling beyond the sting site.
  • Airway: Throat tightness, hoarse voice, stridor, difficulty swallowing.
  • Breathing: Wheezing, shortness of breath, rapid breathing.
  • Circulation: Rapid weak pulse, dizziness, pale/blue skin, loss of consciousness.

Two or more body systems involved after a known exposure = anaphylaxis. Act immediately.

Epinephrine Administration

  1. Use an auto-injector (EpiPen) or draw 0.3 mg (adult) / 0.15 mg (child under 66 lbs / 30 kg) of 1:1,000 epinephrine.
  2. Inject into the outer mid-thigh. Inject through clothing if necessary.
  3. Hold in place for 10 seconds.
  4. Note the time of injection.
  5. If no improvement in 5-15 minutes, administer a second dose.
  6. Position the patient lying down with legs elevated unless breathing is difficult — then allow them to sit upright.
  7. Evacuate immediately. Anaphylaxis can recur (biphasic reaction) 4-12 hours later.
TIP Administer diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 25-50 mg orally as a secondary measure if available. It does not replace epinephrine.

Bite and Sting Treatment by Type

Snake Bites:

Snake Bites

WARNING Do NOT cut the wound, suck out venom, apply a tourniquet, apply ice, or use electric shock. All are harmful and none work.

Identification

Note these features if observed safely:

  • Head shape (triangular vs. rounded).
  • Pupil shape (vertical slits vs. round).
  • Fang marks: two distinct punctures suggest a venomous pit viper; smaller tooth rows suggest non-venomous.
  • Coloring and pattern. Photograph if possible.
NOTE Roughly 20-25% of venomous snake bites are "dry bites" with no venom injected. Treat every bite as envenomation until proven otherwise.

Immediate Treatment

  1. Move the victim away from the snake's striking range (at least 6 feet / 2 m).
  2. Keep the victim calm and still. Increased heart rate accelerates venom spread.
  3. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing from the bitten limb before swelling begins.
  4. Immobilize the bitten limb in a neutral position at or slightly below heart level.
  5. Mark the leading edge of swelling with a pen and note the time.
  6. Clean the wound gently with water. Do not scrub.
  7. Apply a pressure immobilization bandage (PIB) for elapid bites only (coral snakes, cobras, mambas): wrap the entire limb firmly with an elastic bandage from the bite toward the heart at the pressure of an ankle sprain wrap.
CAUTION Do NOT use a pressure immobilization bandage for pit viper bites (rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths). Trapping cytotoxic venom in tissue increases local damage.

Evacuation Criteria

Evacuate ALL suspected venomous snake bites. Antivenom is the definitive treatment and cannot be replicated in the field.

Regional Notes

  • North America: Pit vipers (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth) and coral snakes. "Red touches yellow, kill a fellow" is unreliable outside the U.S.
  • Australia: Assume all snake bites are elapid. Apply PIB immediately.
  • Southeast Asia/Africa: Many species. Assume venomous until confirmed otherwise.

See Venomous Snakes for species identification.

Spider Bites:

Spider Bites

Most spider bites cause only local pain and swelling. Two genera pose serious threats in North America: Latrodectus (widow spiders) and Loxosceles (recluse spiders).

Black Widow (Latrodectus)

Identification: Shiny black body, red hourglass marking on underside (females). Found throughout North America, especially in undisturbed sheltered areas.

Symptoms: Sharp pinprick pain at the bite. Within 30-60 minutes: severe muscle cramping (especially abdomen and back), sweating, nausea, elevated blood pressure, difficulty breathing.

Treatment:

  1. Clean the bite with soap and water.
  2. Apply a cold pack (wrapped, not directly on skin) for 10 minutes on, 10 minutes off.
  3. Administer ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain.
  4. Monitor for systemic symptoms for 6 hours.
  5. Evacuate if muscle cramps are severe, if the victim is a child or elderly, or if breathing difficulty develops.

Brown Recluse (Loxosceles)

Identification: Light brown, violin-shaped marking on cephalothorax, six eyes in three pairs. Found in south-central and southeastern U.S.

Symptoms: Mild sting at bite, often unnoticed. Over 2-8 hours: increasing pain, central blister, expanding area of redness. Over days: necrotic ulcer with purple/black center (not all bites necrose).

Treatment:

  1. Clean with soap and water.
  2. Apply a cold pack intermittently.
  3. Immobilize and elevate the affected area.
  4. Do NOT debride, excise, or apply heat.
  5. Evacuate if the wound develops necrosis, if systemic symptoms (fever, rash, dark urine) develop, or if the bite is on the face or genitals.

See Venomous Spiders for identification details.

Scorpion Stings:

Scorpion Stings

Most scorpion stings cause local pain comparable to a bee sting. The bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus) in the southwestern U.S. and Mexico is the primary North American exception.

Bark Scorpion — Severe Envenomation Signs

  • Numbness and tingling at the sting site spreading to the limb.
  • Roving eye movements (opsoclonus) — a distinctive sign.
  • Muscle twitching, excessive salivation, difficulty swallowing.
  • Respiratory distress (children are most vulnerable).

Treatment

  1. Clean the sting site with soap and water.
  2. Apply a cold pack for 10 minutes on, 10 minutes off.
  3. Administer pain relievers (ibuprofen, acetaminophen).
  4. Do NOT apply a tourniquet or make incisions.
  5. Monitor for systemic symptoms for 4-6 hours.
  6. Evacuate children, elderly, or anyone showing neurotoxic signs.
TIP Shake out boots, clothing, and sleeping bags before use in scorpion territory. Scorpions are nocturnal and seek dark, confined spaces.

Insect Stings:

Insect Stings (Bee, Wasp, Hornet)

Stinger Removal

Remove a honeybee stinger as fast as possible. The method (scraping vs. pulling) matters less than speed — the venom sac continues pumping for 2-3 minutes after detachment.

  1. Scrape the stinger out with a flat edge (credit card, knife blade) or pull it out with fingers or tweezers.
  2. Clean the site with soap and water.
  3. Apply a cold pack to reduce swelling.
NOTE Wasps and hornets do not leave stingers behind. They can sting repeatedly.

Normal Local Reaction

Pain, redness, and swelling at the sting site lasting up to 48 hours. Treat with cold compresses and oral antihistamines.

Large Local Reaction

Swelling greater than 4 inches (10 cm) in diameter, lasting up to 7 days. Not anaphylaxis, but uncomfortable. Treat with antihistamines and ibuprofen.

Multiple Stings

More than 10-20 stings can cause systemic toxicity even without allergy: vomiting, diarrhea, muscle breakdown, kidney failure. Evacuate anyone with more than 20 stings.

See Insect Threats for avoidance strategies.

Tick Bites:

Tick Bites

Ticks transmit Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, and other infections. Disease transmission risk increases with attachment duration — most require 24-48 hours of attachment.

Removal

  1. Grasp the tick as close to the skin surface as possible with fine-tipped tweezers.
  2. Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk.
  3. If mouthparts break off in the skin, remove them with tweezers if easily accessible. If not, leave them and let the skin heal.
  4. Clean the bite area and your hands with rubbing alcohol or soap and water.
WARNING Do NOT use heat (match, cigarette), petroleum jelly, nail polish, or other "suffocation" methods. These cause the tick to regurgitate into the wound, increasing infection risk.

Post-Removal Monitoring

  • Note the date and location of the bite.
  • Watch for a bull's-eye rash (erythema migrans) for 30 days — indicates Lyme disease.
  • Watch for fever, headache, muscle aches, or rash within 2 weeks — indicates possible tick-borne illness.
  • If prophylactic doxycycline is available and the tick was engorged (attached >36 hours) in a Lyme-endemic area: a single dose of 200 mg within 72 hours of removal reduces Lyme risk.

Marine Stings:

Marine Stings (Jellyfish, Man-of-War, Sea Urchin)

Jellyfish and Portuguese Man-of-War

CAUTION Do NOT rinse with fresh water — it causes unfired nematocysts to discharge. Do NOT apply urine (ineffective and unsanitary).

Treatment:

  1. Remove the victim from the water.
  2. Remove visible tentacles using tweezers, a stick, or gloved hands. Do not touch with bare skin.
  3. Rinse the area with vinegar (5% acetic acid) for at least 30 seconds to deactivate nematocysts. If vinegar is unavailable, use saltwater.
  4. Immerse the affected area in hot water — as hot as tolerable without burning, 110-113°F (43-45°C) — for 20-45 minutes.
  5. Administer pain medication as needed.
NOTE Box jellyfish (*Chironex fleckeri*) stings in Australia and Indo-Pacific waters can be lethal within minutes. Apply vinegar immediately and prepare for CPR. Evacuate.

Sea Urchin Spines

  1. Soak the affected area in hot water, 110-113°F (43-45°C), for 30-90 minutes to break down venom proteins.
  2. Remove accessible spines with tweezers. Do not crush spines deeper into tissue.
  3. Spines too deep to remove will often dissolve or be expelled naturally over weeks.
  4. Monitor for infection.

Common Mistakes

  • Applying a tourniquet to a snake bite. Traps venom in the limb, causing massive tissue destruction. Immobilize instead.
  • Sucking venom from a wound. Does not extract meaningful venom. Introduces oral bacteria into the wound.
  • Delaying epinephrine during anaphylaxis. Antihistamines do not stop anaphylaxis. Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment. Give it early.
  • Using fresh water on jellyfish stings. Osmotic change causes remaining nematocysts to fire. Use vinegar or saltwater.
  • Twisting or jerking ticks during removal. Breaks off mouthparts and may cause regurgitation into the wound. Pull straight up with steady force.
  • Ignoring "mild" bites in the field. Infection develops over days. Clean every bite wound and monitor daily.

Quick Reference

Bite/Sting First Action Do NOT Evacuate If
Snake (pit viper) Immobilize limb, remove jewelry Cut, suck, tourniquet, ice All suspected venomous bites
Snake (elapid) Pressure immobilization bandage Delay bandaging All elapid bites
Spider (widow) Clean, cold pack, pain relief — Severe cramps, breathing difficulty
Spider (recluse) Clean, cold pack, elevate Debride, apply heat Necrosis, systemic symptoms
Scorpion Clean, cold pack, pain relief Tourniquet, incision Neurotoxic signs, children
Bee/wasp Remove stinger fast, cold pack Squeeze stinger Anaphylaxis, >20 stings
Tick Pull straight up with tweezers Heat, petroleum jelly Rash, fever within 30 days
Jellyfish Vinegar rinse, hot water soak Fresh water, urine Box jellyfish, breathing difficulty

Anaphylaxis Protocol:

  1. Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (outer thigh) — repeat in 5-15 min if needed.
  2. Position patient supine with legs elevated.
  3. Administer antihistamine if available.
  4. Evacuate immediately.

Wound Infection: Recognition, Treatment, and Evacuation

Identify, treat, and manage wound infections in the field before they become systemic and life-threatening.

DISCLAIMER: This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Systemic infection (sepsis) is a medical emergency. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • All wounds in a survival setting will become contaminated. Aggressive irrigation at the time of injury is the single most effective infection-prevention measure.
  • Infection signs: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaking from the wound, and fever.
  • Red streaking toward the heart (lymphangitis) or fever above 101°F (38.3°C) indicates the infection has spread beyond the wound. Evacuate.
  • Irrigate wounds with at least 500 mL (1 pint) of the cleanest water available under pressure before closing or dressing.
  • Sepsis kills faster than blood loss in prolonged field scenarios. Recognize it early and evacuate.

Infection Timeline

Understanding the typical infection timeline helps distinguish normal healing from dangerous progression.

Time After Injury Normal Healing Infection
0-6 hours Bleeding stops, clot forms Window for effective irrigation
6-12 hours Mild redness, swelling (inflammatory response) Too early to distinguish from normal inflammation
12-48 hours Swelling peaks then begins to recede Increasing redness, warmth, worsening pain
48-72 hours Edges begin to heal, pain decreasing Purulent drainage, expanding redness, fever
3-7 days Granulation tissue forming Red streaking, abscess formation, systemic signs
7+ days Progressive closure Tissue death, sepsis risk
NOTE In warm, humid environments (tropics, swamps), this timeline accelerates. Expect infection signs 12-24 hours earlier than the table above.

Recognizing Infection

Local Signs (at the wound)

  • Increasing redness that expands beyond the wound edges over hours to days.
  • Warmth over and around the wound compared to surrounding tissue.
  • Swelling that worsens after the first 24 hours rather than improving.
  • Purulent drainage — pus (white, yellow, green, or brown fluid). Clear or slightly blood-tinged drainage is normal.
  • Increasing pain at the wound, especially if it was previously improving.
  • Foul smell from the wound.
  • Wound edges separating or tissue breaking down.

Regional Signs (infection is spreading)

WARNING Regional signs mean the infection has moved beyond the wound. Begin antibiotics if available and prepare to evacuate.
  • Red streaking (lymphangitis) — red lines extending from the wound toward the trunk. Follow the streaks toward the heart. Mark the leading edge with a pen and note the time.
  • Swollen, tender lymph nodes — groin nodes for leg wounds, armpit nodes for arm wounds, neck nodes for head/face wounds.
  • Cellulitis — diffuse redness, warmth, and swelling spreading across a broad area without a clear abscess.

Systemic Signs (infection in the bloodstream)

WARNING Any two of the following signs suggest sepsis. This is immediately life-threatening. Evacuate by the fastest means available.
  • Fever above 101°F (38.3°C) or hypothermia below 96.8°F (36°C).
  • Heart rate above 90 beats per minute at rest.
  • Respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute.
  • Confusion, altered mental status, extreme fatigue.
  • Shaking chills (rigors).

Prevention

Irrigation

Irrigation is the most important infection-prevention step. The goal is to physically flush bacteria and debris from the wound under pressure.

  1. Use the cleanest water available: potable water, disinfected water, or saline (1 teaspoon / 5 mL salt per 1 quart / 1 liter water).
  2. Fill a clean plastic bag, water bottle with a hole poked in the cap, or a syringe (at least 20 mL).
  3. Direct a forceful stream into the wound from 2 inches (5 cm) away.
  4. Use at least 500 mL (1 pint) for a small wound, 1-2 liters (1-2 quarts) for large or contaminated wounds.
  5. Irrigate until all visible debris is removed and the fluid runs clear.
TIP A syringe or squeeze bottle produces roughly 8-12 psi of pressure — the effective range for removing bacteria without driving debris deeper. Pouring water over a wound is not irrigation.

Debridement

Remove dead, damaged, or contaminated tissue before dressing. Dead tissue is a bacterial growth medium.

  1. Wash your hands. Wear gloves if available.
  2. Use a sterile blade, scissors, or clean tweezers.
  3. Remove only tissue that is clearly dead (gray, black, or mushy) or foreign material.
  4. Stop if you encounter bleeding tissue — that tissue is alive.
CAUTION Do not debride wounds near tendons, nerves, blood vessels, joints, or the face without surgical training. Irrigate aggressively instead.

Wound Closure vs. Open Management

  • Close clean wounds less than 6 hours old with low contamination risk: clean cuts, surgical wounds.
  • Leave open wounds that are more than 6 hours old, heavily contaminated, caused by bites, or caused by crushing mechanisms.
  • Pack open wounds loosely with moist (saline-dampened) gauze. Change the packing at least once daily.

Field Treatment of Infection

Step 1: Open the Wound

If a closed wound shows infection signs, remove closures (stitches, butterfly strips, staples) and open the wound to allow drainage.

Step 2: Irrigate Aggressively

Flush the wound with at least 1 liter (1 quart) of the cleanest water available under pressure. Irrigate twice daily until infection signs begin to improve.

Step 3: Apply Warm Soaks

Soak the wound in warm water or apply warm, moist compresses for 20-30 minutes, three to four times daily. Heat increases blood flow to the area, bringing white blood cells and antibodies.

Step 4: Antibiotics

Begin oral antibiotics if available and infection signs are worsening despite local care.

CAUTION The dosing table below is for emergency field use only. Confirm no drug allergies before administering. Complete the full course even if symptoms improve.

Antibiotic Dosing Table

Antibiotic Adult Dose Frequency Duration Covers
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) 875/125 mg Every 12 hours 7-10 days Broad spectrum, bite wounds
Cephalexin (Keflex) 500 mg Every 6 hours 7-10 days Skin/soft tissue, cellulitis
Doxycycline 100 mg Every 12 hours 7-10 days Broad spectrum, tick-borne illness
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg Every 12 hours 7-10 days Gram-negative, GI, urinary
Metronidazole (Flagyl) 500 mg Every 8 hours 7-10 days Anaerobic bacteria (deep/puncture wounds)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim DS) 160/800 mg Every 12 hours 7-10 days MRSA, skin abscesses
NOTE For bite wounds (human or animal), use amoxicillin-clavulanate as first choice. For suspected MRSA (abscesses, boils not responding to standard antibiotics), use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline.

Step 5: Drain Abscesses

An abscess is a walled-off pocket of pus. Antibiotics alone cannot clear it — the pus must be drained.

WARNING Do not attempt to drain abscesses near major blood vessels (neck, groin, armpit), near the eyes, or on the face unless you have surgical training. Evacuate.
  1. Clean the skin over the abscess with antiseptic.
  2. Using a sterile blade, make a single incision along the long axis of the abscess through the most prominent point.
  3. Make the incision large enough to allow full drainage — at least half the length of the abscess.
  4. Express all pus by gentle pressure around the edges. Do not squeeze aggressively.
  5. Irrigate the cavity with clean water or saline.
  6. Pack the cavity loosely with moist gauze to keep it open and draining.
  7. Change packing daily. The wound heals from the inside out over days to weeks.

Cellulitis vs. Abscess

Feature Cellulitis Abscess
Appearance Diffuse redness, warm, flat Localized swelling, raised, fluctuant
Borders Indistinct, spreading Defined edges
Palpation Firm, no fluid wave Soft center, fluid moves under pressure
Treatment Antibiotics, warm soaks Incision and drainage + antibiotics
Pain Diffuse Focal, throbbing

Sepsis Recognition and Response

Sepsis is infection that has entered the bloodstream and triggered a systemic inflammatory response. Without IV antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, mortality is high.

Early Sepsis Signs

  • Fever above 101°F (38.3°C) or temperature below 96.8°F (36°C).
  • Heart rate above 90 bpm at rest.
  • Respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute.
  • Known wound infection plus any of the above.

Severe Sepsis / Septic Shock

  • Confusion or altered mental status.
  • Systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg (if you can measure it) or unable to stand without dizziness.
  • Mottled, cool extremities despite fever.
  • Urine output drops to nearly zero.

Field Response

  1. Begin oral antibiotics immediately — use the broadest-spectrum option available.
  2. Push oral fluids aggressively if the patient can swallow: water, ORS, any drinkable fluid.
  3. Manage fever with ibuprofen or acetaminophen.
  4. Keep the patient warm.
  5. Evacuate by the fastest available means. Sepsis requires IV antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation.

Common Mistakes

  • Closing contaminated wounds. Suturing or taping shut a dirty wound traps bacteria inside and guarantees infection. Leave contaminated wounds open.
  • Pouring water over a wound and calling it irrigated. Effective irrigation requires pressure — use a syringe, squeeze bottle, or punctured bottle cap.
  • Stopping antibiotics when symptoms improve. Incomplete courses breed resistant bacteria. Finish the full course.
  • Ignoring red streaking. Lymphangitis means the infection is spreading through the lymphatic system. This is not a "wait and see" situation.
  • Packing an abscess cavity too tightly. Tight packing prevents drainage and creates a new closed space. Pack loosely.
  • Using topical antibiotics (Neosporin) on deep wounds. Topical antibiotics penetrate less than 2 mm. Deep infections require systemic (oral) antibiotics.

Quick Reference

Infection Red Flags — Evacuate Immediately:

  • Red streaking from the wound toward the trunk.
  • Fever above 101°F (38.3°C) with a wound.
  • Confusion or altered mental status.
  • Rapid heart rate (>90 bpm) plus rapid breathing (>20/min).
  • Wound on the face, neck, hands, joints, or genitals with spreading redness.

Daily Wound Care Routine:

  1. Remove old dressing.
  2. Irrigate with clean water under pressure.
  3. Inspect for redness, swelling, pus, streaking, and smell.
  4. Mark redness borders with a pen and note the time.
  5. Apply warm soak for 20-30 minutes if infection is present.
  6. Repack open wounds with moist gauze.
  7. Redress with clean bandage.

Field Saline Recipe:

1 teaspoon (5 mL) table salt per 1 quart (1 liter) of disinfected water.

Dehydration and Waterborne Illness

Recognize and treat dehydration and waterborne diseases in the field when clean water access is limited or compromised.

DISCLAIMER: This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Severe dehydration and cholera can kill within hours. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • Dehydration kills faster than starvation. A person loses function at 5% body water loss and risks death at 10%.
  • Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the most effective field treatment for dehydration — water alone is insufficient because it lacks electrolytes.
  • All surface water in the wilderness should be treated as contaminated. Boil, filter, or chemically treat before drinking.
  • Most waterborne illnesses cause diarrhea, which accelerates dehydration. Break the cycle with ORS and, when available, antibiotics.
  • Dark yellow or amber urine is the earliest reliable sign of dehydration in the field.

Dehydration

Causes

  • Inadequate water intake.
  • Diarrhea and vomiting (the most common accelerator in survival situations).
  • Excessive sweating from heat, exertion, or fever.
  • High altitude (increased respiratory water loss).
  • Burns (fluid loss through damaged skin).

Stages of Dehydration

Stage Body Water Loss Signs Field Treatment
Mild 1-3% (~1-2 lbs / 0.5-1 kg) Thirst, dark urine, dry mouth, slight headache Oral fluids, ORS
Moderate 3-6% (~2-4 lbs / 1-2 kg) Decreased urine output, rapid pulse, dizziness on standing, sunken eyes, loss of skin turgor ORS aggressively, rest in shade
Severe 6-10% (~4-7 lbs / 2-3 kg) No urine output, rapid weak pulse, confusion, unconsciousness, cool/mottled extremities ORS if conscious; evacuate immediately

Skin Turgor Test

Pinch the skin on the back of the hand and release. In a hydrated person, skin snaps back immediately. In moderate dehydration, the skin "tents" and takes 2-3 seconds to flatten. In severe dehydration, the tent persists for more than 3 seconds.

NOTE Skin turgor is unreliable in elderly patients (skin loses elasticity with age) and in cold environments (skin stiffens). Use urine color and mental status as additional indicators.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)

ORS replaces both water and electrolytes lost through diarrhea, vomiting, and sweating. It is absorbed even during active diarrhea because glucose-coupled sodium transport remains functional.

Standard ORS Recipe (WHO formula)

Per 1 quart (1 liter) of clean (disinfected) water:

  • 6 level teaspoons (30 mL) sugar.
  • 1/2 level teaspoon (2.5 mL) table salt.

Stir until fully dissolved. Discard after 24 hours if not refrigerated.

CAUTION Too much salt causes hypernatremia and worsens dehydration. Too much sugar causes osmotic diarrhea. Measure carefully. The solution should taste no saltier than tears.

Alternative ORS Ingredients

If sugar is unavailable:

  • Honey: 6 teaspoons per quart/liter (do not give honey to children under 1 year).
  • Crushed overripe banana or cooked rice water for glucose source (less precise but functional).

If pre-mixed ORS packets are available, follow packet instructions.

Administration

  • Mild dehydration: Drink 1-2 cups (250-500 mL) per hour for 4 hours.
  • Moderate dehydration: Drink 2-4 cups (500 mL-1 liter) per hour for 4 hours. Sip continuously rather than gulping.
  • Severe dehydration with consciousness: Sip ORS constantly. Aim for 4-6 quarts (4-6 liters) over 6-8 hours.
  • Severe dehydration with unconsciousness: Position in recovery position. ORS cannot be given to an unconscious patient. Evacuate for IV fluids.
TIP If the patient vomits, wait 10 minutes, then resume ORS in smaller, more frequent sips — 1 tablespoon every 1-2 minutes.

Field Alternatives for IV Fluids

WARNING Rectal and subcutaneous fluid administration are emergency techniques only. They carry infection risk and should be used only when oral rehydration has failed and evacuation is delayed.

Rectal Rehydration (Proctoclysis):

Fluids administered rectally are absorbed through the rectal mucosa. This technique works when the patient cannot keep oral fluids down.

  1. Use clean, body-temperature water or ORS.
  2. Insert a lubricated flexible tube (catheter, clean flexible tubing) 4 inches (10 cm) into the rectum.
  3. Elevate the fluid bag or bottle 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) above the patient.
  4. Administer slowly — 200-400 mL per hour. If cramping occurs, slow the rate.
  5. Target 1-2 liters over 4-6 hours.

Waterborne Illnesses

WARNING All surface water — streams, rivers, lakes, ponds — should be treated as contaminated even if it appears clear. Treat all water before drinking.

Overview by Pathogen

Giardia:

Giardia (Giardia lamblia)

Source: Contaminated surface water worldwide. Cysts survive cold water and chlorination at standard doses.

Incubation: 1-3 weeks after ingestion.

Symptoms: Explosive, foul-smelling diarrhea (often greasy/floating), gas, bloating, nausea, cramping, sulfurous belching. Low-grade fever occasionally. Symptoms wax and wane over weeks.

Field Treatment:

  1. Push ORS aggressively to offset fluid loss.
  2. Metronidazole 250 mg three times daily for 5-7 days (if available).
  3. Alternative: Tinidazole 2 g single dose.

Prevention: Boiling (1 minute at sea level, 3 minutes above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m), filtration to 1 micron or smaller, or chemical treatment with appropriate contact time.

Cryptosporidium:

Cryptosporidium (Cryptosporidium parvum)

Source: Contaminated water and fecal-oral contact. Oocysts are resistant to chlorine and iodine at standard concentrations.

Incubation: 2-10 days.

Symptoms: Profuse, watery diarrhea, cramping, nausea, low-grade fever. Lasts 1-3 weeks in healthy adults. Can be fatal in immunocompromised individuals.

Field Treatment:

  1. ORS for fluid replacement — this is the primary treatment.
  2. No effective field antibiotic. The illness is self-limiting in healthy adults.
  3. Nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily for 3 days if available.
CAUTION Standard iodine and chlorine tablets do NOT reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Boiling or filtration (1 micron absolute or UV) is required.

Cholera:

Cholera (Vibrio cholerae)

Source: Contaminated water and food in endemic regions (South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Haiti, parts of Central/South America).

Incubation: 12 hours to 5 days.

Symptoms: Sudden onset of painless, massive watery diarrhea ("rice water stool"), vomiting, rapid dehydration. Can lose 1 quart (1 liter) of fluid per hour. Death from dehydration within 12-24 hours without treatment.

WARNING Cholera can kill a healthy adult in under 24 hours through dehydration alone. ORS must begin immediately.

Field Treatment:

  1. Begin ORS immediately — match intake to output. A severely dehydrated cholera patient needs 4-8 quarts (4-8 liters) in the first 4-6 hours.
  2. Doxycycline 300 mg single dose (reduces duration and fluid loss by ~50%).
  3. Alternative: Azithromycin 1 g single dose.
  4. Continue ORS until diarrhea resolves (typically 3-5 days).

E. coli:

Pathogenic E. coli

Source: Fecal contamination of water and food. Multiple pathogenic strains exist.

Incubation: 1-10 days depending on strain.

Symptoms: Watery or bloody diarrhea, cramping, nausea, vomiting. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC/O157:H7) causes bloody diarrhea and can cause kidney failure (hemolytic uremic syndrome).

WARNING Do NOT give antibiotics for suspected EHEC (bloody diarrhea without fever). Antibiotics may increase the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Hydrate and evacuate.

Field Treatment (non-bloody diarrhea):

  1. ORS for fluid replacement.
  2. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days (if available and diarrhea is non-bloody).
  3. Alternative: Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days.

Hepatitis A:

Hepatitis A

Source: Fecal-oral route via contaminated water or food. Common in regions with poor sanitation.

Incubation: 15-50 days (average 28 days).

Symptoms: Fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, low-grade fever. After several days: dark urine, pale stools, jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes).

Field Treatment:

  1. No specific antiviral treatment exists. The illness is self-limiting (2-6 weeks).
  2. Rest and hydration.
  3. Avoid alcohol (additional liver stress).
  4. Maintain caloric intake — small, frequent meals.
  5. Evacuate if jaundice develops, if the patient cannot keep fluids down, or if confusion develops (indicates liver failure).

Prevention: Hepatitis A vaccine provides long-term immunity. Consider vaccination before travel to endemic regions.

Prevention

Water Treatment Methods

Method Effective Against Time Required Notes
Boiling All pathogens 1 min (3 min above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m) Most reliable method
Filtration (0.2 micron) Bacteria, protozoa Immediate Does not remove viruses
Filtration + purifier All pathogens Immediate Purifiers add chemical or UV stage
Chlorine dioxide All pathogens 30 min (4 hours for crypto) Effective against Cryptosporidium
Iodine Bacteria, most viruses, Giardia 30 min NOT reliable for Cryptosporidium
UV (SteriPEN/SODIS) All pathogens 90 sec (SteriPEN) / 6 hours (SODIS) Water must be clear

Hygiene Practices

  • Wash hands with soap and water (or ash and water) before eating, after defecation, and before treating wounds.
  • Dig latrines at least 200 feet (60 m) from any water source and at least 200 feet from camp.
  • Do not share water bottles or eating utensils during a diarrheal illness.

Common Mistakes

  • Drinking untreated water because it looks clean. Clear mountain streams routinely carry Giardia and Cryptosporidium from animal feces upstream.
  • Replacing fluids with water only. Diarrhea depletes sodium, potassium, and glucose. Plain water dilutes remaining electrolytes and can cause hyponatremia. Use ORS.
  • Rationing water in a hot environment. Drink when thirsty. Ration sweat (stay in shade, minimize exertion), not water.
  • Using iodine tablets and assuming all pathogens are killed. Cryptosporidium is iodine-resistant. Boil or filter.
  • Giving antibiotics for bloody diarrhea without fever. Suspected EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) can worsen with antibiotics. Hydrate and evacuate.
  • Ignoring early signs of dehydration. Thirst means you are already 1-2% dehydrated. Drink proactively.

Quick Reference

ORS Recipe (per 1 quart / 1 liter clean water):

  • 6 teaspoons sugar + 1/2 teaspoon salt. Stir. Discard after 24 hours.

Dehydration Assessment:

Check Mild Moderate Severe
Urine color Dark yellow Amber/brown None
Skin turgor Normal Slow return (2-3 sec) Tenting (>3 sec)
Mental status Normal Irritable, dizzy Confused, unconscious
Pulse Normal Rapid Rapid, weak, thready
Action ORS, 1-2 cups/hr ORS, 2-4 cups/hr Evacuate

Waterborne Illness Quick ID:

Disease Onset Key Feature Antibiotic
Giardia 1-3 weeks Sulfurous belching, greasy stool Metronidazole
Cryptosporidium 2-10 days Watery diarrhea, chlorine-resistant Self-limiting
Cholera 12 hrs-5 days Massive rice-water stool Doxycycline
E. coli 1-10 days Watery or bloody diarrhea Ciprofloxacin*
Hepatitis A 15-50 days Jaundice, dark urine None (supportive)

*Do not give antibiotics if bloody diarrhea without fever (suspect EHEC).

Medical

Plant Poisoning: Recognition and Field Treatment

Identify plant poisoning symptoms, administer first aid for ingestion and contact exposure, and avoid commonly confused toxic species.

DISCLAIMER This guide is for educational and emergency preparedness purposes only. It does not replace professional medical training, certification, or the judgment of a licensed medical provider. Plant poisoning can be fatal. Never eat any plant you cannot identify with 100% certainty. Seek professional care as soon as it becomes available.

At a Glance

  • When in doubt, do not eat it. No survival situation improves by adding a poisoning emergency.
  • Do NOT induce vomiting for most plant poisonings — many plant toxins cause more damage on the way back up.
  • Activated charcoal (1 g per kg body weight, or roughly 50 g for an adult) is the primary field treatment for ingestion if given within 1 hour.
  • Cardiac and neurological symptoms after plant ingestion are immediate evacuation criteria.
  • Poison ivy, oak, and sumac cause contact dermatitis — wash skin with soap and cold water within 10 minutes of exposure to prevent rash.

Types of Plant Poisoning

Gastrointestinal Toxicity

The most common presentation. Toxins irritate or damage the GI tract lining.

Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea (sometimes bloody). Onset typically 30 minutes to 6 hours after ingestion.

Caused by: Pokeweed berries, holly berries, daffodil bulbs, horse chestnut, many unidentified mushrooms.

Neurological Toxicity

Toxins affect the central or peripheral nervous system.

Symptoms: Blurred vision, dilated or constricted pupils, dizziness, tremors, seizures, hallucinations, numbness/tingling, paralysis. Onset ranges from 15 minutes to several hours.

Caused by: Water hemlock, poison hemlock, jimsonweed (Datura), nightshade (Atropa belladonna), yew (Taxus).

WARNING Water hemlock (*Cicuta*) is the most violently toxic plant in North America. Seizures begin within 15-60 minutes of ingestion and can be fatal. Evacuate immediately.

Cardiac Toxicity

Toxins interfere with heart rhythm. These are the most immediately life-threatening.

Symptoms: Slow or irregular heartbeat, palpitations, low blood pressure, dizziness, chest pain, cardiac arrest. Onset varies: 30 minutes to several hours.

Caused by: Foxglove (Digitalis), oleander, lily of the valley, rhododendron/azalea, yew berries and foliage, monkshood (Aconitum).

WARNING Cardiac toxins have no field antidote. If any plant ingestion is followed by abnormal pulse or chest symptoms, evacuate immediately.

Dermatological Toxicity (Contact)

Toxins cause skin inflammation on contact, without ingestion.

Symptoms: Itching, redness, blistering (urushiol reactions), burns (sap reactions), photosensitive rash. Onset: minutes to 72 hours.

Caused by: Poison ivy/oak/sumac (urushiol), giant hogweed (phototoxic sap), stinging nettle, wild parsnip.

First Aid for Plant Ingestion

Immediate Actions

  1. Stop eating the plant. Remove any remaining plant material from the mouth.
  2. Save a sample of the plant — leaves, berries, roots, flowers. Wrap in a cloth or bag for identification.
  3. Note the time of ingestion and the amount consumed (even a rough estimate).
  4. Rinse the mouth thoroughly with water. Spit it out — do not swallow.

Activated Charcoal

Activated charcoal binds many plant toxins in the GI tract and prevents absorption. It is most effective within 1 hour of ingestion but may help up to 4 hours.

CAUTION Do NOT give activated charcoal to an unconscious or seizing patient — aspiration risk is lethal. Do NOT give if the patient has ingested a corrosive substance (burning/blistering of the mouth).
  1. Mix 50 g of activated charcoal powder (roughly 1 g per kg body weight for adults) in 8 oz (250 mL) of water.
  2. Stir into a slurry. It tastes gritty and unpleasant.
  3. Have the patient drink it all. If the patient vomits, wait 10 minutes and re-dose.
  4. Children: 1 g per kg body weight, or 25 g for small children.

Vomiting

WARNING Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by poison control or a physician. Most plant toxins cause additional damage to the esophagus on the way back up. Seizure-causing plants (water hemlock, poison hemlock) create aspiration risk if the patient vomits and then seizes.

If vomiting occurs spontaneously:

  1. Position the patient on their side (recovery position) to protect the airway.
  2. Do not suppress spontaneous vomiting unless the patient is at risk of aspiration.
  3. Save vomit for identification if possible.

Monitoring

After any plant ingestion:

  • Check pulse every 15 minutes for irregularities.
  • Monitor breathing rate and mental status.
  • Watch for progressive symptoms (escalation from GI to neuro or cardiac).
  • Keep the patient hydrated with small sips of water.

Evacuation Criteria

Evacuate immediately if any of the following develop:

  • Seizures or tremors.
  • Irregular, slow, or rapid heartbeat.
  • Difficulty breathing.
  • Confusion or altered mental status.
  • Loss of consciousness.
  • Severe or persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake.
  • Known ingestion of water hemlock, oleander, foxglove, yew, or monkshood.

Contact Dermatitis

Poison Ivy, Poison Oak, and Poison Sumac

All three plants produce urushiol, an oily resin that causes allergic contact dermatitis in approximately 85% of people. The rash is not contagious and does not spread from blister fluid.

Identification:

  • Poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans): "Leaves of three, let it be." Grows as a vine or shrub. Eastern and central North America.
  • Poison oak (Toxicodendron diversilobum): Similar leaf-of-three pattern, oak-shaped leaves. Western North America.
  • Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix): 7-13 leaflets per stem, smooth-edged. Swamps and wetlands of eastern North America.
NOTE Urushiol remains active on clothing, tools, pet fur, and dead plants for months to years. Wash all contaminated items.

Prevention:

  • Learn to identify all three plants in all seasons (they look different in spring, summer, and fall).
  • Wear long sleeves and pants in areas where these plants grow.
  • Apply barrier creams (bentoquatam/IvyBlock) before exposure if available.

Treatment:

  1. Wash the exposed skin with soap and cold water (or rubbing alcohol if available) within 10 minutes of contact. Cold water closes pores and prevents deeper urushiol penetration.
  2. Remove and bag contaminated clothing.
  3. Do NOT use hot water — it opens pores and drives urushiol deeper.
  4. If a rash develops (typically 12-72 hours after exposure): apply calamine lotion or hydrocortisone cream.
  5. Take oral antihistamines (diphenhydramine 25-50 mg every 6 hours) for itching.
  6. Cool compresses relieve itch and inflammation.
  7. Do not break blisters — intact blisters protect against infection.
  8. Rash resolves in 1-3 weeks without treatment.
CAUTION Burning poison ivy, oak, or sumac releases urushiol in smoke. Inhaling the smoke causes severe lung inflammation and is a medical emergency. Never burn brush that may contain these plants.

Giant Hogweed and Wild Parsnip

These plants cause phytophotodermatitis — sap on skin combined with sunlight produces severe chemical burns and blistering.

Treatment:

  1. Wash sap off skin immediately with soap and water.
  2. Cover the affected area to block sunlight for 48 hours.
  3. If burns develop, treat as second-degree burns: cool water, clean dressing, pain management.
  4. Blistering and hyperpigmentation can last months.

Universal Edibility Test

Use this test only as a last resort when starvation is a genuine threat. The test takes approximately 24 hours per plant part and is not foolproof.

WARNING The universal edibility test does NOT detect all toxins. Some lethal toxins (amatoxin in death cap mushrooms, cardiac glycosides in oleander) produce no immediate reaction during the test but kill days later. Never use this test on mushrooms.
  1. Separate the plant into parts: leaves, stems, roots, flowers, seeds. Test each part individually.
  2. Skin contact test: Rub the plant part on the inside of your wrist. Wait 15 minutes. If no redness, itching, or burning, continue.
  3. Lip test: Touch the plant part to your outer lip. Wait 15 minutes. If no reaction, continue.
  4. Tongue test: Place the plant part on your tongue. Do not chew. Wait 15 minutes. If no numbness, burning, or bitter taste, continue.
  5. Chew test: Chew a small amount and hold it in your mouth for 15 minutes. Do not swallow. Spit it out. If no reaction, continue.
  6. Swallow test: Eat a small amount (roughly 1 tablespoon). Wait 8 hours. Eat nothing else during this time. If no GI symptoms develop, continue.
  7. Larger portion: Eat 1/4 cup (60 mL) of the plant part. Wait another 8 hours. If no symptoms, the plant part is likely safe in moderate amounts.
NOTE Cooking can neutralize some toxins but concentrate others. If you plan to eat the plant cooked, perform the test with the cooked version.

Commonly Confused Edible and Toxic Species

North America

Edible Toxic Look-Alike Key Difference
Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) Hemlock has smooth purple-blotched stems; wild carrot has hairy green stems
Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) Water hemlock (Cicuta) Water hemlock grows in wet areas, has chambered root with yellow resin
Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) Water hemlock (Cicuta) Elderberry has opposite compound leaves and flat-topped flower clusters
Wild garlic/onion Death camas (Zigadenus) Wild onion always smells like onion; death camas has no onion odor
Blueberries Nightshade berries Blueberries have a crown (calyx) on the end; nightshade berries are smooth
Morel mushrooms False morel (Gyromitra) True morels are hollow inside when sliced lengthwise; false morels have chambered, cotton-like interior

Europe

Edible Toxic Look-Alike Key Difference
Wild garlic (ramsons) Lily of the valley Ramsons smell strongly of garlic when crushed; lily of the valley does not
Wild garlic (ramsons) Autumn crocus (Colchicum) Ramsons appear in spring; autumn crocus leaves appear in spring but lack garlic odor
Chanterelle mushrooms Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) Chanterelles have false gills (blunt ridges); jack-o'-lanterns have true blade-like gills
WARNING If you cannot distinguish the edible species from its toxic look-alike with 100% certainty, do not eat it. A single misidentified plant can be fatal.

Common Mistakes

  • Inducing vomiting after plant ingestion. Most plant toxins cause additional esophageal and airway damage when vomited. Use activated charcoal instead.
  • Assuming a plant is safe because animals eat it. Many animals tolerate toxins that are lethal to humans. Deer eat yew and poison ivy without harm.
  • Relying on taste as a safety indicator. Many lethal plants (death camas, water hemlock root) taste mild or even pleasant.
  • Applying the universal edibility test to mushrooms. Amatoxin (death cap, destroying angel) causes no symptoms for 6-24 hours, then destroys the liver. The edibility test cannot detect it in time.
  • Using hot water on poison ivy exposure. Hot water opens pores and drives urushiol deeper into the skin. Use cold water.
  • Assuming all parts of a "safe" plant are edible. Rhubarb stalks are edible; rhubarb leaves contain lethal levels of oxalic acid. Elderberries are edible when cooked; raw berries, leaves, and stems are toxic.
  • Burning brush containing poison ivy/oak. Urushiol in smoke causes severe respiratory inflammation. Clear these plants by pulling (with gloves) or herbicide — never fire.

Quick Reference

Plant Ingestion Protocol:

  1. Remove plant from mouth. Save a sample.
  2. Rinse mouth with water.
  3. Give activated charcoal (50 g in water) within 1 hour if conscious.
  4. Do NOT induce vomiting.
  5. Monitor pulse, breathing, mental status every 15 minutes.
  6. Evacuate if: seizures, irregular heartbeat, breathing difficulty, confusion.

Contact Dermatitis Protocol (Poison Ivy/Oak/Sumac):

  1. Wash with soap and cold water within 10 minutes.
  2. Remove contaminated clothing.
  3. Apply calamine or hydrocortisone for rash.
  4. Antihistamines for itching.
  5. Do not break blisters.

Universal Edibility Test Timing:

Step Wait Time
Skin contact (wrist) 15 min
Lip test 15 min
Tongue test 15 min
Chew test (spit out) 15 min
Swallow small amount 8 hours
Eat larger portion 8 hours
Total minimum ~17 hours
