  • Olsen, Larry Dean. Outdoor Survival Skills. Chicago Review Press, 1997.
  • National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS). NOLS Wilderness Medicine. Stackpole Books, 2017.
Shelter

Debris Hut Construction

Build a warm, weatherproof A-frame debris hut using only natural materials and no tools.

At a Glance

  • A debris hut traps body heat like a sleeping bag made of forest litter — effective to below 0 F / -18 C with sufficient insulation.
  • Total build time: 3–6 hours for a one-person hut with adequate materials nearby.
  • Minimum debris depth on the roof: 3 feet (1 meter) of loose material, measured from the ribbing outward.
  • Ground insulation is the single most important layer — build it thick.
  • The shelter must be small — barely larger than your body — to retain warmth effectively.

Tools and Materials Needed

No tools are required. Everything is sourced from the forest floor. Having a knife or saw speeds the process but is not essential.

Materials List (One-Person Hut)

Material Quantity Purpose
Ridgepole 1 (9–12 ft / 2.7–3.6 m long) Central spine of the shelter
Ribbing sticks 20–30 (4–6 ft / 1.2–1.8 m long) Framework leaned against ridgepole
Small sticks and brush Several armloads Lattice layer over ribbing
Dead leaves, grass, pine needles, or forest litter A pile the size of a small car Insulation — the bulk of the shelter
Leafy branches or bark slabs Optional Outer weatherproofing layer
Ground insulation material Enough to fill the interior 6–8 in / 15–20 cm deep Sleeping pad replacement

Material Estimation Rule

Stand at your chosen site. If you cannot see enough dead leaves and debris within 50 feet (15 m) to fill a pickup truck bed, the site lacks sufficient material. Move to a better location.

Step 1: Select the Site

Apply all criteria from Shelter Principles:

  1. Check overhead for widow makers and dead branches.
  2. Confirm drainage — the site should be on a slight rise, never in a depression.
  3. Verify wind direction — orient the entrance away from prevailing wind.
  4. Ensure abundant debris within easy carrying distance.
  5. Check for ant mounds, wasp nests, and animal sign at the exact build location.

Step 2: Choose and Place the Ridgepole

The ridgepole is the backbone of the entire structure. Get this right.

Ridgepole Selection

  • Length: 9–12 feet (2.7–3.6 m) for a one-person hut. Measure against your body: lie down and add 2–3 feet (0.6–1 m) beyond your head.
  • Diameter: 3–5 inches (8–13 cm) at the thick end. It must support the weight of hundreds of pounds of debris.
  • Straightness: reasonably straight — slight bends are acceptable; sharp kinks are not.
  • Strength: grab one end and bounce the pole. If it flexes excessively or feels punky/rotten, discard it. Deadwood from hardwoods (oak, maple, hickory) is ideal.
WARNING Test the ridgepole before building on it. A ridgepole that breaks under load collapses the entire shelter while you are inside. Reject any pole that feels weak, heavily rotted, or brittle.

Ridgepole Placement

  1. Find a support point for the elevated end: a sturdy tree crotch, a forked stump, a boulder, or a tripod made from three lashed poles.
  2. Prop the thick end of the ridgepole in the support at chest height when kneeling — approximately 3–3.5 feet (0.9–1.1 m) above the ground. This is the entrance end.
  3. Let the thin end rest on the ground at the far end. The ridgepole tapers downward from entrance to foot end.
  4. The angle from ground to support should be approximately 30–40 degrees.
  5. Lie underneath the ridgepole to verify fit:
  6. Your body fits beneath it with 6–8 inches (15–20 cm) clearance at the chest.
  7. Your shoulders do not touch the eventual ribbing on either side.
  8. The foot end is low — nearly touching the ground.

If the pole is too high, you waste insulation filling the extra volume. If too low, you cannot fit inside. Adjust until it is just right.

Step 3: Install the Ribbing

Ribbing sticks form the sloped walls of the A-frame.

Technique

  1. Gather 20–30 sticks, each 4–6 feet (1.2–1.8 m) long and 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) in diameter.
  2. Lean the sticks against the ridgepole at a 45–60 degree angle, alternating sides.
  3. Space the ribs 4–8 inches (10–20 cm) apart along the length of the ridgepole.
  4. Leave the entrance end (the high end) open — this is your doorway.
  5. At the foot end, pack ribs closely together or block with a solid branch — no large gaps.
  6. The ribs should not extend more than 12–18 inches (30–45 cm) beyond the ridgepole on either side. The goal is a narrow A-frame — just wide enough for your body plus 6 inches (15 cm) of clearance per side.

Width Check

Lie inside the ribbed frame. Your elbows at your sides should not touch the ribs. If the frame is wider than that, the ribs are too long — use shorter ones or push them further up the ridgepole so less extends beyond it.

Step 4: Add the Lattice Layer

Small sticks and brush laid horizontally across the ribs create a lattice that prevents loose debris from falling through.

  1. Gather small sticks (pencil-thickness to finger-thickness), twiggy brush, and evergreen boughs.
  2. Lay them perpendicular to the ribs, across the outside of the frame.
  3. Cover the entire surface — no gaps larger than a fist.
  4. This lattice does not need to be structural — it just holds debris in place.
  5. Work from the foot end toward the entrance.

The shelter now looks like a skeletal tent covered in a mesh of sticks.

Step 5: Layer the Debris

This is the insulation step — the most labor-intensive and the most critical. The debris layer IS the shelter. Everything before this was just scaffolding.

Collecting Debris

  • Ideal materials: dry dead leaves, pine needles, dried grass, bracken fern fronds, forest duff.
  • Acceptable materials: moss, bark strips, cattail fluff, dried seaweed (coastal areas).
  • Avoid: green leaves (compress and rot), wet material (conducts heat), soil/dirt (heavy, poor insulator).
  • Carry debris in armloads. Use a shirt, tarp, or improvised sack to carry more per trip.

Application Technique

  1. Start at the foot end and work toward the entrance.
  2. Pile debris onto the lattice. Push it against the frame — do not stuff it between ribs.
  3. Build the layer to a minimum depth of 3 feet (1 meter) measured from the lattice outward.
  4. The debris should be loose and fluffy — do not compact it. Fluffy debris traps more dead air space.
  5. Continue until the entire shelter (except the entrance) is buried under a mound of debris.

The Arm Test

Push your arm from the outside through the debris layer. If you can see daylight through the inside of the shelter, the layer is too thin at that spot. Add more material until no light penetrates.

Quantity Reference

A properly insulated one-person debris hut requires roughly:

  • 30–40 large armloads of dry leaves, or
  • 60–80 large trash bags worth of debris (if you had bags), or
  • A pile approximately 6 feet wide x 10 feet long x 4 feet tall (1.8 x 3 x 1.2 m) before it compresses onto the frame.

This is far more material than most people initially estimate. When you think you have enough, add the same amount again.

Step 6: Build the Ground Insulation Layer

WARNING Skipping ground insulation negates the entire purpose of the shelter. The ground steals heat 50 times faster than still air. This layer is not optional.
  1. Before climbing in the first time, fill the entire interior floor with insulating material.
  2. Use dry leaves, pine needles, dried grass, or evergreen boughs.
  3. Build the layer 6–8 inches (15–20 cm) deep minimum. It compresses under body weight to 3–4 inches (8–10 cm).
  4. Extend the material from the entrance to the foot end, wall to wall.
  5. If you have a survival blanket (mylar), lay it on top of the ground insulation to reflect body heat.

Testing

Lie on the ground insulation layer for 5 minutes. If you feel cold from below, add more material. You must feel separated from the earth.

Step 7: Construct the Door Plug

An open entrance hemorrhages heat. Seal it.

Construction

  1. Gather a large bundle of debris — leaves, grass, or pine boughs — and stuff it into a bag, shirt, or just compress it into a dense wad.
  2. The plug should fill the entrance opening completely when pushed into place.
  3. Make it slightly oversized so it wedges firmly.
  4. From inside, pull the door plug in behind you after entering.

Alternative Door Methods

  • Backpack — if available, stuff it with leaves and use it as a door plug.
  • Cross-sticks with debris — weave a small lattice panel, pile debris on it, and lean it over the entrance.
  • Poncho or tarp — drape over the opening and weigh down the edges.

Step 8: Add an Outer Weatherproofing Layer (Optional)

In dry conditions, the deep debris layer sheds light rain on its own. In heavy rain or wet climates, add a shingle layer.

Method

  1. Collect broad bark slabs, large leaves (if available), or evergreen boughs.
  2. Layer them on top of the debris like shingles — start at the bottom and overlap each successive layer over the previous one as you work upward.
  3. The goal is to create a water-shedding surface that keeps the underlying insulation dry.
  4. Alternatively, pile an additional 6–12 inches (15–30 cm) of fine, tightly packed debris on the outside. Dense outer material sheds water better than loose, fluffy material.

Time and Effort Estimates

Task Time (Approximate) Notes
Site selection 15–30 minutes Do not rush this step
Ridgepole selection and placement 15–30 minutes Includes testing
Ribbing installation 30–45 minutes 20–30 sticks
Lattice layer 20–30 minutes Small sticks and brush
Debris collection and layering 1.5–3 hours The longest step by far
Ground insulation 20–30 minutes Interior bedding
Door plug 10–15 minutes Simple but critical
Total 3–6 hours Faster with experience, tools, or help

Start building no later than 4 hours before dark. Building in darkness is extremely difficult and the results are poor.

One-Person vs Two-Person Sizing

One-Person Hut

  • Ridgepole: 9–12 ft / 2.7–3.6 m.
  • Interior width at shoulders: 24–30 inches / 60–75 cm.
  • Height at entrance: 3–3.5 ft / 0.9–1.1 m.
  • Total debris needed: 30–40 armloads.
  • Build time: 3–5 hours.

Two-Person Hut

  • Ridgepole: 12–15 ft / 3.6–4.6 m. Must be significantly stronger (4–6 inches / 10–15 cm diameter hardwood).
  • Interior width at shoulders: 40–48 inches / 100–120 cm.
  • Height at entrance: 3.5–4 ft / 1.1–1.2 m.
  • Ribs must be longer and more numerous: 30–40 ribs.
  • Total debris needed: 50–70 armloads. Nearly double the one-person hut.
  • Build time: 5–8 hours.
WARNING A two-person hut requires dramatically more material and time. The larger interior volume is harder to heat with body warmth alone. Two smaller one-person huts may be more thermally efficient if time and materials allow.

Trade-Off

Two bodies generate more heat than one. A two-person hut benefits from shared body warmth, partially offsetting the larger volume. But the structure must be proportionally stronger and better insulated. Evaluate based on available materials, time, and conditions.

Modifications by Environment

Heavy Rain Adaptation

  • Increase the outer debris layer to 4+ feet (1.2+ m) depth.
  • Add a shingle layer of bark, broad leaves, or tightly overlapped evergreen boughs.
  • Dig a drainage channel around the uphill side of the hut — a 4-inch-deep (10 cm) trench diverts runoff around the shelter.
  • Raise the ground insulation with a bed of sticks beneath the leaf layer to create an air gap above puddled water.
  • Angle the ridgepole steeper (40–45 degrees) to improve water runoff from the entrance end.

Snow Conditions

  • Pack snow on top of the completed debris hut. Snow is an excellent insulator — 6–12 inches (15–30 cm) adds significant warmth.
  • Use evergreen boughs instead of deciduous leaves for debris — they resist matting when wet and provide better structure under snow load.
  • Strengthen the ridgepole and ribbing — wet snow is heavy (20 lbs / 9 kg per cubic foot). Use a thicker ridgepole (5–6 inches / 13–15 cm diameter) and heavier ribs.
  • Clear snow from the entrance area to prevent burial.
  • Inside, use a thick layer of evergreen boughs for ground insulation — 8–10 inches (20–25 cm) minimum.
WARNING Snow load can collapse a weakly built debris hut. In snowy conditions, reinforce the ridgepole with a support fork at the midpoint or use a naturally stronger pole.

Coniferous Forest (Pine, Spruce, Fir)

  • Abundant evergreen boughs replace deciduous leaves for insulation and lattice.
  • Pine needles work as debris but compress more than broadleaf litter — add extra depth (4+ feet / 1.2+ m).
  • Bark slabs from dead conifers serve as weatherproofing shingles.
  • Spruce boughs are the best ground insulation material in coniferous forests — aromatic, springy, and rot-resistant.

Deciduous Forest (Oak, Maple, Beech)

  • Ideal environment for debris hut construction — broadleaf litter is the perfect insulation material.
  • Autumn provides the most abundant material. In spring and summer, use dried leaves from previous years or gather green leaves as a last resort (they provide structure but less insulation).
  • Hardwood ridgepoles and ribs are stronger and more durable than softwood equivalents.

Tropical Forest

  • Moisture is the primary enemy. Everything is wet.
  • Elevate the shelter on a platform if possible — even raising it 6 inches (15 cm) on a log framework helps.
  • Use palm fronds for roofing — overlap them thickly for waterproofing.
  • A lean-to design may be more practical than a full debris hut in tropical environments, as enclosed shelters trap humidity and become uncomfortably hot.
  • Prioritize ventilation and rain protection over insulation.

Grassland / Prairie

  • No trees means no ridgepole support and no leaf litter.
  • Improvise: use a depression in the ground covered with bundled grass and a framework of sticks gathered from any available shrubs.
  • Pile grass 4+ feet (1.2+ m) deep. Dry prairie grass is an excellent insulator.
  • Weigh down grass piles with rocks, soil, or green turf to prevent wind from stripping the insulation.
  • Consider a partially buried shelter — dig a body-length trench 18 inches (45 cm) deep and cover it with a grass-and-stick roof.

Entering and Using the Shelter

  1. Crawl in feet-first. This keeps your head near the entrance for fresh air and easy exit.
  2. Pull the door plug in behind you.
  3. Fluff the ground insulation before lying down — it compresses between uses.
  4. If cold during the night, reach outside the entrance and pull additional debris inside to pile on top of your body.
  5. To exit, push the door plug out, crawl out head-first, and replace the plug if you intend to reuse the shelter.

Moisture Management

  • Your body produces moisture throughout the night through respiration and perspiration.
  • In a well-sealed shelter, this moisture condenses on the inner debris layer.
  • Over multiple nights, the inner layer becomes damp. Replace it every 2–3 days with fresh, dry material.
  • If the shelter feels clammy, open the entrance briefly to ventilate.

Maintenance for Multi-Day Use

If staying more than one night:

  1. Refresh ground insulation daily — add new dry material on top of the compressed layer each evening.
  2. Check for settling — debris compacts over time. Add material to any thin spots (use the arm test).
  3. Inspect the ridgepole — weight and moisture stress the pole. Look for bowing or cracking.
  4. Clear drainage — keep any trenches around the shelter open after rain.
  5. Manage the door plug — replace if it becomes wet or compressed.
  6. Add debris after rain — wet outer layers compress and lose insulating value. Pile fresh dry material on top.

Common Mistakes

  • Not enough debris — the most universal error. When you think you have enough, double it.
  • Shelter too large — build it coffin-sized. Extra space is extra air to heat.
  • Skipping ground insulation — the ground is the biggest heat thief. See Shelter Principles: Insulation.
  • Weak ridgepole — a collapsed shelter at 2 AM is a survival emergency inside a survival emergency. Test the pole.
  • No door plug — an open entrance turns the hut into a wind tunnel. Always seal it.
  • Using wet debris — wet insulation conducts heat instead of retaining it. Use dry material or let wet material dry in the sun first.
  • Building too late in the day — start by early afternoon at the latest. A half-finished hut at nightfall provides half the protection.
  • Packing debris too tightly — loose, fluffy material insulates. Compressed material does not. Pile it on loosely.
  • Ignoring overhead hazards — checking for widow makers takes 30 seconds and may save your life.
  • Entering head-first — enter feet-first so your head stays near the entrance for air and quick exit.
  • Forgetting to test — lie inside the frame before adding debris to verify fit. Lie on the ground insulation before sleeping to verify warmth. Use the arm test to verify debris depth.

Quick Reference

Specification One-Person Two-Person
Ridgepole length 9–12 ft / 2.7–3.6 m 12–15 ft / 3.6–4.6 m
Ridgepole diameter 3–5 in / 8–13 cm 4–6 in / 10–15 cm
Entrance height 3–3.5 ft / 0.9–1.1 m 3.5–4 ft / 1.1–1.2 m
Interior width 24–30 in / 60–75 cm 40–48 in / 100–120 cm
Debris depth (roof) 3 ft / 1 m minimum 3 ft / 1 m minimum
Ground insulation depth 6–8 in / 15–20 cm 6–8 in / 15–20 cm
Number of ribs 20–30 30–40
Debris armloads 30–40 50–70
Build time 3–5 hours 5–8 hours

See Also

  • Shelter Principles — site selection, insulation theory, and when not to build.
  • Finding Water in the Wild — locate water near your shelter site.
  • Water Purification — treat water at your shelter camp.

Sources

  • Kochanski, Mors. Bushcraft: Outdoor Skills and Wilderness Survival. Lone Pine Publishing, 1987.
  • Brown, Tom Jr. Tom Brown's Field Guide to Wilderness Survival. Berkley Books, 1983.
  • Canterbury, Dave. Bushcraft 101. Adams Media, 2014.
  • Wiseman, John "Lofty." SAS Survival Handbook. William Collins, 2014.
  • Lundin, Cody. 98.6 Degrees: The Art of Keeping Your Ass Alive. Gibbs Smith, 2003.
  • Mears, Raymond. Essential Bushcraft. Hodder & Stoughton, 2002.
Shelter

Snow Shelters

How to build emergency and semi-permanent shelters from snow in winter and alpine environments.

At a Glance

  • Snow is an excellent insulator — interior temperatures hold near 32°F (0°C) even when outside air drops to -40°F (-40°C).
  • Ventilation holes prevent carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide buildup, which kills silently.
  • Insulate the floor with boughs, a foam pad, or a pack — never sleep directly on snow.
  • The entrance must sit below the sleeping platform so cold air sinks away from you.
  • Choose your shelter type based on snow conditions, available time, and group size.

When to Choose Which Type

Shelter Snow Needed Build Time Best For
Snow trench Any packable snow, 3 ft (1 m) deep 30-60 min Solo, fastest emergency option
Quinzhee Any snow, even powder 3-5 hours (includes settling) 1-3 people, most snow types
Snow cave Deep consolidated snowbank or drift, 8+ ft (2.5+ m) 2-4 hours 1-4 people, existing drifts
Igloo Wind-packed slab snow (sintered) 2-4 hours (experienced builder) Groups, long-term camps

Assessing Snow Conditions

Before choosing a shelter type, evaluate the snow:

  • Grab test: Squeeze a handful. If it holds shape, it is packable and suitable for a quinzhee or trench. If it crumbles to powder, pile and wait longer for sintering.
  • Step test: Step firmly onto the snow surface. If your boot sinks less than 1 inch (2.5 cm), the snow is wind-packed slab — suitable for igloo blocks. If you sink to mid-shin or deeper, the snow is unconsolidated.
  • Probe test: Push a ski pole or long stick straight down. Measure total depth. You need at least 8 ft (2.5 m) of consolidated snow for a snow cave.
  • Temperature check: Snow shelters work best below 25°F (-4°C). Near or above freezing, melt-refreeze cycles weaken walls and cause dripping.

Snow Trench

The fastest emergency snow shelter. Build this when time is critical and hypothermia is approaching.

Construction

  1. Stomp out a trench 3 ft (1 m) wide, 8 ft (2.5 m) long, and 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) deep.
  2. Cut snow blocks from the trench floor or nearby snowpack. Each block should be roughly 18 x 12 x 6 inches (45 x 30 x 15 cm).
  3. Lean blocks against each other across the top of the trench in an A-frame pattern. Alternatively, lay branches, a tarp, or a poncho across the top and pile snow over it.
  4. Leave a gap at one end for entry. Plug it with a pack or snow block after entering.
  5. Poke a ventilation hole through the roof with a ski pole, stick, or fist. Diameter: 2 inches (5 cm) minimum.
  6. Line the floor with boughs, a sleeping pad, or extra clothing.
TIP A snow trench takes 30-60 minutes to build. Prioritize this shelter when you have less than two hours of daylight remaining.

Quinzhee

A pile-and-hollow shelter that works with any type of snow, including powder. This is the most versatile snow shelter.

Construction

  1. Pile snow into a mound 7-8 ft (2-2.5 m) high and 10-12 ft (3-3.5 m) in diameter at the base. Use a shovel, snowshoes, a pot, or your hands.
  2. Pack the outside surface lightly by patting with the flat of a shovel or gloved hands.
  3. Insert 15-20 sticks or poles into the mound, each 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) long. Push them perpendicular to the surface at even spacing. These are thickness gauges.
  4. Wait 1.5-2 hours for the snow to sinter (recrystallize and bond). This step is not optional — skip it and the roof collapses.
  5. Dig an entrance tunnel low on the downwind side. Angle it downward, then up into the mound. The tunnel floor must sit below the interior sleeping platform.
  6. Hollow out the interior. When you hit the inner end of a guide stick, stop digging in that direction. Maintain 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) of wall thickness everywhere.
  7. Carve a flat sleeping platform at least 12 inches (30 cm) above the entrance tunnel floor.
  8. Smooth the interior ceiling into a dome shape. Eliminate flat spots and protrusions — these create drip points.
  9. Poke two ventilation holes through the upper walls at 45-degree angles. Diameter: 2 inches (5 cm) each. Place one on each side.
  10. Glaze the interior walls by lighting a candle or small fire briefly. The slight melt refreezes into an ice layer that strengthens the structure and reduces dripping.
WARNING Never seal the entrance completely. Carbon dioxide accumulates fast in an enclosed snow shelter. Maintain ventilation holes and a partially open entrance at all times.
CAUTION If you skip the 1.5-2 hour settling time, the mound will not bond internally. The roof will collapse during hollowing or while you sleep.

Interior Dimensions

  • Ceiling height at center: 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) sitting height
  • Floor area for two people: roughly 6 x 7 ft (1.8 x 2.1 m)
  • Wall thickness: 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) minimum everywhere

Snow Cave

Requires an existing deep snowbank or wind-deposited drift at least 8 ft (2.5 m) deep. Commonly found on leeward slopes, road cuts, and below ridgelines.

Site Selection

WARNING Evaluate avalanche risk before digging into any slope. Avoid slopes between 25-45 degrees with recent snow loading. If the slope has avalanche debris at the base, do not dig there.

Choose a snowbank on a slope of less than 25 degrees or a flat drift. Probe with a pole or ski to confirm depth of at least 8 ft (2.5 m).

Construction

  1. Dig a horizontal entrance tunnel into the snowbank at the lowest practical point. Make the tunnel 3 ft (1 m) wide and 3 ft (1 m) tall — just large enough to crawl through.
  2. Angle the tunnel slightly upward after the first 3 ft (1 m).
  3. Excavate the main chamber above and behind the tunnel entrance. Carve upward so the sleeping platform sits 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) above the top of the tunnel opening.
  4. Shape the ceiling into a smooth dome. Remove any flat spots or lumps that cause drip points.
  5. Maintain wall and ceiling thickness of at least 12 inches (30 cm). Push a pole through from outside to check.
  6. Carve a shelf for a candle at head height. A single candle raises interior temperature by 2-4°F (1-2°C).
  7. Poke two ventilation holes at 45-degree angles through the roof using a ski pole or long stick.
  8. Smooth and glaze the interior ceiling to prevent dripping.
  9. Place a pack or snow block at the entrance as a partial windbreak. Do not seal it completely.

Cold Sink Design

The entrance tunnel and sleeping platform create a cold sink. Cold air is denser and pools at the lowest point. Position the sleeping platform above the tunnel so warm air from body heat stays at your level and cold air drains downward into the tunnel.

A well-built snow cave with one or two occupants holds 28-32°F (-2 to 0°C) inside regardless of outside temperature.

Igloo

Requires wind-packed slab snow (sintered snow that holds its shape when cut). Test by stepping on the snow surface — your boot should leave a print less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep.

NOTE Igloo construction requires practice. Build at least two practice igloos in non-emergency conditions before relying on this technique in a survival situation.

Block Cutting

  1. Identify a slab snow area. Probe to confirm depth of at least 18 inches (45 cm).
  2. Cut blocks using a snow saw, machete, or long-bladed knife. Standard block size: 24 x 16 x 8 inches (60 x 40 x 20 cm).
  3. Cut blocks from within the planned floor area — this simultaneously creates the sunken interior.
  4. Handle blocks by supporting the bottom. Lift from underneath, not by gripping the sides.

Spiral Construction

  1. Mark a circle on the snow surface: 9 ft (2.7 m) diameter for two people, 12 ft (3.6 m) for four.
  2. Place the first row of blocks around the circle perimeter, angling each block inward 10-15 degrees.
  3. Cut a spiral ramp into the top of the first row. Start at one block and cut diagonally upward across three to four blocks. This ramp allows continuous spiral placement.
  4. Place subsequent blocks along the spiral, increasing the inward lean with each row. Each block leans on the one below it and the one beside it.
  5. Trim the inner face of each block to maintain the dome curve. The angle increases as you build higher.
  6. Place the capstone (keystone block) at the top. Cut it slightly larger than the opening and lower it in from outside, then trim to fit.
  7. Fill all gaps between blocks with loose snow packed firmly.
  8. Cut a low entrance below floor level. Dig a short tunnel or simply cut an arched opening.
  9. Poke two ventilation holes near the top.

Build Time

An experienced two-person team completes an igloo in 1.5-2 hours. A first-time builder should expect 3-5 hours. Practice is essential.

Critical Details for All Snow Shelters

Ventilation

WARNING Carbon monoxide from stoves, candles, or body metabolism accumulates in sealed snow shelters. Maintain at least two ventilation holes at all times. If you feel drowsy, headachy, or nauseous, open the entrance immediately and get fresh air.

Poke ventilation holes at a 45-degree upward angle to prevent rain or meltwater from dripping in. Check holes every few hours — snowfall and frost can seal them. Keep a stick inside the shelter to re-open blocked holes.

Floor Insulation

Never sleep directly on snow. Body heat melts the contact surface, soaking clothing and accelerating heat loss. Layer the floor in this order:

  1. Boughs (spruce, fir, pine) — 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) thick
  2. Sleeping pad or pack frame
  3. Sleeping bag or emergency blanket

Interior Temperature Management

  • A candle raises interior air temperature by 2-4°F (1-2°C).
  • Body heat from two people raises it by 10-15°F (5-8°C).
  • If the interior gets above 32°F (0°C), the ceiling begins to melt and drip. Open a ventilation hole wider or extinguish the candle.
  • Glaze the ceiling by briefly warming it with a candle after construction. The melted surface refreezes into a smooth ice layer that sheds water to the walls instead of dripping.

Entrance Design

  • Orient the entrance away from prevailing wind (downwind side).
  • The entrance floor must be lower than the sleeping platform by at least 12 inches (30 cm).
  • Use a pack, snow block, or jacket as a partial door. Never seal it fully.
  • A right-angle turn in the entrance tunnel blocks wind more effectively than a straight tunnel.

Marking Your Shelter

Mark the shelter exterior with a bright-colored item — a stuff sack, flagging tape, or ski pole. Snow shelters are invisible from a distance and easy to miss, including by search-and-rescue teams.

Wet Clothing Management

Remove wet outer layers before entering the shelter. Brush off all snow from clothing and boots at the entrance — snow tracked inside melts and soaks gear. Hang damp items from sticks pushed into the walls near the ceiling where warm air collects. Do not sleep in wet clothing; strip to dry base layers inside the sleeping bag and use body heat to dry damp socks and gloves overnight.

Common Mistakes

  • Skipping the settling time on a quinzhee. Unsettled snow collapses during hollowing or overnight. Wait the full 1.5-2 hours.
  • Sealing the entrance for warmth. Blocking airflow causes CO2 buildup. Leave ventilation open even if it feels cold.
  • Sleeping on bare snow. Direct contact with snow drains body heat faster than cold air. Always insulate the floor.
  • Making walls too thin. Walls under 12 inches (30 cm) collapse under their own weight or from external loading. Use guide sticks.
  • Building on an avalanche-prone slope. Check slope angle and recent snow conditions before digging into any hillside.
  • Flat ceiling surfaces. Flat spots collect meltwater and drip. Dome the ceiling so meltwater runs down the walls.
  • Entrance at the same level as the sleeping platform. Eliminates the cold sink effect. Dig the entrance lower.

Quick Reference

Detail Specification
Wall thickness (all types) 12-18 in (30-45 cm)
Ventilation holes 2 minimum, 2 in (5 cm) diameter, 45° angle
Sleeping platform 12+ in (30 cm) above entrance floor
Floor insulation 4-6 in (10-15 cm) boughs or pad
Interior target temp 28-32°F (-2 to 0°C)
Quinzhee settling time 1.5-2 hours
Snow trench build time 30-60 min
Quinzhee build time 3-5 hours
Snow cave build time 2-4 hours
Igloo build time 1.5-5 hours (skill dependent)
Igloo block size 24 x 16 x 8 in (60 x 40 x 20 cm)

  • Hypothermia and Heatstroke

Sources

  • Kochanski, Mors. Bushcraft: Outdoor Skills and Wilderness Survival. Lone Pine Publishing, 1987.
  • Wiseman, John "Lofty." SAS Survival Handbook. William Collins, 3rd ed., 2014.
  • U.S. Army. FM 21-76: Survival. Department of the Army, 1992.
  • Mears, Ray. Ray Mears' Outdoor Survival Handbook. Ebury Press, 2001.
  • Fredston, Jill and Fesler, Doug. Snow Sense: A Guide to Evaluating Snow Avalanche Hazard. Alaska Mountain Safety Center, 5th ed., 2011.
Shelter

Desert Shelter

How to build shelters in arid environments where shade, heat management, and water conservation are the primary survival concerns.

At a Glance

  • Shade is the single highest priority in desert shelter — direct sun exposure accelerates dehydration and heat illness.
  • Build or improve shelter during cool hours only (before 10 AM, after 4 PM). Resting in shade during peak heat conserves up to 1 quart (1 liter) of water per hour compared to working in direct sun.
  • Desert temperatures drop 40-60°F (22-33°C) at night. Plan for both extreme heat and near-freezing cold.
  • The double-roof principle (two layers with an air gap) reduces radiant heat transfer by up to 40%.
  • Dig below grade whenever possible — ground temperature 12 inches (30 cm) down is 20-30°F (11-17°C) cooler than the surface.

Shelter Priorities in Desert Environments

Rank shelter needs in this order:

  1. Shade — blocks direct solar radiation, the primary heat source
  2. Insulation from ground — sand and rock surfaces reach 150-170°F (65-77°C) at midday
  3. Wind protection — useful during sandstorms, counterproductive during calm heat (you want airflow)
  4. Rain protection — rare but flash floods occur; avoid washes and low ground
CAUTION Do not build in a dry wash (arroyo/wadi). Flash floods arrive with little warning from storms miles away. Build on elevated ground at least 3 ft (1 m) above the wash floor.

Timing

WARNING Physical labor in direct desert sun between 10 AM and 4 PM causes rapid fluid loss — 1-2 quarts (1-2 liters) per hour. Build shelter during cool hours or at night. If caught without shade at midday, sit on elevated insulation, cover exposed skin, and minimize movement until temperatures drop.

Work schedule:

  • Dawn to 10 AM: Primary construction window.
  • 10 AM to 4 PM: Rest in shade. Minimal activity.
  • 4 PM to dark: Secondary construction or improvement window.
  • Night: Travel, signal, or continue building if moonlight or headlamp allows.

Below-Grade Shelters

Digging below ground level exploits cooler subsurface temperatures. Ground temperature stabilizes approximately 20-30°F (11-17°C) below surface temperature at a depth of 12-18 inches (30-45 cm).

Desert Trench Shelter

  1. Select a site with compacted sand or soil (loose dune sand collapses). Avoid rocky ground that cannot be excavated.
  2. Dig a trench 3 ft (1 m) wide, 7-8 ft (2-2.5 m) long, and 18-24 inches (45-60 cm) deep.
  3. Pile excavated sand along the north side (Northern Hemisphere) to create additional shade during midday.
  4. Span the trench with a tarp, poncho, space blanket, or layered vegetation. Elevate the covering 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) above the trench floor.
  5. If a second layer of material is available, add it 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) above the first layer to create a double-roof air gap.
  6. Anchor the covering edges with sand, rocks, or buried stakes.
  7. Leave both narrow ends partially open for ventilation. Seal one end during sandstorms.

Pit Shelter

For longer stays, dig deeper.

  1. Excavate a pit 4 ft (1.2 m) deep, 4 ft (1.2 m) wide, and 7-8 ft (2-2.5 m) long.
  2. Shore the walls with rocks, branches, or packs if the soil is loose.
  3. Cover with a double-layer roof (see double-roof principle below).
  4. Cut a ramp or steps on one short end for entry.
  5. Line the floor with a ground cloth, vegetation, or clothing to insulate from ground contact.
TIP Combine a below-grade trench with a solar still. Dig the still pit adjacent to the trench and route the condensation collector into a container. See [Finding Water](#finding-water) for solar still construction.

Above-Grade Shade Structures

When digging is impractical (rocky terrain, tool shortage), build shade above ground.

Open Desert Shade

  1. Find or place two vertical supports 6-7 ft (1.8-2.1 m) apart. Use trekking poles, branches, vehicle parts, or rock stacks.
  2. Stretch a tarp, blanket, or space blanket between the supports at 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) height.
  3. Orient the long axis east-west so the shade covers the largest area during midday.
  4. Angle the covering to allow airflow underneath. Do not create an enclosed box — trapped air overheats.
  5. If material allows, add a second layer 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) above the first.

Rock Overhang Evaluation

Natural rock overhangs provide immediate shade. Evaluate before using:

  • Check for loose rock, cracks, or signs of recent rockfall. Do not shelter under unstable formations.
  • Confirm the overhang faces away from prevailing afternoon sun (north-facing in the Northern Hemisphere is ideal).
  • Check for animal sign — scorpions, snakes, and rodents shelter under overhangs. Clear the area before settling in.
  • Deepen the shade by hanging a tarp or space blanket from the overhang lip.
CAUTION Rock surfaces store heat and radiate it for hours after sunset. A south-facing rock wall at dusk can radiate 100-120°F (38-49°C). Position your sleeping area away from sun-heated rock faces.

The Double-Roof Principle

Two layers of material separated by an air gap of 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) reduce radiant heat transfer significantly. The outer layer absorbs solar radiation and heats up. The air gap acts as insulation, preventing that heat from conducting to the inner layer.

  • Outer layer: Any opaque material — tarp, poncho, space blanket (shiny side up), brush, sand-covered fabric.
  • Air gap: 4-6 inches (10-15 cm). Maintain with sticks, rocks, or tied separators.
  • Inner layer: Second tarp, blanket, or vegetation.

A double-roof shelter is 20-40°F (11-22°C) cooler underneath than a single-layer shelter.

TIP A space blanket with the reflective side facing up as the outer layer reflects up to 90% of radiant heat. Use a second tarp below it as the inner layer.

Sand Anchoring Techniques

Desert soil and sand do not hold conventional stakes. Use these methods:

  • Deadman anchor: Tie the guy line to the center of a stick, rock, or stuff sack filled with sand. Bury it 12 inches (30 cm) deep. Pack sand firmly on top.
  • Sand stakes: Fill stuff sacks, bags, or tied-off pant legs with sand. Bury them as anchors.
  • Rock piles: Stack rocks over the guy line or tarp edge. Use 15-20 lb (7-9 kg) minimum per anchor point.
  • Trench-and-bury: Dig a narrow trench, lay the tarp edge in it, and bury with 6 inches (15 cm) of packed sand.

Sandstorm Windbreak

During a sandstorm (haboob), shelter priorities shift to wind protection and breathing safety.

  1. Orient the shelter opening away from the wind direction (downwind).
  2. Seal the windward side completely with a tarp, vehicle panel, or banked sand.
  3. Leave the leeward side partially open to prevent the shelter from pressurizing and collapsing.
  4. Cover your nose and mouth with a damp cloth to filter sand particles.
  5. Protect eyes with goggles, sunglasses, or a wrapped cloth with a narrow slit.
  6. Seal gear in bags or bury under clothing — wind-driven sand penetrates zippers and pockets.

Night Cold Management

Desert air temperatures regularly drop to 35-50°F (2-10°C) at night, and below freezing at higher elevations. Sand and rock lose heat rapidly after sunset.

  • Close open sides of the shelter after sunset while maintaining ventilation.
  • Insulate the floor. Bare sand conducts heat away from the body. Use a pad, vegetation, spare clothing, or a layer of dry brush.
  • Heat rocks in a fire during evening hours. Wrap heated rocks in cloth and place them in the shelter as radiant warmers. Avoid rocks from riverbeds — trapped moisture can cause them to explode when heated.
  • Wear all available layers. Cover the head — 10% of heat loss occurs from an uncovered head.
  • If available, use a space blanket with the reflective side facing inward at night to retain body heat.
NOTE The same shelter that keeps you cool during the day must keep you warm at night. Plan for both extremes during construction.

Water Conservation and Shelter

Shelter choice directly affects water requirements.

Activity Water Loss
Resting in shade 0.5 qt/hr (0.5 L/hr)
Resting in sun 1 qt/hr (1 L/hr)
Working in sun 1-2 qt/hr (1-2 L/hr)
Working in shade 0.5-1 qt/hr (0.5-1 L/hr)

Good shelter reduces water needs by 50% or more. Every hour spent in direct sun instead of shade costs an additional 0.5-1 quart (0.5-1 liter) of sweat.

Solar Still Shelter Combination

A below-grade trench shelter and a solar still share the same construction principles. Build them adjacent to each other to minimize digging effort.

  1. Dig the shelter trench first (see Desert Trench Shelter above).
  2. Dig a second pit 3 ft (1 m) in diameter and 2 ft (60 cm) deep immediately adjacent to the shelter.
  3. Place a collection container at the center bottom of the still pit.
  4. Cover the still pit with clear plastic sheeting. Seal edges with sand.
  5. Place a small rock at the center of the plastic so it sags into a cone shape directly over the container.
  6. Condensation forms on the underside of the plastic and drips into the container. Yield: 0.5-1 quart (0.5-1 liter) per day depending on soil moisture and sun intensity.

Adding green vegetation or urine to the still pit increases moisture output. See Finding Water for full solar still instructions.

Site Selection Criteria

Evaluate potential shelter sites against these factors:

  • Elevation: Build at least 3 ft (1 m) above any wash or drainage. Higher ground catches more breeze.
  • Substrate: Compacted sand or hardpan digs easier than rocky ground. Loose dune sand collapses and requires shoring.
  • Existing shade: A rock overhang, vehicle, or large boulder reduces construction effort. Build adjacent to existing shade sources.
  • Wind exposure: Moderate breeze aids cooling during the day. Excessive wind (sandstorm conditions) requires windbreak construction.
  • Visibility: If rescue is expected, build where the shelter or signal devices are visible from the air and from likely approach routes.

Common Mistakes

  • Building during peak heat. Construction labor in midday sun causes dangerous fluid loss. Build during cool hours only.
  • Single-layer roof. A single tarp in direct sun provides inadequate heat reduction. Use the double-roof principle.
  • Sealing the shelter completely. Trapped air overheats. Maintain airflow on calm days.
  • Sheltering in a dry wash. Flash floods arrive from distant storms without warning. Build on high ground.
  • Ignoring night cold. Planning only for daytime heat. Desert nights are cold enough for hypothermia, especially with dehydration and fatigue.
  • Sleeping on bare ground. Sand and rock conduct heat away from the body at night and burn during the day. Always insulate the floor.
  • Using a dark-colored tarp shiny-side down. Orient reflective surfaces outward during the day to reject solar radiation.

Quick Reference

Detail Specification
Priority order Shade > ground insulation > wind > rain
Work hours Before 10 AM, after 4 PM
Double-roof air gap 4-6 in (10-15 cm)
Trench depth 18-24 in (45-60 cm) minimum
Below-grade temp reduction 20-30°F (11-17°C) cooler
Deadman anchor depth 12 in (30 cm)
Night temp range 35-50°F (2-10°C), lower at elevation
Water savings in shade ~50% reduction vs. sun exposure
Shade orientation Long axis east-west
Space blanket day use Reflective side up (outer layer)
Space blanket night use Reflective side in (toward body)

Shelter

Tarp and Poncho Shelters

How to rig tarps and ponchos into effective shelters using common configurations, knots, and anchoring techniques for any terrain.

At a Glance

  • An A-frame tarp is the most versatile all-weather configuration — rig this first if unsure.
  • The trucker's hitch and taut-line hitch are the only two knots required for most tarp setups.
  • Stake angle matters: drive stakes at 45 degrees away from the tarp for maximum holding power.
  • A 8 x 10 ft (2.4 x 3 m) tarp shelters one to two people. A 10 x 12 ft (3 x 3.7 m) tarp adds gear coverage.
  • Pitch the low side into the wind and angle the roof to direct rain runoff away from the sleeping area.

Tarp Configurations

A-Frame

The most reliable general-purpose setup. Sheds rain, blocks wind from two sides, and provides headroom.

  1. Run a ridgeline between two trees or vertical supports at chest height, roughly 4-5 ft (1.2-1.5 m). Use a trucker's hitch at one end for tensioning.
  2. Drape the tarp over the ridgeline so equal material hangs on each side.
  3. Stake out the four corners at 45-degree angles away from the tarp. Pull the fabric taut.
  4. Stake the midpoints of each long side if the tarp has grommets or tie-out loops there.
  5. Adjust the ridgeline height and stake tension until the tarp is drum-tight with no sagging panels.
TIP Lower one side closer to the ground and face it into the prevailing wind. This deflects rain and wind over the shelter while keeping the leeward side open for entry and ventilation.

Lean-To

Maximum open-side coverage. Best in mild weather or when a fire is built in front for heat reflection.

  1. Run a ridgeline between two trees at 4-5 ft (1.2-1.5 m) height.
  2. Drape the tarp over the ridgeline with roughly two-thirds of the material on one side.
  3. Stake the long rear edge to the ground, pulling it tight and flat.
  4. The short front portion drapes over the ridgeline as a small rain lip.
  5. Stake the two side edges or tie them to diagonal guy lines.

Orient the open face away from the wind. Build a fire 6-8 ft (1.8-2.4 m) in front of the opening — the tarp reflects heat back toward you.

CAUTION Keep all flames at least 6 ft (1.8 m) from any tarp. Silnylon and polyethylene melt and burn. Sparks create holes instantly.

C-Fly (Half Pyramid)

Excellent wind and rain protection with a single attachment point. Works well with one tree or a trekking pole.

  1. Attach one corner of the tarp to a tree or pole at 5-6 ft (1.5-1.8 m) height.
  2. Pull the opposite corner straight back and stake it to the ground.
  3. Stake the two remaining corners wide to the ground, forming a low, swept-back shape.
  4. Tension all three ground stakes until the tarp is smooth.

The result is a low-profile shelter with the high point facing into the wind. Rain runs off the back slope. The open sides provide ventilation.

Diamond Fly

Uses a square tarp rotated 45 degrees. Compact, quick, and effective for one person.

  1. Tie one corner of the tarp to a tree at 4-5 ft (1.2-1.5 m) height. This is the peak.
  2. Stake the opposite corner to the ground directly below and behind where you will sleep. This is the foot end.
  3. Stake the two side corners to the ground, spread wide.
  4. Adjust the peak height and ground tension to eliminate sag.

The diamond fly provides overhead rain protection and wind deflection from three sides. The open front faces the leeward direction.

Hammock Tarp

Covers a hammock from rain and wind. Requires a larger tarp — 10 x 12 ft (3 x 3.7 m) minimum for full coverage.

  1. Run a ridgeline directly above the hammock line, using the same two trees. Tie it 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) above the hammock suspension.
  2. Drape the tarp over the ridgeline, centered on the hammock.
  3. Pull out four corners with guy lines at 45 degrees and stake them.
  4. Ensure the tarp extends at least 12 inches (30 cm) past each end of the hammock to prevent diagonal rain from reaching the occupant.
  5. In heavy rain or wind, lower the tarp sides closer to the hammock. In dry weather, raise them for airflow.
NOTE The tarp ridgeline must be separate from the hammock suspension. Attaching both to the same line transfers rain along the cord directly into the hammock.

Poncho Hooch

A military poncho serves as a single-person shelter. Limited coverage — suitable for short-term use.

  1. Snap the poncho hood closed and tie it off or tuck it in to prevent leaks.
  2. Run a ridgeline through the hood tie-off or over the top of the poncho.
  3. Stake the four corners to the ground in an A-frame or lean-to pattern.
  4. Use the built-in snap closures along the edges to create a tighter seal if two ponchos are available (snap them together for double coverage).

Poncho shelters are fast — 5 minutes from pack to pitched. Trade-off: small coverage area and no floor protection.

Essential Knots

Trucker's Hitch

Provides 3:1 mechanical advantage for tensioning ridgelines and guy lines. This is the primary tensioning knot for tarp shelters.

  1. Tie a fixed loop (directional figure-8 or slip knot) in the standing line, 18-24 inches (45-60 cm) from the anchor point.
  2. Pass the working end around the anchor (tree or stake).
  3. Thread the working end up through the fixed loop.
  4. Pull down to tension. The loop acts as a pulley.
  5. Secure with two half hitches below the loop.

Taut-Line Hitch

An adjustable friction knot for guy lines. Slides to tighten or loosen but grips under load.

  1. Pass the working end around the stake or anchor.
  2. Wrap the working end twice around the standing line, moving toward the tarp (inside the loop).
  3. Make one more wrap around the standing line on the outside (tarp side) of the two inner wraps.
  4. Dress the knot by pulling snug.
  5. Slide the knot along the standing line to adjust tension.
TIP Replace taut-line hitches with a simple prusik loop made from a short cord. Prusiks grip more reliably on slippery modern cord like Dyneema or Spectra.

Additional Useful Knots

  • Bowline: Fixed loop that does not slip or bind. Use for tie-off points on trees.
  • Clove hitch: Quick attachment to a pole or tree. Not secure alone — back up with a half hitch.
  • Sheet bend: Joins two lines of different diameter. Use when extending a guy line with improvised cordage.

See Knots and Lashing for detailed tying instructions.

Ground Cloth Layering

A ground cloth prevents moisture wicking from below and protects the tarp floor from abrasion.

  1. Clear the ground of rocks, sticks, and pinecones.
  2. Lay the ground cloth inside the tarp footprint. Fold edges under so no ground cloth extends beyond the tarp — exposed edges channel rain underneath.
  3. Layer from bottom up: ground cloth, sleeping pad, sleeping bag.

If using a poncho as a shelter, a separate ground cloth is essential. A trash bag, space blanket, or second poncho works.

Staking in Different Soils

Soft Soil and Sand

Standard stakes pull out easily.

  • Use deadman anchors: tie the guy line to a buried stick, rock, or sand-filled bag at 12 inches (30 cm) depth.
  • Drive stakes at 45 degrees away from the tarp and fully bury them.
  • Pile rocks on top of buried stakes for extra holding power.

Rocky Ground

Stakes cannot penetrate.

  • Tie guy lines directly to heavy rocks (15-20 lb / 7-9 kg).
  • Use natural anchors: trees, roots, rock outcrops.
  • Create rock cairn anchors: stack rocks over a guy line loop.
  • Wrap cord around a large rock and use a clove hitch backed with half hitches.

Snow

Stakes melt out of consolidated snow and pull from powder.

  • Use deadman anchors: bury a stick, ice axe, or packed snow ball perpendicular to the pull direction at 12 inches (30 cm) depth.
  • Stamp snow firmly over the buried anchor. Allow 10 minutes to firm up before tensioning.
  • T-stake method: drive the stake horizontally into the snow and pack snow over the top.

Improvised Stakes

  • Sharpened sticks 10-12 inches (25-30 cm) long and 1 inch (2.5 cm) diameter.
  • Forked branches driven with the fork downward to grip the guy line.
  • Tent stake substitutes: large nails, rebar pieces, screwdrivers, butter knives.
  • Loaded stuff sacks or water bottles as deadweight anchors.

Tarp Sizing

Tarp Size Coverage People
5 x 7 ft (1.5 x 2.1 m) Minimal bivy cover 1 (tight)
8 x 10 ft (2.4 x 3 m) Standard shelter 1-2
10 x 12 ft (3 x 3.7 m) Full shelter + gear 2
12 x 16 ft (3.7 x 4.9 m) Group shelter 3-4

Material Considerations

Material Weight Durability Cost Notes
Silnylon Light Moderate High Stretches when wet — retension after rain begins
Silpoly Light Moderate High Less stretch than silnylon when wet
Polyethylene (blue tarp) Heavy Low-Moderate Low Widely available, noisy, bulky
Cuben fiber (DCF) Ultralight Low Very high Does not stretch, tears more easily
Space blanket Ultralight Very low Very low Reflects heat, tears in wind, single-use
Poncho Moderate Moderate Low-Moderate Dual-use (rain gear + shelter), small coverage
CAUTION Silnylon stretches 1-2% when wet. Tension the tarp tightly in dry conditions, then retension after rain begins. Alternatively, use taut-line hitches on all guy lines for quick adjustment.

Wind Load Management

  • Pitch the low side or closed side into the wind.
  • Reduce tarp surface area in high wind by lowering the ridgeline and pulling stakes closer.
  • Angle the windward face at 30-45 degrees so wind deflects over the top.
  • Add mid-panel guy lines to prevent billowing. Attach them at any grommet or use a button-and-cord method on tarp fabric without grommets.
  • In sustained winds above 30 mph (48 km/h), the lean-to and C-fly configurations perform better than the A-frame because of their lower profile.

Rain Runoff Direction

  • Angle the tarp roof so water runs off the rear (downhill side), away from the sleeping area.
  • Dig a shallow trench 2-3 inches (5-8 cm) deep around the uphill and side edges of the shelter to divert ground runoff.
  • Avoid camping in depressions or flat ground where water pools.
  • If the tarp sags and collects a rain pool, push the pool off from inside with a hand or stick. Add a center guy line pulled upward to prevent recurrence.

Common Mistakes

  • Stakes at 90 degrees. Vertical stakes pull out under load. Drive all stakes at 45 degrees away from the direction of pull.
  • Ridgeline sag. A slack ridgeline pools water and reduces headroom. Use a trucker's hitch for mechanical advantage tensioning.
  • Ground cloth extending past the tarp. Exposed ground cloth channels rain underneath the sleeping area. Fold edges under the tarp footprint.
  • Tarp touching the ground on the windward side. Blocks ventilation and causes condensation. Leave a gap of 6-12 inches (15-30 cm) unless blocking wind is critical.
  • Using the hammock line as the tarp ridgeline. Rain follows the cord directly into the hammock. Run a separate ridgeline above.
  • Ignoring guy line tension after rain starts. Silnylon and natural cordage stretch when wet. Retension all lines after precipitation begins.
  • Pitching the open side into the wind. Rain drives horizontally into the shelter. Face the open or high side downwind.

Quick Reference

Detail Specification
Standard tarp size (1-2 people) 8 x 10 ft (2.4 x 3 m)
Ridgeline height (A-frame) 4-5 ft (1.2-1.5 m)
Stake angle 45° away from pull
Fire distance from tarp 6+ ft (1.8+ m) minimum
Primary tensioning knot Trucker's hitch (3:1 advantage)
Primary adjustable knot Taut-line hitch
Deadman anchor depth 12 in (30 cm)
Ground cloth rule Never extend past tarp edge
Hammock tarp extension 12+ in (30 cm) past each hammock end

Fire

Fire Principles

Master the fundamentals of fire creation, management, and safety to survive any situation.

At a Glance

  • Fire requires three elements simultaneously: heat, fuel, and oxygen (the fire triangle).
  • Build fire progressively: tinder catches spark, kindling builds flame, fuel wood sustains it.
  • Choose your fire lay based on purpose: warmth, cooking, signaling, or stealth.
  • Prepare the site before striking the first spark — clear ground, block wind, plan containment.
  • Always extinguish fully and practice leave-no-trace when possible.

The Fire Triangle

Every fire depends on three elements existing together in sufficient quantity:

Heat

Heat provides the ignition energy. Sources include friction, sparks, solar concentration, electrical arc, and chemical reaction. Remove heat and fire dies — this is how water extinguishes flame. The ignition temperature for most wood is 400-500 F (200-260 C). Maintain heat by sheltering flame from wind during the critical early stages.

Fuel

Fuel is any combustible material. In survival fire-making, fuel progresses through three stages (see below). Fuel must be dry enough to ignite — wood above 25% moisture content resists ignition. Dead, standing wood is almost always drier than wood on the ground. Strip wet outer bark to reach dry inner wood.

Oxygen

Air contains roughly 21% oxygen. Fire consumes oxygen rapidly. A smothered fire dies. Ensure airflow reaches the base of the fire at all times. Blow gently on coals to increase oxygen supply. Pack fuel loosely enough for air to circulate between pieces.

WARNING In enclosed spaces (caves, snow shelters, vehicles), fire depletes oxygen and produces carbon monoxide. Ensure ventilation or risk asphyxiation.

Fuel Stages: Tinder, Kindling, Fuel Wood

Tinder

Tinder is any material that ignites from a spark or small flame. It burns hot and fast. Gather at least two handfuls before attempting ignition.

Natural tinder: - Dry grass (dead, golden-colored) - Birch bark (contains flammable oils even when damp) - Cattail fluff - Cedar bark (shredded fine) - Pine resin / fatwood shavings - Dried moss - Seed down (thistle, milkweed, dandelion) - Bird nests (abandoned) - Fungus: cramp ball (Daldinia concentrica), true tinder fungus (Fomes fomentarius)

Prepared / manufactured tinder: - Char cloth - Cotton balls with petroleum jelly - Dryer lint - Steel wool (fine grade, 0000) - Commercial fire starters - Waxed jute twine

Prepare a tinder bundle by forming a loose bird-nest shape approximately 4 in (10 cm) across. Place the finest, most combustible material in the center where the coal or spark will land.

Kindling

Kindling bridges the gap between tinder and fuel wood. Use dry sticks and twigs from pencil-lead thickness up to pencil thickness — roughly 1/8 in to 3/8 in (3-10 mm) diameter. Gather at least two large handfuls. Dead twigs that snap cleanly are dry enough. Twigs that bend without breaking are too green or wet.

Good kindling sources: - Dead twigs still attached to trees (off the ground, drier) - Split wood shavings / feather sticks - Small pieces of fatwood - Dry pine needles in bundles - Thin bark strips

Fuel Wood

Fuel wood sustains the fire. Graduate sizes from thumb-thickness to wrist-thickness to arm-thickness. Start with pieces 1-2 in (2.5-5 cm) diameter and work up. Split wood ignites faster than round wood because it exposes dry interior grain.

Fuel wood by burn characteristics: - Fast / hot burn: Pine, spruce, fir (softwoods) — good for starting, poor for coals. - Slow / steady burn: Oak, hickory, maple, ash (hardwoods) — excellent coals, long duration. - Smoky / resinous: Green wood, damp wood, pine with heavy sap — avoid except for signaling.

Gather three times more fuel wood than you think you need. A night fire in cold conditions consumes a pile roughly 4 ft long x 2 ft high x 2 ft wide (1.2 x 0.6 x 0.6 m) of mixed wood.

Fire Lay Types

Teepee (Tipi)

Lean kindling sticks together to form a cone shape over the tinder bundle. Leave a gap on the windward side for lighting and airflow. As kindling ignites, add progressively larger sticks maintaining the cone shape.

When to use: General purpose. Best for quick ignition and fast heat. Collapses inward as it burns, feeding itself. Ideal for boiling water or lighting larger structures.

Drawbacks: Burns fast, requires frequent feeding. Collapses unpredictably — poor for cooking with a pot or grill.

Log Cabin (Crib)

Stack pairs of sticks in alternating perpendicular layers, like building a small cabin. Place tinder bundle in the center at the base. Each layer uses progressively larger wood.

When to use: Cooking — provides a stable, flat top surface. Produces a uniform coal bed. Good when you need sustained, even heat. Also effective as the outer structure around an inner teepee for signal fires.

Drawbacks: Requires more wood and more preparation time. Slower to ignite than a teepee.

Lean-To

Drive a long stick into the ground at a 30-degree angle, pointing into the wind. Lean kindling against the windward side of this stick. Place tinder underneath at the base.

When to use: Windy conditions. The lean-to structure shields the tinder and flame from wind. Works well when you have only one ignition attempt.

Drawbacks: One-directional heat output. Burns unevenly.

Star Fire (Radial Fire)

Arrange 4-6 logs like spokes of a wheel with the ends meeting in the center. Light a small teepee or tinder bundle at the hub. Push logs inward as the ends burn.

When to use: Long-duration fire with minimal attention. Excellent for overnight warmth. Uses large logs efficiently — no splitting or breaking required. Common in dry grassland and desert environments.

Drawbacks: Low flame height. Slow to establish. Requires periodic pushing of logs inward.

Dakota Hole (Dakota Fire Pit)

Dig two holes roughly 12 in (30 cm) apart. The fire hole is 12 in (30 cm) diameter and 12 in (30 cm) deep. The air hole is 6 in (15 cm) diameter, angled to connect to the bottom of the fire hole. Build the fire inside the fire hole. The air tunnel creates a draft that feeds oxygen from below.

When to use: Tactical / low-visibility situations. Wind protection. Efficient fuel consumption (burns 50-70% less wood than open fire). Excellent for cooking — set a pot directly over the hole. In dry, sandy, or loamy soil the digging is fast.

Drawbacks: Requires digging tools or significant hand effort. Does not work in rocky, frozen, or waterlogged ground. Difficult to extinguish quickly. Radiates almost no warmth sideways — poor for body heating.

WARNING Never build a Dakota hole in peaty or organic soil. Subsurface root fires can smolder for days or weeks and spread underground.

Site Preparation

Clearing Ground

Clear a circle at least 10 ft (3 m) in diameter down to bare mineral soil if possible. Remove dry leaves, pine needles, grass, and duff. Scrape with a stick, boot, or improvised tool. If you cannot reach mineral soil, build the fire on a platform of green logs or rocks.

WARNING Never build fire on wet or river-smoothed rocks. Trapped moisture expands when heated and can cause rocks to explode, sending fragments at lethal velocity.

Wind Considerations

  • Determine prevailing wind direction before selecting your site.
  • Position your shelter upwind of fire for warmth reflection, not downwind (smoke and spark hazard).
  • Use natural windbreaks: rock faces, fallen logs, dense brush lines.
  • In high wind, dig a trench or use the Dakota hole method.
  • Wind above 15 mph (24 km/h) makes open fire dangerous — sparks carry far.

Fire Reflectors

Build a reflector wall on the far side of the fire from your shelter. Stack green logs 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) long in a low wall, 2-3 ft (0.6-1 m) high. Angle the reflector to bounce heat toward your sleeping area. A rock face or earth bank serves the same function. The combination of fire + reflector + shelter behind you creates a heat trap.

Surface Selection

Surface Suitability Notes
Bare mineral soil Best No subsurface spread risk
Sand Excellent Easy cleanup
Gravel Excellent Good drainage
Flat rock Good Avoid wet / porous rock
Snow (on platform) Acceptable Build on green-log platform
Organic duff Dangerous Must clear to mineral soil
Peat Never Subsurface fire risk

The Progression: Spark to Sustainable Fire

Follow this sequence without skipping steps:

  1. Prepare the site. Clear ground, arrange windbreak, position reflector.
  2. Gather all materials before ignition. Tinder, kindling (sorted by size), fuel wood (sorted by size). Place everything within arm's reach.
  3. Build the tinder bundle. Loose, airy, bird-nest shape. Finest material in the center.
  4. Arrange initial kindling. Set up your chosen fire lay around (but not on top of) the tinder, or have kindling ready to add immediately.
  5. Ignite the tinder. Use your chosen method. Place ember or spark into the center of the tinder bundle.
  6. Nurture the ember. Blow gently and steadily at the base. Hold the bundle loosely — do not compress it. Oxygen is critical here.
  7. Transfer to the fire lay. Place the flaming tinder bundle at the base of your prepared kindling structure.
  8. Add kindling progressively. Start with the thinnest sticks. Add each size only after the previous size is burning well. Do not smother the flame.
  9. Graduate to fuel wood. Once kindling is fully engaged, add wrist-thickness fuel wood. Wait for full combustion before adding arm-thickness logs.
  10. Maintain. Feed the fire on a schedule. Do not let it burn down to bare coals until you have added enough fuel to sustain it.
WARNING The most dangerous moment is between steps 7 and 8. Adding too much kindling too fast smothers the flame. Add one or two sticks at a time and wait for each to catch.

Why Fire Fails

Wet Materials

The single most common cause. Even wood that looks dry can hold moisture inside. Test by snapping — a clean snap with an audible crack means dry. A bend or stringy break means wet. Always source dead standing wood over ground wood.

Smothering

Packing fuel too tightly blocks airflow. Leave gaps between sticks. Think "loosely stacked" not "packed solid." Fire needs to breathe.

Skipping Fuel Stages

Jumping from tinder to large fuel wood. The tinder cannot ignite thick logs. Always bridge with kindling. Spend more time on kindling than you think necessary.

Insufficient Tinder

One small pinch of grass is not enough. Gather at least two large handfuls. If your first attempt fails, you need a backup bundle ready.

Wind Mismanagement

Too much wind blows flame away from fuel. Too little wind (or building in a depression) starves fire of oxygen. Moderate, steady airflow at the base is ideal.

Giving Up Too Soon

Friction fire takes 10-45 minutes of sustained effort. Modern methods (ferro rod, lighter) should produce flame in under 2 minutes if materials are dry. If you have been trying for more than 5 minutes with a modern ignition source, stop. Reassess your tinder and kindling — the problem is materials, not method.

Poor Site Selection

Building on damp ground, in a wind tunnel, or on organic soil. Spend 5 minutes selecting and preparing the site. It saves 30 minutes of failed attempts.

Uses of Fire

Warmth

Radiant heat from fire maintains core body temperature in cold conditions. Position yourself 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) from a sustained fire. Use a reflector wall to maximize heat capture. A long fire (built parallel to your body) warms more evenly than a single point source.

Cooking

Coals cook food more evenly than open flame. Allow a hot fire to burn down to a coal bed before cooking. Use a grill of green sticks or flat rocks as a cooking surface. Boiling water requires a sustained, hot flame — use a teepee lay to get to boil quickly.

Water Purification

Bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute at sea level. At elevations above 6,500 ft (2,000 m), boil for 3 minutes. Use a metal container, or heat rocks and drop them into a container of water (stone boiling). Fire is the most reliable purification method when no chemical treatment or filter is available.

Signaling

Build a signal fire in an open, visible location — hilltop, clearing, shoreline. Prepare three fires in a triangle (international distress signal), spaced 100 ft (30 m) apart. For daytime signaling, produce smoke by adding green branches, wet leaves, or damp grass to a hot fire. For nighttime signaling, build a large, bright blaze. Keep signal fires ready to light at a moment's notice.

Psychological Comfort

Fire provides light, warmth, and a sense of security. It reduces panic and improves decision-making. In a group survival situation, fire serves as a morale anchor and gathering point. Do not underestimate this benefit — will to survive is the most critical survival factor.

Predator Deterrence

Most predators avoid fire. Maintain a fire through the night in areas with large predator risk. Keep burning branches available to wave if an animal approaches. Smoke deters insects, particularly mosquitoes — build a smoky fire upwind of your camp during peak insect hours.

Common Mistakes

  • Building the fire too large too fast — wasting fuel and losing control.
  • Failing to gather enough fuel before dark — results in a cold night.
  • Building directly on snow without a platform — the fire melts down into a pit and becomes unreachable.
  • Ignoring wind direction — smoke fills the shelter, sparks ignite nearby materials.
  • Using only one size of kindling — the progression must be gradual.
  • Leaving fire unattended — wind shifts cause spread.
  • Placing wet rocks around the fire ring — explosion hazard.
  • Not having a backup ignition method — always carry two.

Fire Safety and Extinguishing

Containment

Ring the fire with rocks (dry, non-porous) or scrape a bare-earth perimeter at least 2 ft (0.6 m) wide. Never build fire under overhanging branches. Keep the fire only as large as you need — a small, well-managed fire is safer and more fuel-efficient than a bonfire.

Extinguishing

  1. Stop adding fuel and let the fire burn down.
  2. Spread coals out flat with a stick — do not leave them piled.
  3. Drown with water. Pour slowly, stir the ash, pour again. Repeat until no hissing or steam remains.
  4. If no water is available, smother with mineral soil (not organic duff). Cover completely and pack down.
  5. Feel the ash and surrounding soil with the back of your hand. If warm, repeat the process.
  6. Wait 10 minutes and check again.
WARNING Buried coals can reignite up to 24 hours later. If you must leave, ensure the fire is dead cold.

Leave No Trace

In non-emergency situations, practice leave-no-trace fire principles: - Use existing fire rings when available. - Build mound fires on mineral soil carried to a flat rock. - Scatter cold ashes widely after full extinguishment. - Return displaced soil and rocks to their original positions. - Remove all unburned trash and food scraps.

Quick Reference

Item Specification

Kindling diameter range 1/8 - 3/8 in / 3-10 mm
Fuel wood starting size 1-2 in / 2.5-5 cm diameter
Wood ignition temperature 400-500 F / 200-260 C
Boil time (sea level) 1 minute rolling boil
Boil time (above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m) 3 minutes rolling boil
Signal fire spacing 100 ft / 30 m triangle
Maximum safe wind for open fire 15 mph / 24 km/h

  • Spark and Lens Methods — ferro rod, flint and steel, battery, lens, and fire piston techniques.
