Fire

Maintaining Fire

How to manage fuel, bank coals, carry fire, and sustain flame through the night and across distances.

At a Glance

  • A fire without a fuel plan dies. Gather three times more wood than you think you need before dark.
  • Bank coals under ash to preserve fire overnight without tending.
  • Carrying fire between camps saves hours of reignition effort — use punk wood, slow match, or a coal carrier.
  • Hardwood burns slower and produces lasting coals. Softwood burns fast and hot but leaves poor coals.
  • Manage ash buildup. A thick ash layer smothers coals and blocks airflow.

Fuel Management

Fuel Stages and Burn Rates

Different wood types serve different purposes. Match your fuel to your need.

Wood Type Burn Rate Coal Quality Best Use
Pine, spruce, fir (softwood) Fast, hot Poor — burns to powder Quick heat, boiling water, starting fires
Oak, hickory, maple (hardwood) Slow, steady Excellent — long-lasting coals Overnight fire, cooking, banking
Birch Medium-fast Moderate Good all-purpose, bark for tinder
Ash Medium Good Burns well even slightly green
Willow, poplar Fast Poor Emergency fuel only
TIP In temperate hardwood forests, prioritize oak and hickory for overnight fires. One armload of split oak outlasts three armloads of pine.

How Much Fuel to Gather

Underestimating fuel is the most common fire maintenance failure. Use these benchmarks:

  • Overnight fire (8 hours, moderate cold): A woodpile 4 feet long, 2 feet high, and 2 feet wide (1.2 x 0.6 x 0.6 m) of mixed split wood.
  • Cooking fire (2 hours): An armload of wrist-thick hardwood, plus kindling.
  • Signal fire (ready state): Three prepared fire lays plus a reserve pile of dry fuel and green-branch smoke material at each.

Gather all fuel before dark. Searching for wood in darkness is slow, dangerous, and produces poor-quality wet or green wood.

Fuel Sizing

Feed fuel in a steady progression. Jumping from small kindling to large logs smothers the fire.

  1. Once kindling is fully engaged, add thumb-thick sticks, 1-2 inches (2.5-5 cm) diameter.
  2. After 5-10 minutes, add wrist-thick pieces, 3-4 inches (7.5-10 cm) diameter.
  3. For sustained burning, add arm-thick logs, 5-8 inches (13-20 cm) diameter. Split these in half — split wood ignites faster and burns more completely.
NOTE Never add a single large log to a small fire. The log absorbs heat faster than the fire produces it, and the fire dies. Always have an intermediate-size bridge.

Banking Coals for Overnight

Banking is the technique of burying coals under ash to slow combustion and preserve live coals for hours without fuel addition. A properly banked fire survives 6-10 hours.

Procedure

  1. Stop adding fuel 30-45 minutes before you intend to bank. Allow the fire to burn down to a deep coal bed. The coal bed should be at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) thick.
  2. Push all coals into a compact mound in the center of the fire pit.
  3. Cover the mound with a 2-3 inch (5-7.5 cm) layer of fine ash. Pack it gently. Do not use mineral soil unless ash is insufficient — soil insulates but also contaminates the coal bed.
  4. Place 2-3 large, dense hardwood logs (6-8 inches / 15-20 cm diameter) directly on top of the ash mound. The coals slowly consume these from below overnight.

Revival in the Morning

  1. Remove the hardwood logs (they may be partially burned through).
  2. Scrape away the ash to expose the coal bed. Live coals glow red when exposed to air.
  3. Blow gently on the coals. They should brighten within seconds.
  4. Place fine tinder (shaved bark, dry grass, feather stick) directly on the coals.
  5. Continue blowing. The tinder catches flame within 1-3 minutes.
  6. Add kindling and rebuild the fire using standard progression.
CAUTION If no glow appears after scraping and blowing, the coals may be dead. Verify by holding your hand 4 inches (10 cm) above the coal bed. If you feel heat, live coals remain deeper. Continue scraping. If no heat at all, start a new fire.

Carrying Fire

Moving a live coal or ember between locations saves the effort of starting a new fire from scratch. Traditional and indigenous peoples carried fire routinely across long distances.

Punk Wood

Punk wood is soft, spongy, partially decayed wood that smolders slowly without flaming. It is the most common fire-carrying material.

  1. Find a piece of thoroughly dry punk wood from a standing dead tree. It should be soft enough to crumble between your fingers but not wet or powdery.
  2. Touch the punk wood to a live coal. Blow gently until it catches and begins to glow and smolder.
  3. Wrap the smoldering punk loosely in green leaves or bark to slow the burn and protect it from wind. Leave enough airflow to sustain the smolder.
  4. Carry it in your hand or in a bark trough. Check every 30 minutes to ensure it is still smoldering.
  5. At your destination, place the glowing punk wood into a tinder bundle and blow it to flame.
TIP Good punk wood smolders for 2-6 hours depending on piece size and density. Carry a piece the size of your fist for a half-day's travel.

Slow Match

A slow match is a length of cordage or natural fiber that burns slowly along its length, maintaining a coal at the burning tip.

  1. Twist dry plant fibers (cattail, inner bark of cedar or basswood, dried grass) into a loose rope 1/4-1/2 inch (6-13 mm) thick and 3-6 feet (1-1.8 m) long.
  2. Light one end from your fire. The slow match should smolder at the tip, advancing slowly along its length.
  3. Carry the match with the burning end up. Shield from wind.
  4. A 3-foot (1 m) slow match burns for 1-3 hours depending on material density.

Coal Carrier

Build a simple carrier for transporting coals over longer distances.

  1. Line a section of green bark (birch or elm) or a tin can with mineral soil or sand, 1-2 inches (2.5-5 cm) deep.
  2. Place 3-4 live coals on the soil bed.
  3. Cover with a layer of dry punk wood or tinder fungus to insulate.
  4. Add another thin layer of soil.
  5. Wrap loosely in green bark. Leave small air holes.
  6. This carrier preserves coals for 6-12 hours.
NOTE The Pacific Northwest peoples used clam shells lined with damp sand and cedar bark to carry coals in canoes. Adapt the principle to available materials.

Relighting from Coals

Even a seemingly dead fire may contain viable coals buried under ash. Before starting a new fire from scratch, always check the old fire pit.

  1. Scrape away ash to the bottom of the fire pit.
  2. Feel for heat with the back of your hand held 2-4 inches (5-10 cm) above the surface.
  3. If you find a live coal, no matter how small, place a wad of fine, dry tinder directly on it.
  4. Blow steadily from the side. Protect the coal from wind.
  5. A single pea-sized coal can relight a fire in under 2 minutes with good tinder.

Drying Wet Wood Using Existing Fire

An established fire is a wood dryer. Use it to pre-dry the next batch of fuel.

Methods

  • Lean sticks against flanking rocks. Place wet or damp split wood upright, leaning against rocks beside the fire. The radiant heat dries the wood face. Rotate pieces periodically.
  • Ring the fire pit. Lay a ring of fuel wood 12-18 inches (30-45 cm) from the fire's edge. The radiant heat drives moisture out over 30-60 minutes.
  • Overhead drying rack. Build a simple rack from green sticks above the fire (at least 3 feet / 1 m above flames). Lay small-diameter wet wood across it. Heat rises and dries the wood.
CAUTION Do not place wet wood directly on or in the fire to "dry it." This drops the fire temperature, produces excessive smoke, and may extinguish a small fire entirely. Dry wood near the fire, then add it once surface moisture is gone.

Ash Management

Ash accumulates quickly and causes problems if ignored.

  • Too much ash smothers coals. Rake ash away from the active coal bed periodically. Push it to the perimeter of the fire pit.
  • Use ash for banking. Fine ash is the ideal insulating material for overnight coal preservation.
  • Use ash for cooking. Wrap food in leaves and bury it in hot ash for slow baking.
  • Use ash for sanitation. Wood ash mixed with water creates a crude lye solution for cleaning.

Maintain a clear coal bed at the center of the fire with ash pushed to the sides. This ensures oxygen reaches the coals from below.

Fire Watch for Groups

In a group survival situation, assign fire watch shifts to maintain the fire through the night.

Schedule

  • Divide the night into 2-hour shifts. Shorter shifts keep the watcher alert. Longer shifts cause drowsiness and neglect.
  • The fire watcher's duties: add fuel every 15-20 minutes, monitor wind changes, watch for sparks threatening shelters, and maintain the fuel supply.
  • The first and last watches are hardest. Assign your most reliable people to these slots.

Fuel Staging

Pre-stage each watch's fuel supply in separate piles within arm's reach of the fire. Each pile should contain:

  • 6-8 wrist-thick pieces for regular feeding
  • 2-3 arm-thick pieces for sustained burns during the watch
  • A handful of kindling in case the fire needs revival

This prevents the watcher from leaving the fire unattended to search for wood.

When to Maintain vs. When to Let Die

Not every fire needs to last all night. Weigh the cost of maintaining against the effort of restarting.

Maintain the fire when:

  • Nighttime temperature drops below 50°F (10°C) and you lack adequate insulated shelter.
  • Predator activity is likely (large cats, bears, wolves in area).
  • You have injured or hypothermic group members who need continuous warmth.
  • You plan to carry fire to the next camp in the morning.

Let the fire die when:

  • Temperature is mild and shelter is adequate.
  • Fuel is scarce and tomorrow's fire start is easy (dry conditions, reliable ignition source).
  • You are moving camp at dawn and do not need to carry fire.
  • You are in a fire-risk area (dry grassland, drought conditions) and cannot tend it safely.

Fire in Different Weather

Wind

  • In sustained wind above 15 mph (24 km/h), build a windbreak or use a trench/Dakota fire.
  • Reposition fuel additions to the windward side so the fire draws across the fuel.
  • Secure lightweight fuel so it does not blow away before igniting.

Rain

  • See Fire in Wet Conditions for detailed procedures.
  • Keep a reserve of dry kindling and tinder under cover at all times.
  • Feed the fire more frequently. A small fire in rain loses heat faster than in dry conditions.

Extreme Cold

  • Fire consumes fuel faster in extreme cold because more heat energy escapes to the environment.
  • Increase fuel reserves by 50% below 0°F (-18°C).
  • Position a reflector wall to direct heat toward your shelter. Without a reflector, most heat energy radiates uselessly into open air.

Extreme Heat

  • In desert conditions, fire is used primarily for cooking, signaling, and nighttime warmth (desert nights drop sharply).
  • Keep fires small. Large fires waste scarce fuel and add unwanted heat during the day.
  • Fire risk is highest in arid environments. Clear a wide perimeter and never leave fire unattended.

Common Mistakes

  • Not gathering enough fuel before dark. Searching for wood at night produces poor fuel and wastes energy. Stockpile during daylight.
  • Feeding the fire with oversized logs. Large logs smother a small fire. Maintain the size progression even when adding to an established fire.
  • Ignoring ash buildup. Thick ash blankets coals and blocks airflow. Rake coals clear regularly.
  • Placing wet wood directly on the fire. This drops temperature and produces smoke. Pre-dry all fuel near the fire first.
  • Failing to bank before sleeping. Without banking, the fire burns out in 1-2 hours. You wake cold and must restart from scratch.
  • Carrying fire without checking the ember. Check smoldering punk wood or slow match every 30 minutes. A dead ember means starting over at your destination.
  • No fire watcher in groups. An untended overnight fire either dies or spreads. Assign shifts.

Quick Reference

Task Key Detail
Overnight fuel pile 4 x 2 x 2 ft / 1.2 x 0.6 x 0.6 m
Banking ash depth 2-3 in / 5-7.5 cm
Coal bed for banking 3 in / 7.5 cm thick minimum
Banked fire survival 6-10 hours
Punk wood carry time 2-6 hours
Slow match burn rate 1-3 hours per 3 ft / 1 m
Coal carrier survival 6-12 hours
Fire watch shifts 2 hours each
Pre-dry fuel distance 12-18 in / 30-45 cm from fire
Cold-weather fuel increase +50% below 0°F / -18°C

Food

Foraging Basics

Know what to eat, when to eat it, and when foraging is not worth the calories.

At a Glance

  • Wild plants rarely provide enough calories to sustain you — treat them as supplements, not meals
  • The Universal Edibility Test takes 24 hours; do not skip steps or compress the timeline
  • Avoid plants with milky sap, white/yellow berries, or umbrella-shaped flower clusters unless you have positive identification
  • Learn 5-10 plants with absolute certainty rather than 50 with vague familiarity
  • Foraging is most productive in spring and early summer; least productive in deep winter

The Universal Edibility Test

Use this 8-step protocol only when you cannot positively identify a plant. It requires approximately 24 hours and tests only ONE plant part at a time (leaf, stem, root, flower, fruit — each tested separately).

WARNING The Universal Edibility Test does not detect all toxins. Some poisons (oxalic acid, certain alkaloids) cause delayed organ damage with no immediate symptoms. This test reduces risk — it does not eliminate it. Never use it on mushrooms; see [mushroom-identification.md](#mushroom-identification).

Step 1 — Separate the Plant into Parts

Divide the plant into roots, stems, leaves, buds, flowers, and fruit/seeds. Test each part independently. A plant may have edible leaves and toxic roots.

Step 2 — Smell Test

Crush the plant part and smell it. Reject anything with a strong or unpleasant odor (bitter almond scent = cyanide compounds). Allow 5 minutes of exposure.

Step 3 — Contact Test (Skin)

Place the crushed plant part against the inside of your wrist or inner elbow. Hold it there for 15 minutes. Watch for rash, redness, burning, itching, or swelling. If any reaction occurs, discard that plant part.

Step 4 — Wait

After the skin contact test, wait 8 hours. Monitor for delayed skin reactions, nausea, or any ill effects. Do not eat anything else during this period (water only) so you can attribute any reaction to the test plant.

Step 5 — Lip Test

Touch a small portion of the prepared plant part to the corner of your lip. Hold for 3 minutes. Check for burning, tingling, or numbness. If irritation occurs, discard.

Step 6 — Tongue Test

Place a small portion on your tongue. Hold for 15 minutes. Do not chew. Do not swallow. Spit it out. If burning, extreme bitterness, or numbness develops, discard and rinse your mouth.

Step 7 — Chew and Spit

Chew a small amount and hold the chewed material in your mouth for 15 minutes. Do not swallow. Monitor for any adverse reaction. Spit out and rinse. Wait 8 hours. If no ill effects occur, proceed.

Step 8 — Swallow Test

Eat a small portion — approximately 1/4 cup (60 ml). Wait 8 hours. If no nausea, cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, or other symptoms appear, the plant part is likely safe to eat in moderate quantities. Gradually increase portion size over subsequent meals.

Summary Timeline

Step Action Duration
1 Separate parts 5 min
2 Smell test 5 min
3 Skin contact 15 min
4 Wait (skin) 8 hours
5 Lip test 3 min
6 Tongue test 15 min
7 Chew and spit 15 min + 8 hours wait
8 Swallow small amount 8 hours wait
Total ~24 hours

Rules of Foraging

Avoid These Characteristics (General Rules)

  1. White or yellow berries — The majority are toxic. Exception: white mulberries are edible.
  2. Umbrella-shaped flower clusters (umbels) — The carrot/parsley family (Apiaceae) contains some of the deadliest plants on the continent (poison hemlock, water hemlock). Exception: wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace), fennel, and others — but misidentification kills. Avoid unless you have expert-level identification skills.
  3. Milky or discolored sap — Many plants with white, milky latex are toxic (spurge family, some euphorbias). Exceptions: dandelion, lettuce, and figs all produce milky sap and are edible.
  4. Three-leaf growth pattern — "Leaves of three, let it be" applies to poison ivy/oak. Not a food toxicity rule, but a contact dermatitis warning.
  5. Almond or peach smell when crushed — indicates cyanogenic glycosides (cyanide compounds).
  6. Shiny leaves — often (not always) indicate toxic species.
  7. Beans or seeds inside pods — many wild legumes are toxic without extensive preparation.

Positive Indicators (Not Guarantees)

  • Plants you observe animals eating (note: animals tolerate many toxins humans cannot)
  • Aggregate berries (blackberry, raspberry pattern) — no known deadly aggregate berries
  • Plants from known safe families (see below)

The Exception Problem

Every avoidance rule has exceptions. The rules exist to keep you alive when you do not have positive identification. If you positively identify a plant, the rules become secondary to your identification.

When to Forage vs. When Not to Waste Energy

Forage When

  • You are stationary (sheltering in place, awaiting rescue)
  • Abundant, easily identifiable plants surround you
  • You have adequate water (digestion requires water)
  • Temperature and conditions allow safe movement
  • Spring or early summer in temperate climates

Do Not Waste Energy Foraging When

  • You are actively traveling to safety and food is scarce
  • Deep winter with snow cover — caloric expenditure exceeds return
  • You have no water — eating plant material without water accelerates dehydration
  • Unknown terrain with no recognizable species
  • You are already in caloric debt and the available plants provide negligible energy

Caloric Reality of Wild Plants

Most wild greens provide 15-30 calories per cup (240 ml). Compare this to your daily survival need of 1,500-2,500 calories. You would need to eat 50-160 cups of wild greens to meet daily caloric requirements — this is not feasible.

Food Source Calories per cup (240 ml) Feasibility
Wild greens (average) 15-30 Supplement only
Berries (average) 60-85 Supplement
Nuts (acorns, processed) 350-500 Viable staple
Roots/tubers (cattail, burdock) 60-120 Good supplement
Pine inner bark (dried, ground) 500-600 per 100 g Emergency staple
Seeds (collected) 400-550 Labor-intensive but calorie-dense

Bottom line: Prioritize roots, nuts, seeds, and starchy plants over leafy greens. Greens provide essential vitamins and minerals but not survival calories. Combine foraging with trapping (trapping-and-snares.md) and fishing (fishing-improvised.md) for adequate caloric intake.

Tools for Foraging

Carry or improvise the following:

  • Digging stick — hardened in fire, 2-3 ft (60-90 cm) long, sharpened point. Essential for roots and tubers.
  • Knife — cuts stems, strips bark, processes plant material
  • Container — bag, shirt, or improvised bark basket for collecting
  • Cordage — bundling harvested plants for transport
  • Flat rock or board — processing surface for crushing, grinding nuts and seeds

Seasonal Availability (Northern Temperate)

Season Primary Sources Notes
Early Spring Young greens, shoots, bark cambium Highest nutrient density of the year
Late Spring Flowers, expanding leaves, early roots Peak foraging season
Summer Berries, fruits, mature leaves Some greens become bitter/tough
Early Fall Nuts, seeds, late berries, roots Best caloric density (nuts)
Late Fall Roots, bark, remaining seeds Greens dying off
Winter Bark cambium, pine needles (tea), stored nuts Worst season — minimal options

Common Edible Plant Families

Rose Family (Rosaceae)

Includes wild roses (hips), blackberries, raspberries, strawberries, hawthorn, crabapples. Generally recognizable by five-petaled flowers, alternate leaves, and thorny stems. No deadly members, though some seeds contain trace cyanide (apple seeds, cherry pits — avoid eating seeds in quantity).

See edible-plants-temperate.md for specific species.

Mustard Family (Brassicaceae)

Includes wild mustard, shepherd's purse, garlic mustard, watercress, pennycress. Identified by four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross pattern (cruciform), peppery or mustard taste. No deadly members in this family. Excellent source of vitamins A and C.

Legume Family (Fabaceae)

Includes clovers, vetches, wild peas. Identified by butterfly-shaped flowers and seed pods. Many wild legumes require cooking to neutralize toxins. Clovers are safe raw. Approach wild beans and peas with caution — some contain toxic lectins or alkaloids.

WARNING Do not confuse legume-family plants with similar-looking toxic species. Wild lupines (also Fabaceae) contain toxic alkaloids. Stick to species you positively identify.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing multiple plant parts simultaneously — invalidates the edibility test; you cannot determine which part caused a reaction
  • Assuming a plant is safe because an animal eats it — deer eat plants that sicken humans; birds eat berries that kill mammals
  • Foraging near roads, industrial sites, or treated fields — plants absorb heavy metals, pesticides, and pollutants
  • Ignoring preparation requirements — acorns require leaching, some roots require cooking, pokeweed requires multiple boilings
  • Spending 2,000 calories to collect 200 calories of greens — always calculate energy expenditure vs. return
  • Picking every plant in an area — in a long-term situation, leave root stock and seeds to regenerate

Quick Reference

Rule Guidance
White/yellow berries Avoid (exception: white mulberry)
Umbrella flowers Avoid (exception: confirmed wild carrot)
Milky sap Avoid (exception: dandelion, lettuce)
Aggregate berries Generally safe
Edibility test time ~24 hours, no shortcuts
Best calorie sources Nuts, roots, seeds, bark
Worst calorie sources Leafy greens (vitamins yes, calories no)
Best season Late spring through early fall
Worst season Deep winter

Food

Edible Plants — Temperate Forests and Fields

Identify, harvest, and prepare 18 common wild edible plants found across North American and European temperate zones.

At a Glance

  • Focus on plants with no deadly look-alikes first — dandelion, cattail, clover, blackberry
  • Always confirm identification using at least 3 distinguishing features before eating
  • Most wild greens provide vitamins but minimal calories; prioritize roots, nuts, and seeds for energy
  • Preparation matters — some safe plants become toxic (or unpalatable) without proper processing
  • Seasonal timing affects both availability and nutritional content

How to Use This Guide

Each entry includes: identification features, habitat, season, edible parts, preparation, estimated caloric value, and dangerous look-alikes. Calorie estimates are approximate and vary by growing conditions.

Cross-reference with foraging-basics.md for the Universal Edibility Test and general foraging principles. If you find mushrooms, see mushroom-identification.md — different rules apply entirely.

Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale)

Identification: Rosette of deeply toothed leaves radiating from a central base. Single yellow flower head on a hollow, leafless stem. Milky white sap. Taproot is light brown outside, white inside.

Habitat: Lawns, fields, roadsides, disturbed ground. Ubiquitous across temperate zones.

Season: Year-round in mild climates. Best: early spring (tender leaves), fall (roots store energy).

Edible parts: Entire plant — leaves, flowers, roots.

Preparation: - Leaves: eat raw in spring (mild). Summer leaves turn bitter; boil in two changes of water. - Flowers: eat raw, batter and fry, or dry for tea. - Roots: roast at 350 F (175 C) until dark brown, grind for coffee substitute. Or boil as a root vegetable.

Calories: ~25 per cup (55 g) of raw greens. Roots: ~75 per cup.

Look-alikes: Cat's ear (Hypochaeris radicata) — also edible, branching stems. Chicory — also edible, blue flowers. No dangerous look-alikes.

Cattail (Typha latifolia)

Identification: Tall (3-10 ft / 1-3 m), stiff, sword-like leaves. Distinctive brown cylindrical seed head ("corn dog" shape). Grows in dense stands in shallow water.

Habitat: Marshes, pond edges, ditches, slow streams. Found throughout the Northern Hemisphere.

Season: Year-round usability. Spring shoots, summer pollen, fall/winter roots.

Edible parts: Shoots, pollen, roots (rhizomes), immature flower heads.

Preparation: - Young shoots (spring): peel outer layers, eat raw or cooked. Taste similar to cucumber. - Pollen (early summer): shake yellow pollen from male flower head into a bag. Mix with flour or eat directly. High protein. - Roots: peel, then crush in water to release starch. Let starch settle, pour off water, dry the starch. Produces flour. - Immature flower head: boil and eat like corn on the cob.

Calories: Roots yield ~260 calories per cup (120 g) of starch. Pollen: ~450 calories per cup.

WARNING Do not confuse cattail with *Iris pseudacorus* (yellow flag iris), which grows in similar habitats. Iris has a fan-shaped leaf arrangement and yellow flowers — cattails never have colored flowers. Iris is toxic.

Look-alikes: Yellow flag iris (toxic) — fan-shaped leaf base vs. cattail's wrapped cylindrical base. Bur-reed — similar habitat but leaves are triangular in cross-section.

Broadleaf Plantain (Plantago major)

Identification: Low rosette of broad, oval leaves with prominent parallel veins (3-5 veins running lengthwise). Flower stalk is a narrow spike rising from the center. Not related to the banana-family plantain.

Habitat: Lawns, paths, compacted soil, disturbed areas. Extremely common.

Season: Spring through fall. Best in spring when leaves are tender.

Edible parts: Leaves, seeds.

Preparation: - Young leaves: eat raw in salads. Older leaves become stringy — remove veins or cook until tender. - Seeds: collect from mature flower spikes. Eat raw or grind into flour. Related to commercial psyllium.

Calories: ~15 per cup of leaves (35 g). Seeds are more calorie-dense.

Look-alikes: Hosta (ornamental, mildly toxic) — hostas have a more pronounced vein pattern and waxy texture. In the wild, confusion is unlikely.

Clover (Trifolium species)

Identification: Three-part (trifoliate) leaves, often with a lighter chevron marking. Round flower heads — white (T. repens) or red/pink (T. pratense). Low-growing.

Habitat: Fields, lawns, meadows, roadsides. Found across all temperate regions.

Season: Spring through fall. Flowers appear mid-spring to summer.

Edible parts: Leaves, flowers, seeds.

Preparation: - Leaves: eat raw in small quantities. Large amounts may cause bloating — cooking reduces this. - Flowers: eat raw, steep for tea, or dry and grind into flour supplement. - Seeds: small but nutritious. Collect from dried flower heads.

Calories: ~15 per cup of raw leaves.

Look-alikes: Wood sorrel (also edible — see below). Medick (Medicago) — also edible. No dangerous look-alikes for clover.

Wood Sorrel (Oxalis species)

Identification: Three heart-shaped leaflets (not oval like clover). Leaves fold down at night or in rain. Small five-petaled flowers, usually yellow or white. Distinctly sour/tangy taste (oxalic acid).

Habitat: Forest floors, shaded areas, gardens. Widespread.

Season: Spring through fall.

Edible parts: Leaves, flowers, seed pods.

Preparation: Eat raw as a trail nibble or salad addition. The sour flavor makes a good seasoning.

WARNING Contains oxalic acid. Eat in moderation. Avoid large quantities if you have kidney problems. Cooking does not reduce oxalic acid content.

Calories: Negligible (~10 per cup). Value is in vitamins and flavor.

Look-alikes: Clover (also edible). Heart-shaped leaflets distinguish sorrel from clover's rounded leaflets.

Chickweed (Stellaria media)

Identification: Small, low-growing plant with oval, opposite leaves. Tiny white flowers with 5 deeply divided petals (appear as 10). Single line of fine hairs running up one side of the stem, switching sides at each node.

Habitat: Gardens, fields, disturbed ground, shaded areas. Common weed worldwide.

Season: Early spring through late fall. One of the first and last greens available.

Edible parts: Leaves, stems, flowers — entire above-ground plant.

Preparation: Eat raw in salads or as a trail green. Mild, pleasant flavor. Can be cooked like spinach but loses volume drastically.

Calories: ~5-10 per cup. Nutritional value is in vitamins A and C.

Look-alikes: Scarlet pimpernel (Anagallis arvensis) — toxic. Distinguished by orange/red flowers (vs. white) and lacks the single hair line on the stem. Common mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium) — edible but fuzzy-leaved.

Acorns (Quercus species)

Identification: Familiar nut in a cap, produced by oak trees. White oaks (rounded leaf lobes) produce sweeter acorns. Red oaks (pointed leaf lobes) produce more bitter acorns.

Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests throughout temperate zones. Oaks are among the most common trees.

Season: Fall (September-November). Collect from the ground when they drop.

Edible parts: Nut meat (after processing).

Preparation: 1. Shell the acorns and remove the inner skin. 2. Crush or grind the nut meat. 3. Leach tannins by soaking in multiple changes of water. Cold water leaching: 1-2 weeks, changing water daily. Hot water leaching: boil in 3-5 changes of water until bitterness is gone. 4. Dry the meal and use as flour, porridge, or pressed cakes.

WARNING Do not eat unleached acorns. Tannins cause nausea, constipation, and kidney damage in quantity. Taste-test: if still bitter, leach more.

Calories: ~350-500 per cup (100 g) of processed acorn meal. One of the highest-calorie wild foods available.

Look-alikes: Buckeye/horse chestnut — toxic even after processing. Buckeyes have a smooth, round shell without a cap and compound palmate leaves (5-7 leaflets). Oaks have single, lobed leaves. Never confuse them.

Pine (Pinus species)

Identification: Needles in bundles (fascicles) of 2, 3, or 5. Cones. Resinous bark. Distinguished from other conifers by bundled needles (spruce/fir have single needles).

Habitat: Widespread across temperate, boreal, and montane forests.

Season: Year-round.

Edible parts: Needles (tea), inner bark (cambium), nuts (from certain species).

Preparation: - Needle tea: Chop a handful of fresh green needles. Steep in hot (not boiling) water for 10-15 minutes. Rich in vitamin C — historically used to prevent scurvy. Strain and drink. - Inner bark (cambium): Strip outer bark, then scrape the thin, moist inner bark layer. Eat raw (chewy, slightly sweet), dry and grind into flour, or fry into chips. - Pine nuts: Harvest from mature cones of nut-producing species (pinyon pine, stone pine, Korean pine). Pry open scales, extract seeds. Eat raw or roasted.

WARNING Avoid yew (*Taxus*), which resembles pine superficially but has flat needles, red berry-like arils, and no cones. Yew is extremely toxic. Also avoid ponderosa pine needle tea if pregnant — it can cause miscarriage.

Calories: Inner bark: ~500-600 per 100 g dried and ground. Pine nuts: ~670 per 100 g.

Look-alikes: Yew (deadly) — flat needles, no bundling, red fleshy arils. Spruce and fir — edible, similar uses but single needles.

Blackberry and Raspberry (Rubus species)

Identification: Thorny canes (some cultivars thornless). Compound leaves with 3-5 toothed leaflets. White or pink five-petaled flowers. Aggregate berries — blackberries are solid when picked; raspberries are hollow (slip off the receptacle).

Habitat: Forest edges, clearings, hedgerows, roadsides, disturbed areas. Form dense thickets.

Season: Berries ripen mid to late summer (June-September depending on latitude).

Edible parts: Berries, young leaves (tea), young shoots (peeled).

Preparation: Eat berries raw. Dry for later use. Leaves make a mild tea rich in tannins (astringent — useful for diarrhea).

Calories: ~60-70 per cup (150 g) of berries.

Look-alikes: No dangerous look-alikes. All aggregate berries (raspberry, blackberry, thimbleberry, salmonberry, wineberry) are edible. Pokeweed berries look nothing like these but grow in similar areas — pokeweed berries are small, dark purple, in grape-like clusters on a red stem. Avoid pokeweed.

Wild Onion and Wild Garlic (Allium species)

Identification: Grass-like or hollow tubular leaves growing from a bulb. Unmistakable onion or garlic smell when crushed. Globe-shaped flower cluster (umbel) of small white, pink, or purple flowers.

Habitat: Meadows, open woods, rocky slopes. Widespread.

Season: Spring (greens), summer (flowers), fall (bulbs best).

Edible parts: Entire plant — bulb, leaves, flowers.

Preparation: Eat raw or cooked. Use as seasoning for other wild foods. Bulbs can be roasted.

WARNING The smell test is critical. If it does not smell like onion or garlic, DO NOT eat it. Death camas (*Zigadenus*) and star-of-Bethlehem (*Ornithogalum*) look similar but lack the allium smell and are lethally toxic.

Calories: ~60 per cup chopped (160 g).

Look-alikes: Death camas (deadly) — no onion smell, grass-like leaves, white/cream flowers. Crow poison (Nothoscordum bivalve) — faint garlic smell or none, toxic. Always use the smell test.

Burdock (Arctium species)

Identification: Large, broad, heart-shaped leaves with woolly undersides. First-year plants form a basal rosette. Second-year plants send up a tall stalk with purple thistle-like flower heads that become brown burrs (the inspiration for Velcro).

Habitat: Roadsides, waste ground, forest edges. Common in disturbed areas.

Season: Best: first-year roots (fall) or second-year roots (early spring before stalk emerges).

Edible parts: Roots (primary), young leaf stalks (peeled), flower stalks (before flowering).

Preparation: - Roots: scrub, peel, slice. Boil 10-15 minutes or roast. Similar to potato in texture. - Leaf stalks: peel the bitter rind, boil the inner pith.

Calories: ~85 per cup (120 g) of cooked root. Starchy and filling.

Look-alikes: Rhubarb (edible stalks, toxic leaves) — rhubarb has red stalks and no burrs. Cocklebur (Xanthium) seedlings are toxic and can resemble young burdock — cocklebur has narrower, rougher leaves without woolly undersides.

Lamb's Quarters (Chenopodium album)

Identification: Diamond-shaped to triangular toothed leaves. Young leaves have a whitish, mealy coating (powdery, wipes off). Alternate leaves. Green, inconspicuous flower clusters. Grows 1-5 ft (30-150 cm) tall.

Habitat: Gardens, farmland, disturbed soil, waste areas. One of the most common weeds in the world.

Season: Spring through fall. Best when young.

Edible parts: Leaves, young shoots, seeds.

Preparation: - Leaves: eat raw when young. Cook like spinach — excellent flavor and nutrition. Cooking reduces oxalates. - Seeds: collect in fall. Grind into flour or cook as porridge. Related to quinoa.

Calories: ~10 per cup raw greens. Seeds: ~350 per 100 g.

WARNING Contains oxalic acid (like spinach). Cook to reduce oxalate content. Avoid eating large quantities raw.

Look-alikes: Nettles (edible, but sting on contact — different leaf shape). No dangerous look-alikes.

Purslane (Portulaca oleracea)

Identification: Succulent, low-growing. Thick, reddish stems. Small, paddle-shaped, fleshy leaves. Tiny yellow flowers. Breaks cleanly with a snap. Smooth, hairless.

Habitat: Gardens, cracks in pavement, disturbed ground, cultivated fields. Thrives in hot, dry conditions.

Season: Summer. Heat-loving plant.

Edible parts: Leaves, stems, flowers, seeds.

Preparation: Eat raw — crunchy, slightly lemony. Cook by sauteing or adding to soups. Mucilaginous when cooked (thickens liquids).

Calories: ~10 per cup. Notable for high omega-3 fatty acid content (unusual in plants). Excellent source of vitamins A, C, and E.

Look-alikes: Spurge (Euphorbia species) — toxic. Key distinction: spurge produces milky white sap when broken; purslane produces clear sap. Always break a stem and check.

Violets (Viola species)

Identification: Heart-shaped leaves. Distinctive five-petaled flowers (usually purple, also white or yellow). Low-growing, often forming ground cover.

Habitat: Moist woodlands, meadows, gardens. Widespread.

Season: Spring (flowers), spring through fall (leaves).

Edible parts: Leaves, flowers. Avoid roots and seeds of most species.

Preparation: Eat leaves and flowers raw in salads. Steep flowers for tea. Leaves can be cooked like spinach. Flowers make a natural food coloring.

Calories: Negligible. Value is in vitamins A and C.

Look-alikes: Lesser celandine (Ficaria verna) — mildly toxic, has glossy yellow flowers and more rounded leaves. Wild ginger — similar leaf shape but aromatic (edible in small amounts). Confusion is unlikely when flowers are present.

Rose Hips (Rosa species)

Identification: Fruit of wild roses. Small, round to oval, red/orange when ripe. Found below the withered flower petals. Rose bushes have thorns and compound leaves with toothed leaflets.

Habitat: Hedgerows, forest edges, meadows, roadsides. Wild roses are widespread.

Season: Late summer through winter. Best after first frost (softens and sweetens them).

Edible parts: The fleshy outer fruit. Remove seeds and irritating hairs inside.

Preparation: 1. Split the hip open. 2. Scrape out seeds and fine hairs. 3. Eat raw, steep for tea, or cook into jelly/syrup.

WARNING The fine hairs inside rose hips are irritating to the digestive tract. Always remove them. Strain tea through cloth.

Calories: ~45 per cup. Extremely high in vitamin C — up to 40x the vitamin C of an orange by weight.

Look-alikes: No dangerous look-alikes. Other rose-family fruits (hawthorn, crabapple) are also edible.

Wild Strawberry (Fragaria vesca / F. virginiana)

Identification: Three-part toothed leaves on long stalks. White five-petaled flowers with yellow centers. Small red berries with seeds on the surface. Runners (stolons) spread along the ground.

Habitat: Forest edges, meadows, open woods, trailsides.

Season: Late spring to early summer (fruit).

Edible parts: Fruit, leaves (tea).

Preparation: Eat berries raw. Steep leaves for mild tea.

Calories: ~45 per cup. Small size makes collection time-intensive.

Look-alikes: Mock strawberry (Duchesnea indica) — yellow flowers (not white), tasteless fruit. Not toxic, just flavorless. Indian strawberry is the same species. No dangerous look-alikes.

Watercress (Nasturtium officinale)

Identification: Small, round to oval leaflets in pairs along a stem, with a larger terminal leaflet. Grows in flowing water. White, four-petaled flowers (mustard family). Peppery taste.

Habitat: Clean, cold, flowing streams and springs. Avoid stagnant water.

Season: Year-round in mild climates. Best in spring and fall.

Edible parts: Leaves, stems.

Preparation: Eat raw if water source is clean. Cook (boil 5 minutes) if there is any risk of contamination — watercress from streams grazed by livestock can carry liver flukes.

WARNING Water hemlock (*Cicuta*) grows in the same habitat. Water hemlock has compound leaves with sharply toothed, lance-shaped leaflets and a chambered root — it is one of the most toxic plants in North America. Learn the differences thoroughly before harvesting any waterside plant.

Calories: ~5 per cup. Value is in vitamins and minerals (iron, calcium, vitamins A, C, K).

Look-alikes: Water hemlock (deadly) — taller, lance-shaped leaflets, different leaf arrangement. Fool's watercress (Apium nodiflorum) — edible but easily confused with toxic members of the carrot family.

Common Mistakes

  • Relying on a single identification feature — always confirm with at least 3 characteristics (leaf shape, flower, smell, growth habit, habitat)
  • Ignoring preparation requirements — acorns must be leached, some greens must be cooked to reduce oxalates
  • Harvesting from contaminated sites — avoid roadsides with heavy traffic, agricultural field edges (pesticide drift), industrial zones, and areas near standing water treated with herbicides
  • Overestimating caloric yield — greens keep you nourished with vitamins but do not provide survival-level calories. Prioritize nuts, roots, and seeds.
  • Foraging only familiar plants and ignoring abundance — learn whatever is most abundant in your area, even if it is less well-known

Quick Reference

Food

Mushroom Identification for Survival

Mushroom foraging can feed you or kill you — there is no middle ground and no universal safety test.

WARNING Mushroom misidentification kills experienced foragers every year. There is NO universal edibility test for mushrooms — the protocol in [foraging-basics.md](#foraging-basics) does NOT work for fungi. Some of the deadliest mushrooms taste pleasant, show no immediate symptoms, and kill you 3-7 days later through irreversible liver failure. If you have any doubt, do not eat it.
WARNING A single death cap (*Amanita phalloides*) mushroom contains enough toxin to kill an adult. Cooking, drying, freezing, or any other preparation does NOT neutralize the toxin. There is no field antidote.

At a Glance

  • There is no universal test, rule, or trick that distinguishes edible mushrooms from deadly ones
  • Start with species that have NO deadly look-alikes — chicken of the woods, giant puffball, morels
  • Learn the deadly species first so you know what to always avoid
  • Spore prints, gill structure, habitat, and smell are your primary identification tools
  • When in doubt, do not eat it. Period. Ever.

The Reality of Mushroom Foraging

Mushroom identification is not like plant identification. Plants have families with consistent safe/unsafe patterns. Mushrooms do not. Two nearly identical-looking species may differ only in spore color — one is edible, the other is fatal.

What Does Not Work

  • The silver spoon test (myth: a silver spoon turns black near toxic mushrooms) — false
  • The garlic test (myth: garlic turns brown when cooked with toxic mushrooms) — false
  • The peel test (myth: if the cap peels easily, it is safe) — false
  • The insect test (myth: if insects eat it, it is safe for humans) — false. Insects tolerate amatoxins that destroy human livers.
  • The cooking test (myth: cooking destroys all mushroom toxins) — false. Amatoxins survive boiling, frying, and drying.

What Works

Positive identification using multiple features: cap shape and color, gill/pore structure, spore print color, stipe (stem) features, habitat, season, smell, and cross-referencing with reliable field guides.

Safe Beginner Species

These species have distinctive features and no deadly look-alikes when properly identified. Start here.

Chicken of the Woods (Laetiporus sulphureus and related species)

Identification: - Bright orange to yellow-orange shelf/bracket fungus growing on wood - No gills — underside has tiny pores - Grows in overlapping shelves/fans - Soft and fleshy when young; becomes tough and chalky with age - No stem (grows directly from wood) - Size: individual shelves 2-12 in (5-30 cm) wide

Habitat: Dead or living hardwood trees (oak is most common). Occasionally on conifers (some people react poorly to conifer-grown specimens — avoid those).

Season: Late spring through fall.

Edible when: Young and tender (edges should feel soft and moist). Discard any that are tough, dry, or have faded to pale white.

Preparation: Slice and saute in oil or butter for 15-20 minutes. Has a texture often compared to chicken. Cook thoroughly — some people experience GI upset from undercooked specimens.

Calories: ~30-35 per cup (70 g) cooked.

Possible confusion: Older, faded specimens could theoretically be confused with other shelf fungi, but no deadly ones share the bright orange coloring of fresh chicken of the woods. Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms (Omphalotus olearius) are orange but have true gills and grow from buried wood on a central stem — they cause severe GI distress but are not deadly.

WARNING A small percentage of people react to chicken of the woods with GI symptoms regardless of preparation. Eat a small amount the first time and wait 24 hours.

Giant Puffball (Calvatia gigantea)

Identification: - Large, white, round to irregular ball — 4-20+ in (10-50+ cm) diameter - No stem, gills, cap, or any other mushroom structures — just a solid white ball - Interior (gleba) must be uniformly white and firm when sliced open, like a marshmallow - Skin is smooth to slightly rough, white to off-white

Habitat: Meadows, pastures, open woods, lawns. On the ground (not on wood).

Season: Late summer through fall.

The critical test: Slice every puffball in half before eating. The interior must be: - Uniformly pure white - Firm and solid (no soft spots, no discoloration) - No outline of a developing mushroom visible inside

WARNING Young *Amanita* (including death cap and destroying angel) start as white, egg-shaped buttons that can resemble small puffballs. When sliced open, a developing *Amanita* shows the outline of a mushroom (cap, gills, stem) inside. A true puffball is uniformly white with no internal structure. ALWAYS SLICE AND CHECK. If you see any internal structure, any yellow, brown, green, or purple discoloration — discard it.

Preparation: Slice into 1/2 in (1 cm) slabs. Fry, bread and fry, or add to soups. Mild flavor absorbs seasonings well.

Calories: ~20 per cup.

Possible confusion: Only dangerous if you eat small, uncut specimens that could be Amanita buttons. Slicing eliminates this risk completely. Other puffball species (pear-shaped, gem-studded) are also edible when white inside.

Morels (Morchella species)

Identification: - Distinctive honeycomb or sponge-like cap with pits and ridges - Cap is attached to the stem at the base of the cap - Hollow from top to bottom — slice in half to confirm both the cap and stem are hollow - Color ranges from tan/yellow (yellow morel) to dark brown/black (black morel) - Size: 2-6 in (5-15 cm) tall

Habitat: Deciduous forests, burned areas (especially productive 1 year after wildfire), near dead elms, tulip poplars, ash. Well-drained soil.

Season: Spring (April-June depending on latitude). One of the earliest edible mushrooms.

The critical test: Slice in half lengthwise. True morels are completely hollow from cap to stem base. The cap is attached at the base (not hanging free like a skirt).

WARNING: False Morels *Gyromitra esculenta* and related species are brain-like or wrinkled (not pitted/honeycombed). When cut open, false morels are NOT hollow — they contain cottony, chambered, or solid tissue. False morels contain gyromitrin, which metabolizes to monomethylhydrazine (rocket fuel component). Can cause death. Key differences: | Feature | True Morel | False Morel | |---------|-----------|-------------| | Cap surface | Pits and ridges (honeycomb) | Wrinkled, brain-like, lobed | | Interior | Completely hollow | Chambered, cottony, or solid | | Cap attachment | Attached at base of cap | Often attached at top of stem (hangs like a skirt) | | Stem | Single hollow chamber | Irregular chambers or solid |

Preparation: Never eat morels raw — they contain hydrazine compounds that are destroyed by cooking. Saute, fry, or add to soups. Cook for at least 5 minutes at full heat.

Calories: ~20 per cup.

Chanterelles (Cantharellus cibarius and related species)

Identification: - Golden yellow to egg-yolk orange - Funnel or trumpet-shaped when mature, convex when young - False gills: blunt, forking ridges running down the stem (not thin, blade-like true gills) - Flesh is white to pale yellow when cut - Smells fruity or apricot-like - Size: 1-5 in (2-12 cm) cap diameter

Habitat: Forest floors, especially near oaks, conifers, and beech. Mycorrhizal (associated with living tree roots). Found on the ground, never on wood.

Season: Summer through fall (varies by region).

Preparation: Saute dry (without oil initially to cook off moisture), then add fat. Cook 8-10 minutes. Excellent flavor.

Calories: ~20 per cup.

Possible confusion: - Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus olearius) — true, thin, blade-like gills (not blunt ridges). Grows in dense clusters on wood or from buried wood. Orange throughout (chanterelles are white/pale inside). Causes severe vomiting but is not deadly. - False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) — thinner, more regularly-spaced true gills. Darker orange cap center. Less fragrant. Causes GI upset in some people.

Feature True Chanterelle Jack-o'-Lantern
Gills Blunt, forking ridges Thin, blade-like, crowded
Growth Solitary or scattered, from soil Dense clusters, from wood
Flesh color White/pale when cut Orange throughout
Smell Fruity, apricot Unpleasant or neutral

Deadly Species — Learn to Recognize and Always Avoid

Death Cap (Amanita phalloides)

The single most deadly mushroom in the world. Responsible for over 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings globally.

Identification: - Cap: 2-6 in (5-15 cm), greenish-yellow to olive-brown (can be pale or white in some forms) - White gills (free — not attached to stem) - White spore print - White stem with a skirt-like ring (annulus) - Bulbous base enclosed in a cup-like volva (often buried — dig to check) - Pleasant smell (or no distinctive smell) - Pleasant taste (this is what makes it so deadly — victims often enjoy eating it)

Habitat: Near oaks, especially in imported soil. Increasingly common in North America (originally European). Urban parks, landscaped areas, and oak woodlands.

Symptoms: 6-12 hours after ingestion: severe GI symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain). Then a deceptive improvement period (24-72 hours) where the victim feels better. Then liver and kidney failure. Death in 3-7 days without liver transplant. By the time symptoms begin, the damage is already underway.

No treatment exists in the field. If ingestion is suspected, seek emergency medical care immediately.

Destroying Angel (Amanita bisporigera, A. virosa, A. ocreata)

Identification: - Pure white — cap, gills, stem, ring, and volva are all white - Same structure as death cap: free gills, ring on stem, bulbous base with volva - Cap: 2-5 in (5-12 cm), smooth, white - White spore print

Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests. Widespread in North America and Europe.

Symptoms: Identical to death cap. Same amatoxins, same delayed onset, same lethality.

Galerina marginata (Funeral Bell / Deadly Galerina)

Identification: - Small, brown, nondescript mushroom — easily overlooked or dismissed as "just another little brown mushroom" - Cap: 0.5-2.5 in (1.5-6 cm), brown to tawny, smooth, slightly sticky when wet - Brown spore print - Ring on stem (may be faint or missing in older specimens) - Grows on decaying wood

Habitat: Dead wood (logs, stumps, wood chips) in forests.

Why it matters: Contains the same amatoxins as death caps and destroying angels. Commonly confused with edible honey mushrooms (Armillaria), edible Kuehneromyces, and magic mushrooms (Psilocybe). This confusion has killed multiple people.

Distinguishing from honey mushrooms: Galerina has a brown spore print; honey mushrooms have a white to cream spore print. Always take a spore print.

Key Identification Techniques

Taking a Spore Print

  1. Remove the stem from a mature mushroom cap.
  2. Place the cap gill-side down on a piece of paper (half white, half dark — this lets you see both light and dark spore colors).
  3. Cover with a bowl or glass to prevent air drafts.
  4. Wait 4-12 hours.
  5. Lift the cap carefully. The spore deposit reveals color and pattern.
Spore Print Color Indicates
White Many species — both edible and deadly (Amanita)
Brown Possible Galerina (deadly), also many edible species
Pink Possible Entoloma (some toxic), also edible meadow mushrooms
Black/dark purple-brown Possible Agaricus (edible), Coprinopsis (edible), Psathyrella
Rusty orange-brown Galerina (deadly), Cortinarius (some deadly)

Spore print alone never confirms safety. Use it as one of several identification features.

Gill Attachment

  • Free: Gills do not touch the stem. Common in Amanita (many deadly) and Agaricus (mostly edible).
  • Attached (adnate): Gills connect to the stem broadly.
  • Decurrent: Gills run down the stem. Common in chanterelles and oyster mushrooms.
  • Notched (adnexed): Gills narrowly attached.

Cap Features to Note

  • Shape: convex, flat, funnel-shaped, bell-shaped, conical
  • Surface: smooth, sticky, scaly, fibrous, dry
  • Color (note: color changes with age and weather)
  • Margin: even, wavy, striate (lined), inrolled

Stem Features

  • Ring (annulus): present or absent
  • Volva (cup at base): present or absent — DIG to check. A volva suggests Amanita.
  • Texture: smooth, fibrous, scaly
  • Interior: solid, hollow, stuffed (cottony pith)

Smell

  • Anise/licorice: some Agaricus, Clitocybe species
  • Meal/flour (farinaceous): various species
  • Fishy or unpleasant: often a warning sign
  • Apricot/fruity: chanterelles
  • Chlorine/chemical: avoid
  • No smell: inconclusive

Regional Variation

WARNING Mushroom species vary by region, continent, and microclimate. A guide written for the Pacific Northwest may lead you to misidentify a species in the southeastern US or Europe. Use region-specific field guides. Consult local mycological societies. What is common and safe in one area may be absent or have different look-alikes in another.

Common Mistakes

  • Trusting color alone — color varies with age, weather, and genetics. One species can range from pale to dark.
  • Eating any small brown mushroom — the "LBM" (little brown mushroom) category contains numerous deadly species. Avoid all LBMs unless you are an expert.
  • Not digging up the base — the volva of Amanita species is often buried underground. Cutting the stem at ground level hides this critical identification feature.
  • Assuming local knowledge transfers globally — edible species in one region have deadly counterparts in others.
  • Eating raw mushrooms — most wild mushrooms should be thoroughly cooked. Some edible species are toxic when raw.
  • Relying on smartphone apps — misidentification rates in mushroom ID apps are dangerously high. Never trust an app with your life.
  • Collecting specimens of mixed ages — young and old mushrooms of the same species look different. Collect multiple developmental stages for identification.
  • "My friend eats these" — anecdotal identification is how people die. Confirm identification yourself.

Quick Reference

Safe Beginner Species (No Deadly Look-alikes)

Species Key Feature Season Where
Chicken of the Woods Orange shelf fungus, pores not gills Late spring-fall On wood
Giant Puffball Large white ball, pure white inside Late summer-fall Ground, meadows
Morels Honeycomb cap, completely hollow Spring Forest floor
Chanterelles False gills (blunt ridges), apricot smell Summer-fall Forest floor

Always Avoid

Species Key Feature Why
Death Cap Green-olive cap, white gills, volva, ring Destroys liver, fatal
Destroying Angel All white, volva, ring Same toxin as death cap
Galerina marginata Small, brown, on wood, ring Same toxin as death cap
Little Brown Mushrooms (LBMs) Any small, brown, unidentified species Too many deadly possibilities

The One Rule

If you are not 100% certain of your identification, do not eat it. No meal is worth risking amatoxin poisoning. There is no field treatment for liver failure.

Hunting Basics

Track, stalk, and harvest game animals using fundamental skills and improvised weapons when modern tools are unavailable.

At a Glance

  • Hunting burns significant calories — assess whether the expected return justifies the expenditure
  • Tracking is the foundation: learn to read tracks, scat, trails, bedding areas, and feeding signs
  • Wind direction and noise discipline determine whether you get close enough for a shot or strike
  • Improvised weapons are limited in range and lethality — ambush and close-range encounters are your advantage
  • Process kills quickly to prevent spoilage; field dress within 30 minutes in warm weather
WARNING Hunting is regulated by law in every jurisdiction. Seasons, species, methods, and licensing requirements apply. In a non-emergency context, obtain all required permits and follow applicable regulations. In a genuine survival emergency, sustaining your life takes precedence — report any takes to authorities after rescue.

Tracking Fundamentals

Reading Tracks

What to observe: - Species: Shape and size of the print. Cloven hooves = deer, elk, moose, pigs. Paw pads with claws = canines (dog, coyote, fox). Paw pads without visible claws = felines. Long hind feet = rabbits. - Direction of travel: Toes point in the direction of movement. Deeper impression at the toe = the animal was moving quickly. - Age of track: Sharp edges = fresh (hours). Crumbling edges, debris in the print = older (12+ hours). Tracks partially filled with water in mud = made before the water rose. Tracks with frost crystals in cold weather = made before the freeze (overnight or older). - Gait: Walking tracks are evenly spaced. Running tracks are spaced further apart with deeper toe impressions and spray of substrate behind the print.

Common Track Sizes

Animal Front Track Width Notes
White-tailed deer 2-3.5 in (5-9 cm) Cloven hoof, heart-shaped
Rabbit (cottontail) 1 in (2.5 cm) front, 3-4 in (7-10 cm) hind Hind prints land ahead of front
Squirrel 0.5-1 in (1-2.5 cm) Four toes front, five toes hind
Turkey 4-4.5 in (10-11 cm) Three forward toes, distinctive
Raccoon 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) Hand-like, five toes
Wild boar/feral pig 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) Cloven, rounder than deer

Scat (Droppings)

Scat reveals diet, species, and recency.

  • Deer: Piles of small, oval pellets (3/4 in / 2 cm). Soft/clumped when feeding on green browse. Hard, separated pellets on dry diet.
  • Rabbit: Small, round, fibrous pellets. Often near burrow entrances.
  • Carnivore scat: Twisted, tapered, often containing hair and bone fragments.
  • Bird (turkey, grouse): J-shaped or cylindrical with a white uric acid cap.
  • Freshness: Moist, dark, strong-smelling = fresh (hours). Dry, gray, crumbling, odorless = old (days to weeks).

Trails and Runs

  • Deer trails: 6-12 in (15-30 cm) wide, worn through vegetation, often connecting bedding areas (thick cover on high ground) to feeding areas (meadows, crop edges) and water.
  • Rabbit runs: 4-6 in (10-15 cm) wide tunnels through grass or brush. Used repeatedly. Excellent locations for snares (see trapping-and-snares.md).
  • Game highways: Near water sources, multiple species use the same approach routes. Look for overlapping tracks of different species.

Bedding Areas

  • Deer bed in thick cover, usually on elevated ground with sight lines and escape routes.
  • Look for flattened ovals in grass, leaves, or snow — 3-4 ft (1-1.2 m) long for deer.
  • Droppings and hair near bedding confirm use.
  • Do not hunt in bedding areas — you will push animals out permanently. Hunt between bedding and feeding/water instead.

Feeding Signs

  • Browse lines: Ragged, torn ends on twigs and branches (deer lack upper incisors and tear rather than cut cleanly).
  • Rooting: Disturbed soil where pigs or bears have dug for roots, grubs, or tubers.
  • Scratching/rubbing: Antler rubs on trees (deer). Bark stripped by bears. Scratched ground under nut trees (turkeys, squirrels).
  • Crop and mast damage: Edge of agricultural fields, under oak or beech trees (acorn mast).

Stalking Technique

Wind Direction

Wind carries your scent. A deer can smell you from over 300 yards (275 m) downwind.

  • Always approach from downwind — the wind blows from the animal toward you.
  • Check wind direction constantly: wet a finger and feel for cooling, drop light debris and watch it drift, observe smoke direction.
  • If the wind shifts, stop. Reposition or abort the stalk.
  • Thermals: in the morning, cool air flows downhill (hunt above your target). In the afternoon, warm air rises uphill (hunt below).

Noise Discipline

  • Step placement: Place the ball of your foot first, feel for sticks and debris, then lower your heel. Avoid stepping on dry leaves, twigs, or gravel.
  • Speed: Move one slow step at a time. Pause between steps. Natural background noise (wind, running water, other animals) provides cover — move when the wind gusts.
  • Clothing: Avoid synthetic fabrics that swish and scrape. Wool and soft cotton are quieter.
  • Equipment: Secure anything that rattles, clanks, or jingles. Tape or tie loose items.

Movement Patterns

  • Move in short segments: 3-5 steps, then stop and observe for 30-60 seconds.
  • Use the terrain: stay behind ridgelines, use trees and brush for concealment.
  • Avoid skylining yourself (appearing as a silhouette on a ridgeline or hilltop).
  • Break your outline — humans are recognized by their upright, symmetrical shape.
  • Approach from higher ground when possible — animals watch for threats at their level, not above.
  • Best times to stalk: dawn and dusk (animals are active and feeding, light is low).

The Final Approach

  • Inside 50 yards (45 m), every movement matters. Animals at close range detect the smallest twitch.
  • Move only when the animal's head is down (feeding, drinking).
  • Freeze when the animal looks up — motion triggers flight response, but a stationary shape may not.
  • Be in position before you need to be. Set up on a trail, a water approach, or a feeding area and let the animal come to you (ambush) rather than closing the final distance.

Kill Zones by Animal Type

Effective shots or strikes must hit vital areas. With improvised weapons, range is limited — proximity and accuracy matter enormously.

Deer / Large Ungulates

  • Heart/lung zone: Behind the front shoulder, lower third of the body. This is the primary target. Heart sits low, lungs fill the chest cavity. A broadside shot into this area is the most lethal placement.
  • Size of kill zone: Approximately 8-10 in (20-25 cm) diameter.
  • Avoid: Head shots (small target, easy to wound), gut shots (slow death, meat contamination), leg shots (cripples without killing).

Rabbit

  • Head/upper body: Small target. A blunt impact weapon (throwing stick) to the head or body is effective.
  • Behavior advantage: Rabbits freeze when startled and rely on camouflage before bolting. This freeze moment is your opportunity.

Birds (Turkey, Grouse, Pheasant)

  • Head/neck: For birds, target the head and neck — the body is protected by thick feathers that deflect weak projectiles.
  • On the ground: Ground-dwelling birds are easier targets than birds in flight. Turkeys and grouse often walk rather than fly when disturbed.
  • At roost: Birds on a roosting branch at dusk are stationary targets.

Small Mammals (Squirrel, Raccoon)

  • Body shot: Center mass. Small mammals do not present a large kill zone — aim for the torso.
  • Trapping is more efficient for these species. See trapping-and-snares.md.

Improvised Weapons

WARNING Improvised weapons are far less effective than purpose-built hunting tools. Expect a high miss rate. Supplement with passive trapping and fishing methods.

Throwing Stick (Rabbit Stick)

The simplest hunting weapon — a heavy, curved stick thrown sidearm at close-range targets.

Construction: 1. Select a hardwood stick or branch, slightly curved, 18-30 in (45-75 cm) long, 1-2 in (2.5-5 cm) diameter. 2. Weight should be concentrated toward one end (a natural club shape works well). 3. Smooth any knots that affect flight.

Technique: - Throw sidearm with a flat trajectory, 2-4 ft (60-120 cm) off the ground. - Effective range: 15-30 ft (5-10 m). Beyond this, accuracy drops rapidly. - Best against: rabbits, ground birds, roosting birds at close range. - Carry 2-3 throwing sticks — you get one throw before the animal flees.

Bola

Two or three weights connected by cordage. Thrown at the legs or body of an animal to entangle it.

Construction: 1. Select 2-3 smooth, heavy stones, each 4-8 oz (110-225 g). 2. Wrap each stone in a pouch of fabric or rawhide and tie securely. 3. Connect the pouches with cordage 18-24 in (45-60 cm) long. For a three-stone bola, tie all three cords together at a central point.

Technique: - Hold the center knot and whirl the bola overhead. - Release toward the target at close range — 15-30 ft (5-10 m). - The spinning weights spread and wrap around legs, wings, or neck. - Best against: ground birds (turkeys, geese), medium mammals in the open.

Sling

A pouch attached to two cords. Whirled overhead to launch a stone at high velocity.

Construction: 1. Cut a pouch from leather, sturdy fabric, or woven plant fiber — approximately 3 x 5 in (7.5 x 12.5 cm). 2. Punch holes at each end of the pouch. 3. Attach two cords, each 24-36 in (60-90 cm) long. One cord has a finger loop; the other has a knot or smooth end for release.

Technique: 1. Place a round, egg-sized stone (1.5-2 in / 4-5 cm) in the pouch. 2. Grip the loop on one cord with your index finger, hold the release cord between your thumb and forefinger. 3. Whirl overhead or beside you (vertical or horizontal). 4. Release the free cord at the right moment in the arc to send the stone at the target. 5. This requires extensive practice. Accuracy improves dramatically with repetition.

Effective range: 30-100 ft (10-30 m) with practice. Lethal to small-medium game. Can take rabbits, birds, and even stun or kill larger animals with well-placed head shots.

Atlatl (Spear Thrower) — Concept

A lever arm that extends the length of the throwing arm, increasing spear velocity and range.

Concept: 1. Cut a straight branch 18-24 in (45-60 cm) long. 2. Carve or attach a hook/spur at one end that catches the butt of a dart (light spear). 3. Carve darts: straight shafts 4-6 ft (1.2-1.8 m) long with fire-hardened or stone/bone tips. 4. Place the dart butt against the spur, hold the atlatl behind the dart, and throw in an overhand motion — the atlatl acts as a lever.

Advantages: Doubles effective range and increases impact force compared to hand-thrown spears. Used by humans for tens of thousands of years before the bow.

Limitations: Requires significant practice. Darts must be straight and consistent. Not a weapon you build and use effectively on day one.

Field Processing

Detailed butchering procedures are covered in field-butchering.md. The essentials:

  1. Field dress immediately — within 30 minutes, especially in warm weather. Gut bacteria multiply rapidly and taint meat.
  2. Open the body cavity from sternum to pelvis. Remove all internal organs.
  3. Save the heart and liver — the most nutrient-dense organs.
  4. Drain blood — hang or prop the carcass to drain. Blood attracts predators and accelerates spoilage.
  5. Cool the meat — get air circulating inside the body cavity. In warm weather, shade the carcass and consider quartering for faster cooling.
  6. Protect from flies — flies lay eggs within minutes. Cover the meat with cloth or place in a game bag. Smoke deters insects.

Energy Expenditure vs. Caloric Return

This is the critical calculation in a survival situation. Hunting burns enormous calories — often for zero return.

The Math

Activity Calories Burned per Hour Success Probability Expected Caloric Return
Stalking deer (improvised weapon) 200-400 Very low (under 5%) High if successful: 25,000-40,000 cal
Sitting in ambush 80-120 Low-Moderate (5-15%) Variable
Rabbit hunting (throwing stick) 150-300 Low (10-20%) Moderate: 500-800 cal per rabbit
Bird hunting (throwing stick/sling) 150-250 Low (5-15%) Low-Moderate: 200-600 cal per bird
Setting snares (labor) 150-250 (one-time) Moderate (20-40% per trap line/night) Moderate: 500-800 cal per rabbit
Fishing (active, improvised) 100-200 Moderate-High (30-60%) Variable: 200-1,000+ cal per session
Fishing (passive, traps/nets) 200-400 (one-time build) Moderate-High (40-70% ongoing) Ongoing: hundreds of calories daily

When Hunting Is Worth It

  • You have a high-probability ambush opportunity (game at close range, moving toward you)
  • You are sheltered in place with time and energy to spare
  • Large game is present (one deer feeds you for weeks)
  • You have an effective weapon (even improvised) and have practiced with it
  • Terrain allows close-range encounters (thick forest, narrow valleys)

When Hunting Is Not Worth It

  • You are calorie-depleted and physically weak — a failed hunt worsens your situation
  • Only small game is available and terrain makes approach difficult
  • You have no effective weapon and no materials to make one
  • Open terrain prevents close-range stalking
  • Better alternatives exist (fishing, trapping, foraging)

General rule: Passive methods (traps, nets, set lines) are almost always more calorie-efficient than active hunting. Set traps and fish first; hunt only when opportunity presents itself or when large game justifies the energy investment.

Legal and Ethical Framework

Survival Context

In a genuine survival emergency, preserving your life is the priority. Most legal systems recognize a necessity defense for taking game out of season or without a license when your life is at risk. After rescue:

  • Report what you took, when, and where to the relevant wildlife agency
  • Cooperate fully with any investigation
  • Document your situation if possible (the survival context justifies the take)

Non-Survival Context

  • Obtain all required licenses and permits before hunting
  • Follow all season, method, and bag limit regulations
  • Use the most humane method available
  • Track and retrieve all wounded animals — do not leave them to suffer
  • Respect private property and obtain permission
  • Follow all firearm/weapon safety regulations

Ethical Principles (All Contexts)

  • Take only what you need
  • Use all edible parts of the animal
  • Kill cleanly — target vital areas for quick, humane kills
  • Do not hunt breeding animals with dependent young when avoidable
  • Respect the animal — it is giving its life to sustain yours

Common Mistakes

  • Hunting when you should be trapping — active hunting burns calories with low success rates. Set traps first.
  • Ignoring wind direction — this is the number one reason stalks fail. Check constantly.
  • Moving too fast — patience is the stalker's primary weapon. Slow down by half, then slow down again.
  • Targeting too-large game with inadequate weapons — an improvised spear against a deer is a very low-probability gamble. Focus on small game unless you have a clear advantage.
  • Not scouting first — spend time observing before hunting. Learn the animals' patterns, routes, and timing.
  • Hunting in bedding areas — you push animals out and they relocate. Hunt travel routes instead.
  • Failing to field dress quickly — meat spoils within hours in warm weather. Process immediately.
  • Underestimating the difficulty of the kill shot — animals are fast, vital areas are small, and adrenaline ruins accuracy. Practice with your weapon before you depend on it.

Quick Reference

Element Key Principle
Wind Always approach from downwind
Movement Slow, deliberate, pause frequently
Timing Dawn and dusk — peak animal activity
Kill zone (deer) Behind front shoulder, lower third
Kill zone (rabbit) Head/upper body — blunt impact
Kill zone (bird) Head and neck
Best improvised weapon Throwing stick (simplest, most versatile)
Field dress Within 30 minutes
Energy rule Passive methods (traps/fishing) before active hunting
