Food

Trapping and Snares

Traps work while you sleep — invest time building them, then spend your energy on other survival tasks.

At a Glance

  • Trapping is more calorie-efficient than active hunting in most survival situations
  • Set a minimum of 6-12 traps to have a reasonable chance of catching anything
  • Check traps at least every 12 hours — animal suffering, predator theft, and spoilage are real problems
  • Game trails, water sources, and funneling terrain are your highest-probability trap sites
  • Know the legal framework: trapping is heavily regulated in non-survival contexts
WARNING Trapping animals is illegal in most jurisdictions outside of genuine survival emergencies. Regulations cover trap types, species, seasons, and licensing. In a non-emergency context, obtain proper permits and follow all applicable laws.

Game Trail Identification

Before building any trap, find where animals travel. A trap on a trail catches game; a trap in a random spot catches nothing.

Signs of Active Game Trails

  • Tracks: Clear prints in soft soil, mud, or snow. Note size and frequency — multiple overlapping prints indicate a well-used trail.
  • Scat (droppings): Fresh droppings near a trail confirm recent and active use. Dry, crumbling droppings indicate old or abandoned routes.
  • Runs: Narrow, worn paths through grass or underbrush, 4-8 in (10-20 cm) wide for rabbits, wider for deer.
  • Browse lines: Chewed vegetation at consistent heights along a path.
  • Hair/fur: Caught on branches, bark, or fencing along the route.
  • Funneling terrain: Natural narrowing points — between rocks, along fence lines, through gaps in brush, between water and a hillside. Animals follow paths of least resistance.

Best Trap Locations

  • Trail bottlenecks (natural funnels)
  • Near water sources (streams, ponds)
  • Along fence lines or walls
  • Entrances to burrows and dens
  • Feeding areas (nut-producing trees, berry patches)
  • Between bedding areas and food/water

Simple Snare

The most fundamental survival trap. A wire or cordage loop positioned on a game trail that tightens around an animal as it passes through.

Materials

  • Wire: 20-24 gauge brass or stainless steel wire, 2-3 ft (60-90 cm) length. Ideal material.
  • Cordage alternative: Paracord inner strands, bank line, or strong natural cordage (rawhide, sinew, braided plant fiber). Wire is far superior — cordage can be chewed through.
  • Anchor: Sturdy stake, tree, or heavy drag (log/branch)

Construction

  1. Form a small loop at one end of the wire by twisting the wire around itself 4-5 times. This creates the locking eye.
  2. Thread the free end through the small loop, creating an adjustable noose.
  3. Size the noose opening:
  4. Rabbit: 3-4 in (7.5-10 cm) diameter, bottom of loop 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) off the ground
  5. Squirrel: 2-2.5 in (5-6 cm) diameter
  6. Larger game: scale accordingly
  7. Anchor the free end to a solid stake driven deep into the ground, or tie to a tree/heavy log.
  8. Position the noose across the game trail, supported by small twigs or natural features so it hangs in the path at head height for the target animal.
  9. Add guide sticks on either side of the trail to funnel the animal through the snare loop.

Placement Tips

  • Set the snare in a slight narrowing of the trail.
  • Use sticks and brush to create a subtle funnel directing animals through the loop. Do not create an obvious barrier — animals will divert.
  • Minimize ground disturbance and human scent. Wear gloves if available. Rub the snare with local vegetation or soil.
  • Wire maintains its shape in wind and rain; cordage may sag.

Drag Snare

A snare attached to a drag (heavy branch or log) instead of a fixed anchor. The animal pulls the drag, which catches on vegetation and exhausts the animal without the snare breaking from the force of a panicked animal hitting a fixed point.

Materials

Same as simple snare, plus a drag — a branch 3-5 ft (1-1.5 m) long with side branches that catch on brush.

Construction

  1. Build the snare loop as described above.
  2. Instead of anchoring to a fixed point, tie the free end to the drag branch.
  3. Position the drag near the trail but not directly in the path.
  4. The animal enters the snare, pulls the drag, and the drag tangles in surrounding vegetation.

When to Use

  • When a fixed anchor is not available
  • For larger animals that might break a fixed snare
  • When you cannot drive stakes into frozen or rocky ground

Spring Snare

Uses a bent sapling or branch under tension to lift the caught animal off the ground, keeping it away from scavengers and preventing escape.

Materials

  • Snare wire or cordage (noose)
  • Flexible sapling or bent branch (spring pole), 5-8 ft (1.5-2.5 m) long
  • Trigger mechanism (carved sticks)
  • Cordage connecting spring pole to snare via trigger
  • Anchor stake

Trigger Mechanisms

Two-Pin Toggle Trigger

  1. Carve two small sticks, each 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) long, with a notch near one end.
  2. Drive one stick (the base pin) into the ground at a slight angle.
  3. Tie the spring pole line to the second stick (the toggle pin).
  4. Hook the notches together so the tension of the spring pole holds them in place.
  5. Attach the snare loop so that when an animal pulls on it, the toggle pin disengages from the base pin, releasing the spring pole.

L-Hook Trigger

  1. Carve two sticks into L-shapes (or carve notches to create hook shapes).
  2. One L-hook drives into the ground; the other attaches to the spring pole line.
  3. The hooks interlock under tension. The snare loop attaches so that any lateral pull disengages the hooks.

Construction Steps

  1. Identify or plant a flexible sapling near the trail.
  2. Bend the sapling down and test its spring — it must lift the target animal clear of the ground.
  3. Set the trigger mechanism at ground level on the trail.
  4. Connect the spring pole to the trigger.
  5. Attach the snare noose to the trigger assembly so pulling the noose releases the trigger.
  6. Position the noose across the trail at the target animal's head height.
  7. Test the trigger by gently pulling the snare loop — it should release smoothly.
WARNING Spring snares are under tension. Keep your face and hands clear of the spring pole path during setup. A sapling snapping back can cause serious injury.

Deadfall Traps

Use a heavy weight (flat rock or log) propped up by a trigger mechanism. When the trigger is disturbed, the weight falls and kills the animal.

Figure-4 Deadfall

The most well-known deadfall trigger. Three sticks notched to interlock in a figure-4 pattern.

Materials

  • Heavy flat rock, 5-15 lbs (2-7 kg) depending on target animal (heavier for larger animals)
  • Three sticks: upright, diagonal, and horizontal (bait bar), each 6-10 in (15-25 cm) long
  • Knife for carving notches
  • Bait

Construction

  1. Upright stick (vertical post): Flatten one end to rest on the ground. Carve a square notch near the top (the diagonal stick hooks here). Carve a second square notch midway (the horizontal bait bar hooks here).
  2. Diagonal stick (prop): Carve a point at the top that rests against the underside of the rock. Carve a square notch at the bottom that interlocks with the top notch of the upright.
  3. Horizontal stick (bait bar): Carve a point or notch at the end that engages the mid-point notch of the upright. The other end supports the rock edge. Bait goes on the free end.
  4. Assembly:
  5. Stand the upright on its flat base.
  6. Hook the diagonal stick into the upright's top notch, angling upward to prop the rock.
  7. Hook the bait bar into the upright's middle notch, extending under the rock.
  8. Balance the rock on the diagonal stick (top) and bait bar (side).
  9. The three sticks and rock should be in equilibrium. When an animal touches the bait bar, the system collapses.

Tips

  • Practice carving and assembling the figure-4 without the rock until you can do it smoothly.
  • The notches must be precise — too tight and the trap will not fire; too loose and wind triggers it.
  • Position the rock so it falls cleanly on the kill zone (where the animal reaches for bait).
  • Flat rocks work best. Round rocks roll off-target.

Paiute Deadfall

Simpler and faster to build than a figure-4. Uses a toggle and cordage system.

Materials

  • Heavy flat rock
  • One upright stick, 6-8 in (15-20 cm)
  • One toggle stick, 2-3 in (5-7 cm) — a small, thin stick
  • Short length of cordage, 4-6 in (10-15 cm)
  • Bait stick, 6-10 in (15-25 cm)

Construction

  1. Tie one end of the cordage to the top of the upright stick.
  2. Tie the other end to the center of the small toggle stick.
  3. Stand the upright under the rock's edge, propping it up.
  4. Lay the bait stick with one end under the rock and the other end extending out (bait on the free end).
  5. Wrap the cordage once around the bait stick and hook the toggle against the rock underside. The friction of the cordage on the bait stick and the toggle against the rock hold everything in balance.
  6. When the bait stick is disturbed, the toggle slips, the upright falls, and the rock drops.

Fish Traps

Funnel Trap (Basket Trap)

A woven enclosure with a funnel-shaped entrance that guides fish in but prevents them from finding the exit.

Materials

  • Flexible branches or split wood strips (willow, hazel, bamboo)
  • Cordage for binding
  • Bait

Construction

  1. Weave a cylindrical basket, 18-36 in (45-90 cm) long, 8-12 in (20-30 cm) diameter.
  2. Construct a funnel (cone) from the same material, with the wide end matching the basket opening and the narrow end 1-2 in (2.5-5 cm) diameter.
  3. Insert the funnel into the basket opening with the narrow end pointing inward.
  4. Secure the funnel to the basket with cordage.
  5. Close the opposite end of the basket (or leave a small opening tied shut for bait access and fish removal).
  6. Bait the trap with crushed insects, fish scraps, or bread-like material.
  7. Place in a stream facing upstream, or in still water near shore.

See fishing-improvised.md for additional fish trap designs and fishing techniques.

Weir

A V-shaped wall of rocks or stakes in a stream that funnels fish into a narrow collection point.

Construction

  1. Build two walls of stacked rocks or driven stakes in a stream, forming a V shape pointing downstream.
  2. The opening at the V's point should be narrow — 6-12 in (15-30 cm).
  3. Place a basket trap or enclosure at the narrow point.
  4. Fish swimming upstream enter the wide end of the V and are funneled into the collection point.
  5. In tidal areas, build the weir to trap fish as the tide recedes.

Trap Line Management

How Many Traps

A single trap has a low probability of success on any given night. Increase your odds through numbers:

  • Minimum: 6 traps across different locations
  • Recommended: 12+ traps for reliable food production
  • Mix trap types: Some snares on trails, some deadfalls near dens, a fish trap in the stream

Checking Frequency

  • Check every trap at least every 12 hours (twice daily — morning and evening)
  • Reasons: animal suffering, meat spoilage in warm weather, predators stealing your catch, trapped animals chewing through cordage
  • Plan a trap line route that is efficient to walk

Trap Line Principles

  • Spread traps across different animal habitats (forest edge, waterside, meadow)
  • If a trap has not caught anything in 48 hours, relocate it
  • Rebait deadfalls after rain (scent washes away)
  • Repair and reset traps immediately after a catch
  • Mark trap locations with subtle indicators so you find them on your route

Bait Selection

Target Animal Effective Baits
Rabbit No bait needed — place snares on runs. Rabbits follow habit trails.
Squirrel Nuts, seeds, peanut butter
Raccoon Fish scraps, sweet foods, shiny objects near bait
Opossum Fish, fruit, carrion
Birds Seeds, berries, insects
Fish Insects, worms, fish scraps, crushed shellfish
WARNING Bait also attracts predators. A baited deadfall may attract bears, coyotes, or other large animals. Be aware of the predator community in your area.

Ethical and Legal Considerations

In a Survival Emergency

Use whatever methods keep you alive. Survival overrides game regulations. After rescue, report what you caught and where. Most jurisdictions explicitly exempt genuine survival situations from trapping regulations.

In All Other Contexts

  • Trapping is regulated by state, provincial, and national wildlife agencies
  • Permits and licenses are required in virtually all jurisdictions
  • Legal trap types, target species, and seasons are strictly defined
  • Many trap types described here (deadfalls, snares) are illegal for recreational trapping in many areas
  • Body-gripping traps may be banned or restricted
  • Check all local and national regulations before building or setting any trap

Ethical Principles

  • Check traps frequently to minimize suffering
  • Kill trapped animals quickly if found alive (a sharp blow to the base of the skull)
  • Do not set traps you cannot check regularly
  • Release non-target animals unharmed when possible
  • Do not waste — use all edible parts of caught animals

Common Mistakes

  • Setting only 1-2 traps — the probability of catching anything with a single trap on any given night is low. You need volume.
  • Poor placement — a perfect trap in the wrong location catches nothing. Invest time finding active trails.
  • Over-engineering triggers — a trigger that is too stable will not fire. A trigger that is too sensitive fires in the wind. Test before leaving.
  • Leaving human scent — handle traps and triggers with gloves or rubbed with local vegetation and dirt.
  • Not checking traps — unchecked traps mean spoiled meat, suffering animals, and wasted effort.
  • Building traps too close to camp — animals avoid areas with heavy human activity. Set traps at least 100 yards (90 m) from your shelter.
  • Ignoring fish traps — fish traps in productive water can be the most reliable passive food source. See fishing-improvised.md.

Quick Reference

Trap Type Target Materials Complexity Effectiveness
Simple snare Rabbit, squirrel Wire/cordage, stake Low Moderate
Drag snare Rabbit, larger game Wire/cordage, drag log Low Moderate
Spring snare Rabbit, squirrel Wire, sapling, trigger sticks Medium High
Figure-4 deadfall Rodents, small mammals Rock, 3 carved sticks Medium Moderate
Paiute deadfall Rodents, small mammals Rock, 2 sticks, cordage Low-Medium Moderate
Funnel fish trap Fish Woven branches, cordage High High
Weir Fish Rocks or stakes High (labor) High

Food

Improvised Fishing

Fish are the highest-probability wild protein source in most environments — learn to catch them with whatever you have.

At a Glance

  • Fish provide dense, complete protein with less caloric expenditure than hunting land animals
  • Improvise hooks from thorns, bone, wire, safety pins, or carved wood (gorge hooks)
  • Paracord inner strands, dental floss, and plant fibers serve as fishing line
  • Passive methods (traps, weirs, set lines) produce food while you do other tasks
  • Cook all freshwater fish thoroughly — parasites are common and dangerous
WARNING All freshwater fish should be assumed to carry parasites (tapeworms, flukes, roundworms). Cook to an internal temperature of 145 F (63 C) or until flesh is opaque and flakes easily. Do not eat raw freshwater fish in a survival situation.

Improvised Hooks

Thorn Hooks

Natural thorns from hawthorn, honey locust, acacia, or blackthorn make functional hooks.

Construction: 1. Select a thorn 0.5-1 in (1-2.5 cm) long with a sharp, curved point. 2. Trim the branch end to a short stub for line attachment. 3. Lash the line to the stub with multiple wraps and secure with a half-hitch. 4. For a stronger hook, lash two thorns together in an L-shape or V-shape with their points opposing.

Limitations: Fragile. Best for panfish, small trout, and other small species. Replace frequently.

Bone Hooks

Carved from bird or small mammal bones (wishbone, rib, leg bone).

Construction: 1. Select a thin, hard bone. Bird wishbones work well. 2. Break or grind to a hook shape — a curved piece with a sharp point and a shank for line attachment. 3. Sharpen the point on a rock. 4. Carve a notch or groove at the shank end for line attachment.

Durability: Stronger than thorn hooks. Suitable for medium-sized fish.

Safety Pin Hooks

If you have a safety pin, you have a hook.

Construction: 1. Open the safety pin fully. 2. Bend the pointed end into a hook shape using pliers or by bending against a hard surface. 3. Create a small barb by nicking the wire just below the point and bending it slightly outward. 4. Tie the line to the circular end (the spring loop).

Wire Hooks

Any small-gauge wire (picture hanging wire, electrical wire stripped of insulation, baling wire) makes an excellent hook.

Construction: 1. Cut a 3-4 in (7-10 cm) length of wire. 2. Bend one end into a J-shape or circle hook shape. 3. Sharpen the point on a rock. 4. Form an eye (small loop) at the other end for line attachment. 5. Create a barb by cutting a small notch and bending out a sliver of wire near the point.

Carved Gorge Hook

The oldest and most universal improvised hook. A straight, double-pointed piece that lodges crosswise in the fish's throat when swallowed.

Construction: 1. Carve a piece of hardwood, bone, or thorn into a straight piece 1-2 in (2.5-5 cm) long. 2. Sharpen both ends to points. 3. Carve a groove or notch at the center for line attachment. 4. Tie the line to the center so the gorge hangs parallel to the line. 5. Embed the gorge in bait so the fish swallows it whole. 6. When the fish swallows and you pull the line, the gorge turns sideways and lodges in the throat or stomach.

Technique: Do not set the hook immediately — wait for the fish to swallow the bait, then pull steadily (not sharply).

Improvised Line

Paracord Inner Strands

Standard 550 paracord contains 7 inner strands, each rated to approximately 35 lbs (16 kg). Each strand contains 2-3 smaller filaments.

Extraction: Cut the outer sheath and pull out the inner strands. Use individual strands for fishing line. For lighter line, separate into individual filaments.

Dental Floss

Surprisingly strong — waxed dental floss tests at 2-5 lbs (1-2.3 kg) breaking strength. Sufficient for panfish and trout. Braid multiple strands for heavier fish.

Plant Fiber Line

Materials: Dogbane, milkweed, stinging nettle, yucca, cattail leaves, inner bark of basswood, elm, or cedar.

Construction: 1. Harvest long plant fibers by stripping bark and separating the inner fibers. 2. Dry the fibers slightly (too wet = weak; too dry = brittle). 3. Use the reverse wrap (two-ply twist) method: - Take a bundle of fibers and twist them tightly in one direction. - Fold the bundle in half at the midpoint. - Hold the fold and let the two halves twist around each other in the opposite direction. - Splice in new fibers by overlapping 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) as you twist. 4. Test line strength before use. Rebuild if it breaks below expected load.

Breaking strength: Varies. Well-made plant fiber cordage can hold 10-30 lbs (4.5-13.5 kg).

Other Line Materials

  • Unwound thread from clothing seams
  • Shoelaces (braided types are strong)
  • Hair — human or horsehair braided together
  • Thin strips of plastic bag, twisted

Rod Alternatives

A rod is not essential. Many improvised fishing methods work without one.

  • Hand line: Wind line around a stick, can, or smooth rock. Cast by swinging and releasing. Retrieve by winding.
  • Pole: Cut a straight, flexible sapling, 6-10 ft (1.8-3 m) long. Tie line to the tip. This is the simplest and most effective configuration.
  • Set line (trotline): Tie a main line between two fixed points (trees, stakes) across or along water. Attach multiple shorter lines with baited hooks at intervals. Check periodically.
  • Jug line: Tie a baited line to a sealed bottle or jug. Set it floating and check for movement.

Hand Fishing (Noodling)

Reaching into underwater holes, cavities, and undercut banks to grab fish by hand — primarily catfish.

Technique

  1. Locate underwater cavities: submerged logs, rock crevices, undercut banks, hollow tree roots.
  2. Wade or swim to the cavity.
  3. Slowly insert your hand into the opening.
  4. When a fish bites or you feel its mouth, grip the lower jaw firmly.
  5. Pull the fish out and secure it.
WARNING Noodling carries serious risks. Underwater cavities may contain snapping turtles, water moccasins (cottonmouths), or other hazards. Risk of drowning from entanglement is real. Never noodle alone. Not recommended unless other methods are unavailable.

Where It Works

  • Muddy rivers and lakes with catfish populations
  • Areas with abundant underwater structure
  • Warm water (catfish are most active in warm months)

Spear Fishing

Two-Prong Spear

Materials: Straight sapling or branch, 6-8 ft (1.8-2.4 m) long. Knife or sharp stone.

Construction: 1. Select a straight piece of green wood, 1-1.5 in (2.5-4 cm) diameter. 2. Split the working end 6-8 in (15-20 cm) using a knife (batoning). 3. Insert a small wedge (twig) into the split to spread the two prongs. 4. Lash below the split to prevent further splitting (wrap cordage tightly around the shaft just below where the split ends). 5. Sharpen both prong tips. 6. Fire-harden the tips by rotating them slowly over hot coals (do not burn — just heat until the surface darkens slightly and dries).

Four-Prong (Gig) Spear

Construction: 1. Split the working end into a cross pattern — make two perpendicular splits. 2. Insert two crossed wedge twigs to spread the four prongs. 3. Lash below the splits. 4. Sharpen all four prong tips. 5. Optionally carve small backward-facing barbs on each prong to prevent fish from sliding off.

Spearing Technique

  • Stand on a bank, rock, or wade into shallow water.
  • Hold the spear above and slightly behind the target.
  • Account for refraction: the fish appears shallower than it actually is. Aim below where you see the fish.
  • Strike quickly and pin the fish to the bottom. Do not try to lift immediately — press down first, then slide a hand down to secure the fish.
  • Best in shallow, clear water with visible fish.
  • Dawn and dusk are prime times — fish feed in shallows.
  • Use a light source at night (torch, flashlight) — fish are attracted to and immobilized by light.

Fish Traps and Weirs

Funnel Trap

See trapping-and-snares.md for detailed construction. Summary:

  1. Weave a cylindrical basket from flexible branches.
  2. Create a funnel-shaped entrance — wide opening at the basket end, narrow (1-2 in / 2.5-5 cm) at the interior end.
  3. Insert the funnel into one end of the basket.
  4. Bait inside.
  5. Place in current facing upstream, or weight down in still water near shore.

Rock Weir

  1. Build a V-shaped or U-shaped wall of stacked rocks in a shallow stream.
  2. The opening points downstream.
  3. Fish swimming upstream enter the wide mouth and are trapped at the narrow end.
  4. Collect by hand or with a net/basket.
  5. Works best at natural choke points — shallow riffles, stream narrows.

Tidal Trap

In coastal areas:

  1. Build a circular or semicircular rock wall in the intertidal zone during low tide.
  2. As the tide rises, fish swim over and through the wall.
  3. As the tide falls, fish are trapped inside the enclosure.
  4. Collect at low tide.

Gill Net from Cordage

A gill net hangs vertically in water. Fish swim into it and are caught by their gill covers when they try to back out.

Construction

  1. Cut two horizontal lines (top and bottom) the desired length — 10-30 ft (3-9 m) is practical.
  2. Cut vertical strands 2-4 ft (60-120 cm) long — enough to span the water depth.
  3. Tie vertical strands to the top line at intervals matching your target fish size:
  4. Small fish (panfish): 1-1.5 in (2.5-4 cm) mesh openings
  5. Medium fish (trout-size): 2-3 in (5-7.5 cm) mesh openings
  6. Large fish: 4+ in (10+ cm) mesh openings
  7. Knot vertical strands together in alternating rows to create a diamond mesh pattern (standard netting knot: sheet bend).
  8. Attach floats (bark, sealed bottles, wood chunks) to the top line.
  9. Attach weights (rocks tied with cordage) to the bottom line.
  10. Set across a stream or along a shoreline.
WARNING Gill nets are indiscriminate. They catch everything that swims into them. In regulated waters, gill nets are typically illegal for recreational use. Use only in genuine survival situations.

Setting a Gill Net

  • Across a stream: anchor both ends to stakes or trees on opposite banks.
  • Along a shoreline: one end anchored on shore, the other weighted and extending into the water.
  • Check at least twice daily — fish deteriorate quickly in nets.

Bait Selection

Bait How to Obtain Target Fish
Earthworms Dig in moist soil, under logs/rocks Most freshwater species
Grubs/larvae Under bark, in rotting wood Trout, panfish
Insects (grasshoppers, crickets) Catch by hand in fields Trout, bass, panfish
Crayfish Turn over rocks in streams Bass, catfish, large trout
Minnows Trap in shallows with fabric/shirt Bass, pike, walleye
Fish entrails From previously caught fish Catfish, carp
Berries Forage near water (edible-plants-temperate.md) Panfish, trout
Dough/bread From supplies Carp, panfish
Bright cloth/feather (lure) Clothing, birds Trout, bass (aggressive species)

Improvised Lures

  • Wrap a small piece of bright cloth, tinfoil, or feather around a hook.
  • Carve a small fish shape from wood, attach a hook, and paint or scratch a scale pattern.
  • Use a spinner: small piece of shiny metal (spoon, can lid) attached above the hook.

Fish Stunning

WARNING Fish stunning (using rocks to strike the water or natural plant-based piscicides) is illegal in most jurisdictions and causes ecological damage. Include here for completeness in genuine survival contexts only.

Rock stunning: In shallow pools, drop or throw heavy rocks into small, enclosed pools to stun fish. Collect stunned fish immediately before they recover.

Natural piscicides: Certain plants (green walnut hulls, mullein seeds, certain tropical species) contain compounds that stun or suffocate fish when introduced to still or slow water. This method contaminates the water and kills indiscriminately. Use only as a last resort in survival situations.

Best Times and Locations

When to Fish

Time Productivity Reason
Dawn (30 min before/after sunrise) High Fish feed actively in low light
Dusk (30 min before/after sunset) High Same — low light feeding period
Overcast days Moderate-High Reduced light all day
After rain High Insects wash into water, fish feed aggressively
Midday, bright sun Low Fish retreat to deep water and cover
Night (with light) Moderate-High Some species (catfish, walleye) feed nocturnally

Where to Fish

  • Eddies and pools: Behind rocks, below waterfalls, in river bends — fish rest in slow water adjacent to fast water where food drifts past.
  • Undercut banks: Fish shelter under overhanging banks.
  • Submerged structure: Fallen trees, rock piles, weed beds — cover attracts fish.
  • Stream inlets: Where a tributary enters a larger body — food concentrates here.
  • Shaded areas: In hot weather, fish seek shade.
  • Shallow riffles: In cooler weather, fish feed in shallow, oxygenated water.

Fish Preparation and Parasite Warnings

Cleaning

  1. Kill the fish immediately with a sharp blow to the head.
  2. Scale by scraping from tail to head with a knife blade held at 45 degrees.
  3. Gut: insert knife into the vent (anus) and cut forward to the jaw. Remove all entrails.
  4. Remove gills.
  5. Rinse in clean water. Save entrails for bait or trap bait.

Cooking Methods

  • Direct flame: Skewer on a green stick and roast over coals. Turn frequently. Cook until flesh is opaque and flakes.
  • Hot rock: Heat flat rocks in a fire. Place fish on the hot rocks. Flip once.
  • Wrapped in mud or leaves: Coat whole fish (ungutted) in a thick layer of wet clay or large green leaves. Bury in coals. Cook 20-30 minutes. The skin and scales peel off with the clay.
  • Smoking: For preservation. Build a rack 2-3 ft (60-90 cm) above a low, smoky fire. Smoke for 12-24 hours. Smoked fish lasts days to weeks depending on conditions.
  • Boiling: If you have a container, boil fish in water to make a broth that captures fats and nutrients that would otherwise drip away in roasting.

Parasite Risks

Parasite Found In Risk
Broad fish tapeworm Pike, perch, freshwater species GI symptoms, B12 deficiency
Liver flukes Freshwater fish near livestock Liver damage
Anisakis (roundworm) Saltwater fish Severe GI pain
Diphyllobothrium Salmon, trout Tapeworm infection

Prevention: Cook thoroughly. Freezing at 0 F (-18 C) for 7 days also kills parasites, but this is rarely achievable in the field. Do not eat raw freshwater fish.

Common Mistakes

  • Fishing only during midday — fish at dawn, dusk, and after rain for best results
  • Fishing in open, featureless water — find structure, shade, and current breaks
  • Using hooks too large for available fish — scale your hook to the fish you expect to catch. A large hook catches nothing in a stream full of panfish.
  • Jerking the line on a gorge hook — gorge hooks must be swallowed. Wait, then pull steadily.
  • Not accounting for refraction when spearing — aim below the visible position of the fish
  • Neglecting passive methods — set lines, traps, and nets catch fish while you do other things. Set them first, then actively fish.
  • Discarding fish guts — use them as bait for the next catch or for traps
  • Eating raw freshwater fish — parasites are ubiquitous and some cause serious illness

Quick Reference

Method Effort Level Best For Passive?
Hook and line (hand line) Low All species No
Gorge hook Low Bottom feeders, catfish Semi (set line)
Spear fishing Medium Shallow, clear water No
Funnel trap High (build), Low (operate) Streams, all species Yes
Rock weir High (build), Low (operate) Shallow streams Yes
Gill net High (build), Low (operate) All water types Yes
Noodling Low Catfish No
Tidal trap High (build) Coastal areas Yes

Navigation

Map and Compass Navigation

Core land navigation using topographic maps and magnetic compass — the primary backup when GPS fails.

At a Glance

  • A compass points to magnetic north, not true north — adjust for declination or every bearing is wrong
  • Triangulation with three bearings fixes your position on a map within 100 meters (330 feet) in most terrain
  • Pace counting is the only reliable way to track distance without electronics
  • Always orient your map to north before plotting or reading anything
  • Combine compass bearings with terrain features — never rely on compass alone

Compass Anatomy and Terminology

A baseplate compass (the standard for land navigation) has these parts:

  • Baseplate — flat, transparent plate with a direction-of-travel arrow
  • Rotating bezel (housing) — numbered ring from 0 to 360 degrees
  • Magnetic needle — red end points to magnetic north
  • Orienting arrow — fixed inside the bezel, used to align with the needle ("red in the shed")
  • Orienting lines — parallel lines inside the bezel that align with map grid lines
  • Index line — where the bezel meets the direction-of-travel arrow; read your bearing here
  • Declination adjustment screw — on better compasses, allows you to set local declination once
NOTE Lensatic (military) compasses use a different sighting method but the same principles apply. The procedures below work with either type.

Declination: Magnetic vs. True North

True north is the geographic North Pole. Magnetic north is where compass needles point — currently in the Canadian Arctic, roughly 500 miles (800 km) from true north.

The angle between true north and magnetic north at your location is magnetic declination. It varies by region and changes slowly over time.

Finding Your Local Declination

  1. Check the margin of your topographic map — declination is printed there with the date of measurement.
  2. Use the NOAA Magnetic Declination Calculator (online, before your trip).
  3. In the continental US, declination ranges from 20 degrees west (Washington state) to 20 degrees east (Maine).

Adjusting for Declination

CAUTION Ignoring declination causes an error of roughly 1 mile (1.6 km) for every 20 miles (32 km) traveled per degree of declination. At 15 degrees declination, that is 15 miles (24 km) of drift over 20 miles.

West Declination:

Magnetic north is west of true north. Add the declination to your map bearing to get a compass bearing. Memory aid: "West is best, add to the rest."

East Declination:

Magnetic north is east of true north. Subtract the declination from your map bearing. Memory aid: "East is least, subtract at least."

If your compass has a declination adjustment screw, set it once and all readings convert automatically.

Taking a Bearing

A bearing is the direction from your position to a target, measured in degrees from north.

Field Bearing (compass to terrain)

  1. Hold the compass flat at waist height with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing at the target.
  2. Rotate the bezel until the orienting arrow frames the red end of the needle ("red in the shed").
  3. Read the number at the index line. That is your bearing in degrees.

Map Bearing (map to compass)

  1. Place the compass on the map with the baseplate edge connecting your position to your destination.
  2. Ensure the direction-of-travel arrow points toward the destination, not away from it.
  3. Rotate the bezel until the orienting lines are parallel to the map's north-south grid lines, with the orienting arrow pointing toward the top of the map.
  4. Read the bearing at the index line.
  5. Adjust for declination before following this bearing in the field.

Following a Bearing

  1. Set the desired bearing at the index line.
  2. Hold the compass level and rotate your entire body until the red needle sits inside the orienting arrow.
  3. Look along the direction-of-travel arrow and pick a visible landmark on that line — a specific tree, rock, or ridge feature.
  4. Walk to that landmark. Do not stare at the compass while walking.
  5. At the landmark, repeat the process: recheck the bearing, pick the next landmark, walk.
TIP In thick forest or fog, use a partner. Send them ahead and direct them onto the bearing line by voice or hand signals.

Map Reading Basics

Contour Lines

Contour lines connect points of equal elevation. Learn these patterns:

  • Close together — steep slope
  • Far apart — gentle slope or flat ground
  • Concentric circles — hilltop or depression (depressions have tick marks pointing inward)
  • V-shapes pointing uphill — valleys and stream drainages
  • V-shapes pointing downhill — ridgelines and spurs

The contour interval (elevation change between lines) is printed in the map margin. Common intervals: 20 feet (6 m), 40 feet (12 m), or 10 meters.

Scale

Map scale tells you the ratio of map distance to real distance. On a 1:24,000 map, 1 inch (2.5 cm) on the map equals 24,000 inches (2,000 feet / 610 m) on the ground. Use the bar scale in the margin for quick measurement.

Legend

Read the legend before navigating. Key symbols: trails (dashed lines), water (blue), vegetation (green tint), roads (red or black lines), buildings (small black squares).

Triangulation

Triangulation determines your position using bearings to known landmarks.

  1. Identify two or three features visible both in the terrain and on the map (peaks, towers, lake points, road intersections).
  2. Take a field bearing to the first feature.
  3. Convert to a map bearing (apply declination in reverse).
  4. On the map, place the compass edge on that feature with the bearing set.
  5. Draw or visualize a line from the feature back toward you (the back bearing).
  6. Repeat for the second and third features.
  7. Your position is where the lines intersect. Three lines form a small triangle — you are inside it.
NOTE Use landmarks at least 30 degrees apart for the best fix. Landmarks close together produce a vague, elongated intersection zone.

Orienting a Map

Before reading or plotting on a map, orient it so map-north faces real-world north.

  1. Set the bezel to 0 degrees (or your declination value if pre-adjusted).
  2. Place the compass on the map with the baseplate edge along a north-south grid line.
  3. Rotate the map and compass together until the red needle sits in the orienting arrow.
  4. The map now matches the terrain. Features on your left in the real world are on your left on the map.

Route Planning

  1. Orient the map.
  2. Mark your start and destination.
  3. Identify handrails — linear features (rivers, ridgelines, trails, power lines) that run roughly parallel to your direction of travel. Follow these instead of a raw bearing when possible.
  4. Identify catching features — large, unmissable features (roads, rivers, lakeshores) that tell you when you have gone too far.
  5. Identify backstops — features beyond your destination that confirm you overshot.
  6. Break the route into legs. Take a bearing and estimate distance for each leg.
  7. Note the terrain for each leg: elevation gain, water crossings, thick vegetation, cliff bands.

Pace Counting

Pace counting measures distance traveled by counting steps.

Calibrate Your Pace Count

  1. Mark a known distance of 100 meters (330 feet) on flat ground.
  2. Walk it at a natural pace, counting every time your left foot hits the ground.
  3. Repeat three times and average. Most people get 62-68 paces per 100 meters on flat ground.

Adjustments

Condition Adjustment
Uphill Add 2-5 paces per 100 m
Thick brush Add 3-5 paces per 100 m
Snow (deep) Add 5-10 paces per 100 m
Downhill (steep) Add 1-3 paces per 100 m
Sand/gravel Add 3-5 paces per 100 m

Use ranger beads or knots in a cord to track groups of 100 meters.

Deliberate Offset

When navigating to a feature on a linear landmark (a bridge on a river, a cabin on a trail), do not aim straight at it. Aim deliberately 5-10 degrees to one side.

When you hit the linear feature, you know which direction to turn to reach your target. Aiming straight risks hitting the linear feature and not knowing whether to go left or right.

Aiming Off

Aiming off is the same concept applied to any target near a catching feature. Offset your bearing intentionally so that when you reach the catching feature, the direction to your target is unambiguous.

Handrail Navigation

A handrail is any linear feature roughly parallel to your direction of travel: a ridge, river, trail, fence line, power line, or edge of a forest. Follow handrails whenever possible. They reduce navigation to a single task: stay near the feature.

Night Compass Navigation

CAUTION Travel at night only when necessary. The risk of injury from falls, unseen obstacles, and disorientation increases dramatically.
  1. Take your bearing during remaining daylight if possible.
  2. Use a red-light headlamp to preserve night vision while reading the compass.
  3. Choose landmarks silhouetted against the sky — ridgelines and lone trees stand out at night.
  4. Shorten your legs. Move 50-100 meters (165-330 feet) at a time.
  5. Have a partner walk ahead with a light as a moving reference point.
  6. Use Polaris (North Star) as a constant reference in the Northern Hemisphere. Check your bearing against its position every few minutes.

When GPS Fails

GPS fails for predictable reasons: dead batteries, broken screen, lost signal under dense canopy or in deep canyons, satellite geometry errors in narrow valleys.

Carry a compass and paper map as primary backup on every trip. Practice compass navigation before you need it. A GPS-dependent navigator who loses the device is functionally lost.

TIP Print or photograph key map sections on your phone before the trip. A phone with a dead cell signal still displays stored images and many have a built-in magnetic compass app.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting declination adjustment. This is the single most common navigation error. Every uncorrected bearing drifts further from the true line.
  • Following the compass needle instead of the bearing. The needle points north, not at your destination. Align the needle in the orienting arrow, then follow the direction-of-travel arrow.
  • Not calibrating pace count. Using someone else's pace count or an uncalibrated guess produces cumulative distance errors.
  • Navigating without catching features. Walking on a bearing with no backstop means overshooting the target with no way to know it.
  • Holding the compass near metal. Belt buckles, knives, firearms, vehicles, and power lines deflect the needle. Hold the compass away from your body and metal objects by at least 18 inches (45 cm).
  • Aiming directly at a target on a linear feature. Use deliberate offset instead.

Quick Reference

Task Key Steps
Take a bearing Point at target, red in shed, read index line
Follow a bearing Set bearing, red in shed, pick landmark, walk
Declination (west) Add to map bearing
Declination (east) Subtract from map bearing
Orient map Compass on grid line, rotate map until red in shed
Triangulate Bearings to 2-3 known features, back-plot lines, position at intersection
Pace count (flat) ~65 paces per 100 m (330 ft) — calibrate your own
Deliberate offset Aim 5-10 degrees to one side of target on a linear feature

See Also

  • Natural Navigation
  • Signaling for Rescue

Navigation

Natural Navigation

Direction-finding without instruments using the sun, stars, moon, terrain, vegetation, and environmental patterns.

At a Glance

  • The shadow stick method gives a reliable east-west line anywhere the sun is visible
  • Polaris (Northern Hemisphere) and the Southern Cross (Southern Hemisphere) provide true north and south within 2-3 degrees
  • Moss on trees is not a reliable direction indicator — tree growth asymmetry caused by prevailing wind and sun exposure is
  • No single natural method is accurate enough alone — combine at least two methods and cross-check
  • Terrain association (rivers flow downhill, drainages merge) is the most practical way to find civilization

Sun-Based Methods

The sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. At solar noon it is due south in the Northern Hemisphere and due north in the Southern Hemisphere. These facts power all sun-based navigation.

NOTE Near the equator (between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn), the sun passes directly overhead and may be north or south depending on the season. Sun methods are less reliable in the tropics.

Shadow Stick — Equal-Length Method

This method takes 2-3 hours but gives a true east-west line.

  1. Place a straight stick 3 feet (1 m) tall vertically in flat, open ground.
  2. Mark the tip of the shadow with a stone or scratch.
  3. Wait 2-3 hours. The shadow tip moves in an arc.
  4. Mark the new shadow tip position.
  5. Draw a straight line between the two marks. This line runs approximately east-west. The first mark is west, the second is east (in the Northern Hemisphere the shadow moves from west to east).
  6. A perpendicular line gives you a north-south line.

Shadow Stick — Shortest Shadow Method

This method takes most of a day but is more accurate.

  1. Set up the stick before midday.
  2. Mark the shadow tip every 15-20 minutes from mid-morning through mid-afternoon.
  3. The shortest shadow points true north in the Northern Hemisphere (true south in the Southern Hemisphere).
  4. Connect the arc of shadow tips to get an accurate east-west line.

Watch Method

Northern Hemisphere:

  1. Hold an analog watch (or visualize a clock face using the current time) flat with the hour hand pointing at the sun.
  2. The midpoint between the hour hand and the 12 o'clock position is approximately south.
  3. Before 12:00, bisect the angle clockwise from the hour hand to 12. After 12:00, bisect counterclockwise.

Southern Hemisphere:

  1. Point the 12 o'clock position at the sun.
  2. The midpoint between the 12 and the hour hand is approximately north.
CAUTION The watch method gives rough direction only — expect 15-20 degrees of error. It degrades further at high latitudes and near the equator. Use it as a quick check, not primary navigation.

If using a digital watch, draw a clock face on the ground with the current time and apply the same technique.

Star Navigation

Northern Hemisphere — Polaris (the North Star)

Polaris sits within 1 degree of true north. Find it with these methods:

Using the Big Dipper (Ursa Major):

  1. Locate the Big Dipper — seven bright stars forming a ladle shape.
  2. Find the two "pointer stars" at the outer edge of the dipper's bowl (Dubhe and Merak).
  3. Extend a line from Merak through Dubhe approximately five times the distance between them.
  4. That line hits Polaris, which is the last star in the handle of the Little Dipper (Ursa Minor).

Using Cassiopeia:

  1. Locate Cassiopeia — five bright stars forming a W or M shape.
  2. Polaris is roughly between the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia, at a similar distance from each.
  3. Useful when the Big Dipper is below the horizon or obscured by trees.

Southern Hemisphere — The Southern Cross

There is no bright star at the south celestial pole. Use the Southern Cross (Crux) to find due south.

  1. Locate the Southern Cross — four bright stars forming a cross shape, with a fifth dimmer star offset.
  2. Extend the long axis of the cross (from the top star through the bottom star) 4.5 times its length.
  3. That point is approximately the south celestial pole.
  4. Drop a vertical line from that point to the horizon. Where it meets the horizon is due south.
TIP Distinguish the Southern Cross from the False Cross (which is larger and dimmer) by looking for the two bright "pointer stars" (Alpha and Beta Centauri) to the left of the true Southern Cross.

Moon Direction Indicators

The moon provides rough directional information:

  • Crescent moon: Draw an imaginary line through the two tips (horns) of the crescent down to the horizon. In the Northern Hemisphere, this point is approximately south. In the Southern Hemisphere, it indicates approximately north.
  • Full moon: Rises in the east at sunset, is due south (Northern Hemisphere) or due north (Southern Hemisphere) at midnight, and sets in the west at sunrise.
  • First quarter moon (right half lit, Northern Hemisphere): Due south at sunset.
  • Last quarter moon (left half lit, Northern Hemisphere): Due south at sunrise.
NOTE Moon methods give rough bearings only — within 20-30 degrees. Combine with other methods.

Prevailing Wind Indicators

North America:

Prevailing winds blow from the west/southwest across most of the continental US and southern Canada. In the Arctic, expect winds from the north and northeast. Coastal areas have onshore-offshore wind cycles that override prevailing patterns.

Europe:

Westerly winds dominate from the Atlantic. In Scandinavia, expect northwest prevailing winds. The Mediterranean has complex local wind patterns (mistral, sirocco).

Southern Hemisphere:

Prevailing winds blow from the west/northwest across temperate zones (Roaring Forties). In Australia, the southeast trade winds dominate the northern half.

Wind-shaped trees (flagging) lean away from the prevailing wind. Snow cornices form on the leeward (downwind) side of ridges. Sand dunes migrate downwind. Use these as directional clues, not precise bearings.

Vegetation Patterns

The Moss Myth

Moss grows on all sides of trees. It prefers moisture and shade, not north-facing surfaces exclusively. In dense forest, moss distribution tells you nothing reliable about direction. Do not use moss for navigation.

Tree Growth Asymmetry (Reliable)

In open areas with consistent wind or sun exposure, trees show directional growth patterns:

  • Sun-favored growth: In the Northern Hemisphere, trees in open areas grow fuller and have more branches on the south-facing side (more sunlight). The reverse is true in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • Wind shaping: Isolated trees in exposed areas lean away from the prevailing wind. Branches on the windward side are shorter and stunted.
  • Bark differences: On some species (birch, beech), bark is thicker and more weathered on the windward side.
CAUTION Vegetation indicators require open-grown, isolated trees. In dense forest, microclimates override directional patterns. Do not use vegetation indicators in thick canopy.

Snow Melt Patterns

In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive more direct sunlight. Snow melts faster on south-facing slopes and on the south sides of rocks, trees, and ridges. In the Southern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes melt first.

Look for:

  • Uneven snow line on ridges — the bare side faces the equator
  • Snow melted away from the south side of tree trunks (Northern Hemisphere)
  • South-facing rock faces cleared of snow first

These patterns are reliable in winter and spring in temperate latitudes above 35 degrees.

Animal Behavior Indicators

Animal behavior gives general clues, not precise bearings.

  • Birds: Many migratory species fly south in autumn and north in spring. Geese and other waterfowl follow flyways tied to major river systems.
  • Spiderwebs: In open areas, spiders tend to build webs on the south side of trees and structures (Northern Hemisphere) for warmth. Unreliable in dense forest.
  • Ant mounds: In some temperate regions, ant mounds tend to be on the south/southwest side of trees. The correlation is weak — use only as a supporting clue.
NOTE Animal indicators are the least reliable natural navigation method. Never use them as a primary method.

River and Drainage Following

Rivers and streams flow downhill and merge into larger waterways. Larger waterways lead to civilization in most inhabited regions. This makes drainage following the most practical method for reaching help when lost.

  1. Find any stream and follow it downstream.
  2. Streams merge into larger rivers. Stay with the largest waterway.
  3. In most inhabited areas, rivers lead to roads, bridges, towns, or other infrastructure within 5-30 miles (8-48 km).
WARNING Do not follow rivers through canyons or gorges — the terrain may become impassable with cliff bands, waterfalls, and swift water. If the drainage narrows into a canyon, climb out and contour above it.

Terrain Association

Terrain association uses the shape of the land to determine location and direction.

  • Ridgelines are natural travel corridors with better visibility.
  • Valleys contain water and easier footing but limit visibility.
  • Saddles (low points between peaks) are natural pass points.
  • Drainages form predictable patterns: small gullies merge into creeks, creeks into rivers.
  • Elevation changes confirm direction of travel against known terrain.

Compare what you see around you with what the map shows. Match at least three terrain features to confirm your position.

Cultural Indicators

In non-wilderness areas, human infrastructure reveals direction and proximity to civilization.

  • Satellite dishes: In North America and Europe, most point roughly south (toward geostationary satellites on the equatorial arc).
  • Power lines: Follow them to reach roads and towns. Higher voltage lines (taller towers, more wires) connect larger population centers.
  • Roads and trails: Follow them downhill or toward wider/better-maintained surfaces.
  • Church architecture: In traditional European churches, the altar faces east. The main entrance faces west.
  • Aircraft contrails: Major flight routes follow known corridors. Frequent parallel contrails indicate a major air route, often between cities.

Combining Methods for Accuracy

No single natural method is precise enough for reliable navigation. Use this approach:

  1. Establish a rough direction with the best available method (shadow stick or stars).
  2. Cross-check with a second independent method (terrain association, wind indicators, cultural features).
  3. If the two methods disagree by more than 30 degrees, add a third method.
  4. Favor the method with the strongest physical basis (shadow stick and stars over vegetation and animal behavior).
  5. Reassess periodically — conditions change as you travel.

Common Mistakes

  • Relying on moss for direction. Moss grows where moisture exists, regardless of compass bearing. It is not a reliable indicator.
  • Using a single method without cross-checking. Every natural method has error margins of 10-30 degrees. One method alone causes dangerous drift over distance.
  • Applying Northern Hemisphere rules in the Southern Hemisphere. Sun, shadow, snow melt, and vegetation patterns reverse. Confirm which hemisphere you are in before interpreting indicators.
  • Following rivers blindly into canyons. Always assess downstream terrain before committing to drainage following. Climb to a vantage point first if possible.
  • Trusting the watch method as precise navigation. The watch method gives rough direction for orientation, not a bearing accurate enough to navigate to a specific point.
  • Ignoring cultural indicators. A power line or road is a faster route to help than any wilderness navigation technique.

Quick Reference

Method Accuracy Time Required Works At Night
Shadow stick (equal-length) ~5-10 degrees 2-3 hours No
Shadow stick (shortest) ~3-5 degrees Most of a day No
Watch method ~15-20 degrees Instant No
Polaris ~1-2 degrees Instant (clear sky) Yes
Southern Cross ~3-5 degrees Instant (clear sky) Yes
Moon (crescent) ~20-30 degrees Instant Yes
Snow melt patterns ~10-20 degrees Observation N/A
Wind/tree shaping ~15-30 degrees Observation Daylight
Drainage following N/A (route, not bearing) Continuous Risky

Navigation

Signaling for Rescue

Make yourself big, bright, and unmistakable — rescuers cannot save what they cannot find.

At a Glance

  • Three of anything means distress. Three fires, three whistle blasts, three gunshots, three flashes. This is the universal pattern.
  • Signal mirrors are the single most effective non-electronic signaling device, visible up to 100 mi / 160 km in clear conditions.
  • Electronic beacons (PLB/EPIRB) provide the highest probability of rescue. Carry one and know how to activate it.
  • Contrast is everything. Use colors, shapes, and movement that do not exist naturally in your environment.
  • Signal continuously and on schedule. Rescuers search in patterns and time windows — your signal must be active when they pass overhead.

Ground-to-Air Signals

International Ground-to-Air Emergency Symbols

Construct these symbols at least 10 ft / 3 m tall per character, with proportions of 6:1 (length to width). Use materials that contrast sharply with the ground — dark rocks on snow, light fabric on dark earth, trampled paths in tall grass.

Symbol Meaning
V Require assistance
X Require medical help
N No / Negative
Y Yes / Affirmative
F Need food and water
→ (Arrow) Traveling in this direction
I Require doctor — serious injury
II Need supplies
LL All is well

SOS Layout

Spell SOS in letters large enough to read from 1,000 ft / 305 m altitude. Each letter should be at least 10 ft / 3 m high and 3 ft / 1 m wide. Use trenches, rocks, logs, or any high-contrast material. Maintain sharp, straight edges — nature does not produce straight lines, so searchers notice them immediately.

WARNING Signals that are too small, too low-contrast, or placed under tree canopy are invisible from the air. Always construct signals in the largest clearing available.

Panel Signals

If you have brightly colored fabric, a tarp, an emergency blanket, or even a tent rainfly, spread it flat in an open area. International orange, red, and bright yellow are the most visible colors from the air. Anchor panels securely — a signal that blows away is worse than no signal, because you have lost the material.

Arrange panel signals in geometric shapes (triangle, cross, straight line) rather than random piles. Geometric shapes register as artificial and attract attention.

Signal Mirrors

A signal mirror is the most underrated survival signaling tool. On a clear day, the flash from a 3 x 5 in / 7.5 x 12.5 cm glass mirror is visible at distances exceeding 100 mi / 160 km. Even a improvised reflector — a CD, phone screen, belt buckle, or aluminum wrapper — produces a visible flash at several miles.

Aiming Technique (Sighting Method)

You cannot see your own flash hitting a distant target. Use this method:

  1. Hold the mirror close to your face, just below one eye.
  2. Extend your free hand to full arm's length toward the target (aircraft, ship, distant ridge).
  3. Form a peace sign (V) with your index and middle fingers, placing the target between them.
  4. Tilt the mirror until the reflected sun spot falls on your extended fingers.
  5. Slowly sweep the flash across and through the V, bracketing the target.

The reflected beam spreads over distance, so even imprecise aiming produces a visible flash at range. Sweep continuously — a moving flash is far more noticeable than a static one.

When No Target Is Visible

Flash the horizon in a slow, continuous sweep. Aircraft may be beyond visual range but within mirror-flash range. Sweep 360 degrees every few minutes during daylight hours. This "blind flashing" has resulted in documented rescues where the survivor never saw the aircraft that spotted them.

Signal Fires

Fire is visible by day (smoke) and night (flame). It is one of the oldest and most reliable signaling methods.

Three Fires in a Triangle

The international distress signal is three fires arranged in an equilateral triangle, spaced approximately 100 ft / 30 m apart. Prepare all three fire sites in advance with tinder, kindling, and fuel so you can ignite them rapidly when you hear or see a search aircraft.

If three fires are not feasible, build one large fire in the most open, visible location available.

Smoke Generation

During daylight, smoke is more visible than flame. Maximize smoke production:

  • White smoke (best against dark backgrounds like forests): Add green vegetation, fresh leaves, or damp moss to a hot fire.
  • Black smoke (best against light backgrounds like snow, sand, or overcast sky): Add rubber, plastic, oil-soaked materials, or petroleum products if available.
WARNING Burning plastics and rubber produces toxic fumes. Stand upwind and avoid inhaling smoke directly.

Build the hottest base fire you can first, then add smoke-generating materials on top. A smoldering, weak fire produces thin, low smoke that dissipates quickly. A hot fire with green material piled on top produces a dense, rising column visible for miles.

Platform Fires for Wet Ground

In swamps, snow, or saturated terrain, fire on the ground surface will extinguish itself. Build a platform:

  1. Lay a base of green logs or thick branches in a grid pattern, 3-4 ft / 1-1.2 m square.
  2. Stack a second layer perpendicular to the first.
  3. Build your fire on top of the platform.

The platform insulates the fire from moisture and elevates it for better visibility. In deep snow, the platform also prevents the fire from melting downward and disappearing into a pit.

Whistle Signals

Three short blasts on a whistle is the universal auditory distress signal. Repeat every few minutes when you believe searchers may be in range.

A whistle carries farther than the human voice (up to 1 mi / 1.6 km in open terrain vs. 600 ft / 183 m for shouting), requires far less energy, and does not cause throat damage from prolonged use.

WARNING Do not waste energy shouting. A whistle is louder, travels farther, and costs almost no calories. Carry one on your person at all times in the backcountry.

If you do not have a whistle, bang rocks together, strike a tree with a stick, or use any method that produces a sharp, repetitive sound in groups of three.

Bright Clothing and Markers

Wear or display the brightest colors available. Prioritize:

  1. International orange — the single most visible color against natural backgrounds
  2. Red
  3. Bright yellow

Hang brightly colored items from tree branches at the edge of clearings where they can catch wind and move. Movement attracts the eye far more effectively than static color.

Create trail markers if you move from your initial position: strips of fabric tied to branches, arrows made of rocks, or scratches on tree bark. Mark your direction of travel and the date if possible. Search teams follow these markers.

Improvised Markers

  • Tie clothing to a long pole and wave it when aircraft approach.
  • Stomp large arrows or letters into snow, mud, or sand.
  • Arrange rocks or logs in unnatural geometric patterns in clearings.

Electronic Signaling

Personal Locator Beacons (PLB)

A PLB transmits a 406 MHz distress signal to the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system, which relays your GPS coordinates to rescue authorities. Activation-to-alert time is typically 5-15 minutes.

  • Register your PLB before you need it (in the U.S.: beaconregistration.noaa.gov).
  • Test it according to the manufacturer's schedule.
  • Carry it on your person, not in your pack — if you are separated from your gear, the beacon goes with you.
  • Activate it only in genuine emergencies. False activations waste SAR resources and may result in penalties.

EPIRBs (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons)

EPIRBs function identically to PLBs but are designed for maritime use. Many models activate automatically upon immersion in water. If you are in a maritime survival situation, ensure the EPIRB is deployed, antenna is upright, and the unit is not submerged.

Satellite Messengers

Devices such as the Garmin inReach, SPOT, and Zoleo provide two-way messaging and SOS capability via satellite networks. Advantages over PLBs:

  • Two-way communication allows you to describe your situation and receive instructions.
  • Tracking features let others monitor your position in real time.
  • Non-emergency messaging reduces unnecessary SAR activations.

Carry charged batteries or a backup power source. Cold temperatures reduce battery life by 30-50% — keep the device inside your clothing in cold weather.

Cell Phone Tips

Cell phones are unreliable in the backcountry but may work in some situations:

  • Text before you call. SMS requires less signal strength and a shorter connection window than voice. A text may transmit where a call cannot connect.
  • Climb for signal. Gain elevation. Move to ridgelines, hilltops, or open terrain. Even 100 ft / 30 m of elevation gain can make the difference.
  • Conserve battery. Switch to airplane mode when not actively attempting to signal. Disable Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and background apps. Reduce screen brightness to minimum.
  • Dial emergency services (911 / 112). Emergency calls can connect through any available carrier network, not just your own.
  • Leave a voicemail. If the call connects briefly and drops, the voicemail may still record your message and location.
WARNING Do not rely on a cell phone as your primary signaling device. Carry a PLB or satellite messenger as your primary electronic signal.

Improvised Reflectors and Flags

When purpose-built signaling tools are unavailable, improvise:

Material Use
CD/DVD Signal mirror — use sighting technique
Aluminum foil / wrapper Crumple loosely around a stick for a waving reflector
Glass or clear plastic Angle toward the sun to produce a flash
Phone or watch screen Use as an improvised mirror
Belt buckle, knife blade Short-range reflector, effective to 1-3 mi / 1.6-5 km
Garbage bag (clear or white) Spread flat as a ground panel or tie to a pole as a flag
Space blanket / emergency blanket Extremely reflective; spread flat or hang vertically

For flags, attach material to the longest available pole. Elevation and movement are key. A flag waving 15 ft / 4.5 m above ground level is visible at far greater distances than one at waist height.

When to Signal vs. When to Self-Rescue

This decision can determine whether you live or die. Apply these criteria:

Stay and Signal When:

  • Someone knows your itinerary and expected return time.
  • You are near your last known position or planned route.
  • You are injured and movement risks worsening your condition.
  • You have adequate shelter, water, and signaling resources.
  • Terrain between you and help is unknown, hazardous, or impassable.

Self-Rescue When:

  • No one knows where you are or when to expect you.
  • You are certain of the direction to help and the distance is manageable.
  • Your current location is dangerous (rising water, fire, rockfall zone).
  • You have been signaling for an extended period with no response and conditions are deteriorating.
  • You have the physical ability, navigation tools, and supplies to travel safely.
WARNING If you choose to self-rescue, leave clear markers at your departure point indicating your direction of travel, the date and time, your condition, and your intended destination. Search teams may arrive after you leave.

Night Signaling

Fire

Fire is the dominant night signal. A single bright fire is visible up to 20 mi / 32 km on flat terrain in clear conditions. Maintain three fires in a triangle pattern if possible. Keep fuel stacked and ready to build up the flames rapidly when you detect a potential rescuer.

Flashlight SOS

Flash SOS in Morse code using any light source:

  • S: Three short flashes (dot-dot-dot)
  • O: Three long flashes (dash-dash-dash)
  • S: Three short flashes (dot-dot-dot)

Pause, then repeat. "Short" is approximately 1 second on. "Long" is approximately 3 seconds on. Pause 3 seconds between letters and 7 seconds between repetitions.

Aim the flashlight toward likely search areas: trails, roads, ridgelines, or the direction of the nearest settlement.

Chemical Lights (Chemlights / Glow Sticks)

Chemlights are visible at 1-2 mi / 1.6-3.2 km in darkness. Tie one to a length of cordage (3 ft / 1 m) and swing it in a circle overhead. The moving circle of light is highly visible and immediately identifiable as a human-made signal.

Attach chemlights to your shelter, your signal panel, or an elevated pole to mark your location passively through the night.

Aviation Search Patterns

Understanding how search aircraft operate helps you position yourself for detection.

Common Search Patterns

  • Parallel track (creeping line): The aircraft flies back and forth in parallel lines across the search area. Position yourself in open terrain along the likely search corridor.
  • Expanding square: The aircraft spirals outward from a central point (usually your last known position). Stay as close to your last known position as feasible.
  • Sector search: The aircraft flies outward from a point along different compass headings. Open ground near the center of the search area is optimal.

How to Be Visible

  • Stand in the open. Never signal from under tree canopy. Move to clearings, riverbanks, ridgelines, or shorelines.
  • Create contrast. Wear or display colors that oppose the background. Orange on green, dark on snow, light on dark rock.
  • Move. Wave both arms overhead in a slow, deliberate motion. A moving figure is far more detectable than a stationary one.
  • Lie flat and spread out if wearing high-contrast clothing on low-contrast ground — this maximizes your visible surface area from above.
  • Shadow matters. At low sun angles, your shadow is longer than your body. Position yourself where your shadow falls on open, light-colored ground for additional contrast.

Signaling an Aircraft Directly

When an aircraft approaches:

  1. Face the aircraft.
  2. Raise both arms overhead in a Y shape — this is the international "Yes, I need help" signal.
  3. If you do not need help (e.g., you are signaling for someone else nearby), raise one arm and extend the other downward, forming a diagonal line — this means "No, do not land here."
  4. Flash your signal mirror directly at the cockpit.
  5. Deploy smoke if available — smoke gives the pilot wind direction for landing and visually marks your exact position.

Do not assume the aircraft has seen you on the first pass. Continue signaling through every pass until you receive a definitive acknowledgment (wing waggle, circle pattern, or radio contact).

Common Mistakes

  • Building signals under tree cover. Canopy blocks ground signals entirely from aerial view. Always signal from the largest clearing available.
  • Relying on a single signal type. Combine methods: mirror + fire + ground symbol + whistle. Redundancy saves lives.
  • Signaling only when you hear an aircraft. Prepare all signals in advance. By the time you hear an engine, you have seconds, not minutes.
  • Using low-contrast materials. Gray rocks on gray soil are invisible from altitude. Prioritize contrast above all else.
  • Letting fires go out. Maintain signal fires or keep ignition materials immediately at hand at all times. A dead fire signals nothing.
  • Forgetting to signal at night. Many searches continue after dark with night-vision equipment or thermal imaging. Keep fire burning and light signals active.
  • Draining electronic device batteries. Activate your PLB and then conserve all other battery power. Do not play with your phone.

Quick Reference

Method Range Day/Night Notes
Signal mirror Up to 100 mi / 160 km Day Most effective daytime visual signal
Signal fire (smoke) 10-50 mi / 16-80 km Day White smoke on dark background, black on light
Signal fire (flame) Up to 20 mi / 32 km Night Three fires in a triangle = distress
Whistle 1 mi / 1.6 km Both Three blasts = distress; minimal energy cost
PLB/EPIRB Global (satellite) Both Highest probability of rescue; 5-15 min alert
Flashlight SOS 1-5 mi / 1.6-8 km Night Three short, three long, three short
Ground-to-air symbols Visible at 1,000+ ft / 305+ m Day Minimum 10 ft / 3 m tall, high contrast
Chemlight on cord 1-2 mi / 1.6-3.2 km Night Swing in a circle for maximum visibility

See Also

  • Wiseman, John "Lofty". SAS Survival Handbook. William Collins, 2014.

Wildlife

Bear Safety and Encounter Protocol

Identify the bear, prevent the encounter, survive the confrontation.

At a Glance

  • Black bears and grizzlies demand opposite responses — misidentification kills.
  • Bear spray is more effective than firearms in stopping a charge (92% vs 67% success rate).
  • Store all food, toiletries, and scented items at least 200 ft (60 m) from your sleeping area.
  • A mother with cubs is the single most dangerous scenario in bear country.
  • Most bear encounters end without contact if you respond correctly in the first 5 seconds.

Identification

Black Bear

  • Size: 200–400 lb (90–180 kg); up to 600 lb (270 kg) in exceptional cases.
  • Shoulder: No pronounced hump.
  • Face profile: Straight or slightly convex from forehead to nose ("Roman nose").
  • Ears: Tall, pointed, prominent relative to head size.
  • Claws: Short, curved, 1.5 in (4 cm). Dark colored. Designed for climbing.
  • Tracks: Front track about 4.5 in (11 cm) long. Toes tightly spaced in an arc.
  • Color: Misleading. Ranges from blonde to cinnamon to jet black. Do NOT rely on color alone.

Grizzly / Brown Bear

  • Size: 400–800 lb (180–360 kg); coastal brown bears exceed 1,000 lb (450 kg).
  • Shoulder: Prominent muscular hump above the shoulders. This is the defining field mark.
  • Face profile: Concave, dish-shaped. Forehead dips before the nose.
  • Ears: Short, rounded, appear small relative to the massive head.
  • Claws: Long, slightly curved, 2–4 in (5–10 cm). Light colored. Designed for digging.
  • Tracks: Front track about 5–7 in (13–18 cm) long. Toes more widely spaced and less arced.
  • Color: Varies from blonde to dark brown. Guard hairs often silver-tipped ("grizzled").

Track Analysis

Measure the front track width. Under 4 in (10 cm) is almost certainly black bear. Over 5 in (13 cm) is almost certainly grizzly. Between 4–5 in (10–13 cm), look at the toe arrangement: draw a straight line across the tops of the outer toes. In a black bear track, the line crosses through the middle toes. In a grizzly track, the middle toes fall below the line.

Prevention

Food Storage

Use one of three approved methods:

  1. Bear canister: Required in many wilderness areas. Place it on flat ground at least 200 ft (60 m) from camp. Do NOT place near cliffs or water where a bear could bat it out of reach.
  2. Bear hang (PCT method): Use a stuff sack, 50 ft (15 m) of paracord, and a carabiner. Hang food at least 12 ft (3.7 m) off the ground, 6 ft (1.8 m) from the trunk, and 6 ft (1.8 m) below the branch.
  3. Bear box/locker: Use established metal food lockers at designated campsites. Close and latch them fully.
WARNING "Odor-proof" bags reduce smell but do NOT eliminate it. Use them inside a canister or hang, never as a standalone method.

Scent Discipline

  • Cook and eat at least 200 ft (60 m) from your tent, preferably downwind.
  • Never sleep in clothing you cooked in.
  • Store toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm, insect repellent, and menstrual products with your food.
  • Strain dishwater and pack out solids. Broadcast strained water at least 200 ft (60 m) from camp.
  • Do NOT bury food scraps. Bears will dig them up.

Trail Behavior

  • Make noise: clap, talk loudly, call out "Hey bear!" before blind corners and dense brush.
  • Travel in groups of three or more. Groups of four or more have a near-zero attack rate.
  • Stay on established trails when possible.
  • Avoid hiking at dawn, dusk, or night in active bear areas.
  • Watch for fresh sign: scat, tracks, digging, torn-apart logs, claw marks on trees.
  • If you find a large animal carcass, leave the area immediately. Bears cache kills and defend them.

Encounter Protocol

Step 1: Identify the Bear

Before anything else, determine whether you face a black bear or a grizzly. Your survival response depends entirely on this identification.

Step 2: Assess the Behavior

Defensive behavior (the bear feels threatened): - Huffing, jaw-popping, swatting the ground. - Ears back, head low. - Bluff charges (stops short, veers away). - Common near cubs, a food source, or when surprised.

Predatory behavior (the bear views you as food): - Quiet, deliberate approach. - Follows you persistently. - Ears forward, head up, staring fixedly. - Circles to get downwind of you. - Approaches at night.

Step 3: Respond

Black Bear — Any Behavior

  • Stand your ground. Do NOT play dead.
  • Make yourself as large as possible. Raise your arms, open your jacket wide.
  • Shout, bang pots, throw rocks.
  • If it makes contact, fight back. Target the nose and eyes.
  • Black bears that attack are almost always treating you as prey. Playing dead guarantees injury.

Grizzly — Defensive Attack

  • Deploy bear spray at 20–30 ft (6–9 m).
  • If contact is made, play dead. Drop face-down, spread your legs for stability, lace your fingers behind your neck.
  • Keep your pack on — it protects your back.
  • Remain motionless until you are certain the bear has left. Wait at least 20 minutes.
  • If the attack continues beyond 2 minutes, the bear may have switched to predatory behavior. Start fighting back.

Grizzly — Predatory Attack

  • Do NOT play dead.
  • Fight with everything available. Target the eyes and nose.
  • Use rocks, sticks, trekking poles, knives.
  • This is a fight for your life.
WARNING If a grizzly enters your tent at night, it is a predatory attack regardless of circumstances. Fight back immediately.

Bear Spray

Selection

  • Choose EPA-registered bear spray with a minimum of 2% capsaicin and related capsaicinoids (CRC).
  • Minimum canister size: 7.9 oz (225 g). Larger is better.
  • Minimum spray range: 16 ft (5 m). Most quality sprays reach 25–35 ft (8–11 m).
  • Check the expiration date before every trip.

Deployment

  1. Remove the safety clip with your thumb.
  2. Grip with both hands. Hold the canister slightly below eye level.
  3. Aim at a downward angle toward the bear's face, just above ground level. Do NOT aim high.
  4. Fire a 1–2 second burst when the bear is within 30 ft (9 m).
  5. Adjust aim based on the spray cloud. Fire additional bursts as needed.
  6. Create a wall of spray between you and the bear, then back away.
  7. If the wind is at your back, spray freely. If the wind is in your face, wait until the bear is closer (15 ft / 4.5 m) and fire anyway — partial exposure still deters.

Carry Position

Keep bear spray in a hip holster or chest harness. Never bury it in your pack. Practice drawing and removing the safety at least 10 times before entering bear country.

Mother with Cubs

  • Never position yourself between a mother and her cubs.
  • If you see cubs, immediately scan for the mother. She is close.
  • Speak in calm, low tones and back away slowly.
  • Do NOT approach cubs, even if they appear orphaned. The mother is likely watching.
  • If a mother charges, this is almost always defensive. Stand your ground, deploy bear spray. If she makes contact and she is a grizzly, play dead.

Night Encounters

  • Keep bear spray inside your tent, next to your hand.
  • Sleep with a headlamp around your neck or within reach.
  • If a bear is investigating your tent, speak in a firm voice. Bang pots.
  • If the bear begins tearing into the tent, use bear spray immediately and exit the opposite side.
  • Any bear that enters your tent at night is exhibiting predatory behavior. Fight back.
  • Run your headlamp. Bears generally avoid confrontation when they lose the advantage of darkness.

Camp Setup in Bear Country

Follow the bear-muda triangle layout:

  1. Cooking area: Downwind from sleeping area. At least 200 ft (60 m) away.
  2. Food storage: At least 200 ft (60 m) from both cooking and sleeping areas. Use a bear hang, canister, or locker.
  3. Sleeping area: Upwind. Away from trails, water sources, and berry patches.

Do NOT camp on game trails, near salmon streams, or in areas with abundant fresh bear sign. Choose open sites where you have good visibility.

Common Mistakes

  • Relying on color to identify the species. Color is unreliable. Use the shoulder hump, face profile, and ear shape.
  • Playing dead with a black bear. This is almost always fatal. Fight back.
  • Running from any bear. Bears run at 35 mph (56 km/h). You cannot outrun them. Running triggers a pursuit response.
  • Climbing a tree. Black bears are excellent climbers. Grizzlies can climb or shake you out. This is not a reliable escape.
  • Storing food in your tent or vehicle with open windows. Bears that obtain human food become habituated and are eventually destroyed.
  • Keeping bear spray in your pack. You have 2–5 seconds to respond. An inaccessible canister is a useless canister.
  • Approaching a bear for photographs. Maintain at least 100 yd (91 m) distance.

Quick Reference

Scenario Black Bear Grizzly (Defensive) Grizzly (Predatory)
First response Stand tall, yell Stand ground, speak calmly Stand tall, prepare to fight
Bear charges Hold ground, spray Hold ground, spray Hold ground, spray
Contact made Fight back — eyes, nose Play dead — face down Fight back — eyes, nose
Night tent entry Fight back Fight back Fight back
Bear spray range 20–30 ft (6–9 m) 20–30 ft (6–9 m) 20–30 ft (6–9 m)

See Also

  • Big Cats — Mountain lion encounters share some protocols (appear large, fight back) but differ in key ways.
  • Venomous Snakes — Watch-where-you-step discipline applies in all wildlife areas.
  • Insect Threats — Scented repellents can attract bears; choose unscented options when possible.

Sources

  • Smith, T. S., et al. "Efficacy of Bear Deterrent Spray in Alaska." Journal of Wildlife Management, vol. 72, no. 3, 2008, pp. 640–645.
