Wildlife

Big Cat Encounters

Face the cat, stand tall, fight back — never run, never crouch, never look like prey.

At a Glance

  • Mountain lions are ambush predators. If you can see one, you have already disrupted its attack pattern.
  • Running triggers pursuit. Stand your ground every time.
  • Children are disproportionately targeted. Keep them close and pick them up immediately.
  • Fatal mountain lion attacks average 1 per year in North America. Lightning kills 20.
  • Most big cat encounters end without contact if you deny the cat an easy target.

Mountain Lion / Cougar

Range and Habitat

Mountain lions (Puma concolor) occupy the largest range of any terrestrial mammal in the Western Hemisphere: from British Columbia to Patagonia. In North America, established populations exist throughout the western states and provinces, Florida (the Florida panther subspecies), and expanding territory in the Midwest and East.

Preferred habitat includes: - Rugged terrain with dense cover (canyons, rock outcrops, thick brush). - Transition zones between forest and open areas. - Proximity to deer populations (their primary prey). - Elevations from sea level to 10,000 ft (3,000 m).

Behavior

  • Primarily crepuscular and nocturnal. Most active at dawn and dusk.
  • Solitary except during mating or when a female has kittens.
  • Territorial. Males maintain ranges of 50–150 sq mi (130–390 sq km).
  • Kill by ambush: stalk from behind, leap onto the back, deliver a bite to the base of the skull or throat.
  • Almost never attack from the front when the target is facing them and alert.
  • Cache large kills by covering them with leaves, dirt, and debris. Return to feed over several days.

Signs of Presence

Tracks

  • Round, 3–3.5 in (7.5–9 cm) wide. Wider than long.
  • Four toes, no claw marks (retractable claws).
  • Leading edge of the heel pad has two lobes; trailing edge has three lobes.
  • Distinguish from canine tracks: canines show claws, are longer than wide, and have a single-lobed heel pad leading edge.

Scat

  • Segmented, blunt-ended.
  • Contains hair and bone fragments.
  • Often partially buried or covered with debris (scraping behavior).

Scrapes

  • Mounds of dirt, leaves, or pine needles 6–12 in (15–30 cm) long, often with urine.
  • Found along ridgelines, trail junctions, and territory boundaries.
  • Indicate an active territorial cat. Increase your alertness.

Cached Kills

  • Deer or other large prey partially covered with debris.
  • Strong odor of decomposition.
WARNING If you find a cached kill, leave the area immediately. The cat is nearby and will defend this food source aggressively. Do NOT investigate. See also [Bear Safety](#bear-safety) — bears also cache kills and react similarly.

Encounter Protocol

When You See a Mountain Lion

  1. Stop. Do NOT run. Do NOT turn your back.
  2. Face the cat directly. Maintain eye contact.
  3. Appear large. Raise your arms overhead. Open your jacket wide. Stand on a rock if available.
  4. Speak firmly. Use a loud, authoritative voice. Do NOT scream — high-pitched sounds can mimic prey.
  5. Do NOT crouch or bend down. This makes you look like a four-legged animal. If you need to pick something up, squat while maintaining eye contact.
  6. Back away slowly if possible. Give the cat a clear escape route. Never corner a mountain lion.
  7. Throw objects if the cat holds its ground or approaches. Rocks, sticks, water bottles, trekking poles. Aim for the body.

If the Cat Charges

  • Hold your ground. Many charges are bluff charges — the cat pulls up short.
  • Deploy bear spray if you carry it. Effective at 15–20 ft (4.5–6 m). See Bear Safety for spray technique.
  • Use trekking poles offensively: thrust at the face.

If the Cat Makes Contact

  • Fight back aggressively. There is no "play dead" protocol for big cats.
  • Target the eyes and nose. These are the most sensitive areas.
  • Use any available weapon: knife, rock, trekking pole, bare hands.
  • Protect your neck and throat — cover them with one arm while striking with the other.
  • Gouge the eyes. This is not the time for restraint.
  • Mountain lions often release and retreat once prey fights back effectively.
WARNING Never play dead with a mountain lion. Every mountain lion attack is predatory. Playing dead confirms you as food.

Children and Group Safety

Children

  • Mountain lions preferentially target small, fast-moving beings that appear prey-sized.
  • Keep children within arm's reach in cat country. Do NOT let them run ahead on the trail.
  • If a cat appears, pick children up immediately — even if you must crouch briefly to do so. Put them on your shoulders.
  • Instruct children to face the cat, raise their arms, and shout if they are old enough to follow directions.
  • Never let children play alone in areas with known mountain lion presence.

Group Dynamics

  • Travel in groups. Mountain lions almost never attack groups of three or more.
  • If a cat appears, group together. Stand shoulder to shoulder. Raise arms collectively.
  • Place children and smaller individuals in the center.
  • Present a unified, large, loud front.
  • Do NOT scatter. A fleeing individual becomes an irresistible target.

Night Hiking in Cat Country

Night hiking in active mountain lion territory substantially increases your risk. Mountain lions rely on stealth and darkness.

  • Carry a powerful headlamp (300+ lumens) and sweep it regularly.
  • Keep the beam slightly above eye level to catch eyeshine. Cat eyes reflect brightly — usually green or amber.
  • Make more noise than usual: talk, sing, strike trekking poles together.
  • Keep your group tight. No stragglers.
  • If you detect eyeshine that does not retreat, stop, face the source, and make yourself large.
  • Carry bear spray in a hip holster with the safety removed while actively hiking.
  • Avoid wearing earbuds or headphones. Your ears are your best early warning system.

Statistics

North America (Mountain Lion)

  • Fatal attacks: approximately 27 confirmed deaths from 1890 to 2025.
  • Average: roughly 1 fatality per 5 years historically, increasing to approximately 1 per year in recent decades as habitat overlap grows.
  • Non-fatal attacks: approximately 200 confirmed from 1890 to 2025.
  • Most victims: solo adults or unaccompanied children. Children under 16 are overrepresented.
  • Most attacks: dawn, dusk, or full darkness.
  • Most common regions: British Columbia, California, Colorado.

Context

  • Deer kill approximately 200 people per year in the US (vehicle collisions).
  • Domestic dogs kill approximately 30–50 people per year in the US.
  • Lightning kills approximately 20 people per year in the US.
  • Mountain lions kill approximately 1 person per year in the US and Canada combined.

Your risk is real but statistically low. Proper behavior reduces it to near zero.

Jaguar

The jaguar (Panthera onca) ranges from the southwestern US (rare, limited sightings in Arizona and New Mexico) through Central and South America.

  • Significantly more powerful than a mountain lion. Males reach 200–250 lb (90–113 kg).
  • Kills by biting through the skull (unique among big cats).
  • Attacks on humans are extremely rare. Jaguars prefer to avoid people entirely.
  • If encountered: follow the same protocol as for mountain lions. Face the cat, appear large, fight back if attacked.
  • Jaguars are strong swimmers and excellent climbers. Climbing a tree is not a reliable escape.

Leopard

The leopard (Panthera pardus) ranges across sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.

  • Most adaptable of the big cats. Thrives near human settlements.
  • Significantly more likely to attack humans than mountain lions, particularly in India.
  • Man-eating leopards are a documented phenomenon, historically and currently.
  • Encounter protocol: identical to mountain lion. Face it, stand tall, fight back.
  • Leopards are nocturnal and excel at ambush. Avoid walking alone at night in leopard territory.
  • In camp, keep fires burning and sleep inside a tent or enclosed structure.

Common Mistakes

  • Running. The single most dangerous thing you can do. A mountain lion runs at 50 mph (80 km/h) in short bursts. Running triggers hard-wired pursuit behavior.
  • Crouching or bending down. This transforms your silhouette from an upright human (not typical prey) to a four-legged animal shape (typical prey).
  • Turning your back. Mountain lions attack from behind. Face the cat at all times.
  • Playing dead. No big cat respects this. You become an easy meal.
  • Ignoring signs of presence. Fresh tracks, scrapes, and especially cached kills mean a cat is actively using the area. Increase your vigilance or reroute.
  • Letting children run ahead. A small, fast-moving figure at a distance from the group is the ideal target.
  • Wearing earbuds on the trail. You lose your most important sense for detecting approach.
  • Approaching a sighting for photos. Maintain at least 100 yd (91 m) distance and leave the area.

Quick Reference

Situation Action
Cat spotted at distance Stop, face it, appear large, speak firmly, back away slowly
Cat approaching Stand ground, shout, throw objects, deploy spray
Cat charges Hold ground (likely bluff), spray, thrust with poles
Contact made Fight aggressively — eyes, nose, throat
Children present Pick them up, place in center of group
Night eyeshine detected Stop, face source, light it up, appear large
Cached kill found Leave the area immediately
Fresh tracks/scrapes Increase alertness, make noise, tighten group

See Also

  • Bear Safety — Bear spray is effective against mountain lions. Camp layout principles overlap.
  • Venomous Snakes — Different threat, same terrain. Maintain awareness of ground-level and eye-level threats simultaneously.
  • Insect Threats — Tick checks after off-trail travel in cat country.

Sources

  • Mattson, D., et al. "Contexts of Mountain Lion Predatory Behavior toward Humans." Wildlife Society Bulletin, vol. 35, no. 2, 2011, pp. 62–73.
  • California Department of Fish and Wildlife. "Living with Mountain Lions." wildlife.ca.gov. Accessed 2025.
  • Colorado Parks and Wildlife. "Mountain Lion Safety." cpw.state.co.us. Accessed 2025.
  • Quigley, H., and Herrero, S. "Characterization and Prevention of Attacks on Humans by Mountain Lions." Proc. of the 5th Mountain Lion Workshop, 1996.
Wildlife

Venomous Snake Identification and Bite Protocol

Identify the region, respect the distance, treat the bite — not the snake.

At a Glance

  • Approximately 7,000–8,000 venomous snakebites occur in the US annually; fewer than 5 are fatal.
  • Do NOT attempt to catch or kill the snake for identification. Photograph it from a safe distance if possible.
  • The only effective treatment for a significant envenomation is antivenom administered in a medical facility.
  • Prevention is simple: watch where you step, where you reach, and where you sit.
  • "Dry bites" (no venom injected) occur in 20–50% of venomous snake strikes.

Identification by Region

North America

Rattlesnakes (Crotalus and Sistrurus)

  • Range: All 48 contiguous US states except Maine, Alaska, and Hawaii. Southern Canada. Mexico. Most diverse in the southwestern US.
  • Identification: Segmented rattle on the tail (may be missing in juveniles or if broken off). Broad, triangular head. Vertical pupils. Heat-sensing pits between the eye and nostril.
  • Size: Varies by species. Timber rattlesnake: 36–60 in (91–152 cm). Western diamondback: 48–72 in (122–183 cm). Eastern diamondback: up to 96 in (244 cm) — the largest venomous snake in North America.
  • Behavior: Generally rattle before striking. May NOT rattle if startled or if they have learned that rattling attracts predators. Strike range is approximately one-half to two-thirds body length.
  • Venom type: Primarily hemotoxic. Destroys tissue, disrupts clotting, causes massive local swelling.

Copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix)

  • Range: Eastern and central US from Massachusetts to Nebraska to Texas.
  • Identification: Hourglass-shaped crossbands (wider on sides, narrow on spine). Copper-colored head. Heat pits. Vertical pupils. Stocky body.
  • Size: 24–36 in (61–91 cm).
  • Behavior: Freeze-and-rely-on-camouflage. Most bites occur when the snake is stepped on. Often does NOT rattle, flee, or warn.
  • Venom type: Mildly hemotoxic. Least dangerous of North American pit vipers. Rarely fatal but causes significant pain and swelling.

Cottonmouth / Water Moccasin (Agkistrodon piscivorus)

  • Range: Southeastern US. Aquatic and semi-aquatic habitats — swamps, rivers, lakes, drainage ditches.
  • Identification: Heavy-bodied. Dark (often black) in adults. Juveniles have distinct crossbands. When threatened, opens mouth wide to display white interior ("cottonmouth"). Heat pits. Vertical pupils.
  • Size: 30–48 in (76–122 cm). Up to 72 in (183 cm).
  • Behavior: Stands its ground rather than fleeing. Swims with body on the surface (nonvenomous water snakes swim with body submerged and head up). Can bite underwater.
  • Venom type: Hemotoxic. More potent than copperhead. Can cause tissue necrosis and systemic effects.
WARNING Many nonvenomous water snakes are killed because they are mistaken for cottonmouths. If you are unsure, leave the snake alone and give it a wide berth.

Coral Snake (Micrurus fulvius and relatives)

  • Range: Southeastern US (eastern coral snake), Arizona and New Mexico (Arizona coral snake). Also Mexico and Central/South America.
  • Identification: Bright bands of red, yellow/white, and black encircling the body. Small head, not triangular. Round pupils. No heat pits. This snake is an elapid, not a pit viper.
  • Size: 20–30 in (51–76 cm). Slender.
  • The rhyme: "Red touches yellow, kill a fellow. Red touches black, friend of Jack."
  • Limitations of the rhyme: Works ONLY for North American species. Central and South American coral snakes, and Old World species, vary enormously. Some have aberrant color patterns. Some nonvenomous mimics break the pattern rule. Do NOT rely on the rhyme outside the US, and even within the US, treat any brightly banded red/black/yellow snake with extreme caution.
  • Behavior: Reclusive, fossorial (burrowing). Rarely encountered. Must chew to envenomate effectively — the fangs are small and fixed.
  • Venom type: Neurotoxic. Causes progressive paralysis, respiratory failure. Symptoms may be delayed 6–12 hours. This delay is dangerous — victims feel fine and delay seeking treatment.
WARNING Coral snake bites may initially cause minimal pain and swelling. Do NOT mistake the lack of immediate symptoms for a dry bite. Seek emergency medical care for any confirmed or suspected coral snake bite regardless of symptoms.

General Venomous Indicators (and Why They Are Unreliable)

Common field marks taught to identify venomous snakes:

Feature "Rule" Why It Is Unreliable
Triangular head Venomous snakes have triangular heads Many nonvenomous snakes flatten their heads when threatened, appearing triangular. Coral snakes have small, rounded heads.
Vertical pupils Venomous = vertical; nonvenomous = round Requires getting dangerously close to the snake's face. Also, coral snakes have round pupils.
Heat pits Pit between eye and nostril = venomous Only applies to pit vipers. Coral snakes lack pits. Requires close observation.
Single anal plate Venomous snakes have a single row of subcaudal scales Requires handling the snake. Absolutely never do this.

The practical rule: If you cannot positively identify a snake as nonvenomous, treat it as venomous. Maintain a distance of at least 6 ft (1.8 m) and leave it alone.

Bite Protocol

What TO Do

  1. Move away from the snake's strike range — at least 6 ft (1.8 m). A snake can strike again.
  2. Stay calm. Increased heart rate accelerates venom distribution. Panic causes more harm than venom in most cases.
  3. Remove jewelry and constrictive clothing from the bitten extremity immediately, before swelling begins. Rings, watches, bracelets, tight sleeves, boots.
  4. Immobilize the bitten limb. Splint it if possible. Keep it at or slightly below heart level.
  5. Mark the edge of swelling with a pen or marker and note the time. Repeat every 15–30 minutes. This information helps the medical team assess progression.
  6. Photograph the snake from a safe distance if possible. Do NOT pursue, capture, or kill it.
  7. Evacuate to a medical facility. Walk the victim out if possible. If the bite is on a leg, carry or improvise transport. Call 911 or activate an emergency beacon.
  8. Monitor for anaphylaxis. Some people have allergic reactions to venom independent of the envenomation itself. Watch for hives, facial swelling, difficulty breathing. See Insect Threats for anaphylaxis management.
  9. Note the time of the bite and any symptoms as they develop.

What NOT to Do

  • Do NOT apply suction. Extractor devices and mouth suction do not remove clinically significant venom and cause additional tissue damage.
  • Do NOT apply a tourniquet. Trapping venom in a limb concentrates tissue destruction and increases the risk of amputation.
  • Do NOT apply ice. Cold vasoconstriction concentrates venom locally and increases tissue necrosis.
  • Do NOT cut the wound. Incision increases bleeding, infection risk, and tissue damage without removing venom.
  • Do NOT apply electric shock. This myth persists. It causes burns and does nothing to venom.
  • Do NOT drink alcohol. Alcohol vasodilates and accelerates venom absorption.
  • Do NOT attempt to capture or kill the snake. This is the most common cause of second bites and third-party bites.
WARNING Every minute spent applying folk remedies is a minute not spent evacuating. The only definitive treatment is hospital-administered antivenom.

Pressure Immobilization Technique (Elapids Only)

For coral snake bites (and overseas elapids like cobras, mambas, taipans), apply a pressure immobilization bandage:

  1. Wrap a broad elastic bandage (ACE bandage, torn clothing strip) starting at the bite site and wrapping toward the heart.
  2. Wrap firmly — as tight as for a sprained ankle. You should be able to slide a finger under the bandage.
  3. Splint the entire limb to prevent movement.
  4. Do NOT remove the bandage until the victim reaches a medical facility with antivenom available.

Do NOT use pressure immobilization for pit viper bites (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth). Their hemotoxic venom causes local tissue destruction, and trapping it increases necrosis.

Dry Bites

A "dry bite" occurs when a venomous snake strikes but injects no venom or only a trivial amount.

  • Occurs in an estimated 20–50% of pit viper bites and up to 50% of coral snake bites.
  • The snake controls venom delivery. Defensive strikes are more likely to be dry.
  • Treat every bite as envenomated until proven otherwise. Monitor for at least 8 hours (24 hours for coral snake) before concluding a dry bite.
  • Even dry bites carry infection risk from the snake's oral bacteria. Clean the wound and seek medical evaluation.

Antivenom

  • CroFab (crotalidae polyvalent immune fab) is the standard antivenom for North American pit viper bites. Anavip is an alternative.
  • Antivenom is most effective when administered within 4–6 hours of the bite.
  • Delayed administration (up to 24 hours) can still be beneficial for coagulopathy.
  • Antivenom is expensive ($20,000–$100,000+ per treatment course) and not stocked at every hospital. Confirm availability with the receiving facility.
  • Allergic reactions to antivenom (serum sickness) occur in approximately 5–10% of cases. The medical team manages this.
  • There is currently limited availability of coral snake antivenom (Pfizer's product was discontinued; remaining stock exists but is scarce). This makes prevention even more critical.

Prevention

Watch Where You Step

  • Never step over a log without looking on the other side first. Step onto the log, then down.
  • Avoid placing your hands on ledges, in rock crevices, or into holes you cannot see into.
  • Use a trekking pole to probe ahead in dense vegetation, tall grass, or rocky terrain.
  • Stay on established trails when possible. Avoid bushwhacking through snake habitat.

Footwear and Clothing

  • Wear boots that cover the ankle. Leather or heavy synthetic.
  • Wear loose-fitting long pants. Many bites do not penetrate two layers of fabric.
  • Consider snake gaiters in areas with high rattlesnake density. Gaiters cover from ankle to knee and resist fang penetration.
  • Wear gloves when collecting firewood, moving rocks, or handling debris.

Camp

  • Shake out boots, clothing, and sleeping bags before use.
  • Zip your tent fully. Snakes seek warmth and shelter.
  • Do NOT place your sleeping bag directly on the ground in open-air bivy setups in snake country.
  • Use a headlamp when moving around camp at night. Many snakes are nocturnal.
  • Keep the area around your tent clear of debris, woodpiles, and rock piles that attract rodents (which attract snakes).

Awareness by Season and Time

  • Snakes are most active in spring (emergence from brumation) and fall (returning to dens).
  • Peak activity times: dusk and dawn in warm months; midday in spring and fall.
  • In extreme heat, snakes become nocturnal. Increase night vigilance.
  • Cool nights (below 50 F / 10 C) reduce snake activity significantly.

Common Mistakes

  • Attempting to catch or kill the snake. Causes the majority of second bites. Leave the snake alone.
  • Applying tourniquets, suction, or ice. Outdated first aid that worsens outcomes.
  • Assuming a lack of immediate symptoms means a dry bite. Coral snake envenomation can be asymptomatic for hours before respiratory failure.
  • Relying on the triangular head rule. Misidentifies many nonvenomous snakes and misses coral snakes entirely.
  • Wearing sandals or going barefoot in snake habitat. Ankle-covering boots prevent the majority of fang-to-skin bites.
  • Reaching into blind spaces. Never reach where you cannot see. Use a stick.
  • Walking at night without a light. Many venomous snakes are nocturnal, especially in warm weather.

Quick Reference

Action Correct Incorrect
First response Back away, stay calm Chase or kill the snake
Bitten limb Immobilize, keep at heart level Tourniquet, ice, elevation
Wound care Mark swelling, note time Cut, suck, apply suction device
Jewelry Remove immediately Leave on
Transport Evacuate to hospital ASAP Wait and see
Coral snake Pressure immobilization bandage Same as pit viper treatment
Any bite Treat as envenomated Assume dry bite without monitoring

See Also

  • Venomous Spiders — Similar bite-area-first-aid principles. Same camp hygiene practices (shake out boots).
  • Bear Safety — Watch-where-you-step discipline overlaps. Different threat, same terrain awareness.
  • Insect Threats — Anaphylaxis protocols for allergic reactions to venom.
  • Big Cats — Terrain awareness in rugged environments.

Sources

  • Seifert, S. A., et al. "AAPCC Database Characterization of Native US Venomous Snake Exposures, 2001–2005." Clinical Toxicology, vol. 47, no. 4, 2009, pp. 327–335.
  • Norris, R. L., and Bush, S. P. "Bites by Venomous Reptiles in the Americas." Wilderness Medicine, 7th ed., Elsevier, 2017.

Wildlife

Venomous Spider Identification and Bite Protocol

Identify the spider if safe, treat symptoms — most "spider bites" are something else entirely.

At a Glance

  • Only two spiders in North America pose significant medical risk: the black widow and the brown recluse.
  • Most suspected spider bites are actually MRSA (staph) infections, insect bites, or other skin conditions.
  • No spider actively hunts humans. Bites are almost always defensive (trapped against skin).
  • Prevention is straightforward: shake out boots, check bedding, wear gloves when moving debris.
  • Deaths from spider bites in the US are extremely rare — fewer than 7 per year, and most of those involve the very young, the very old, or those with compromised health.

Black Widow (Latrodectus spp.)

Identification

  • Size: Female body 0.5 in (13 mm). With legs, approximately 1.5 in (38 mm) across. Males are much smaller and rarely bite.
  • Color: Shiny jet black (southern and western black widows). Northern black widow may have red/white dorsal markings.
  • Field mark: Red hourglass marking on the ventral (underside) abdomen. This is the defining feature. In some species, the hourglass is broken into two separate triangles or is orange rather than red.
  • Web: Irregular, tangled, strong. No organized pattern. Found low to the ground.

Range

All 48 contiguous US states, southern Canada, Mexico, and much of the temperate world. Five species of Latrodectus occur in North America. Most common in the South and West.

Habitat

  • Dark, undisturbed spaces: woodpiles, stone walls, sheds, garages, outhouses, crawl spaces.
  • Under rocks, logs, and debris.
  • In boots, gloves, and clothing left outdoors or in storage.
  • Outdoor furniture, mailboxes, meter boxes.
  • Rarely found in occupied, well-lit, frequently-used indoor spaces.

Bite and Symptoms (Latrodectism)

The bite itself may feel like a pinprick or go unnoticed.

Timeline:

  • 0–30 minutes: Small red mark at bite site. Minor local pain.
  • 30–60 minutes: Pain intensifies and begins spreading. Muscle cramping starts, typically in the large muscle groups nearest the bite.
  • 1–6 hours: Full-body muscle cramping, rigidity, and pain (especially abdomen, back, and chest). Abdominal rigidity can mimic appendicitis or peritonitis. Sweating, nausea, vomiting, elevated blood pressure, headache.
  • 6–24 hours: Symptoms peak. Severe cases include hypertension, tachycardia, respiratory difficulty.
  • 24–72 hours: Gradual resolution in most cases. Residual muscle pain and weakness can persist for weeks.
WARNING If the victim develops severe abdominal rigidity, chest tightness, or difficulty breathing, evacuate immediately. These symptoms indicate significant envenomation requiring medical intervention.

Treatment

  • Clean the bite with soap and water.
  • Apply ice wrapped in cloth for 10–15 minutes to manage pain.
  • Over-the-counter pain relief (ibuprofen, acetaminophen). Opioids may be needed for severe pain.
  • Seek medical care for moderate to severe symptoms. Antivenom (Antivenin Latrodectus mactans) exists and is effective but is reserved for severe cases due to allergic reaction risk.
  • Muscle relaxants (benzodiazepines) and IV calcium gluconate are standard hospital treatments.
  • Most healthy adults recover fully within 1–3 days with supportive care.

Brown Recluse (Loxosceles reclusa)

Identification

  • Size: Body 0.25–0.5 in (6–13 mm). Leg span approximately 1 in (25 mm).
  • Color: Tan to dark brown, uniform. Legs are slightly lighter, no banding.
  • Field mark: Dark violin-shaped marking on the cephalothorax (fused head-chest segment), with the neck of the violin pointing toward the abdomen. This mark is subtle and requires close inspection.
  • Eyes: Six eyes arranged in three pairs (dyads). Most spiders have eight eyes. This is the most reliable identification feature but requires magnification.
  • Web: Small, irregular, loosely woven. Not used for prey capture — the recluse hunts actively.

Range

Central and south-central US: a band from Nebraska to Ohio, south to Texas and Georgia. This range is frequently overstated. Brown recluses are NOT established in California, the Pacific Northwest, New England, or most of the western US.

WARNING If you are outside the established range of the brown recluse (roughly the central US), a suspected "recluse bite" is far more likely to be a MRSA skin infection. See a physician for proper diagnosis. Do NOT self-diagnose or self-treat for a recluse bite.

Habitat

  • True to its name: reclusive. Found in dark, undisturbed areas.
  • Closets, attics, basements, crawl spaces, storage boxes.
  • Behind furniture, inside wall voids, under baseboards.
  • In clothing, shoes, and bedding that has been undisturbed for weeks.
  • Outdoors: under bark, rocks, and debris in protected locations.
  • Can establish large populations in a single building (hundreds to thousands) without any bites occurring, because they avoid contact with humans.

Bite and Progression

The bite is often painless at first.

Timeline:

  • 0–2 hours: Mild stinging or nothing at all. Small red area.
  • 2–8 hours: Pain increases. Red area develops a white center (vasoconstriction) surrounded by a red ring — the "red, white, and blue" or "bull's-eye" pattern.
  • 8–24 hours: A blister or vesicle may form at the bite center.
  • 24–72 hours: In moderate to severe cases, the central tissue begins to darken (necrosis). The area becomes purple or black.
  • 3–14 days: The necrotic area may enlarge to an ulcer. Size varies from a dime to 6+ in (15+ cm) across in severe cases. This is dermonecrosis.
  • 2–8 weeks: The ulcer slowly heals by secondary intention (from the edges inward). Scarring is common.
  • Systemic symptoms (rare, <1% of bites): Fever, chills, nausea, hemolytic anemia, kidney failure (loxoscelism). Most common in children and debilitated individuals. Can be fatal.

Treatment

  • Clean the bite with soap and water.
  • Apply ice wrapped in cloth for 10–15 minutes at a time to slow tissue destruction.
  • Immobilize the bite area and keep it elevated.
  • Seek medical evaluation within 24 hours for any suspected recluse bite with progressive symptoms.
  • No FDA-approved antivenom exists for brown recluse bites in the US. Treatment is supportive.
  • Wound care: keep the ulcer clean, apply antibiotic ointment, cover with a sterile bandage. Change dressings daily.
  • Surgical debridement may be needed for large necrotic wounds, but early surgery is generally avoided — it often worsens outcomes. Allow the wound to declare itself over 1–2 weeks before surgical intervention.
  • Dapsone and other systemic therapies are sometimes used but remain controversial.

Hobo Spider (Eravus agrestis)

  • Range: Pacific Northwest US and southern British Columbia.
  • Previously considered: A significant medical threat causing necrotic bites similar to brown recluse.
  • Current understanding: The CDC removed the hobo spider from its list of medically significant spiders. Evidence for necrotic bites is weak and largely based on flawed studies. Most "hobo spider bites" are likely misdiagnosed MRSA infections.
  • Identification: Brown, funnel-web builder, 12–18 mm body, herringbone pattern on abdomen. Difficult to distinguish from many similar species.
  • Practical approach: If bitten by any spider in the Pacific Northwest and necrotic symptoms develop, seek medical care. Treat the wound, not the species identification.

Funnel-Web Spider (Atrax and Hadronyche spp.)

  • Range: Eastern Australia, particularly within 100 mi (160 km) of Sydney.
  • Significance: The Sydney funnel-web (Atrax robustus) is arguably the most dangerous spider in the world.
  • Size: Body up to 1.4 in (35 mm). Robust, glossy black.
  • Behavior: Aggressive when cornered. Rears up and strikes downward with large fangs. Can bite through fingernails and soft shoes.
  • Venom: Neurotoxic (atracotoxin). Causes excitatory neurotransmitter release. Symptoms include profuse sweating, muscle fasciculations, salivation, tearing, tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema. Can kill within 15 minutes in severe cases (children).
  • Treatment: Apply a pressure immobilization bandage immediately (same technique as for elapid snakebites — see Venomous Snakes). Evacuate to a hospital with antivenom. Since the introduction of antivenom in 1981, no deaths have occurred from confirmed funnel-web bites in Australia.
  • Prevention: Shake out shoes and clothing. Check under toilet seats. Do not leave laundry on the ground. Pool fences and water features attract wandering males.
WARNING If bitten by a funnel-web spider, apply a pressure immobilization bandage to the entire limb immediately and do NOT remove it until you reach a hospital. This is a life-threatening emergency.

Bite First Aid (General)

  1. Remain calm. Spider bites are rarely life-threatening.
  2. Identify the spider if safe to do so. Trap it under a glass or photograph it. Do NOT handle it.
  3. Clean the bite with soap and water.
  4. Apply ice wrapped in cloth, 10–15 minutes on, 10–15 minutes off.
  5. Monitor for symptom progression. Mark the border of any redness with a pen and note the time.
  6. Seek medical care if: severe pain develops, muscle cramping begins, the wound develops a bull's-eye pattern, necrosis appears, or systemic symptoms (fever, nausea, difficulty breathing) occur.
  7. Update tetanus vaccination if not current (within the past 10 years).

When to Evacuate

Evacuate immediately (call emergency services or activate a beacon) if:

  • The victim is a child under 5, elderly, or immunocompromised.
  • Severe muscle cramping, rigidity, or abdominal pain develops (likely black widow).
  • Difficulty breathing, chest tightness, or cardiovascular symptoms appear.
  • Signs of anaphylaxis: hives, facial swelling, wheezing. See Insect Threats for anaphylaxis management.
  • Rapidly spreading redness, streaking (red lines extending from the bite), or fever — these suggest secondary bacterial infection, not spider venom, and require antibiotics.
  • In Australia: any suspected funnel-web bite.

Prevention

Shake and Check

  • Shake out boots, shoes, and clothing before putting them on, especially if stored outdoors or in undisturbed areas.
  • Check sleeping bags and bedding before entering.
  • Inspect gloves before putting them on.
  • Check under toilet seats (particularly relevant for funnel-webs in Australia and black widows in outhouses).

Camp and Shelter

  • Keep your tent zipped at all times. Even a small gap admits spiders.
  • Do not leave clothing or gear on the ground overnight.
  • Store boots inside your tent or stuff sack, upside down.
  • Shake out any gear that sat on the ground before packing it.

Handling Debris

  • Wear leather gloves when moving firewood, rocks, lumber, or stored equipment.
  • Break apart woodpiles from the outside. Do not reach into the center.
  • Use a stick to flip rocks and logs rather than your hands.
  • Tap or shake items before picking them up. Vibration causes most spiders to flee.

Around Structures

  • Seal cracks and gaps in building foundations, window frames, and door frames.
  • Remove woodpiles, rock piles, and debris from directly against structures.
  • Use sticky traps in garages, basements, and storage areas to monitor spider populations.
  • Reduce clutter in storage spaces. Cardboard boxes are preferred habitat for recluses; switch to sealed plastic bins.

Myth-Busting

"Most spider bites are from spiders"

They are not. Multiple studies show that 60–80% of lesions diagnosed as "spider bites" by patients and even by some physicians are actually:

  • MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) skin infections — by far the most common misdiagnosis.
  • Other bacterial infections (cellulitis, abscesses).
  • Insect bites (mosquitoes, fleas, bedbugs, mites — see Insect Threats).
  • Herpes simplex, diabetic ulcers, Lyme disease, fungal infections.
  • Chemical burns, vasculitis, and other dermatological conditions.

A confirmed spider bite requires either witnessing the spider biting you or capturing the spider on your body immediately after feeling the bite. Waking up with a lesion is not a spider bite until proven otherwise.

"Brown recluse bites always cause necrosis"

They do not. Most confirmed recluse bites heal without significant necrosis. Only approximately 10% of bites develop moderate to severe dermonecrosis.

"All brown spiders in the US are brown recluses"

False. Hundreds of brown spider species exist in North America. The brown recluse has a specific, limited range. Outside that range, a brown spider is almost certainly not a recluse.

"Daddy longlegs are the most venomous spider but their fangs are too small to bite"

False on every count. "Daddy longlegs" refers to harvestmen (not spiders, no venom glands), cellar spiders (minimal venom, can bite, no medical significance), or crane flies (not arachnids). This myth has no factual basis.

Common Mistakes

  • Self-diagnosing a skin lesion as a spider bite. Seek medical evaluation. MRSA requires antibiotics, not wound care for envenomation.
  • Applying a tourniquet to a spider bite. Never appropriate for spider envenomation.
  • Cutting, sucking, or applying suction to a spider bite. Ineffective and harmful.
  • Early surgical excision of a brown recluse bite. Usually worsens the wound. Allow the lesion to fully declare itself first.
  • Ignoring camp hygiene. Spiders enter open tents, get into boots, and nest in piled clothing. Prevention takes 30 seconds per item.
  • Panicking over a spider sighting. Most spiders are harmless and provide pest control. Identify, avoid, and move on.

Quick Reference

Spider Key ID Venom Effect First Aid Urgency
Black widow Shiny black, red hourglass (underside) Neuromuscular (latrodectism) — cramping, rigidity Ice, pain relief, evacuate if severe Moderate to high
Brown recluse Tan-brown, violin on cephalothorax, 6 eyes Dermonecrotic — ulceration Ice, clean, monitor, medical eval in 24 h Low to moderate
Funnel-web (Australia) Glossy black, large, aggressive posture Neurotoxic — rapid systemic collapse Pressure immobilization bandage, evacuate NOW Critical
Hobo spider Brown, funnel web, PNW range Disputed — likely minimal Treat as general bite Low

Wildlife

Insect and Arthropod Threats

Insects and arachnids kill more people than every other animal on Earth combined — prevention is everything.

At a Glance

  • Mosquitoes are the deadliest animal on the planet: over 700,000 human deaths annually via disease transmission.
  • Ticks transmit Lyme disease to approximately 476,000 people per year in the US alone.
  • Anaphylaxis from bee and wasp stings kills more Americans annually than snakes, spiders, bears, and mountain lions combined.
  • DEET remains the gold standard for insect repellent. Apply it to skin. Apply permethrin to clothing.
  • Proper tick removal (fine-tipped tweezers, steady upward pull) prevents most disease transmission.

Mosquitoes

Disease Vectors

Mosquitoes transmit some of the most lethal pathogens on the planet:

Disease Pathogen Regions Symptoms Notes
Malaria Plasmodium spp. Sub-Saharan Africa, South/SE Asia, Central/South America Cyclic fever, chills, anemia, organ failure ~600,000 deaths/year. Prophylaxis available.
Dengue Dengue virus Tropics worldwide, expanding range High fever, severe joint pain ("breakbone fever"), hemorrhagic in severe cases No specific treatment. Second infection more dangerous.
Zika Zika virus Americas, SE Asia, Pacific Islands Mild fever, rash, joint pain — but causes microcephaly in fetuses Critical risk for pregnant travelers.
West Nile West Nile virus US, Europe, Africa, Middle East Usually asymptomatic. Severe: encephalitis, meningitis Most common mosquito-borne illness in continental US.
Yellow Fever Yellow fever virus Sub-Saharan Africa, South America Fever, jaundice, hemorrhage, organ failure Vaccine available and required for some countries.
Chikungunya Chikungunya virus Africa, Asia, Americas Fever, severe joint pain lasting weeks to months No vaccine, no specific treatment.

Prevention

Chemical Repellents

  • DEET (N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide): Apply to exposed skin. Concentrations of 20–30% provide 6–8 hours of protection. Higher concentrations last longer but are not more effective per hour. Safe for adults and children over 2 months.
  • Picaridin: Apply to skin. 20% concentration matches DEET effectiveness. Odorless, does not damage plastics or synthetics. Preferred by many travelers.
  • Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE/PMD): Plant-derived. 30% concentration provides 4–6 hours of protection. Not as long-lasting as DEET. Do NOT use on children under 3 years.
  • IR3535: Available in some commercial formulations. Moderate effectiveness, shorter duration.
WARNING "Natural" repellents (citronella, lavender, peppermint, etc.) provide minimal protection lasting 20–60 minutes at most. Do NOT rely on them in areas with disease-carrying mosquitoes.

Permethrin-Treated Clothing

  • Apply 0.5% permethrin spray to clothing, tents, mosquito nets, and gear. Allow to dry fully before wearing.
  • Treated fabric kills mosquitoes, ticks, and other arthropods on contact.
  • Lasts through 5–6 wash cycles (spray-applied) or 70+ washes (factory-treated, e.g., Insect Shield).
  • Do NOT apply permethrin to skin. It is a contact insecticide, not a repellent for skin use.
  • Combine with DEET on exposed skin for maximum protection.

Physical Barriers

  • Sleep under a mosquito net. Treat the net with permethrin. Ensure edges are tucked under the mattress or sleeping pad.
  • Wear long sleeves and long pants during peak mosquito hours (dusk through dawn for most species).
  • Use head nets in areas of extreme mosquito density.
  • Screen tent doors and windows. Repair any holes in netting.

Environmental Controls

  • Eliminate standing water around camp: empty containers, overturn buckets, drain puddles.
  • Camp on high ground with breeze when possible. Mosquitoes are weak fliers.
  • Build a smoky fire (add green wood or damp leaves) upwind of your sitting area. Smoke repels mosquitoes.
  • Avoid camping near stagnant water, swamps, or marshes.

Ticks

Disease Threats

Disease Pathogen Tick Species Region Key Symptom
Lyme disease Borrelia burgdorferi Blacklegged (deer) tick Northeast, upper Midwest US; Europe Bull's-eye rash (erythema migrans) in ~70% of cases
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Rickettsia rickettsii American dog tick, Rocky Mountain wood tick Eastern US, despite the name Spotted rash, high fever, can be fatal without treatment
Anaplasmosis Anaplasma phagocytophilum Blacklegged tick Northeast, upper Midwest US Fever, headache, muscle pain
Ehrlichiosis Ehrlichia spp. Lone star tick Southeast, south-central US Fever, headache, fatigue
Babesiosis Babesia microti Blacklegged tick Northeast, upper Midwest US Malaria-like: fever, chills, anemia
Alpha-gal syndrome Immune response to tick saliva Lone star tick Eastern US Delayed allergic reaction to red meat, 3–6 hours after eating

Tick Removal

Use fine-tipped (pointed) tweezers. Blunt tweezers crush the tick body and may force pathogens into the wound.

  1. Grasp the tick as close to the skin surface as possible. Grip the mouthparts, not the body.
  2. Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do NOT twist, jerk, or rock the tick.
  3. If the mouthparts break off in the skin, remove them with tweezers if easily accessible. If not, leave them alone — the skin will expel them naturally.
  4. Clean the bite area with rubbing alcohol, iodine, or soap and water.
  5. Dispose of the tick: submerge in alcohol, flush down a toilet, or seal in tape. Do NOT crush between your fingers.
  6. Save the tick in a sealed bag with a damp cotton ball if you want it identified or tested later. Note the date.

What NOT to do: - Do NOT apply petroleum jelly, nail polish, heat (match, cigarette), or other "suffocation" methods. These delay removal and may cause the tick to regurgitate pathogens into the wound. - Do NOT squeeze the tick's body. - Do NOT use bare fingers to remove a tick if possible (use tweezers, or a cloth/leaf as a barrier).

Tick Check Protocol

Perform a full-body tick check within 2 hours of leaving tick habitat. Ticks generally take 24–36 hours of attachment to transmit Lyme disease. Earlier removal dramatically reduces transmission risk.

Check these areas carefully:

  • Scalp and hairline (run fingers through hair).
  • Behind and inside the ears.
  • Neck, especially the nape.
  • Armpits.
  • Inside the navel.
  • Waistband and belt line.
  • Groin and inner thighs.
  • Behind the knees.
  • Between the toes.

Shower within 2 hours of returning indoors. Tumble-dry clothing on high heat for 10 minutes to kill ticks (washing alone does not reliably kill them — it is the heat that matters).

Tick Prevention

  • Wear permethrin-treated clothing. This is the single most effective tick prevention measure.
  • Apply DEET or picaridin to exposed skin.
  • Tuck pants into socks. Tuck shirt into pants. Wear light-colored clothing to spot ticks.
  • Walk in the center of trails. Avoid brushing against vegetation.
  • Avoid sitting directly on logs, stone walls, or the ground in tick habitat.

Bees, Wasps, and Hornets

Anaphylaxis Recognition

Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that can kill within minutes. Recognize these signs:

  • Skin: Hives, flushing, swelling (especially face, lips, tongue, throat).
  • Respiratory: Wheezing, shortness of breath, throat tightness, stridor (high-pitched breathing), coughing.
  • Cardiovascular: Rapid pulse, low blood pressure, dizziness, fainting.
  • Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea.
  • Neurological: Confusion, anxiety, sense of impending doom.

Two or more body systems affected after a sting = anaphylaxis. Treat immediately.

EpiPen Use

  1. Remove the blue safety cap.
  2. Grip the orange tip end firmly in your fist. Do NOT put your thumb over the end.
  3. Swing and press firmly into the outer thigh (through clothing if necessary).
  4. Hold in place for 10 seconds.
  5. Remove and massage the injection site for 10 seconds.
  6. Note the time. Symptoms may return in 15–20 minutes (biphasic reaction). A second dose may be needed.
  7. Always evacuate to a medical facility after using an EpiPen, even if symptoms resolve. A biphasic reaction can be fatal.

Field Treatment Without EpiPen

If no EpiPen is available:

  • Administer 50 mg diphenhydramine (Benadryl) orally if the victim can swallow.
  • Position the victim on their back with legs elevated (shock position). If vomiting, turn on their side.
  • If the victim carries an asthma inhaler, administer 2 puffs. Albuterol helps with bronchospasm.
  • Keep the victim warm.
  • Prepare for CPR if breathing stops.
  • Evacuate immediately. This is a life-threatening emergency.
WARNING Antihistamines (Benadryl) do NOT stop anaphylaxis. They only manage mild allergic reactions. Without epinephrine, severe anaphylaxis is likely fatal. Carry an EpiPen if you have any history of severe sting reactions.

Sting Prevention

  • Avoid bright-colored clothing and floral patterns.
  • Do not wear perfume, cologne, or scented products.
  • Cover food and drinks outdoors. Bees and wasps are attracted to sugar.
  • Remain calm around individual bees/wasps. Swatting provokes them.
  • If a swarm attacks, run in a straight line. Cover your face. Do NOT jump into water — the swarm will wait. Seek an enclosed space (vehicle, building, tent).
  • Yellowjackets nest in the ground. Watch for ground holes and heavy insect traffic near the trail.

Stinger Removal

Honeybees leave barbed stingers embedded in the skin. Remove the stinger as quickly as possible by any method — scrape, flick, or pull. Speed matters more than technique. Each second the stinger remains, more venom is injected from the attached venom sac.

Scorpions

Dangerous Species

Most scorpion stings are painful but not dangerous. The primary exception in North America:

  • Arizona bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus): Found in the southwestern US (Arizona, New Mexico, SE California, southern Nevada, Utah). 2–3 in (5–7.5 cm) long. Light brown to yellowish. Slender body with thin pincers.
  • Worldwide, approximately 25 species of ~2,500 are dangerous. The Androctonus (North Africa/Middle East), Tityus (South America), and Leiurus (Middle East) genera contain the most lethal species.

Habitat

  • Under rocks, bark, and debris during the day.
  • Inside boots, clothing, and bedding.
  • Active at night. Glow under ultraviolet light — a UV flashlight is an effective detection tool.
  • Excellent climbers. Can ascend walls, trees, and tent fabric.
  • Attracted to moisture and shelter in arid environments.

Sting Protocol

  1. Clean the sting site with soap and water.
  2. Apply ice wrapped in cloth, 10 minutes on, 10 minutes off.
  3. Immobilize the affected limb.
  4. Monitor for systemic symptoms: muscle twitching, roving eye movements (opsoclonus), difficulty swallowing, slurred speech, excessive salivation, respiratory distress.
  5. Administer pain relief (ibuprofen, acetaminophen).
  6. Seek medical care for bark scorpion stings, stings in children under 5, or any sting with systemic symptoms. Antivenom (Anascorp) is available for severe bark scorpion envenomation.
  7. Most non-bark-scorpion stings resolve in 24–48 hours with pain management.

Prevention

  • Shake out boots, clothing, and sleeping bags every time.
  • Sleep on a cot or elevated surface when possible in scorpion country.
  • Check under and around your tent with a UV flashlight at night.
  • Do not walk barefoot at night in scorpion habitat.
  • Do not reach under rocks, logs, or debris without gloves.

Fire Ants (Solenopsis invicta)

  • Range: Southeastern US, expanding. Also South America, Australia, parts of Asia.
  • Behavior: Extremely aggressive colony defense. Swarm and sting en masse when the mound is disturbed.
  • Sting: Each ant bites to anchor, then stings repeatedly in a circular pattern. Venom is alkaloid-based.
  • Symptoms: Immediate burning pain. Within 24 hours, characteristic white pustules form at each sting site. In sensitive individuals, anaphylaxis is possible — treat as per bee sting anaphylaxis protocol above.
  • Treatment: Clean with soap and water. Apply ice. Do NOT pop the pustules (infection risk). Take antihistamines for itching. Monitor for anaphylaxis.
  • Prevention: Watch for mounds (dome-shaped, 6–24 in / 15–61 cm tall, no visible entry hole on top). Avoid standing on or near mounds. If swarmed, brush ants off immediately — they grip with their jaws and will not release easily.

Assassin Bugs and Chagas Disease

  • Range: Americas, from the southern US to Argentina. Known as "kissing bugs" (Triatoma spp.) because they bite near the mouth at night.
  • Disease: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi). Transmitted not through the bite itself but through the bug's feces, which are deposited near the bite wound. The victim scratches the bite, rubbing feces into the wound or mucous membranes.
  • Acute symptoms: Swelling at the bite site (Romana sign if near the eye), fever, fatigue. Often asymptomatic.
  • Chronic disease: 20–30% of infected individuals develop cardiac disease (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias) or GI disease (megacolon, megaesophagus) years to decades later.
  • Prevention: Sleep in tightly sealed shelters. Use mosquito netting tucked under the sleeping surface. Inspect bedding. Kissing bugs are nocturnal and hide in cracks in walls, thatched roofs, and behind furniture during the day.
  • If bitten: Do NOT scratch. Clean the bite area thoroughly. Seek medical evaluation for testing if you are in an endemic area.

Improvised Repellents

When commercial repellents are unavailable:

Smoke

  • Build a small, smoky fire (add green wood, damp leaves, or damp grass to a hot fire).
  • Sit in the smoke plume. Smoke repels mosquitoes, black flies, and most biting insects.
  • Dry your clothing over smoke to impart short-term repellent properties.
  • Create a smudge pot: carry smoldering punk wood or a bundle of smoldering damp grass in a container.

Mud

  • Apply a thin layer of mud to exposed skin. The physical barrier deters biting insects.
  • Reapply as it dries and cracks. Effectiveness is moderate and short-lived.
  • Better than nothing in a no-repellent emergency.

Plant-Based Options

These provide limited, short-duration (20–60 minute) protection:

  • Wild mint/pennyroyal: Crush fresh leaves and rub on skin. Contains pulegone.
  • Yarrow: Crush leaves and rub on exposed skin.
  • Birch bark: Peel thin strips of papery bark and burn them for smoke. Contains compounds mosquitoes avoid.
  • Citronella grass (Cymbopogon nardus): If available in tropical regions, crush and rub on skin.
  • Pine/spruce resin: Apply sparingly to pulse points. Sticky but somewhat effective.
WARNING Plant-based repellents provide vastly inferior protection compared to DEET or picaridin. Do NOT rely on them in areas where mosquitoes carry malaria, dengue, or other life-threatening diseases. Use them only as a supplement or emergency backup.

Common Mistakes

  • Applying DEET under clothing. Apply to exposed skin only. Apply permethrin to clothing.
  • Using "suffocation" methods for tick removal. Vaseline, heat, and nail polish delay removal and may increase disease transmission.
  • Ignoring mild sting reactions in someone with no allergy history. Anaphylaxis can develop at any age with no prior warning. Always carry an EpiPen if traveling in remote areas.
  • Popping fire ant pustules. Leads to secondary infection. Leave them intact.
  • Assuming mosquito nets alone are sufficient. Nets must be permethrin-treated and properly tucked to be effective. Mosquitoes find gaps.
  • Scratching insect bites and assassin bug bites. Scratching is the primary transmission route for Chagas disease and introduces bacteria into any bite wound.
  • Relying on citronella candles. Studies show minimal effectiveness beyond a 3 ft (1 m) radius, and even that is marginal.

Quick Reference

Threat Prevention Immediate Treatment Evacuate If
Mosquitoes DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing, nets N/A (treat diseases) Fever develops after travel to endemic area
Ticks Permethrin clothing, DEET, tick checks Fine tweezers, steady pull, clean site Bull's-eye rash, fever, or joint pain within 30 days
Bee/wasp stings Avoid scents, cover food, stay calm Remove stinger fast, ice, antihistamine Any sign of anaphylaxis
Scorpions Shake out boots, UV light checks, sleep elevated Ice, immobilize, pain relief Systemic symptoms, child under 5, bark scorpion
Fire ants Avoid mounds, brush off immediately Soap/water, ice, do not pop pustules Anaphylaxis signs
Assassin bugs Sealed shelter, netting, do not scratch Clean bite, do not scratch, seek testing Facial swelling (Romana sign), fever

See Also

  • Venomous Snakes — Anaphylaxis can occur from venom allergies. Same evacuation principles apply.
  • Venomous Spiders — Many "spider bites" are actually insect bites. Cross-reference for differential diagnosis.
  • Bear Safety — Scented repellents can attract bears. Choose unscented DEET formulations in bear country.
  • Big Cats — Tick prevention matters in off-trail terrain shared with big cats.

  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Mosquito-Borne Diseases," "Ticks," "Insect Repellents." cdc.gov. Accessed 2025.

  • Fradin, M. S., and Day, J. F. "Comparative Efficacy of Insect Repellents against Mosquito Bites." New England Journal of Medicine, vol. 347, no. 1, 2002, pp. 13–18.
