Scenarios

Lost in the Woods

A step-by-step survival walkthrough from the moment you realize you are lost through rescue or self-extraction.

At a Glance

  • Apply the STOP protocol immediately: Sit, Think, Observe, Plan.
  • Shelter and warmth kill faster than hunger — prioritize them over food.
  • Stay put unless you have a compelling, logical reason to move.
  • Make yourself visible and audible to search and rescue teams.
  • Manage your psychology as aggressively as you manage your resources.

The STOP Protocol

S — Sit Down

Stop moving the instant you realize you are lost. Every step you take from this point without a plan increases the search area SAR must cover. Sit on your pack, a log, or the ground. Drink water if you have it.

T — Think

Recall your last known position. Think about landmarks you passed. Estimate how long you have been walking since your last confirmed location. Do not let panic override this step.

O — Observe

Survey your immediate surroundings. Note terrain features: ridgelines, water, trails, clearings. Check the sun's position to establish rough cardinal directions. Listen for roads, rivers, trains, or human activity. Inventory everything on your person and in your pockets.

P — Plan

Decide: stay or move. Base this decision on the decision tree below, not on emotion.

Stay Put vs. Move: Decision Tree

Answer these questions in order:

  1. Does anyone know your planned route and expected return time?
  2. Yes: Stay put. SAR will search your planned route first.

  3. No: Continue to question 2.

  4. Do you have a confirmed direction to a road, trail, or town within 3 miles (5 km)?

  5. Yes: Consider moving, but leave markers at your current position.

  6. No: Stay put.

  7. Is your current location dangerous (flash flood zone, exposed ridge in lightning, unstable slope)?

  8. Yes: Move to the nearest safe location, then stay put.

  9. No: Stay put.

  10. Have you been waiting more than 72 hours with no sign of rescue and no one knows you are missing?

  11. Yes: Consider self-extraction by following water downhill.
  12. No: Stay put.
WARNING The urge to "just walk out" kills more lost people than exposure. Statistically, staying put is almost always the correct decision if anyone knows your approximate area.

Immediate Actions (First 2 Hours)

1. Assess Resources on Your Person

Empty every pocket. Check your pack thoroughly. Common overlooked items: - Cell phone (try emergency calls even with no signal — 911 can route through any carrier tower) - Lighter, matches, or ferrocerium rod - Knife or multitool (see Knife Use and Care) - Cordage or paracord (see Cordage) - Trash bag or emergency blanket - Whistle - Mirror or reflective surface - Snack food or water

2. Establish Your Shelter Site

Select a location that is: - Protected from wind (leeward side of a hill, dense tree stand) - Near water but above flood level — at least 20 ft (6 m) above the waterline - Visible from the air if possible (near a clearing) - Away from dead standing trees (widowmakers)

3. Build or Improvise Shelter

Your body loses heat 25 times faster on wet ground than in still air. Insulate from below first. - Leaf litter bed: Pile dry leaves, pine needles, or grass at least 6 in (15 cm) deep. - Debris hut: Ridgepole at 45 degrees, ribs of branches on both sides, piled with leaves and brush. Body-width only — smaller is warmer. - Trash bag shelter: Cut open a bag for a lean-to or wrap yourself in it as a vapor barrier.

4. Start a Fire

Fire provides warmth, water purification, signaling, and morale. Build it near your shelter but not so close that sparks threaten your debris hut. - Gather tinder, kindling, and fuel before striking your first spark. - Three fires in a triangle (spaced 25 ft / 8 m apart) is a recognized distress signal. - Add green branches or damp leaves to a hot fire to produce signal smoke.

Water Priority

You can survive roughly 3 days without water, but your cognitive function degrades within hours of dehydration. Find water within the first day.

Finding Water

  • Follow animal trails downhill — they converge on water.
  • Listen for running water; sound carries far in quiet woods.
  • Look for green vegetation concentrated in a line (indicates subsurface water).
  • Collect morning dew by dragging a cloth through grass, then wring it into your mouth.
  • Rain catchment using a tarp, poncho, trash bag, or large leaves funneled into a container.

Purifying Water

  • Boiling: Roll boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m). This is the most reliable field method.
  • No container for boiling? Use a rock with a natural depression, heat stones in a fire, and drop them into the water (hot rock boiling).
  • Chemical treatment: 2 drops of unscented household bleach per quart/liter. Wait 30 minutes.
WARNING Do not drink untreated water from streams or ponds unless you are in immediate danger of dying from dehydration. Giardia, cryptosporidium, and bacterial infections will make your situation dramatically worse within 24-48 hours.

Signaling

Ground-to-Air Signals

  • Clear a large area and arrange rocks, logs, or trampled snow into a V (need assistance) or X (need medical help). Make each arm at least 10 ft (3 m) long.
  • Use contrasting colors: dark materials on snow, light materials on dark ground.

Audible Signals

  • Three blasts on a whistle = universal distress. Repeat every few minutes.
  • Yell, bang pots, or strike rocks together if you have no whistle.
  • Sound carries best at dawn and dusk.

Visual Signals

  • Signal mirror: aim reflected sunlight at aircraft by holding the mirror near your face, extending your other hand to frame the aircraft between your fingers, and sweeping the reflected light across your fingers. Effective up to 10 miles (16 km).
  • Smoky fire during the day. Bright fire at night.
  • Hang brightly colored clothing in tree canopies near clearings.

Electronic Signals

  • Cell phone: turn off to preserve battery. Power on periodically at high points.
  • If you have signal, send a text with GPS coordinates rather than calling — texts require less bandwidth and may get through when calls cannot.

Navigation if You Decide to Move

Use these methods only if the decision tree above supports moving.

Following Water Downhill

Water flows to civilization more often than not. Follow a stream or creek downstream. It will merge with larger waterways, and larger waterways attract roads, bridges, and towns.

WARNING Do not follow water through deep gorges or box canyons. If terrain becomes impassable, climb above the waterway and parallel it from higher ground.

Finding Trails

  • Look for cut stumps, blazes on trees, or worn ground.
  • Game trails may lead to water but not to civilization. Human trails are wider, more consistent in direction, and show boot prints or litter.

Natural Navigation

  • Sun: Rises approximately east, sets approximately west. In the Northern Hemisphere at midday, the sun is due south.
  • Stick shadow method: Plant a stick upright. Mark the tip of its shadow. Wait 15 minutes. Mark the new shadow tip. A line from the first mark to the second runs approximately west-to-east (first mark = west).
  • Stars: In the Northern Hemisphere, locate Polaris (North Star) by following the two "pointer stars" on the Big Dipper's cup edge. Polaris indicates true north.
  • Vegetation: Moss grows on all sides of trees and is not a reliable indicator of direction. Disregard this myth.

Marking Your Route

Leave clear markers as you travel so SAR can track you or so you can return if the route fails. - Break branches at head height, bending them to point your direction of travel. - Stack three rocks in a cairn at each turn. - Drag a stick to leave a visible trail on soft ground.

Day 1 vs Day 2+ Priorities

Day 1

  1. STOP protocol
  2. Shelter and insulation from ground
  3. Fire
  4. Water procurement and purification
  5. Signaling (visual and audible)

Day 2+

  1. Improve shelter (wind resistance, rain proofing)
  2. Establish a reliable water source
  3. Expand signaling (ground-to-air symbols, signal fire ready to light)
  4. Forage only for easily identifiable, safe food (do not eat wild mushrooms or unfamiliar plants)
  5. Maintain fire through the night
  6. Consider snares or fishing if near water (see Cordage for trap construction lines)
WARNING Expending calories to hunt or forage aggressively before Day 3 is almost always counterproductive. Your body's fat reserves are substantial. Focus on water, warmth, and being found.

Psychological Management

Fear and panic kill faster than cold or thirst. Manage your mental state deliberately.

  • Accept the situation. Denial wastes time. Say out loud: "I am lost. I will survive this."
  • Set small tasks. Gather firewood. Improve shelter. These give purpose and reduce helplessness.
  • Talk to yourself. Narrate your actions. This maintains cognitive function and prevents spiraling thoughts.
  • Control breathing. Box breathing: inhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds, exhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds. Repeat until your heart rate drops.
  • Sleep discipline. Rest when dark. Sleep deprivation destroys judgment. Even in cold conditions, sleep in shifts (if alone, set small fires to keep waking you to tend them).
  • Assign meaning. Think about who and what you are surviving for. People with strong reasons to live consistently outperform those without.
  • Reject the timeline. Do not tell yourself "if I'm not rescued by tomorrow..." Set no deadline for hope.

What Search and Rescue Actually Does

How SAR Searches

  • Hasty teams deploy first: small, fast groups checking the most likely locations (trails, campsites, water sources, your planned route).
  • Grid search follows if hasty teams fail: crews walk in systematic patterns across the search area.
  • Air assets (helicopters, drones, fixed-wing) scan open terrain, ridgelines, and waterways.
  • Dog teams track your scent. If you stay put, your scent concentrates in one area. If you wander, you dilute it across a wide zone.

SAR Timelines

  • If you filed a trip plan, SAR may be notified within hours of your expected return.
  • Without a trip plan, SAR depends on someone reporting you missing, which may take days.
  • Most wilderness rescues occur within 72 hours of activation.
  • SAR does not stop looking after a fixed period. Searches continue based on probability of detection and survivability estimates.

How to Be Found

  • Stay in the open when you hear aircraft. Lie flat with arms and legs spread on contrasting ground.
  • Wave with both arms crossed overhead (not one arm — one arm can look like a casual wave).
  • Keep your signal fire fueled and ready to ignite at the sound of aircraft or voices.
  • Respond to shouts with three whistle blasts or three yells.
  • At night, keep your fire burning. Fire is visible from the air for miles.

Common Mistakes

  • Walking aimlessly in hopes of stumbling onto a road.
  • Abandoning a shelter to build a new one instead of improving the current one.
  • Rationing water too aggressively — drink when thirsty, find more water.
  • Eating snow directly (lowers core temperature; melt it first).
  • Separating from your group if lost together.
  • Discarding gear that seems useless (every item has potential survival applications).
  • Giving up signaling after a few hours.
  • Travelling at night over unfamiliar terrain.

Quick Reference

Priority Timeframe Action
1 Immediate STOP protocol
2 First 30 min Assess resources, pick shelter site
3 First 2 hours Build shelter, start fire
4 First 6 hours Find and purify water
5 Ongoing Signal (visual, audible, fire)
6 Day 2+ Improve shelter, maintain water, forage

Rule of Threes: - 3 minutes without air - 3 hours without shelter (in harsh conditions) - 3 days without water - 3 weeks without food

  • Knots and Lashing — structural knots for shelter construction
  • Cordage — making rope from natural fibers for snares and lashing

  • Wiseman, John "Lofty." SAS Survival Handbook. William Morrow, 2014.
  • Lundin, Cody. 98.6 Degrees: The Art of Keeping Your Ass Alive. Gibbs Smith, 2003.

Scenarios

Animal Attack

Decision flowcharts and survival protocols for encounters with dangerous wildlife, from prevention through post-attack wound care.

At a Glance

  • Identify the animal before reacting — wrong responses get you killed.
  • Bear attacks require opposite responses depending on species and motivation.
  • Fight back against mountain lions, predatory black bears, and wild boar. Never play dead with these animals.
  • Snake bites: immobilize, keep below heart level, evacuate. Do not cut, suck, or tourniquet.
  • After any attack, infection is the primary ongoing threat.

Decision Flowchart: What Is Attacking You?

Ask in order:

  1. Is it a bear? Go to Bear Attack.
  2. Is it a large cat (mountain lion / cougar)? Go to Mountain Lion.
  3. Is it a canine (wolf, coyote, dog)? Go to Wolf Pack or Dog Attack.
  4. Is it a moose? Go to Moose.
  5. Is it a wild boar / feral hog? Go to Wild Boar.
  6. Is it a snake? Go to Snake Bite Protocol.
  7. Is it an alligator or crocodile? Go to Alligator and Crocodile.

Bear Attack

Step 1: Identify the Bear

Feature Black Bear Grizzly / Brown Bear
Shoulder hump No Yes — prominent muscular hump
Face profile Straight from forehead to nose Concave (dished)
Ears Tall, pointed Short, rounded
Claws Short, dark, curved (1.5 in / 4 cm) Long, light, straighter (2-4 in / 5-10 cm)
Size 200-400 lb (90-180 kg) 400-800 lb (180-360 kg)

Step 2: Determine Motivation

Defensive attack (most common for grizzlies): - The bear charges because you surprised it, threatened cubs, or approached a food cache. - Signs: woofing, jaw-popping, bluff charges, ears back.

Predatory attack (rare but lethal): - The bear stalks you, circles, approaches silently, or follows you. - The bear is calm, focused, and deliberate. - More common with black bears than grizzlies.

Step 3: Respond

Grizzly — Defensive Attack: 1. Do not run. Bears sprint at 35 mph (56 km/h). You cannot outrun one. 2. Stand your ground during bluff charges. 3. Deploy bear spray at 20-30 ft (6-9 m) in a slight downward angle. 4. If contact occurs: play dead. Lie face down, hands clasped behind your neck, legs spread to resist being flipped. Keep your pack on for spine protection. 5. Remain motionless until the bear leaves the area. Grizzlies often return to check.

Black Bear — Defensive Attack: 1. Stand tall and make yourself look large. Speak in a firm, loud voice. 2. Back away slowly. Do not turn your back. 3. Use bear spray at 20-30 ft (6-9 m). 4. If it bluff-charges, hold your ground and keep shouting.

Any Bear — Predatory Attack: 1. Do not play dead. This bear wants to eat you. 2. Face the bear. Make yourself as large as possible. 3. Fight with everything available: rocks, sticks, knife, fists. 4. Target the nose, eyes, and face. 5. Shout aggressively. Do not stop fighting.

WARNING If a bear enters your tent at night, this is virtually always predatory. Fight immediately with maximum aggression.

Mountain Lion

Mountain lions (cougars, pumas) are ambush predators. If one is facing you and has not attacked, you have likely already deterred it by detecting it.

Response — Always Fight

  1. Face the animal. Never turn your back or run — running triggers a chase response.
  2. Make yourself appear as large as possible. Raise your arms, open your jacket wide, stand on a rock or log.
  3. Shout, throw rocks, use sticks. Be aggressive.
  4. If it attacks: fight back with everything. Target eyes, nose, and throat.
  5. Use a knife if available (see Knife Use and Care). Stab the throat, eyes, or base of the skull.
  6. Do not play dead. Mountain lions will continue feeding on a passive target.
WARNING Children are at highest risk. In mountain lion territory, keep children between adults, not trailing behind.

Wolf Pack

Unprovoked wolf attacks on humans are extremely rare. Most documented attacks involve habituated wolves or rabid individuals.

Response

  1. Do not run. Wolves are pursuit predators.
  2. Make yourself appear large. Group together if with others.
  3. Back away slowly while facing the wolves.
  4. Maintain aggressive posture: shout, wave arms, throw objects.
  5. If attacked, fight back targeting the nose and eyes.
  6. Climb a tree if possible — wolves cannot climb. Get at least 12 ft (3.7 m) up.
  7. Build or maintain a fire — wolves generally avoid fire.

Moose

Moose injure more people than bears and wolves combined in North America. A bull moose weighs up to 1,500 lb (680 kg) and can kick in any direction.

Signs of Aggression

  • Ears pinned back.
  • Hair raised on the hump (hackles).
  • Licking lips.
  • Lowering the head.

Response

  1. Give moose at least 50 ft (15 m) of space. They have a larger personal-space threshold than bears.
  2. If it charges: run. Unlike bears and cats, moose often do not pursue far. They want you away from them.
  3. Put a large object between you and the moose: a tree, a car, a boulder.
  4. If knocked down, curl into a ball, protect your head and neck with your arms, and stay down until the moose leaves. Getting up triggers repeated stomping.
  5. Do not approach a cow with calves — this is the most dangerous moose encounter.
WARNING Moose are most aggressive during rut (September-October) and calving season (May-June). Give extra distance during these periods.

Wild Boar

Wild boar (feral hogs) weigh 100-400 lb (45-180 kg) and have razor-sharp tusks. They are fast, aggressive when cornered, and will charge without warning.

Response

  1. Climb. Get off the ground onto a tree, boulder, vehicle, or any elevated surface. Boar cannot climb.
  2. If you cannot climb, sidestep the charge — boar run in straight lines and turn poorly.
  3. If knocked down, protect your femoral arteries (inner thighs) and abdomen. Curl on your side with knees drawn up.
  4. Fight back with a knife, spear, or heavy stick targeting the head and eyes.
  5. A boar will usually disengage once it perceives the threat is neutralized. Do not chase it.

Snake Bite Protocol

Immediate Actions

  1. Move away from the snake to avoid a second bite.
  2. Note the snake's appearance (color, pattern, head shape) for identification, but do not attempt to catch or kill it.
  3. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the bite — swelling begins rapidly.
  4. Immobilize the bitten limb. Splint it in a neutral position if possible (see Injured and Alone).
  5. Keep the bite at or below heart level.
  6. Mark the edge of swelling with a pen or charcoal and note the time. This tracks progression for medical responders.
  7. Evacuate to medical care immediately. Antivenom is the only effective treatment for envenomation.

Do NOT

  • Cut the wound.
  • Suck the venom (mouth or extractor pump — neither works).
  • Apply a tourniquet (traps venom in the limb, causing tissue death).
  • Apply ice (increases tissue damage).
  • Drink alcohol (accelerates venom absorption).
  • Apply electric shock (myth with no medical basis).
WARNING Roughly 25% of venomous snake bites are "dry bites" with no venom injected. Evacuate regardless — you cannot determine envenomation status in the field.

Pit Viper vs Coral Snake (North America)

  • Pit vipers (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth): triangular head, vertical pupils, heat-sensing pits between eye and nostril. Cause immediate local pain and swelling.
  • Coral snakes: red-yellow-black banding ("red touches yellow, kills a fellow"). Neurotoxic venom may produce delayed symptoms. Seek medical care even if you feel fine.

Alligator and Crocodile

Myth Busted: Zigzag Running

The old advice to run in a zigzag pattern is wrong. Alligators and crocodiles are fast in a straight line for short distances (up to 20 mph / 32 km/h on land) but tire quickly. Run straight and fast away from the water. Zigzagging slows you down for no benefit — these animals do not chase prey on land for extended distances.

If Grabbed

  1. Target the eyes — gouge, poke, stab. The eyes are their most sensitive point.
  2. Hit the snout and palatal valve (the flap at the back of the throat that prevents water intake). If you can wedge something into the valve, the animal will open its jaws.
  3. Do not try to pry the jaws open — the closing force exceeds 2,000 psi, but the opening muscles are weak. A strong person can hold a gator's mouth shut with bare hands, but cannot force it open.
  4. If dragged underwater, fight. These animals drown prey. Resistance to the death roll is your only option.

Prevention

  • Never swim, wade, or stand at the water's edge in known alligator/crocodile habitat, especially at dawn, dusk, or night.
  • Stay at least 15 ft (4.5 m) from the water's edge.
  • Never feed alligators — this eliminates their fear of humans.

Dog Attack

Domestic and feral dogs account for far more attacks than all wild animals combined.

Prevention

  • Do not run from an aggressive dog.
  • Avoid direct eye contact (perceived as a challenge).
  • Stand sideways to reduce your profile.
  • Speak in a calm, firm voice.

During an Attack

  1. Wrap your non-dominant forearm in a jacket, shirt, or pack strap and offer it as a sacrifice target.
  2. When the dog latches on, strike the back of the skull, the nose, or the ribs with your free hand, a rock, or a stick.
  3. If knocked down, curl into a ball protecting your neck and face.
  4. If you have a knife, target the throat or the base of the skull.
  5. A rear chokehold around the dog's neck can cause it to release.

After the Attack: Wound Care

Immediate Wound Management

  1. Control bleeding with direct pressure. Apply a tourniquet only for life-threatening limb hemorrhage (see Injured and Alone).
  2. Irrigate the wound with the cleanest water available — high volume, moderate pressure. Use a water bottle with a small puncture in the cap to create a jet.
  3. Remove visible debris (dirt, teeth, quills) with clean fingers or improvised tweezers (two small sticks).
  4. Do not close bite wounds with tape or sutures in the field — bite wounds are contaminated and must drain.
  5. Cover loosely with the cleanest material available.

Infection Prevention

  • Change dressings at least twice daily.
  • Monitor for signs of infection: increasing redness, swelling, warmth, red streaks from the wound, fever, or foul-smelling discharge.
  • If you have a first aid kit, apply antibiotic ointment.
  • Animal bites carry high infection risk: bacteria from the animal's mouth, soil, and your skin all enter the wound.
WARNING All mammal bites carry rabies risk. Any bite from a bat, raccoon, skunk, fox, or feral dog requires post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible. Rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms appear.

Evacuation Decision

Evacuate immediately if: - Bleeding cannot be controlled. - The wound is on the face, neck, or over a joint. - Signs of envenomation develop (snake, spider). - Any puncture wound is deeper than 0.5 in (1.3 cm). - Bone, tendon, or muscle is visible. - The victim shows signs of shock (pale, cold, rapid pulse, confusion). - You suspect rabies exposure.

Common Mistakes

  • Running from predators that have chase instincts (bears, cats, wolves, dogs).
  • Playing dead with the wrong species (never play dead with a black bear in predatory mode or a mountain lion).
  • Attempting to suck venom from a snake bite.
  • Running zigzag from alligators/crocodiles.
  • Neglecting wound irrigation after the immediate danger has passed.
  • Closing bite wounds in the field (traps bacteria).
  • Failing to monitor for infection in the hours and days after the attack.
  • Approaching a "dead" or injured animal.

Quick Reference

Animal Primary Response Secondary Response
Grizzly (defensive) Bear spray, play dead Protect neck, stay down
Grizzly (predatory) Fight back Target face
Black bear (defensive) Stand tall, yell Back away slowly
Black bear (predatory) Fight back Target nose and eyes
Mountain lion Fight always Appear large, be loud
Wolf Stand tall, back away Climb a tree, use fire
Moose Run, get behind cover Curl up if knocked down
Wild boar Climb Sidestep charge
Snake Move away, immobilize limb Evacuate for antivenom
Alligator/Croc Run straight from water Gouge eyes if grabbed
Dog Offer wrapped forearm Strike nose, skull, ribs

  • Lost in the Woods — survival priorities if an animal encounter leaves you disoriented
  • Knife Use and Care — defensive knife use and wound care tool
  • Cordage — making improvised tourniquets and lashing for splints

Scenarios

Injured and Alone

Self-assessment, self-treatment, and self-rescue protocols when you are hurt in the wilderness with no one to help.

At a Glance

  • Run the ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) on yourself before doing anything else.
  • Stop catastrophic bleeding first — everything else is secondary.
  • A one-handed tourniquet can save your life; practice the technique before you need it.
  • The decision to self-rescue vs stay and signal depends on injury severity, mobility, and rescue probability.
  • Your greatest enemy is not the injury. It is the psychological spiral that follows it.

Self-Assessment: The First 60 Seconds

Adrenaline masks pain. You may not realize the extent of your injuries immediately. Force yourself through this checklist before acting.

The ABCs

A — Airway - Can you breathe freely through your nose and mouth? - Is there blood, vomit, or debris in your mouth? Clear it. - If your jaw is broken, prop yourself on your side so fluids drain out.

B — Breathing - Take a deep breath. Is it painful? Pain on one side may indicate broken ribs or a pneumothorax (collapsed lung). - Count your breaths for 15 seconds and multiply by four. Normal: 12-20 per minute. Above 24 suggests shock, pain, or chest injury. - If you hear a sucking sound from a chest wound, seal it immediately with any airtight material (plastic wrapper, duct tape, a gloved hand) taped on three sides to create a flutter valve.

C — Circulation - Check for bleeding. Run your hands over your entire body — head, neck, armpits, chest, abdomen, groin, thighs, back. Look at your hands after each area. - Life-threatening bleeds feel warm, wet, and fast. Arterial blood is bright red and spurts. - Check your pulse at the wrist. If you cannot find it, check the neck (carotid). A rapid, weak pulse indicates blood loss or shock.

Full Body Survey

After ABCs, systematically check: - Head: Feel the skull for depressions, swelling, or boggy spots. Check ears and nose for clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid leak = skull fracture). - Neck and spine: Can you move your head without electric/shooting pain down your arms or legs? If not, minimize spinal movement. - Shoulders and arms: Squeeze each arm, check range of motion. - Chest and ribs: Press gently. Instability or grinding (crepitus) = fracture. - Abdomen: Press gently in all four quadrants. Rigidity or guarding = internal injury. You cannot treat this in the field — prioritize evacuation. - Pelvis: Press inward on both hip bones. Instability = pelvic fracture. Do not repeat this test — you can worsen bleeding. - Legs: Squeeze each leg from hip to ankle. Check ankles and feet for sensation and movement.

WARNING Abdominal rigidity, a pelvic fracture, or signs of significant internal bleeding (rapid pulse, cold skin, confusion without external blood loss) mean you must signal for rescue immediately. These injuries cannot be self-treated.

Stopping Catastrophic Bleeding

Direct Pressure

  1. Place the cleanest cloth available directly on the wound.
  2. Press hard — harder than feels comfortable. Use your body weight.
  3. Hold for a minimum of 10 minutes without checking. Lifting to look resets clotting.
  4. If blood soaks through, add more material on top. Do not remove the first layer.

Wound Packing

For deep wounds (stab, gunshot, gaping laceration): 1. Push clean cloth directly into the wound cavity with your fingers. 2. Pack tightly, filling the entire space. 3. Apply direct pressure on top of the packing.

One-Handed Tourniquet Application

If you are bleeding heavily from a limb and your other arm is functional:

With a manufactured tourniquet (CAT, SOFTT-W): 1. Slide the tourniquet onto the injured limb, 2-3 in (5-8 cm) above the wound. Never place over a joint. 2. Pull the free end through the buckle with your teeth and free hand. 3. Twist the windlass until bleeding stops. 4. Secure the windlass in the clip. 5. Note the time. Write it on the tourniquet or on your skin with any marking implement.

Improvised one-handed tourniquet: 1. Use a belt, strip of fabric (at least 1.5 in / 4 cm wide), or a triangular bandage folded. 2. Wrap it around the limb above the wound. 3. Tie a half knot. Place a stick, pen, or sturdy twig on the knot. Tie a full knot over the stick. 4. Twist the stick until bleeding stops. Secure the stick against the limb by tying or taping it in place.

WARNING A tourniquet causes severe pain. This is expected. Do not loosen it. A properly applied tourniquet can remain in place for up to 2 hours without causing limb loss. Losing the limb is preferable to losing your life.

Self-Splinting

General Principles

  • Immobilize the joint above and below the fracture.
  • Pad between the splint and skin to prevent pressure sores.
  • Check circulation below the splint after application: feel for a pulse, check skin color (pink = good, blue/white = too tight), and test sensation.

Arm or Wrist Fracture

  1. Find two rigid objects (sticks at least 12 in / 30 cm long, trekking pole sections, rolled magazine or bark).
  2. Place one on each side of the break.
  3. Pad with cloth, moss, or clothing.
  4. Lash in place above and below the fracture using strips of cloth, paracord, or natural cordage. Use a clove hitch to start each lashing.
  5. Fashion a sling from a shirt, bandana, or belt to support the arm against your chest.

Lower Leg Fracture

  1. Straighten the leg gently by pulling traction from the ankle (pull along the length of the leg, not upward).
  2. Place a rigid splint on the outside of the leg from hip to past the foot.
  3. Place a second splint on the inside from groin to past the foot if material is available.
  4. Pad the ankle, knee, and groin.
  5. Lash at the ankle, below the knee, above the knee, and at the hip.

Improvised Splint Materials

  • Trekking poles (adjustable length, rigid)
  • Branches stripped of nubs (at least thumb-thickness)
  • SAM splint if in your kit (moldable aluminum)
  • Rolled bark stripped from a dead tree
  • Foam sleeping pad rolled and taped
  • Your own body: splint a broken finger to the adjacent finger, a broken leg to the other leg

Ankle Sprain or Fracture

  1. Do not remove the boot if the ankle is swelling — the boot acts as a compression splint.
  2. Lash a figure-eight pattern of cloth or cordage around the boot and ankle for additional stability.
  3. If the boot is already off, wrap the ankle in cloth and splint with sticks on both sides.

Treating Your Own Wounds

Wound Irrigation

  • Use the cleanest water available in the highest volume you can manage.
  • Punch a small hole in a water bottle cap and squeeze — this creates adequate irrigation pressure (approximately 8 psi).
  • Flush the wound from the cleanest edge outward, washing debris away.
  • Use at least 500 ml (1 pint) per wound.

Wound Closure

  • Close clean, straight cuts with butterfly closures (adhesive strips) or improvised tape strips.
  • Do not close dirty wounds, bite wounds, or punctures — these must drain to prevent infection.
  • Steri-strips: apply perpendicular to the wound edges, pulling the skin together. Alternate sides for even tension.

Burns

  • Cool with clean water for 10 minutes.
  • Do not pop blisters — intact skin is a sterile barrier.
  • Cover with a clean, non-adhesive dressing.
  • Burns larger than your palm (approximately 1% body surface) or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals require evacuation.

Infection Signs (Monitor Continuously)

  • Increasing pain after the first 24 hours (pain should be decreasing, not increasing).
  • Spreading redness beyond the wound edge.
  • Red streaks extending from the wound toward the heart (lymphangitis — this is urgent).
  • Pus (yellow/green discharge).
  • Fever, chills, or malaise.
  • Foul smell.

Pain Management Without Medication

Breathing Techniques

  • Box breathing: Inhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds, exhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds. Repeat for 5 minutes. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system and measurably reduces pain perception.
  • Slow exhale: Inhale for 4 seconds, exhale for 8 seconds. The extended exhale triggers a relaxation response.

Cold Application

  • Apply cold water, snow wrapped in cloth, or a cool mud pack to injuries with swelling. Apply for 15 minutes, remove for 15 minutes.
  • Do not apply ice or snow directly to skin — frostbite compounds the injury.

Positioning

  • Elevate injured limbs above heart level to reduce swelling and throbbing pain.
  • For rib fractures, sit upright leaning slightly toward the injured side. This limits chest wall movement on the broken side.

Distraction and Mental Techniques

  • Count objects in your environment. Name every tree species you can see. Recite song lyrics. Mental engagement reduces pain signal processing.
  • Visualize the pain as a color or shape. Mentally shrink it. This technique has clinical support in pain management literature.
  • Set small, timed goals: "I will manage this for the next 10 minutes." Repeat.

Natural Analgesics (Use with Caution)

  • Willow bark contains salicin (related to aspirin). Chew the inner bark of willow species. Provides mild anti-inflammatory and analgesic effect. Do not use if allergic to aspirin or if you have a bleeding wound (salicin has a mild blood-thinning effect).
  • Do not eat unknown plants in hopes of pain relief.

Mobility with Injuries

Improvised Crutch

  1. Find a Y-shaped branch (forked at the top) approximately armpit height.
  2. Pad the fork with cloth or moss to prevent armpit nerve damage.
  3. Trim nubs and rough bark from the shaft.
  4. Test weight-bearing before trusting it fully.
  5. Walk with the crutch on the opposite side of the injury: if your right leg is hurt, the crutch goes under your left arm.

Walking with a Leg Splint

  • Use the crutch or two trekking poles.
  • Take short steps. Place the crutch/poles first, then swing the injured leg through, then step with the good leg.
  • On downhill terrain, lower the crutch/poles first, then step down with the good leg, then ease the injured leg down.

Crawling Techniques

When you cannot walk at all: - Army crawl: Lie prone, pull with forearms, push with the good leg. Slow but effective over flat or slightly downhill terrain. - Seated scoot: Sit on your backside, push with arms and the good leg. Works on moderate terrain. - Log roll: For short, flat distances or to reach a specific point. Protect the injured limb by holding it against your body.

WARNING Crawling is exhausting. If you must crawl, do so toward a signaling position (clearing, ridgetop, road) rather than attempting to crawl out of the wilderness. A 1 mile (1.6 km) crawl on rough terrain can take 8-12 hours.

Self-Rescue vs Stay-and-Signal Decision

Stay and Signal if:

  • Someone knows your location and expected return.
  • You cannot walk or can only crawl.
  • You have shelter, water access, and signaling capability at your current position.
  • The terrain between you and help is technical, steep, or hazardous.
  • The weather is deteriorating.

Attempt Self-Rescue if:

  • No one knows where you are.
  • You can walk (even slowly) and know the direction to a road or trailhead.
  • Your current position is exposed to elements with no way to improve it.
  • You are confident the route is manageable with your injuries.
  • Remaining in place will worsen your condition (e.g., rising water, extreme cold with no shelter materials).

If You Move

  • Mark your starting position with a note, ground-to-air symbol, or trail marker.
  • Travel during the safest hours (daylight, moderate temperatures).
  • Rest frequently — your calorie burn is massively elevated when injured.
  • Reassess at every rest stop: is continuing smarter than stopping here?
  • See Lost in the Woods — Navigation for route-finding techniques.

Psychological Challenge of Solo Injury

Being injured alone is the most psychologically demanding survival scenario. The combination of pain, helplessness, and fear of death creates a powerful downward spiral.

Immediate Psychological First Aid

  1. Breathe. Pain and fear make you hyperventilate. Force slow, deep breaths.
  2. Talk out loud. Narrate your actions: "I am checking my bleeding. I am applying pressure." Verbal processing keeps your prefrontal cortex (logical brain) engaged over your amygdala (panic center).
  3. Triage your emotions. Acknowledge fear. Say it: "I am scared." Then set it aside and focus on the next physical task.

Ongoing Mental Discipline

  • Assign yourself a routine: check wound, gather firewood, improve shelter, signal. Repeat. Routine creates normalcy.
  • Set micro-goals measured in minutes, not miles or days.
  • Do not make permanent decisions based on temporary despair. "I can't do this" is always temporary if you are still breathing.
  • Anger is a useful emotion in survival. Channel it toward survival tasks, not toward self-blame.
  • If you feel yourself giving up, focus on one person you refuse to let down.

Prioritization When You Cannot Do Everything

If your injuries limit you to only a few actions, prioritize in this order:

  1. Stop life-threatening bleeding. Nothing else matters if you bleed out.
  2. Protect your airway and breathing. Position yourself so you will not choke if you lose consciousness.
  3. Get out of immediate environmental danger (water, lightning, rockfall).
  4. Signal for rescue — whistle, mirror, fire, ground-to-air symbol.
  5. Insulate from the ground. Pull leaves, branches, or gear under you.
  6. Water — only after the above are handled.
  7. Splint and stabilize injuries to prevent further damage.
  8. Everything else (shelter improvement, food) is bonus.

Common Mistakes

  • Failing to check for bleeding due to adrenaline masking the wound.
  • Removing a boot from a swelling ankle (the boot is your best splint).
  • Loosening a tourniquet because of pain.
  • Attempting to relocate (reduce) a dislocation without training.
  • Moving with a suspected spinal injury unnecessarily.
  • Closing a dirty wound (traps bacteria, causes abscess).
  • Refusing to rest ("I'll push through it") and collapsing in a worse location.
  • Crawling for miles when staying put and signaling would bring faster rescue.
  • Waiting too long to apply a tourniquet during arterial bleeding.

Quick Reference

Injury Type Immediate Action Key Rule
Arterial bleeding Tourniquet or direct pressure Tourniquet pain is expected; do not release
Broken limb Splint in place, immobilize two joints Check circulation below the splint
Chest wound (sucking) Seal on three sides One open side = flutter valve
Snake bite Immobilize, below heart level Do not cut, suck, or tourniquet
Spinal injury suspected Minimize movement, signal for rescue Do not move unless immediate danger
Burn Cool water 10 min, do not pop blisters Cover with non-adhesive dressing
Head injury Monitor consciousness level, rest Evacuate if confused, vomiting, unequal pupils

Survival Glossary

Comprehensive A-Z glossary of survival terminology. Use this as a quick-reference when encountering unfamiliar terms throughout the guides.

A

ABCDE (Primary Survey) — The standard trauma assessment sequence: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure. Used to identify and treat life-threatening conditions in priority order.

Azimuth — A compass bearing measured in degrees clockwise from true north (0-360 degrees). Used to navigate toward a target.

AMS (Acute Mountain Sickness) — Illness caused by rapid ascent to high altitude, characterized by headache, nausea, and fatigue. Onset typically above 8,000 feet (2,400 m).

B

Baseplate Compass — A compass mounted on a transparent rectangular base with a direction-of-travel arrow, used for taking bearings from a map and navigating in the field.

Batoning — Striking the spine of a knife with a baton (a short, heavy stick) to split wood along its grain. Used to produce kindling and access dry inner wood.

Bearing — The direction from one point to another, expressed in degrees from north. A compass bearing accounts for magnetic declination.

Bivouac (Bivy) — A temporary, minimalist camp or shelter, often just a sleeping bag and a lightweight waterproof cover.

Bug-Out Bag (BOB) — A pre-packed emergency bag containing supplies for 72 hours of self-sufficiency during an evacuation. See also: EDC, INCH bag.

Bushcraft — The skill set of thriving in a wilderness environment using knowledge and minimal tools. Encompasses fire craft, shelter building, foraging, tracking, and tool making.

C

Cairn — A man-made stack of stones used as a trail marker or navigational reference in open terrain.

Char Cloth — Cotton or linen fabric that has been partially burned (pyrolyzed) in the absence of oxygen to create a material that catches sparks easily and holds an ember.

Conduction — Heat transfer through direct contact between objects. A major cause of heat loss when lying on cold ground without insulation.

Convection — Heat transfer through moving air or water across the body. Wind chill is a convection effect.

CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) — An emergency procedure combining chest compressions and rescue breaths to maintain circulation and oxygenation when the heart stops. Standard adult rate: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

D

Dead Reckoning — Navigating by tracking your direction and distance traveled from a known starting point, without external references.

Debris Hut — A small, low shelter built from a ridgepole propped against a support, covered with layers of leaves, branches, and forest debris for insulation. See Debris Hut.

Declination — The angular difference between magnetic north (where a compass needle points) and true north (geographic north). Varies by location and must be accounted for when navigating with map and compass.

Dehydration — A dangerous deficit of body water. Symptoms progress from thirst and dark urine to confusion, rapid heartbeat, and organ failure. A leading cause of death in survival situations.

E

EDC (Everyday Carry) — The essential items a person carries daily for emergency preparedness: knife, lighter, flashlight, cordage, and similar tools.

Edibility Test (Universal Edibility Test) — A multi-step protocol for testing unknown plants for toxicity. Involves skin contact, lip contact, tongue contact, chewing, and small ingestion with 8-hour waits between steps. See Foraging Basics.

Ember — A small, glowing piece of combustible material produced by friction fire methods or char cloth. Placed into a tinder bundle and blown into flame.

Evaporation — Heat loss caused by moisture turning to vapor on the skin surface. Wet clothing dramatically increases heat loss through this mechanism.

Exposure — Prolonged subjection to extreme environmental conditions (cold, heat, wind, rain) without adequate protection. A primary killer in wilderness emergencies.

F

Fatwood — Resinous wood found in the stumps and heartwood of dead conifers, particularly pine. Extremely flammable and effective as fire-starting material even when wet.

Ferro Rod (Ferrocerium Rod) — A metallic fire-starting tool that produces a shower of sparks exceeding 5,000°F (2,760°C) when scraped with a hard edge. Works when wet.

Fire Lay — The arrangement of tinder, kindling, and fuel wood before ignition. Common types: teepee, log cabin, lean-to, star, and platform.

Fire Triangle — The three elements required for combustion: heat, fuel, and oxygen. Remove any one element and the fire goes out.

Fording — Crossing a body of water on foot. Requires assessment of depth, current speed, and footing.

Foraging — Gathering wild plants, fungi, insects, or other natural foods from the environment. See Foraging Basics.

G

GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite) — A weather satellite system used by NOAA. Relevant to understanding weather forecasting tools and satellite-based communication.

Ground-to-Air Signal — A large visual marker laid out on the ground to communicate with search aircraft. Standard symbols include V (need assistance), X (need medical help), and an arrow (traveling this direction).

H

Handrail (Navigation) — A linear terrain feature (river, ridge, road, fence line) used as a navigation guide to follow toward a destination or catching feature.

Hardtack — A simple, long-lasting survival biscuit made from flour, water, and salt. Historical emergency ration.

Hemostatic Agent — A substance (such as QuikClot or Celox) applied to a wound to accelerate blood clotting and control severe hemorrhage.

Hypothermia — A dangerous drop in core body temperature below 95°F (35°C). Progresses through shivering, confusion, loss of coordination, and cardiac arrest. See Hypothermia and Heatstroke.

Heatstroke — A life-threatening condition in which the body's core temperature rises above 104°F (40°C) and the thermoregulation system fails. Requires immediate aggressive cooling. See Hypothermia and Heatstroke.

I

INCH Bag (I'm Never Coming Home) — A long-term survival pack designed for indefinite self-sufficiency, as opposed to a 72-hour bug-out bag.

Insulation — Material that traps dead air to slow heat transfer. In shelters, provided by leaves, grass, boughs, or snow. In clothing, provided by down, wool, or synthetic fill.

J

Jerky — Lean meat that has been trimmed, sliced thin, and dried to prevent spoilage. A critical food-preservation technique in wilderness survival.

K

Kindling — Small, dry sticks and twigs (pencil-thickness or smaller) placed over tinder to catch fire and build heat for larger fuel wood. See Fire Principles.

Knot (Bowline) — A fixed-loop knot that does not slip under load. One of the most essential survival knots. See Knots and Lashing.

L

Lean-To — A simple shelter constructed by leaning branches or a tarp against a horizontal support, creating a single sloped wall for wind and rain protection.

Lensatic Compass — A military-style compass with a sighting lens and wire for precise bearing measurement. Standard issue in US military (e.g., Cammenga 3H).

LNT (Leave No Trace) — Seven principles for minimizing environmental impact during outdoor activities: plan ahead, travel on durable surfaces, dispose of waste properly, leave what you find, minimize campfire impacts, respect wildlife, be considerate of others.

M

MARCH (Massive hemorrhage, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia) — A tactical trauma assessment protocol used in TCCC (Tactical Combat Casualty Care). Prioritizes life threats in combat or austere environments.

Morse Code (SOS) — The international distress signal: three short, three long, three short (... --- ...). Transmitted by light, sound, or radio.

N

NPA (Nasopharyngeal Airway) — A flexible tube inserted through the nostril to maintain an open airway in a semiconscious patient. Tolerated better than oral airways.

O

Orienteering — The skill of navigating between points using a map and compass. Fundamental to wilderness travel and search-and-rescue.

P

PLB (Personal Locator Beacon) — A device that transmits a distress signal on 406 MHz to the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system, alerting rescue authorities to your GPS position.

Potable — Safe to drink. Water is potable when it has been treated to remove or kill pathogens, chemical contaminants, and particulates.

Pressure Dressing — A bandage applied with firm pressure to a wound to control bleeding. Maintains direct pressure without requiring someone to hold it.

Primitive Fire — Fire created without modern ignition tools, using methods such as bow drill, hand drill, fire plow, or fire saw. See Friction Methods.

Prusik Knot — A friction hitch that grips a rope when weighted and slides freely when unweighted. Used for ascending ropes, tensioning ridgelines, and self-rescue.

Q

Quarantine (Water) — The practice of isolating collected water and allowing sediment to settle before filtering or treating. Improves the effectiveness of purification methods.

R

Radiation (Heat) — Heat loss through infrared emission from the body to cooler surroundings. Occurs without contact or air movement. A reflective survival blanket counters this.

Ridgepole — The central, horizontal support beam of a shelter (especially a debris hut or A-frame), running from the raised front opening to the ground at the rear. See Shelter Principles.

Rule of Threes — A survival prioritization framework: 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter (in harsh conditions), 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food.

S

Shelter-in-Place — Remaining in your current location and fortifying it rather than traveling. Appropriate when travel is more dangerous than staying put.

Signal Mirror — A reflective device used to flash sunlight toward aircraft or distant rescuers. Effective range exceeds 10 miles (16 km) in clear conditions. See Signaling for Rescue.

Snare — A trap using a loop of wire or cordage to capture small game by tightening around the animal as it moves through the loop. See Trapping and Snares.

SODIS (Solar Water Disinfection) — A water purification method using UV radiation from sunlight. Clear water in a transparent PET bottle is exposed to direct sunlight for at least 6 hours (or 2 days under overcast skies). See Purification.

Spindle — The vertical, rotating component of a friction fire set (bow drill or hand drill) that presses into the fireboard to create heat through friction.

Splint — A rigid or semi-rigid support applied to immobilize a fractured or dislocated bone. Constructed from sticks, SAM splints, or improvised materials padded with cloth. See Fractures and Splints.

STOP Protocol — A survival mnemonic: Stop (do not panic), Think (assess the situation), Observe (inventory resources and surroundings), Plan (decide on a course of action). See Survival Mindset.

T

TCCC (Tactical Combat Casualty Care) — A set of evidence-based trauma care guidelines developed by the US military for use in combat and austere environments. Emphasizes hemorrhage control and hypothermia prevention.

Tinder — The finest, most combustible material in a fire lay. Must catch a spark or ember and sustain flame long enough to ignite kindling. Examples: dry grass, birch bark, cedar shavings, char cloth. See Fire Principles.

Tinder Bundle — A bird's-nest-shaped collection of fine, dry tinder material into which an ember is placed and blown into flame.

Tourniquet — A constricting device applied to a limb to cut off arterial blood flow and stop life-threatening hemorrhage. Applied 2-3 inches (5-7.5 cm) above the wound, tightened until bleeding stops. See Trauma and Triage.

Triage — The process of sorting casualties by severity to allocate treatment resources. Categories: immediate, delayed, minimal, expectant. See Trauma and Triage.

Turbidity — The cloudiness or haziness of water caused by suspended particles. High turbidity reduces the effectiveness of UV and chemical purification methods. Pre-filter turbid water before treatment.

U

Universal Edibility Test — See Edibility Test.

UV Purification — Water treatment using ultraviolet light to destroy the DNA of pathogens, rendering them unable to reproduce. Devices like SteriPEN deliver a measured UV dose. Requires low-turbidity water.

V

Vapor Barrier — A waterproof layer (plastic sheet, trash bag) placed close to the body inside insulation to prevent moisture from saturating insulating layers. Used in extreme cold.

W

WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature) — An environmental heat stress index that accounts for temperature, humidity, wind, and solar radiation. Used to assess risk of heatstroke.

Wicking — The movement of moisture away from the skin through capillary action in fabric. Base layers made of wool or synthetic materials wick sweat to keep the skin dry.

Windbreak — A barrier (natural or constructed) that blocks or deflects wind to reduce convective heat loss at a camp or shelter site.

Wound Packing — The technique of filling a deep wound cavity with hemostatic gauze or plain gauze, pressing firmly to apply direct pressure to the bleeding source from within.

X

XSTAT — A hemostatic device consisting of small, compressed sponges injected into a wound cavity where they expand to apply internal pressure and stop bleeding. Military and specialized first-aid use.

Y

Yucca — A genus of plants found in arid environments with strong leaf fibers used for cordage and roots that produce a soapy lather for cleaning.

Z

Z-Fold Gauze — Gauze that is folded in a zigzag pattern for rapid deployment in wound packing. Standard component of trauma first-aid kits (e.g., IFAK).

Recommended Survival Reading List

Curated reading list organized by category. These books form the foundation of wilderness survival, emergency medicine, and preparedness knowledge.

Core Survival Manuals

Title Author Best For
SAS Survival Handbook John "Lofty" Wiseman The single most comprehensive general survival reference, covering every environment and scenario.
FM 21-76 (FM 3-05.70) Army Survival Manual US Department of the Army Systematic military survival doctrine covering evasion, shelter, water, food, and navigation in all climates.
Hawke's Green Beret Survival Manual Mykel Hawke Practical survival strategies from a Special Forces veteran, with clear decision-making frameworks.
98.6 Degrees: The Art of Keeping Your Ass Alive Cody Lundin Thermoregulation-focused survival philosophy emphasizing core temperature as the primary survival priority.
Build the Perfect Bug Out Bag Creek Stewart Step-by-step emergency kit building with gear lists and load-out strategies for 72-hour preparedness.

Bushcraft and Skills

Title Author Best For
Bushcraft 101 Dave Canterbury Foundational bushcraft skills organized around the "5 Cs of Survivability" (cutting, combustion, cover, container, cordage).
Advanced Bushcraft Dave Canterbury Deeper techniques for long-term wilderness living, including trapping, hide tanning, and tool construction.
Tom Brown's Field Guide to Wilderness Survival Tom Brown Jr. Nature awareness and primitive skills from a legendary tracker, with strong emphasis on the spiritual dimension of survival.
Camping and Woodcraft Horace Kephart Classic early-20th-century reference on camp craft, cooking, and backcountry travel technique.
Primitive Technology: A Survivalist's Guide to Building Tools, Shelters, and More in the Wild John Plant Visual guide to building structures, tools, and implements from raw natural materials with no modern tools.

Wilderness Medicine

Title Author Best For
Wilderness Medicine (Textbook) Paul Auerbach The definitive medical reference for austere environments, covering every injury and illness encountered far from hospitals.
Medicine for the Outdoors Paul Auerbach A condensed, field-practical version of the full textbook, written for non-physicians.
NOLS Wilderness Medicine Tod Schimelpfenig Scenario-based wilderness medical training used in NOLS and WMA certification courses.
Where There Is No Doctor David Werner Community health manual for situations without access to physicians, covering diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.
Wilderness & Travel Medicine: A Comprehensive Guide Eric Weiss Pocket-sized field reference for backcountry medical emergencies.

Psychology and Decision-Making

Title Author Best For
Deep Survival: Who Lives, Who Dies, and Why Laurence Gonzales Understanding the psychology of survival, why some people survive and others do not, and how the brain functions under extreme stress.
The Unthinkable: Who Survives When Disaster Strikes and Why Amanda Ripley How ordinary people respond to disasters, the stages of the survival arc (denial, deliberation, action), and training the brain for crisis.
Surviving the Extremes Kenneth Kamler Medical and psychological case studies from the most extreme environments on Earth.
The Survivor's Club Ben Sherwood Research-based exploration of the traits, behaviors, and luck that determine survival outcomes.

Navigation and Weather

Title Author Best For
Wilderness Navigation Bob Burns, Mike Burns Map and compass fundamentals, GPS use, and route-finding for backcountry travel.
Be Expert with Map and Compass Bjorn Kjellstrom The classic orienteering manual, thorough on declination, bearings, and triangulation.
Weather Forecasting (BSA Merit Badge Series) Boy Scouts of America Accessible introduction to reading clouds, barometric pressure, and predicting weather changes in the field.

Foraging and Wild Food

Title Author Best For
Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide Thomas Elias, Peter Dykeman Photographic identification of 200+ edible species with habitat, season, and preparation details.
Peterson Field Guide to Medicinal Plants and Herbs Steven Foster, James Duke Identification and traditional uses of medicinal plants in eastern and central North America.
The Forager's Harvest Samuel Thayer In-depth profiles of wild edible plants with practical harvesting and preparation methods based on firsthand experience.
Stalking the Wild Asparagus Euell Gibbons The classic foraging narrative that launched modern wild food interest, with recipes and plant profiles.
Mushrooms Demystified David Arora The comprehensive mushroom identification reference for North America.

Preparedness and Self-Reliance

Title Author Best For
The Prepper's Blueprint Tess Pennington Structured preparedness planning from short-term emergencies through long-term societal disruption.
When All Hell Breaks Loose Cody Lundin Urban and suburban disaster preparedness with emphasis on practical, low-cost solutions.
Emergency: This Book Will Save Your Life Neil Strauss One journalist's journey through survival training, providing an accessible entry point to the preparedness world.

Fire and Primitive Skills

The Book of Fire William Herring Dedicated deep-dive into every aspect of fire making, from primitive friction methods to modern ignition tools.
Participating in Nature Thomas Elpel Primitive living skills including brain-tanning, bow making, and friction fire, taught through immersive outdoor experience.

Master Source List

Authoritative sources referenced throughout the WilderThings survival guide collection. Organized by type for easy lookup.

Military Field Manuals

  • FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 — Survival. US Department of the Army. The foundational military survival manual covering evasion, shelter, water, fire, food, navigation, and survival in all climate zones. Superseded by ATP 3-50.3 but remains widely referenced.
  • ATP 3-50.21 — Survival, Evasion, and Recovery. US Department of the Army. Current doctrine for personnel recovery and survival operations in military contexts.
  • TCCC Guidelines (Tactical Combat Casualty Care). Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC), Joint Trauma System. Evidence-based trauma care protocol for combat and austere environments. Updated annually. Available at: jts.health.mil.
  • FM 4-25.11 — First Aid. US Department of the Army. Military first-aid procedures for battlefield injuries including hemorrhage control, airway management, and shock treatment.
  • FM 3-97.6 — Mountain Operations. US Department of the Army. Mountain warfare manual covering cold-weather survival, high-altitude medicine, and mountain navigation.
  • MCRP 3-02F — Survival, Evasion, and Recovery. US Marine Corps. Marine Corps survival doctrine with emphasis on evasion and coastal/jungle environments.
  • STP 21-1-SMCT — Soldier's Manual of Common Tasks. US Department of the Army. Includes fundamental survival, first aid, and navigation tasks required of all soldiers.

Medical References

  • Wilderness Medical Society (WMS) Clinical Practice Guidelines. Peer-reviewed, evidence-based guidelines for wilderness medicine topics including hypothermia, altitude illness, wound management, anaphylaxis, and lightning injuries. Published in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine journal. Available at: wms.org.
  • American Red Cross — First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual. Standard civilian first-aid training reference covering bleeding control, shock, burns, fractures, CPR, and AED use.
  • American Heart Association (AHA) — Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Current evidence-based standards for CPR technique, compression rate, rescue breathing, and AED protocols. Updated every five years.
  • NAEMT PHTLS (Prehospital Trauma Life Support). National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians. Textbook and course covering trauma assessment and treatment in prehospital settings.
  • WAFA/WEMT Curriculum — Wilderness First Aid / Wilderness EMT. Standardized wilderness medical training curricula used by NOLS Wilderness Medicine, SOLO, and WMA.
  • Merck Manual — Professional and Consumer Versions. Comprehensive medical reference for disease identification, symptoms, and treatment. Available at: merckmanuals.com.
  • Wilderness & Environmental Medicine (Journal). Peer-reviewed journal of the Wilderness Medical Society publishing original research on wilderness injuries, environmental illness, and austere-environment care.

Government Sources

  • NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration). Weather forecasting, storm warnings, tide tables, and climate data. Available at: noaa.gov.
  • NWS (National Weather Service). Real-time weather observations, forecasts, and severe weather alerts. Part of NOAA. Available at: weather.gov.
  • CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention). Guidelines on waterborne illness, vector-borne disease, travel health, and emergency preparedness. Available at: cdc.gov.
  • EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) — Water Treatment Guidelines. Standards for safe drinking water including turbidity limits, disinfection methods, and contaminant thresholds. Available at: epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water.
  • USGS (United States Geological Survey). Topographic maps, geological data, and water resource information. Topographic maps available at: usgs.gov/programs/national-geospatial-program.
  • NPS (National Park Service). Backcountry safety guidelines, Leave No Trace principles, and wildlife encounter protocols. Available at: nps.gov.
  • FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency). Disaster preparedness guides, emergency planning resources, and community resilience frameworks. Available at: fema.gov.
  • COSPAS-SARSAT. International satellite-based search and rescue distress alert system. Technical documentation on PLB and EPIRB operation. Available at: cospas-sarsat.int.

Organizations

  • NOLS (National Outdoor Leadership School). Wilderness skills education including leadership, navigation, and wilderness medicine certification (WAFA, WFR, WEMT). Available at: nols.edu.
  • WMA (Wilderness Medical Associates International). Wilderness medicine training and certification programs. Develops curricula for WAFA and WFR courses. Available at: wildmed.com.
  • Boy Scouts of America (BSA). Merit badge programs in wilderness survival, first aid, orienteering, and camping. Field manuals and handbooks provide foundational outdoor skills. Available at: scouting.org.
  • SOLO (Stonehearth Open Learning Opportunities). Wilderness medicine education provider offering WFA, WFR, and WEMT courses. Available at: soloschools.com.
  • Leave No Trace Center for Outdoor Ethics. Seven principles of outdoor ethics for minimizing environmental impact. Available at: lnt.org.
  • International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG). UN coordination body for urban search and rescue, publishing guidelines on disaster response methodology.
  • Mountain Rescue Association (MRA). Standards for mountain rescue operations in North America. Available at: mra.org.

Academic and Research Sources

  • Journal of Wilderness Medicine. Early peer-reviewed journal (now merged into Wilderness & Environmental Medicine) covering wilderness injury and illness research.
  • Forgey, William. Wilderness Medicine: Beyond First Aid (7th edition). Textbook used in wilderness medical training covering diagnosis and treatment in backcountry settings.
  • Gonzales, Laurence. Deep Survival: Who Lives, Who Dies, and Why. Research-based analysis of survival psychology drawing on neuroscience, accident investigation, and case studies.
  • Ripley, Amanda. The Unthinkable: Who Survives When Disaster Strikes and Why. Research into human behavior during disasters including the denial-deliberation-action model.
  • Leach, John. "Cognitive Paralysis in an Emergency: The Role of the Supervisory Attentional System." Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. Academic paper on the freeze response and why 75% of people become bewildered and unable to act in emergencies.
  • Giesbrecht, Gordon. Research publications on hypothermia, cold water immersion, and thermoregulation. University of Manitoba. Key researcher in cold-exposure survival physiology.

Key Textbooks

  • Auerbach, Paul. Wilderness Medicine (7th edition). Elsevier, 2017. The definitive 2,500-page medical reference for wilderness and austere-environment medicine. Covers every injury, illness, and environmental hazard encountered in remote settings.
  • Wiseman, John "Lofty." SAS Survival Handbook (revised edition). William Morrow, 2014. Comprehensive general survival manual by a former SAS instructor. Covers all environments, climates, and core survival skills.
  • Canterbury, Dave. Bushcraft 101. Adams Media, 2014. Foundational bushcraft reference organized around the "5 Cs of Survivability." Practical and field-tested.
  • Lundin, Cody. 98.6 Degrees: The Art of Keeping Your Ass Alive. Gibbs Smith, 2003. Thermoregulation-focused survival guide emphasizing core body temperature as the central survival priority.
  • Hawke, Mykel. Hawke's Green Beret Survival Manual. Running Press, 2012. Field-practical survival strategies from a career Special Forces officer.
  • Brown, Tom Jr. Tom Brown's Field Guide to Wilderness Survival. Berkley, 1983. Primitive skills and nature awareness from one of America's most well-known trackers.
  • Angier, Bradford. How to Stay Alive in the Woods. Black Dog & Leventhal, 1956 (revised 2001). Classic guide to wilderness self-sufficiency.
  • Elias, Thomas, and Peter Dykeman. Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide. Sterling, 2009. Photographic field guide to 200+ edible species with preparation details.
  • Foster, Steven, and James Duke. Peterson Field Guide to Medicinal Plants and Herbs (3rd edition). Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2014. Standard field reference for medicinal plant identification in eastern and central North America.
  • US Department of the Army. FM 21-76: Survival. 1992 (reprinted by various publishers). The foundational military survival field manual.

First Aid Checklist

Use this checklist when responding to any injury or medical emergency in the field. Follow the steps in order. Do not skip scene safety.

Checklist

Scene Safety

  • [ ] Stop and assess the scene for hazards (falling objects, fire, traffic, unstable ground, electrical lines, hostile wildlife)
  • [ ] Ensure the scene is safe before approaching the patient
  • [ ] Put on gloves or use a barrier if available
  • [ ] Determine the mechanism of injury (fall, cut, burn, animal attack, environmental)
  • [ ] Count the number of patients and call for help if overwhelmed

Primary Survey (ABCDE)

  • [ ] A — Airway. Check if the airway is open. Perform jaw thrust (if spinal injury suspected) or head-tilt/chin-lift. Clear obstructions
  • [ ] B — Breathing. Look, listen, and feel for breathing. If absent, begin rescue breathing or CPR. See CPR and Choking
  • [ ] C — Circulation. Check for a pulse. Identify and control life-threatening bleeding immediately (see Bleeding Control below)
  • [ ] D — Disability. Assess level of consciousness (AVPU: Alert, Verbal, Pain, Unresponsive). Check pupils for equal size and reactivity
  • [ ] E — Exposure. Remove or cut away clothing to find hidden injuries. Protect the patient from environmental exposure (cold ground, wind, rain) immediately after examination

Bleeding Control

  • [ ] Apply direct pressure with a clean dressing or cloth
  • [ ] If blood soaks through, pack the wound with gauze and apply more pressure (do not remove the first dressing)
  • [ ] Elevate the injured limb above the heart if possible
  • [ ] For life-threatening limb bleeding that does not stop with pressure, apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches (5-7.5 cm) above the wound
  • [ ] Tighten the tourniquet until bleeding stops completely
  • [ ] Note and record the time the tourniquet was applied
  • [ ] Apply a hemostatic agent (QuikClot, Celox) to junctional wounds (groin, armpit, neck) if available

Shock Treatment

  • [ ] Lay the patient flat on their back
  • [ ] Elevate the legs 6-12 inches (15-30 cm) unless spinal injury, head injury, or leg fracture is suspected
  • [ ] Maintain body temperature: insulate from the ground, cover with blankets or extra clothing
  • [ ] Do not give food or water if evacuation is imminent or the patient is not fully conscious
  • [ ] Monitor breathing and pulse continuously
  • [ ] Keep the patient calm and still

Burn Treatment

  • [ ] Remove the patient from the heat source
  • [ ] Cool the burn with clean, cool (not ice-cold) water for at least 10 minutes
  • [ ] Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts
  • [ ] Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-stick dressing
  • [ ] Do not pop blisters
  • [ ] Do not apply butter, toothpaste, or other home remedies
  • [ ] For large or deep burns (larger than the patient's palm, or charred/white skin), treat for shock and evacuate

Fracture Management

  • [ ] Immobilize the injury in the position found (do not attempt to straighten an angulated fracture unless circulation is compromised below the break)
  • [ ] Splint above and below the fracture site
  • [ ] Pad the splint to prevent pressure points
  • [ ] Check circulation below the splint (pulse, sensation, skin color, warmth) before and after application
  • [ ] Secure the splint with bandages, strips of cloth, or cordage
  • [ ] Recheck circulation every 15-30 minutes and loosen the splint if numbness, tingling, or color change develops
  • [ ] See Fractures and Splints for detailed splinting techniques

Notes

  • The primary survey (ABCDE) is always performed in order. Treat each life threat as you find it before moving to the next letter.
  • Tourniquets are safe for field use. Do not loosen a tourniquet once applied unless directed by a physician.
  • In a wilderness context, definitive care may be hours or days away. Monitor the patient closely and plan evacuation early.
  • Document all injuries, treatments, and times. This information is critical for the receiving medical team.
WARNING If you suspect a spinal injury, do not move the patient unless the scene is immediately life-threatening. Stabilize the head and neck in the position found.

Fire Starting Checklist

Use this checklist whenever building a fire, whether for warmth, signaling, water purification, or cooking. Follow the steps in order from site selection through sustainable fire.

Checklist

Site Selection

  • [ ] Choose a location sheltered from wind (use terrain, rocks, or trees as a natural windbreak)
  • [ ] Ensure the ground is dry, or create a platform of green logs or flat rocks to insulate the fire from wet or snowy ground
  • [ ] Clear a circle at least 10 feet (3 m) in diameter of dry leaves, grass, and other combustible debris
  • [ ] Check overhead for low branches, dead snags, or dry canopy that could catch fire
  • [ ] Position the fire site where heat reflects toward your shelter (a rock wall or log behind the fire works as a reflector)
  • [ ] Consider proximity to your water source and firewood supply

Material Gathering

  • [ ] Tinder. Collect two generous handfuls of fine, dry, combustible material: shredded bark (birch, cedar), dry grass, cattail fluff, fatwood shavings, or char cloth
  • [ ] Kindling. Gather a double armload of dry sticks ranging from matchstick thickness to pencil thickness
  • [ ] Small fuel. Collect an armload of dry sticks from thumb thickness to wrist thickness
  • [ ] Main fuel. Gather larger pieces of dry, dead wood from forearm thickness to leg thickness
  • [ ] Test wood by snapping it: dry wood breaks cleanly with a snap; wet wood bends or splinters
  • [ ] Source dead, standing wood (off the ground) whenever possible; ground wood absorbs moisture
  • [ ] Keep all materials organized and within arm's reach of the fire site

Fire Lay Construction

  • [ ] Form the tinder into a loose, bird's-nest-shaped bundle (airflow is critical)
  • [ ] Select a fire lay type appropriate to the situation:
  • Teepee: Lean kindling in a cone over the tinder bundle (good general purpose)
  • Log cabin: Stack kindling in alternating layers around the tinder (good for coals and cooking)
  • Lean-to: Lean kindling against a larger stick placed over the tinder (good in light wind)
  • Platform/upside-down fire: Large logs on bottom, smaller wood on top (good on wet or snowy ground)
  • [ ] Leave an opening in the fire lay on the windward side for oxygen flow and ignition access
  • [ ] Stage small fuel and main fuel within arm's reach, organized by size

Ignition

  • [ ] Shield the fire lay from wind with your body or a windbreak
  • [ ] Ignite the tinder using your available method:
  • Lighter/matches: Apply flame directly to the base of the tinder bundle
  • Ferro rod: Strike sparks into the finest tinder material at the base
  • Bow drill/hand drill: Transfer the ember into the tinder bundle, fold gently, and blow. See Friction Methods
  • Spark methods: See Spark Methods
  • [ ] Blow gently and steadily at the base of the tinder to feed oxygen to the growing flame
  • [ ] Do not smother the fire; let the tinder catch fully before adding kindling

Building to a Sustainable Fire

  • [ ] Add kindling one piece at a time, starting with the thinnest pieces
  • [ ] Wait for each piece to catch before adding the next
  • [ ] Gradually increase the size of wood added (matchstick to pencil to thumb to wrist)
  • [ ] Maintain airflow: do not pack wood too tightly
  • [ ] Once a solid bed of coals forms, add main fuel logs
  • [ ] Adjust fuel placement to control heat output (closer together for more heat, spread apart to reduce)
  • [ ] Maintain the fire by adding fuel before it burns down to weak coals

Notes

  • Gather three times more material than you think you need, especially tinder and kindling.
  • In wet conditions, split wood to access dry inner material. Fatwood from dead conifer stumps ignites even when wet.
  • Never leave a fire unattended. Before sleeping, reduce the fire and clear the area of stray sparks.
  • To extinguish: spread coals, douse with water, stir the ash, douse again, and feel with the back of your hand for remaining heat.
CAUTION In dry, windy conditions, an uncontrolled fire spreads rapidly. Always have water or dirt available to suppress the fire if it escapes the cleared area.
